questions.title: Russian Roulette I
questions.problem: You and a high-stakes friend want to play Russian Roulette together. A revolver with $6$ chambers is loaded with one bullet. Initially, the cylinder is spun to randomize the order of the chambers. The two of you take turns pulling the trigger until the person who fires the gun loses. Given that the cylinder is not re-spun after each turn, what is the probability that you win if your friend goes first?
questions.solution: Suppose the chambers are labelled $1-6$, where $1$ is the chamber that shoots off first. Your friend dies if the bullet is in chambers $1,3,$ or $5$, as they will be shooting on odd chambers. However, you die if the bullet is in chambers $2,4,$ or $6$, as the revolver is alternated. Therefore, as you win in $3$ of the $6$ possible outcomes, the answer is 3 6 = 1 2 6 3 = 2 1 .

questions.title: Russian Roulette II
questions.problem: You and a high-stakes friend want to play Russian Roulette together. A revolver with $6$ chambers is loaded with one bullet. Initially, the cylinder is spun to randomize the order of the chambers. The two of you take turns pulling the trigger until the person who fires the gun loses. Given that the cylinder is re-spun after each turn, what is the probability that you win if your friend goes first?
questions.solution: Since we spin the cylinder after each turn, the game is essentially unchanged except for the player that starts. Let $p$ the probability of you winning (i.e. your friend losing) when your friend is the starting player in the game. Note that 1 − 1−p is the probability of your friend winning, as the two probabilities must sum to 1 1. With probability $1/6$, your friend shoots themselves on the first trial, which means you automatically win. Otherwise, with probability $5/6$, your friend does not shoot themselves and the revolver is passed to you. We now have the same game, but you are the one that starts. In other words, you can view this as the roles of you and your friend being swapped. From the discussion above, there is a probability 1 − 1−p of you winning, as the starting player had probability 1 − 1−p of winning. By Law of Total Probability, this yields = 1 6 + 5 6 ⋅ ( 1 − ) ⟺ = 6 11 p= 6 1 + 6 5 ⋅(1−p)⟺p= 11 6

questions.title: Russian Roulette III
questions.problem: You and a high-stakes friend want to play Russian Roulette together. A revolver with $6$ chambers is loaded with two bullets. Initially, the cylinder is spun to randomize the order of the chambers. The two of you take turns pulling the trigger until the person who fires the gun loses. Your friend pulls the trigger and they live. Find the probability of you living when you spin the barrel.
questions.solution: Spinning the barrel randomizes the order of the bullets within the chambers. $2$ of the $6$ chambers will be occupied by bullets, so there is a probability $2/6 = 1/3$ that a bullet lies in the chamber when you shoot. Therefore, there is a probability 2 3 3 2 that you live.

questions.title: Russian Roulette IV
questions.problem: You and a high-stakes friend want to play Russian Roulette together. A revolver with $6$ chambers is loaded with two bullets. Initially, the cylinder is spun to randomize the order of the chambers. The two of you take turns pulling the trigger until the person who fires the gun loses. Your friend pulls the trigger and they live. Find the probability of you living when you don't spin the barrel.
questions.solution: If you do not spin the barrel, there are $5$ chambers remaining. Given that your friend lived, you know that $2$ of the $5$ chambers do have a bullet in them. Therefore, the probability of bullet being shot when you pull the trigger is 2 5 5 2 . By complementation, the probability of you living is 3 5 5 3 . The results of this problem and "Russian Roulette III" implies that you should roll the barrel before shooting.

questions.title: Russian Roulette V
questions.problem: You and a high-stakes friend want to play Russian Roulette together. A revolver with $6$ chambers is loaded with two bullets in consecutive chambers. The two of you take turns pulling the trigger until the person who fires the gun loses. Your friend pulls the trigger and they live. Find the probability of you living when you spin the barrel.
questions.solution: Spinning the barrel randomizes the order of the bullets within the chambers. $2$ of the $6$ chambers will be occupied by bullets, so there is a probability $2/6 = 1/3$ that a bullet lies in the chamber when you shoot. This doesn't change, even with the information of having consecutive bullets, as there are $6$ possibilities for the pairs of locations for the bullets, and exactly $2$ of those will have a bullet in the first chamber shot. Therefore, there is a probability 2 3 3 2 that you live.

questions.title: Russian Roulette VI
questions.problem: You and a high-stakes friend want to play Russian Roulette together. A revolver with $6$ chambers is loaded with two bullets in consecutive chambers. The two of you take turns pulling the trigger until the person who fires the gun loses. Your friend pulls the trigger and they live. Find the probability of you living when you don't spin the barrel.
questions.solution: If you don't spin the barrel, there are $5$ barrels that remain that could have the bullets. For simplicity, say that the chambers are labelled $1-6$ and your friend shot chamber $1$. Since the bullets are consecutive, the bullets can only be in the following pairs of chambers: $(2,3), (3,4), (4,5),$ and $(5,6)$. Out of these $4$ possibilities, only one of them kills you next turn, so there is a 3 4 4 3 probability that you will live when pulling the trigger. This result and that of "Russian Roulette V" imply that you should not spin the chamber between turns.

questions.title: Missing Money I
questions.problem: You make it onto a game show that presents you with $N$ doors. There is a large prize behind one of the doors, while the others are empty. The host lets you spin a prize a wheel that will either reveal to you the door that the money is behind with probability p or nothing with probability 1 − 1−p. If you don't receive any information from the wheel, you guess uniformly at random. Find your probability of locating the prize when = 1 / 3 p=1/3 and = 5 N=5.
questions.solution: You can win by either getting information from the spin or by not getting information from the spin and guessing correctly. These two cases are disjoint, as you can't both obtain and not obtain information from the wheel. You obtain information from the wheel with probability p by the question. You receive no information from the wheel with probability 1 − 1−p, and then you guess uniformly at random among the N doors. The probability of you guessing the door that does have the prize is 1 N 1 , as one of the N doors has a prize. Adding these together, the answer is + 1 − p+ N 1−p . With the specified values, the answer is 7 15 15 7 .

questions.title: First and Last I
questions.problem: How many anagrams of KANGAROO start and end with the same letter?
questions.solution: The only repeated letters are A and O. Since there are only two replicates of each of these letters, the first and last letter must either be A or O. This gives us $2$ options for the first and last letter (both A or O). WLOG, assume that A was fixed as the first and last letter. The number of remaining anagrams is the same in both cases, so we can just take one and multiply by 2 2. Once the two A's are fixed in the first and last spot, there are 6 6 remaining letters, of which 2 2 of them are O and the remaining are distinct. Therefore, there are ( 6 2 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 ) = 6 ! 2 ! 1 ! 4 = 6 ! 2 ( 2,1,1,1,1 6 )= 2!1! 4 6! = 2 6! anagrams of the remaining letters. This is a direct application of the multinomial coefficient. We must multiply this above answer by 2 2 to account for either A or O being the first and last. Doing so, this yields a total number of anagrams of 2 ⋅ 6 ! 2 = 6 ! = 720 2⋅ 2 6! =6!=720

questions.title: First and Last II
questions.problem: How many anagrams of MISSISSIPPI start and end with the same letter?
questions.solution: The repeated letters in this word are I, S, and P. S and I each have $4$ replicates, while P only has $2$. We will need to break up into cases as to whether or not the letter at the start and end has $2$ replicates vs. $4$ replicates, as the number of anagrams for each case is different. Let's start with the case that P is at the start and end. Those are the only 2 P's in the anagram, so of the 1$1$1 letters, 9 9 are left, where 4 4 are I, 4 4 are S, and 1 1 is M. Hence, there are ( 9 4 , 4 , 1 ) = 9 ! 4 ! 4 ! ( 4,4,1 9 )= 4!4! 9! distinct anagrams in this case. Next, let's move to the two letters that have 4 4 replicates. We have 2 2 possible options for the letter that we place at beginning or end that have 4 4 replicates total (S or I), so we can just consider one of the two cases and multiply by 2 2 to account for the other case. WLOG, let's say S is at the start and end. This means that there are 9 9 letters left, where 4 4 are I, 2 2 are S, 2 2 are P, and 1 1 is M. By the multinomial coefficient, there are ( 9 4 , 2 , 2 , 1 ) = 9 ! 4 ! 2 ! 2 ! ( 4,2,2,1 9 )= 4!2!2! 9! ways to arrange the remaining letters in an anagram. Adding up the two cases and multiplying the second by 2 2 to account for the choice of S or I, the total number of anagrams satisfying this is 9 ! 4 ! 4 ! + 9 ! 4 ! 2 ! = 8190 4!4! 9! + 4!2! 9! =8190

All of the first k candies must be red, so we are permuting r red candies to k spots, which can be done in ( , ) P(r,k) ways. Next, we are also permuting the b blue candies to the remaining k spots, which can be done in ( , ) P(b,k) ways. Therefore, by the multiplicative principle, there are ( , ) ( , ) P(r,k)P(b,k) ways to arrange the candies such that they satisfy our condition. This yields a probability of ( , ) ( , ) ( + , 2 ) P(r+b,2k) P(r,k)P(b,k) With our specified values, the probability is 10 ⋅ 9 ⋅ 8 ⋅ 7 18 ⋅ 17 ⋅ 16 ⋅ 15 = 7 102 18⋅17⋅16⋅15 10⋅9⋅8⋅7 = 102 7

questions.title: Spotify Music
questions.problem: Armaan is creating a playlist on Spotify. There are $s$ total songs in the playlist, of which $w \geq 1$ of them are written by The Weeknd and $b \geq 2$ of them are written by Bruno Mars. You may assume $s \geq w + b$. Armaan orders the songs in the playlist uniformly at random. Find the probability that all of The Weeknd's songs come before the second Bruno Mars song when $w = 8$ and $b = 4$.
questions.solution: We only care about the orderings of The Weeknd's songs and Bruno Mars' songs, so we can just disregard the remaining songs that aren't by either of them, as they don't change the ordering of the songs by these artists relative to each other. For all of The Weeknd's songs to come before the second Bruno Mars song, it must be the case that in the first + 1 w+1 spots of the + b+w songs that are occupied by these two artists, there must be all w The Weeknd songs and 1 1 Bruno Mars song. We now need to determine the number of distinct ways this can happen. We know that, in total, there are ( + ) ! (b+w)! ways to arrange the songs with no restrictions, as we are permuting + b+w songs to + b+w spots in the playlist. Afterwards, we know that in the first + 1 w+1 spots, we must pick a song by Bruno Mars to be in there (can be done in b ways), choose a location for that Bruno Mars song in the first + 1 w+1 spots (can be done in + 1 w+1 ways), and then permute the w songs by The Weeknd to the remaining w spots (can be done in ! w! ways). Once this is done, we can just permute the other − 1 b−1 songs by Bruno Mars to the remaining − 1 b−1 spots that remain, which can be done in ( − 1 ) ! (b−1)! ways. By the multiplicative principle and the fact that Armaan makes these playlists uniformly at random, the probability of this event is ⋅ ( + 1 ) ⋅ ! ⋅ ( − 1 ) ! ( + ) ! = ( + 1 ) ! ⋅ ! ( + ) ! (b+w)! b⋅(w+1)⋅w!⋅(b−1)! = (b+w)! (w+1)!⋅b! With our specified values, the answer is 1 55 55 1 .

questions.title: Missing Values I
questions.problem: $n$ integers are going to be selected from the set [ ] = { 1 , 2 , … , } [n]={1,2,…,n} with repetition allowed. Find the probability that every integer is selected exactly once when $n = 5$.
questions.solution: To compute this probability, we need to find the total number of ways in which we select one of each value and divide that by the total number ways to select the n values. If there are no restrictions, since we select with replacement, there would be n options from $[n]$ that we can select at trial, so there would be a total of $n^n$ ways to select $n$ values by the multiplication principle. If we are required to draw one of each value from $[n]$, then we are essentially picking without replacement from $[n]$, as each of the values drawn must be distinct to be able to select all $n$ of them. There are $n!$ total ways to draw out the values without replacement, so the probability of this is ! n n n! With $n = 5$, the answer is 120 3125 = 24 625 3125 120 = 625 24 .

questions.title: Final Digit
questions.problem: $k \geq 1$ integers are independently selected from the set [ 9 ] = { 1 , 2 , … , 9 } [9]={1,2,…,9} with replacement. Find the probability that the product of all k of these integers has a ones digit of $1,3,7,$ or $9$ when $k = 3$.
questions.solution: For the product of the integers to end in $1,3,7,$ or $9$, all of the integers must be $1,3,7,$ or $9$. If any of the integers selected are even, then the product will be even and hence not even with an odd integer. However, if $5$ is selected, then the product will end with $5$ or $0$, which is also not any of the integers listed above. However, multiplying any combination of $1,3,7,$ or $9$ together results in an integer whose last digit is also $1,3,7,$ or $9$, which can be checked by pairwise multiplication of the integers and checking their last digit. Therefore, we just need to find the probability all $k$ integers are one of $1,3,7,$ or $9$. There is a probability 4 9 9 4 per digit selected that it is one of those $4$ there, as there are $9$ integers in $[9]$ total and we select uniformly at random. Since each selection is independent of each other, the probability all $k$ integers are $1,3,7,$ or $9$ is ( 4 9 ) ( 9 4 ) k . With $k = 3$, the answer is 64 729 729 64 .

questions.title: Matching Royals
questions.problem: A reduced deck of $16$ cards ( $4$ suits of each face cards and the $4$ aces) is dealt out to $4$ people. Find the probability that each of the $4$ people receive one of each rank of card. Round to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: To compute this probability, we first need to find the total number of ways that the cards can be dealt to the $4$ people. Since we are dealing multiple cards to groups of people, multinomial is the way to go. In particular, there are $16$ distinct cards, of which each person receives $4$, so there are ( 16 $4$ , $4$ , $4$ , $4$ ) ( 4,4,4,4 16 ) ways to distribute the cards to the people. This counts the number of ways to distribute the cards to people that ignores the order of the cards in the hand. However, we still do care about the suits of the cards that each person receives. Therefore, we need to count the number of ways to distribute the cards to the people such that only the suits are relevant. For each rank, there are 4 4 cards ( 1 1 per suit) and 4 4 people that those cards can go to. Therefore, for each rank, there are 4 ! 4! ways to permute the cards to the 4 4 different people. Since there are 4 4 such cards we are permuting to the people, the number of distinct arrangements is ( 4 ! ) 4 (4!) 4 . Thus, our answer is ( 4 ! ) 4 ( 16 4 , 4 , 4 , 4 ) = ( 4 ! ) 8 16 ! ( 4,4,4,4 16 ) (4!) 4 = 16! (4!) 8

questions.title: 3 Consecutive Cards II
questions.problem: $k \geq 1$ standard decks are combined together to form a large deck. $3$ cards are selected uniformly at random from this large deck without replacement. Let $p_k$ be the probability these three cards form a three card straight (following similar rules to the standard poker straight, which means that an Ace can either be the lowest card or the highest card) when there are k decks combined. Find lim ⁡ → ∞ k→∞ lim p k . Note that a straight flush is allowed in this.
questions.solution: As $k \rightarrow \infty$, it is as if you are selecting with replacement from the deck, as there are essentially infinitely many cards compared to the three that are selected. Therefore, it is as if you are selecting with replacement from the deck, as the removed cards are negligible when compared to the total number of cards in the deck. Since the decks that are being combined are all standard decks, all of them have the same proportions of cards, so we can just consider one deck. If we were selecting with replacement from one deck, there would be 52 3 52 3 total outcomes. There would still be 12 12 possibilities of the lowest ranked card for a 3 3 card straight, which are Ace to Queen. There are 3 ! = 6 3!=6 ways to arrange the order in which the ranks are selected. Afterwards, once the lowest ranked card is selected, this fixes the three cards in the straight. Since there are 4 4 suits of each card, there are 4 3 4 3 total ways to pick the cards of the three ranks, as we have 4 4 options of suit per rank. Therefore, the probability of drawing a 3 3 card straight in this case is 12 ⋅ 3 ! ⋅ 4 3 52 3 = 72 2197 52 3 12⋅3!⋅4 3 = 2197 72 This is also lim ⁡ → ∞ k→∞ lim p k by the argument above that the limit of the sampling without replacement case is just sampling with replacement. This can also be verified by taking the limit as → ∞ k→∞ in the result of "3 Consecutive Cards I", which yields the same value.

questions.title: Risk Manager
questions.problem: Suppose you purchase $1$ share of stock $A$. A share of stock $A$ has mean return μ A and return variation 2 σ A 2 . You also want to purchase stock $B$. $1$ share of $B$ has mean return μ B and return variation 2 σ B 2 . Additionally, the returns of $A$ and $B$ are correlated with coefficient ρ. How many units of stock $B$ should you purchase so that the variance of your portfolio consisting of both $A$ and $B$ is minimized? Fractional shares are valid. Solve this with = − 1 / 3 , = 4 , = 6 , 2 = 16 , ρ=−1/3,μ A =4,μ B =6,σ A 2 =16, and 2 = 4 σ B 2 =4
questions.solution: Let $R_A$ and $R_B$ be the returns of stock $A$ and $B$, respectively. If you purchase $k$ shares of stock $B$, then the return of your portfolio is given by + R A +kR B , as you have one unit of $A$ and $k$ units of $B$. The goal here is to minimize Var ( + ) Var(R A +kR B ). This is a sum of random variables that are not independent, so we have to use the variance of a sum formula. By the variance of a sum formula, we have that Var ( + ) = Var ( ) + Var ( ) + 2 Cov ( , ) = Var ( ) + 2 Var ( ) + 2 Cov ( , ) Var(R A +kR B )=Var(R A )+Var(kR B )+2Cov(R A ,kR B )=Var(R A )+k 2 Var(R B )+2kCov(R A ,R B ) The last equality is via the properties of variance and covariance. Var ( ) = 2 Var(R A )=σ A 2 and Var ( ) = 2 Var(R B )=σ B 2 from the question itself. From the definition of correlation, Cov ( , ) = Cov(R A ,R B )=ρσ A σ B . Thus, we have that the variance (as a function of k) is 2 2 + 2 + 2 k 2 σ B 2 +2ρσ A σ b k+σ A 2 . We are looking to minimize the variance in k, so we should take a derivative in k. Note that this is a quadratic function in k, so to find the minimum in k, we need to take a derivative of the above function with respect to k. The derivative is 2 2 + 2 = 0 2kσ B 2 +2ρσ A σ B =0, which means that ∗ = − k ∗ =− σ B ρσ A minimizes the variance. With the specified values, the answer is 2 / 3 2/3.

questions.title: Positive Stars
questions.problem: Let $1 \leq k \leq n$. Find the number of positive integer solutions to the equation 1 + ⋯ + = x 1 +⋯+x k =n when $k = 6$ and $n = 11$.
questions.solution: This looks very similar to the typical stars and bars scenario, except the restriction here is that the integers are positive rather than non-negative. Since the stars in stars and bars are not distinct, what we can do is fix a value of 1 1 for each of the $x_i$ automatically. In other words, if you were thinking of there being $n$ balls being distributed to $k$ bins and $x_i$ being the number of balls in bin $i$, we are fixing one ball per bin automatically. Afterwards, we can distribute the remaining − n−k balls as we please, since the condition of having at least one ball per bin is satisfied apriori. In this scenario, we just fix a value of 1 1 per $x_i$ from the start. Therefore, there are an equal number of solutions to the equation in question as the equation 1 + ⋯ + = − x 1 +⋯+x k =n−k with each $x_i$ non-negative (rather than positive). By stars and bars, there are ( ( + ) + − 1 − 1 ) = ( − 1 − 1 ) ( k−1 (n+k)+k−1 )=( k−1 n−1 ) solutions to this. With the specified values, the answer is $252$.

questions.title: Poker Pair
questions.problem: A pair in poker is a $5$ card hand where you have $2$ cards of the same rank and $3$ other cards of distinct ranks. Find the probability that a randomly drawn $5$ card poker hand from a standard deck is a pair. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: To create a pair, we need to choose the rank of the pair, which two suits of the rank we want to select, as well as the ranks and suits of the three other cards. There are $13$ choices for the rank of the rank that has $2$ suits. Then, we are picking $2$ of the $4$ suits to be in our hand, so there are ( 4 2 ) ( 2 4 ) ways to pick those $2$ suits. Afterwards, we must pick $3$ ranks to select $1$ suit each from. Since each of these only have $1$ card, we should be performing a "choose" here, as opposed to a permutation, as the order in which we select the ranks to be in our hand is irrelevant. Namely, there would be ( 12 3 ) ( 3 12 ) ways to pick 3 3 ranks from the remaining $12$. For each of these ranks, there are $4$ suits we can select from, which yields 4 3 4 3 ways we can pick the suits once the ranks are selected. By the multiplication rule, this yields 13 ⋅ ( 4 2 ) ⋅ ( 12 3 ) ⋅ 4 3 13⋅( 2 4 )⋅( 3 12 )⋅4 3 ways to pick the hand such that it is a pair. There are ( 52 5 ) ( 5 52 ) total ways to select 5 5 cards from the standard deck, as the order of the selection of cards is irrelevant. Thus, the probability of a pair is 13 ( 4 2 ) ( 12 3 ) 4 3 ( 52 5 ) ≈ 0.423 ( 5 52 ) 13( 2 4 )( 3 12 )4 3 ≈0.423

questions.title: Arithmetic Arrangement
questions.problem: How many valid arithmetic expressions using only ∗ ∗ and $+$ are there that include the values $123456789$ exactly once in some order? Some examples include 123456789 , 6 ∗ 42 + 375 ∗ 18 + 9 , 123456789,6∗42+375∗18+9, and 9 ∗ 3 ∗ 7 ∗ 5 + 48 ∗ 21 + 6 9∗3∗7∗5+48∗21+6. Some non-examples are 887 ∗ 654321 887∗654321 and $+123975468$.
questions.solution: We can see that a valid arithmetic expression will have the numbers $1-9$ in some order and (potentially) a symbol between consecutive digits. Note that there can't be a symbol at the absolute front or back, as this is not a valid arithmetic expression. Thus, symbols can only go between digits. We can then format a valid arithmetic expression as follows: − − − − − − − − D−D−D−D−D−D−D−D−D, where D is a digit and − − is some operation. Note that there are 9 9 digits and 8 8 operations to be placed between them. There are 9 ! 9! ways to permute the numbers 1 − 9 1−9 to the digit spots, as they can be arranged in any order. For the operation slots, these can either by + , ∗ , +,∗, or nothing at all, as a "nothing" would just concatenate the digits and form a 2 − 2−digit number. For example, in this format, 6 ∗ 42 + 375 ∗ 18 + 9 6∗42+375∗18+9 is really 6 ∗ 4 ∣ 2 + 3 ∣ 7 ∣ 5 ∗ 1 ∣ 8 + 9 6∗4∣2+3∣7∣5∗1∣8+9, where ∣ ∣ means a blank. Thus, there are really 3 3 options per blank in each of the 8 8 blanks, so there are 3 8 3 8 total ways to determine the arrangements of the operation spots. By multiplication principle, the total number of arrangements is 9 ! ⋅ 3 8 9!⋅3 8 .

questions.title: Marble Transfer I
questions.problem: You have two bins in front of you, say $1$ and $2$. Bin $i$ has $r_i$ red and $b_i$ blue marbles inside. $1$ marble uniformly at random is selected from bin $1$ and is transferred to bin $2$. Afterwards, a marble is selected uniformly at random from bin $2$. Find the probability that the marble drawn is blue when $1$ = 4 , 1 = 3 , 2 = 5 , r 1 =4,b 1 =3,r 2 =5, and 2 = 3 b 2 =3.
questions.solution: The probability of drawing a blue in bin $2$ is dependent on the color of the marble that is transferred to it. Therefore, the key idea is to condition on the color of the marble that is drawn from urn $1$. Let $B_1$ and $R_1$ be the events that a blue and red marble, respectively, are drawn from urn $1$. Similarly, let $B_2$ be the event that a blue marble is drawn from bin $2$. Then by the law of total probability, [ 2 ] = [ 2 ∣ $1$ ] [ 1 ] + [ $2$ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] P[B 2 ]=P[B 2 ∣B 1 ]P[B 1 ]+P[B 2 ∣R 1 ]P[R 1 ] Since the marbles are drawn uniformly at random from bin 1 1, [ 1 ] = 1 1 + 1 P[B 1 ]= r 1 +b 1 b 1 and [ 1 ] = 1 1 + 1 P[R 1 ]= r 1 +b 1 r 1 . Now, we compute the conditionals. If a blue marble is transferred to bin 2 2, there are 2 + 1 b 2 +1 blue and 2 r 2 red marbles, so [ 2 ∣ 1 ] = 2 + 1 2 + 2 + 1 P[B 2 ∣B 1 ]= r 2 +b 2 +1 b 2 +1 . Similarly, if a red is transferred, there are 2 b 2 blue and 2 + 1 r 2 +1 red marbles, so [ 2 ∣ 1 ] = 2 2 + 2 + 1 P[B 2 ∣R 1 ]= b 2 +r 2 +1 b 2 . Therefore, plugging into the Law of Total Probability, [ 2 ] = 1 ( 2 + 1 ) + 1 2 ( 1 + 1 ) ( 2 + 2 + 1 ) P[B 2 ]= (b 1 +r 1 )(b 2 +r 2 +1) b 1 (b 2 +1)+r 1 b 2 With the specified values, the answer is [ 2 ] = 8 21 P[B 2 ]= 21 8

questions.title: Murder Mystery
questions.problem: Someone was murdered! A witness claims that the murderer had a red car. Suppose that witnesses are correct with probability $a$. In this particular city, all cars are red or blue, of which 100 % 100r% of them are red. questions.title: Three of a Kind
questions.problem: A $5-$card hand is called a three-of-a-kind if it consists of $3$ cards of one rank and $2$ cards of two other distinct ranks. To the nearest ten-thousandth, find the probability that a random $5$ card hand drawn from a standard deck of cards is a three-of-a-kind.
questions.solution: To have a three-of-a-kind, you must pick the rank for which $3$ suits are drawn, pick the two ranks that have $1$ suit drawn, and also pick the suits drawn. The total number of $5$ card hands that can be drawn from a standard deck is ( 52 5 ) ( 5 52 ), as the order of the cards drawn is irrelevant. We must determine the number of ways to draw the three-of-a-kind hand. There are $13$ ways to pick the rank that will have $3$ of its suits drawn out. Once the rank is selected, there are ( $4$ 3 ) ( 3 4 ) ways to pick the three suits of that rank that are selected, as the order of those suits being selected is irrelevant. Once those are picked, we need to select two more cards of two distinct suits. There are ( 12 2 ) ( 2 12 ) ways to pick the two ranks of cards that will occupy our last two spots, as the order of their selection is irrelevant. Once we have selected the two ranks, there are 4 4 suits of each of those ranks to select from, so we multiply by 4 2 4 2 to account for the number of ways to pick the suits. By the mulitplication principle, the number of three-of-a-kind hands is 13 ⋅ ( 4 3 ) ( 12 2 ) ⋅ 4 2 13⋅( 3 4 )( 2 12 )⋅4 2 Therefore, the probability of a three-of-a-kind is 13 ⋅ ( 4 3 ) ( 12 2 ) ⋅ 4 2 ( 52 5 ) ≈ 0.0211 ( 5 52 ) 13⋅( 3 4 )( 2 12 )⋅4 2 ≈0.0211

questions.solution: There are a couple approaches that can be taken here. This question is looking to count events where either one event or another happens, and those events are not disjoint. Thus, one should either work with the complement or use inclusion-exclusion. In this case, both of them work, and the easier one is complementation, as you can visualize it on the blanks directly. The complement of the event in question is that the string must begin with 0 0 and not end with 00 00. The rest of the string is unrestricted. Therefore, there is only 1 1 option for the first spot, and there are three options for the last two spots: 01 , 10 , 01,10, or 11 11. In the other − 3 n−3 spots, there are no restrictions, so there are 2 2 options for each of those − 3 n−3 spots. Thus, the number strings where the string starts with 1 1 or ends with 00 00 is 2 − 3 ⋅ 2 − 3 2 n −3⋅2 n−3 , as there are 2 2 n total strings of length n ( 0 0 or 1 1 for each of n spots). With = 10 n=10, the answer is 1024 − 384 = 640 1024−384=640.

questions.title: Quick Blue
questions.problem: A bowl has $3$ red and $4$ blue marbles inside. The marbles are drawn out one-by-one until without replacement. Find the probability that it takes more than $5$ draws to draw out the last blue marble.
questions.solution: For all $4$ blue marbles to be removed within the first $5$ draws, there must be exactly $1$ red marble in the first $5$ draws. We know that there is at least $1$ red marble in the first $5$ draws no matter what, as there are only $4$ blue marbles total. If there were at least $2$ red marbles in the first $5$ draws, there could only be at most $3$ blue marbles in the first $5$ draws, meaning that the last blue marble would be outside of the first $5$ draws. Therefore, the only time that all $4$ blue marbles are removed in the first $5$ draws is if there is exactly $1$ red marble in the first $5$ draws. In other words, the last two draws must both be red. Since sampling without replacement is an exchangeable process, the probability that the last two marbles drawn are red is the same as the probability that the first two are red. The probability that the first marble drawn is red is 3 7 7 3 , as 3 3 of the 7 7 marbles at the start are the red. Afterwards, the probability that the second marble is red is 2 6 = 1 3 6 2 = 3 1 , as there would be 2 2 red marbles left out of 6 6 total. Multiplying these together, the probability that the last two marbles are red is 3 7 ⋅ 1 3 = 1 7 7 3 ⋅ 3 1 = 7 1 . This implies that the probability that all 4 4 blue marbles are drawn out in the first 5 5 turns is 1 7 7 1 , meaning the probability that it takes more than 5 5 turns is 1 − 1 / 7 = 6 / 7 1−1/7=6/7.

If any person lands a heads, that person wins, meaning player 1 1 would not win. If all players land a tails, then the coin goes back to player 1 1, and they have probability α of winning in this case, as the situation of the game is completely unchanged from the fact that the coin went through a full revolution and is back at player 1 1. Therefore, by Law of Total Probability, = + ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) − 1 ⟺ = 1 − ( 1 − ) α=p+(1−p)(1−p) n−1 α⟺α= 1−(1−p) n p With the given values, the answer is 81 211 211 81 .

questions.title: Colorful Run I
questions.problem: A bowl consists of $n$ red and $n$ blue marbles. Marbles are drawn from this bag one-by-one without replacement until there are no marbles left in the bag. The order that the marbles are drawn in is noted. questions.solution: The number of runs is equal to the number of starts of runs, as every single run must have a start. Since we are looking for the expected count of something occurring in sampling without replacement, linearity of expectation is the way to go. The first task is to set up appropriate indicators. Since we want to count the expected number of runs, let X i be the indicator of the event that the ith marble drawn out is the start of a new run. = 1 + 2 + ⋯ + 2 T=X 1 +X 2 +⋯+X 2n gives the total number of runs in our sequence. Note that all of these except one are identically distributed. Namely, 1 = 1 X 1 =1 always, as there is no marble prior to it that it needs to differ in color from, so it must be the start of a run. However, the other 2 − 1 2n−1 random variables are all exchangeable, as we are sampling without replacement and the probability of being the start of a new run only depends on there being a previous marble to compare to, in which all of them have a marble to compare to. By linearity of expectation and exchangeability, [ ] = 1 + ( 2 − 1 ) [ 2 ] E[T]=1+(2n−1)E[X 2 ] Note that we have to choose 2 X 2 since 1 X 1 has a different distribution than the rest. [ 2 ] E[X 2 ] is the probability that the second marble drawn is the start of a new run. This means that the color of the first and second marbles drawn differ. Since each marble color is equally likely for the first draw, we can fix it arbitrarily. WLOG, say it is red. To start a new run, the second marble must be blue. There are n blue marbles in the bowl at this point out of 2 − 1 2n−1 total, as we sample without replacement, so [ 2 ] = 2 − 1 E[X 2 ]= 2n−1 n . Plugging this in, [ ] = + 1 E[T]=n+1. With = 100 n=100, the answer is 101 101.

questions.solution: Note that $X$ and $Y$ are not necessarily IID, so we can't just say it is $1/2$. However, we can use the case where 1 = 2 λ 1 =λ 2 as a litmus test for the solution to ensure that it is $1/2$ in that case. Computing this probability is best done by integrating over the joint PDF, as the random variables are not identically distributed. We want to integrate over $0 < x < y < \infty$, as that is the region where $x < y$. The joint PDF is easily obtained by multiplying the PDFs of $X$ and $Y$ together to get ( , ) = $1$ 2 − ( 1 + 2 ) ( 0 , ∞ ) ( ) ( 0 , ∞ ) ( ) f(x,y)=λ 1 λ 2 e −(λ 1 x+λ 2 y) I (0,∞) (x)I (0,∞) (y). The integral we must evaluate is [ < ] = ∫ 0 ∞ ∫ ∞ 1 2 − ( 1 + 2 ) ( 0 , ∞ ) ( ) ( 0 , ∞ ) ( ) = ∫ 0 ∞ 1 − ( 1 + 2 ) = 1 1 + 2 ∫ 0 ∞ ( 1 + 2 ) − ( 1 + 2 ) P[X<Y]=∫ 0 ∞ ∫ x ∞ λ 1 λ 2 e −(λ 1 x+λ 2 y) I (0,∞) (x)I (0,∞) (y)dydx=∫ 0 ∞ λ 1 e −(λ 1 +λ 2 )x dx= λ 1 +λ 2 λ 1 ∫ 0 ∞ (λ 1 +λ 2 )e −(λ 1 +λ 2 )x dx The interior of the last integral is the PDF of an Exp ( 1 + 2 ) Exp(λ 1 +λ 2 ) distribution. We are integrating this PDF over its entire support, so the integral must be 1 1. Therefore, the probability in question is 1 1 + 2 λ 1 +λ 2 λ 1 . Intuitively, this answer makes sense. Suppose you have a machine producing red cards at a rate of 1 λ 1 per time unit on average and 2 λ 2 blue cards per time unit on average, independently of one another. Then the probability that the first card produced is red should intuitively just be the average amount of red cards produced in the period, 1 λ 1 , out of the average total amount of cards produced in the period, 1 + 2 λ 1 +λ 2 . When 1 = 2 λ 1 =λ 2 , we can see that the fraction above reduces to 1 / 2 1/2, which is what we would expect in the IID case. With the specified values in the problem, the answer is 2 / 5 2/5.

questions.title: Opposite Parity Heads I
questions.problem: We flip a coin that has a probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip $n \geq 2$ times. Given that the first and last flip are of opposite parity, compute the expected number of heads obtained when $p = 3/4$ and $n = 10$.
questions.solution: Let $T$ be the total number of heads in the $n$ flips and $P$ be the event that the first and last flip are of opposite parity. We can write = 1 + 2 T=T 1 +T 2 , where $T_1$ is the number of heads obtained in the first and last flip (i.e. restricting to the two flips of interest) and $T_2$ is the number of heads in the remaining − 2 n−2 flips. The reason we want to do something like this is because the information that we are given says that 1 = 1 T 1 =1, as there is one heads and one tails among the first and last flip. In other words, [ ∣ ] = [ 1 + 2 ∣ ] = [ 1 ∣ ] + [ 2 ∣ ] = 1 + [ 2 ∣ ] E[T∣P]=E[T 1 +T 2 ∣P]=E[T 1 ∣P]+E[T 2 ∣P]=1+E[T 2 ∣P] The number of heads in the remaining − 2 n−2 flips is independent of the event P, as P is only concerned with the first and last flip, while 2 T 2 counts the number of heads in the remaining − 2 n−2 flips. Thus, [ 2 ∣ ] = [ 2 ] E[T 2 ∣P]=E[T 2 ]. As 2 T 2 counts the number of heads obtained in − 2 n−2 flips of a coin with probability p of heads per flip, 2 ∼ Binom ( − 2 , ) T 2 ∼Binom(n−2,p). The mean is therefore [ 2 ] = ( − 2 ) E[T 2 ]=p(n−2). This implies [ ] = 1 + ( − 2 ) E[T]=1+(n−2)p With the specified values, the answer is 7 7.

questions.title: Opposite Parity Heads II
questions.problem: We flip a coin that has a probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip $n \geq 2$ times. Let $P$ be the event that the first and last flip are of opposite parity. For what value(s) of $p$ (potentially dependent on $n$) does the knowledge of $P$ occurring not impact the expected number of heads in the $n$ flips? Report the sum of all such values of $p$ when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: Let $T$ be the total number of heads in the $n$ flips and $P$ be the event that the first and last flip are of opposite parity. We essentially want to find the value of $p$ such that [ ∣ ] = [ ] E[T∣P]=E[T]. With no information, $T$ counts the number of heads that are obtained in $n$ flips of a fair coin that has probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip, so ∼ Binom ( , ) T∼Binom(n,p). This has mean [ ] = E[T]=np. From "Opposite Parity Heads I", [ ∣ ] = 1 + ( − 2 ) E[T∣P]=1+(n−2)p. Thus, we must solve 1 + ( − 2 ) = 1+(n−2)p=np. This has solution $p = 1/2$ by rearrangement, independent of $n$. This result makes intuitive sense. With $p = 1/2$, there would be an average of $2 \cdot 1/2 = 1$ head among the first and last flip, and the information given is that there indeed is $1$ head among the first and last flip, so the information given doesn't impact the expectation.

Namely, we get 2 + 3 − 2 + 5 − 3 + 7 − 4 − 4.5 − 5 9 = − 1 6 9 2+3−2+5−3+7−4−4.5−5 =− 6 1

questions.title: Miami Hurricanes
questions.problem: A family has a sign with the letters MIAMI on the front. A hurricane hits Miami for the $10$th time this year, so two random letters have fallen off this sign. However, if they are not the same, it is not guaranteed that the sign will read correctly again. Thus, the best approach is to condition on whether the two letters that fell off are the same or not. The goal is to compute [ ] = [ ∣ ] [ ] + [ ∣ ] [ ] P[C]=P[C∣M]P[M]+P[C∣M c ]P[M c ] [ ] P[M] is just the probability that the two letters that fell off match. Therefore, [ ] = 2 / 10 = 1 / 5 P[M]=2/10=1/5, which implies [ ] = 1 − 1 / 5 = 4 / 5 P[M c ]=1−1/5=4/5. Therefore, the total probability that the bug reaches a vertical side is 1 4 + 3 4 ⋅ 1 2 = 5 8 4 1 + 4 3 ⋅ 2 1 = 8 5

One of these is an outcome where Amber wins, while the other is where Billy rolls a larger number than Amber. Thus, there are 2 − 2 2 n 2 −n outcomes where Amber rolls a strictly larger number than Billy. Adding the two cases, there are 2 − 2 + = 2 + 2 2 n 2 −n +n= 2 n 2 +n outcomes where Amber rolls at least as large as Billy. Thus, the probability Amber rolls larger than Billy i.e. wins is ( − 1 ) / 2 ( + 1 ) / 2 = − 1 + 1 n(n+1)/2 n(n−1)/2 = n+1 n−1 With = 10 n=10, the answer is 9 11 11 9 .

questions.solution: Since the coin is fair, we can just count sequences of coin flips, rather than working with the binomial distribution. In a problem like this, since $5$ is a small number of flips, it's best to enumerate the forms of the outcomes. The sequence of outcomes must be in the form − , , − HHHT−,THHHT,or−THHH, where $-$ can be either heads or tails. This implies that there are $2$ outcomes of the first and last form, while there is exactly $1$ outcome of the middle form. This is because $-$ has two options. Thus, there are $5$ total outcomes yielding exactly $3$ consecutive heads. There are 2 5 = 3$2$ 5 =32 total outcomes of the flipping sequence, as each flip has 2 2 options, so the probability of obtaining exactly $3$ consecutive heads is 5 32 32 5 .

To have at least $3$ consecutive heads consecutively, there can be exactly $3,4,$ or $5$ consecutive heads. In "Consecutive Heads I", we found that $5$ sequences had exactly $3$ consecutive heads. It is easy to see that the only sequence with $5$ consecutive heads is $HHHHH$. This is a single sequence. To have exactly $4$ consecutive heads, the sequence must either be $HHHHT$ or $THHHH$, which is $2$ possible outcomes. Adding all of these together, we obtain $8$ total outcomes out of 2 5 = 32 2 5 =32 total, so the answer is $8/32 = 1/4$.

questions.title: Prior Die Sum II

questions.solution: Since we are looking at the probability that an event occurs before some other event disjoint to it, the paradigm of "Prior Event I" is particularly appealing to solve this problem. Clearly, the events of rolling a sum of 2 2 and a sum of 4 4 are disjoint on a given trial. By writing out the PMF table of the sum of two dice, sums of 2 2 and 4 4 occur with respective probabilities 1 36 36 1 and 3 36 = 1 12 36 3 = 12 1 . These sum to at most 1 1, so the result of "Prior Event I" yields that the probability of obtaining a sum of 4 4 before a sum of 2 2 is 3 / 36 1 / 36 + 3 / 36 = 3 4 1/36+3/36 3/36 = 4 3 .

questions.title: Multiballs I
questions.problem: You have two urns in front of you, say $1$ and $2$. Urn $1$ has $m$ red and $n$ blue marbles inside, while urn $2$ has $n$ red and $m$ blue marbles inside. Assume that $m,n \geq 1$. You select one urn uniformly at random and select $2$ marbles uniformly at random without replacement. In your selection, you observe $1$ red and $1$ blue marble. Find the probability that you drew from urn $1$ when $m = 7$ and $n = 4$.
questions.solution: We are given information here about what appears in the sequence of draws, so using the definition of conditional probability/Bayes' Theorem here is most relevant. Let $U_1$ and $U_2$ be the events that we select from urns $1$ and $2$, respectively. Similarly, let $S$ be the event that we obtain a selection of $1$ red and $1$ blue marble among $2$ marbles drawn without replacement. If we know which urn we selected, then it's quite easy to determine the probability of obtaining the selection above, as we know the counts of the marbles in the urn. Therefore, we should condition on the selected urn. Namely, [ ∩ 1 ] = [ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] P[S∩U 1 ]=P[S∣U 1 ]P[U 1 ]. [ 1 ] = 1 / 2 P[U 1 ]=1/2, as you select the urn uniformly at random to start. As there are + m+n marbles in the urn and we select 2 2, there are ( + 2 ) ( 2 m+n ) ways to do this without restriction. There are n ways to pick the one blue marble and m ways to pick one red marble from urn 1 1. Thus, [ ∣ 1 ] = ( + 2 ) P[S∣U 1 ]= ( 2 m+n ) mn . We compute [ ] P[S] in a similar way. As per the above, we condition on the urn that is being drawn from to obtain [ ] = [ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] + [ ∣ 2 ] [ 2 ] P[S]=P[S∣U 1 ]P[U 1 ]+P[S∣U 2 ]P[U 2 ]. The first term is exactly the numerator. We also know that [ 2 ] = 1 2 P[U 2 ]= 2 1 , as each urn is equally likely to be selected from at first. Then, given that we selected from urn 2 2, we must find the probability of obtaining the desired selection. There are ( + 2 ) ( 2 m+n ) ways to pick the marbles without restriction once again. In this case, the roles of m and n are reversed, as the other bag has n red and m blue marbles. Therefore, [ ∣ 2 ] = ( + 2 ) P[S∣U 2 ]= ( 2 m+n ) nm . Plugging all of this in, we obtain [ 1 ∣ ] = ( + 2 ) ( + 2 ) + ( + 2 ) = + = 1 2 P[U 1 ∣S]= ( 2 m+n ) mn + ( 2 m+n ) mn ( 2 m+n ) mn = mn+mn mn = 2 1 This answer makes intuitive sense, as the information that is given is symmetric between the two urns. In other words, drawing one red and one blue marble gives no information at all regarding which urn was selected, as the information says that we draw one marble of each color, and the urns are also symmetric in their counts of each type of marble. questions.title: Same Sequence I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob both flip fair coins $n$ times. Find the probability that Alice and Bob obtain the same sequence when $n = 6$.
questions.solution: As the coin is fair, all sequences are equally likely, so we can fix Alice's sequence arbitrarily. Of all of the sequences that Bob can flip, exactly $1$ of them is the one Alice has. There are $2^n$ equally likely sequences of flips that Bob can obtain, as each of the $n$ flips has the option to be either heads or tails. Therefore, the probability that Alice and Bob flip the same sequence is 1 2 = 2 − 2 n 1 =2 −n . With $n = 6$, the answer is 1 64 64 1 .

questions.title: Same Sequence III
questions.problem: Alice and Bob flip coins with respective probabilities $0 < p < 1$ and $0 < q < 1$ of heads $n$ times each. Find the probability that Alice and Bob obtain the same sequence when $n = 4, p = 1/3,$ and $q = 1/4$.
questions.solution: We can't employ the same approach as "Same Sequence I" because of the fact that the sequences are not equally likely now. To reduce the problem, consider the case of $n = 1$. In $1$ flip, Alice and Bob flip the same sequence if they either both obtain a head or both obtain a tail. Since their flips are independent, the probability they both obtain a head is $pq$, while the probability that they both obtain a tail is ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) (1−p)(1−q). As these two cases are disjoint, the probability that the both obtain the same sequence in $1$ flip is + ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) pq+(1−p)(1−q). However, we can note that for Alice and Bob to obtain the same sequence of $n$ flips, each of the individual $n$ flips must be the same. Each flip is independent, so the probability of all $n$ flips being the same is just the same as the product of the probabilities each individual flip is the same. However, each individual flip is the same with probability + ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) pq+(1−p)(1−q) by the above. Therefore, the probability that all n flips are the same i.e. they have the same sequence is ( + ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) ) (pq+(1−p)(1−q)) n . With the specified values, the answer is 2401 20736 20736 2401 .

Plugging these in, we get [ ∣ ∩ ∣ ] = ⋅ ⋅ = E[∣A∩B∣]=n⋅ n a ⋅ n b = n ab With the specified values, the answer is 4 4.

questions.title: Modular Pairs
questions.problem: What is the minimum number of pairs of integers $(a,b)$ that are needed to guarantee that there exist two pairs ( 1 , 1 ) (a 1 ,b 1 ) and ( 2 , 2 ) (a 2 ,b 2 ) such that 1 mod = 2 mod a 1 modn=a 2 modn and 1 mod = 2 mod b 1 modn=b 2 modn, where $n \geq 2$ is an integer? Solve this when $n = 7$.
questions.solution: Note that there are $n$ options for the equivalence class that $a_1$ and $a_2$ both belong to. Similarly, there are $n$ options for the equivalence class that both $b_1$ and $b_2$ belong to. Therefore, by the multiplication principle, there are $n^2$ total ways to pick the pair of equivalence classes that the $a_i$ s and the $b_i$ s belong to. By the Pigeonhole Principle, if there are at least 2 + 1 n 2 +1 pairs, there must exist two pairs that satisfy the above, as there are only $n^2$ pigeonholes (pairs of equivalence classes). With less than 2 + 1 n 2 +1 pairs, it is possible that no two belong to the same pigeonhole, so 2 + 1 n 2 +1 is the absolute minimum. With the specified value here, the answer is $50$.

questions.title: Ice Cream Orders
questions.problem: An ice cream store sells cups and cones. A cup can hold small, medium, and large scoops, while a cone can only hold small and medium scoops. There are $8$ cup toppings and $12$ cone toppings. How many one-topping ice cream orders are there?
questions.solution: The size of the ice cream order allowed is dependent on whether a cone or cup is selected. Therefore, it's best to break up this problem into two cases: Cone and cup. These cases are disjoint (you can't have both a cone and cup) and exhaustive (every ice cream order uses either a cone or cup). For the cup case, there are 3 3 size options and 8 8 toppings, meaning there are 3 ⋅ 8 = 24 3⋅8=24 ice cream options with a cup. For a cone, there are only 2 2 sizes and 12 12 toppings, so there are 2 ⋅ 12 = 24 2⋅12=24 ice cream options with a cone. Adding these together, we have 48 48 total orders.

questions.title: Modified Full House I
questions.problem: How many $5-$card hands from a standard $52-$card deck consist of $2$ cards of one suit and $3$ cards of another suit?
questions.solution: The first thing we need to ask ourselves is: Does the ordering of suits matter? The answer is yes because we are selecting only $2$ of one, but $3$ of the other, so if we swap the two suits around, we do indeed get a different full house. Thus, we first have to permute $k=2$ suits from $n=4$ total suits in the deck, as which suit receives $3$ cards vs. $2$ cards matters. There are $P(4,2)$ ways to do this. For the suit that has $3$ replicates in the hand, the order of the cards selected is irrelevant, so we want a subset of size $k = 3$ from a set of $n = 13$ cards of that suit, which can be selected in ( 13 3 ) ( 3 13 ) ways. Then, for the suit with $2$ replicates, by the same logic, there are ( 13 2 ) ( 2 13 ) ways to pick $2$ cards from the other suit. By the multiplication principle, the answer is ( 4 , 2 ) ⋅ ( 13 3 ) ⋅ ( 13 2 ) = 267696 P(4,2)⋅( 3 13 )⋅( 2 13 )=267696

Let A be the event that Diego correctly answers at least 2 2 questions. $A^c$ is the event that he answers either $0$ or $1$ question correctly, as these outcomes ensure Diego did not answer at least $2$ questions correctly. Since we are looking at the number of correct answers in Diego's exam and we know each sequence of answers to the $10$ questions are equally likely, we should set up the sample space as all possible sequences of $10$ answers that Diego can submit. Each answer has $4$ options, so there are 4 10 4 10 possible ways to answer the exam. The events of obtaining exactly $0$ correct answers and exactly $1$ correct answer are disjoint events. Therefore, if we let $C_0$ and $C_1$ be the events that Diego gets $0$ and $1$ questions correct, respectively, = 0 ∪ 1 A c =C 0 ∪C 1 . By finite disjoint additivity, [ ] = [ 0 ] + [ 1 ] P[A c ]=P[C 0 ]+P[C 1 ] [ 0 ] P[C 0 ] is the probability he selects a wrong answer for all $10$ questions. There are $3$ wrong answers per question of the $4$ questions, so there are ∣ 0 ∣ = 3 10 ∣C 0 ∣=3 10 ways he can answer every question wrong. Therefore, [ 0 ] = 3 10 / 4 10 P[C 0 ]=3 10 /4 10 . For the other $9$ questions, there are $3$ ways to pick a wrong answer. By the multiplication rule, there are ∣ 1 ∣ = 10 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 3 9 = 10 ⋅ 3 9 ∣C 1 ∣=10⋅1⋅3 9 =10⋅3 9 ways to get one answer correct. Therefore, [ 1 ] = 10 ⋅ 3 9 / 4 10 P[C 1 ]=10⋅3 9 /4 10 . Substituting x as both + s+t and t into the expression fro the beginning, [ > + ] = − ( + ) P[X>s+t]=e −λ(s+t) and [ > ] = − P[X>t]=e −λt . This result makes intuitive sense by thinking about the meaning of the Exponential distribution. The memorylessness property here says that given you have waited at least t time units for the first occurrence event, the probability you must wait at least + t+s time units for the first occurrence of the event is just the probability you must wait s time units (as if it was from the beginning). Imagine the following scenario: You are watching for a certain type of bird, and you wait t units of time for the bird to appear, and it still doesn't. After t units of time, your friend comes in to substitute for you in watching for the bird. The probability that the total time spent watching the bird is at least + t+s is therefore just the probability your friend spends at least s units of time watching for the bird. Since the bird hasn't appeared yet, it's as if your friend had started watching from the beginning again, as the state is the exact same. In rough terms, the memorylessness property says: The amount of time that you have already waited for an event to occur does not give any information about how much longer you must wait for an event to occur. With this intuition in mind, we can conclude that the limit is $0$ for all $k$.

questions.title: Rank and Suit Diff

questions.solution: Since there are the same number of ranks and suits among all different ranks/suits, fix the first card arbitrarily. There are now $51$ cards in the deck remaining. Therefore, there are $12 \cdot 3 = 36$ valid cards that can be selected for the second card, so the answer is $36/51 = 12/17$.

questions.title: Die Duo I
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. While your die is a standard fair $6-$sided die, your friend's die has the values $111666$ on the sides. Both of you roll the die one time. questions.solution: To roll strictly higher than your friend, they must obtain a $1$ on their die, as it's not possible for your to obtain a strictly larger value than $6$. Your friend rolls $1$ with probability $1/2$. Given your friend rolls a $1$, you must obtain some value strictly larger than $1$. This occurs with probability $5/6$ on your die, as all outcomes but $1$ are strictly better than your friend's roll. Therefore, the answer is $5/6 \cdot 1/2 = 5/12$.

questions.solution: When $p = 0$, the person who lost the previous game wins the next game. In this case, Bob wins the first game guaranteed. questions.title: Scotty Bugatti
questions.problem: Scotty has a Bugatti and parks it in a row of $N$ parking spots. He doesn't park in one of the endpoints of the row. After parking his car, he leaves to go skiing. Upon returning, Scotty sees exactly 1 ≤ ≤ − 2 1≤k≤N−2 cars are in the parking lot. Assume that all cars park among the open spots uniformly at random and that at most 1 1 car is in a given spot. Find the probability that Scotty's car is between two vacant spots when = 15 N=15 and = 6 k=6. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The knowledge that Scotty's car is on the interior reduces the problem complexity, as it's irrelevant exactly where he parked his car, since any interior spot has $2$ cars that are adjacent to it. This question now reduces to: How many arrangements of the other cars have none on either side of Scotty's car? This can be done as a counting problem because all arrangements are equally likely. The total number of ways to park the other − 1 k−1 cars in the − 1 N−1 open spots with no restrictions is ( − 1 − 1 ) ( k−1 N−1 ), as their order of parking is irrelevant. To ensure that Scotty's car is between two vacant spots, the spots immediately left and immediately right of his car must be empty. questions.title: Shakey Hands
questions.problem: A room of $N > 3$ people contains at least one person that has not shaken hands with every other person. Find the maximum number of people that have shaken hands with every other person when $N = 50$.
questions.solution: WLOG, suppose the people are labelled $1$ to $N$, and person $1$ is someone who hasn't shaken hands with every other person. This means there is someone that person $1$ has not shaken hands with. To maximize the number of people that have shaken hands with everyone else, suppose there is only $1$ person that person $1$ hasn't shaken hands with, and let this be person $2$. By default, since $1$ and $2$ haven't shaken hands, person $2$ also has not shaken the hands of every other person in the room. However, people $3$ to $N$ can all shake each other's hands, as well as the hands of people $1$ and $2$, so they have shaken hands with everyone else in the room. Thus, the maximum number of people that have shaken hands with everyone else is − 2 N−2. With $N = 50$, the answer is $48$.

questions.title: Kitten Box
questions.problem: A box has $15$ kittens in it. $8$ of the kittens are black and $7$ of the kittens are white. You randomly pull kittens out of the box until its empty. What is the probability that when the last white kitten is pulled out of the box, there are exactly $3$ black kittens left in the box?
questions.solution: A good strategy for questions like this is to use counting methods to determine the probability. In this case we want the probability that the when the last white kitten is pulled out there are exactly three black kittens still in box. If we think about the sequence of kittens that we pull out and denote each black kitten as B and each white kitten as W, then the probability will be the number of sequences of kittens that end in WBBB divided by the total number of sequences of kittens. If a sequence of kittens ends with WBBB then that means there are 11 remaining kittens to pull out of the box. Of these 11 kittens, 6 of them must be white. Thus, there are ( 11 6 ) ( 6 11 ) total kitten sequences that end in WBBB, since we need to fill 6 of the 11 spots with a white kitten. Similarly, if we want to determine the total number of kitten sequences, there are 15 spots in total and of these 15 we need to choose 7 of them to be a white kitten, so that there are ( 15 7 ) ( 7 15 ) total kitten sequences. Thus the final probability is, ( 11 6 ) ( 15 7 ) = 14 195 ( 7 15 ) ( 6 11 ) = 195 14

questions.title: Strictly Increasing Dice

The second is that the dice must be appropriately ordered, so that the first is lower than the second, the second is lower than the third, and the third is lower than the fourth. To find [ Strictly increasing sequence ∣ All dice are different ] P[Strictly increasing sequence∣All dice are different], note that if all dice are different then there is exactly one ordering of those dice that forms a strictly increasing sequence. Since every sequence is equally likely, and since we are rolling 4 dice, this probability is equal to 1 4 ! 4! 1 . questions.title: Product of 6
questions.problem: If you roll $2$ standard fair $6-$sided dice, what is the probability that the product of their faces is divisible by $6$?
questions.solution: In order for the product of the two rolls to be divisible by $6$ we must be able to write the product as $6k$, where $k$ is some integer. Since $2 \times 3 = 6$, any pair of dice rolls whose product contains a factor of $2$ and $3$ will be divisible by $6$. This means our possible pairs are $(3,4), (3,2), (4,3), (2,3),$ and any pair where one of the dice is a $6$, or both are $6$. In the case of one of the dice being a $6$, there are $10$ total possibilities since there are $5$ other possible values for the other dice, and $2$ ways to decide which of the two dice is $6$. In the case of both dice being $6$, there is only one possible pair. Since there are 6 2 = 36 6 2 =36 total possible pairs for the dice rolls the final probability is, [ product of faces is divisible by 6 ] = 4 + 10 + 1 36 = 15 36 = 5 12 P[product of faces is divisible by 6]= 36 4+10+1 = 36 15 = 12 5

questions.title: Breaking Even
questions.problem: Lewis and Lilly are playing a game with a coin. The coin is going to be tossed $10$ times. After a toss, Lewis will give Lilly $\$1$ if the toss is heads, and Lilly will give Lewis $\$1$ if it is tails. As long as Lewis and Lilly both have at least $\$1$, they will toss again. If one of them has a balance of $\$0$, then the game ends. If they both start out with $\$5$, what is the probability that they break even? That is, what is the probability that both finish the game with $\$5$?
questions.solution: In order for both players to finish the game with $\$5$, two things must occur. The first is that they each need to win and lose $5$ times, since otherwise their total at the end of the game would not be $\$5$. The second thing that needs to happen is that none of the players can ever go to $\$0$, because then the game stops. The number of length $10$ sequences of coin flips that consist of $5$ heads and $5$ tails is given by ( 10 5 ) ( 5 10 ), since out of the $10$ flips, we need to choose $5$ of them to be tails. However, $2$ of these flips violate the second condition that we need. Specifically, the sequence $HHHHHTTTTT$ and $TTTTTHHHHH$, since if we flip $5$ heads or $5$ tails in a row right from the beginning, then one of the players will reach a balance of $\$0$, and the game will stop. Thus, there are ( 10 5 ) − 2 = 250 ( 5 10 )−2=250 sequences of coin flips that meet our criteria. The total number of possible coin flips is given by 2 10 2 10 , since each of the $10$ coin flips can be either heads or tails. Thus, since every sequence of coin flips occurs we equal probability, the probability that both players break even is, 250 2 10 = 125 512 2 10 250 = 512 125

questions.title: Choosing a Die
questions.problem: Suppose that you are playing a game with two fair dice $-$ one which is $6-$sided and one which is $8-$sided. You first roll the $6-$sided die and have the option to keep the value on that die, or to roll the $8-$sided die instead and keep that value. questions.solution: To optimize our expected earnings, we will decide to only roll the second dice if doing so provides a benefit (in expectation). Since the expected value of the $6-$sided die is $3.5$, and the expected value of the $8-$sided die is $4.5$, we should decide to reroll the first die if we roll anything below a $5$. If we roll a $5$ or $6$, we should keep the result of the first dice, since we expect to only get $4.5$ (on average) if we decide to roll the $8-$sided die. To find the expected value of this strategy, let $R$ be the value we roll from the $6-$sided die, and let $V$ denote our payout. On average, Alice rolls 2 2 times before stopping, as there is probability 1 / 2 1/2 per roll of her rolling a stopping value. Thus, at the time of stopping, she has $ 2 $2 in her bank on average. With probability 2 / 3 2/3, she stopped on a value that allows her to keep the $ 2 $2, so the expected amount Alice receives is 2 ⋅ 2 / 3 = 4 / 3 2⋅2/3=4/3.

Therefore, the key is to apply Law of Total Expectation and condition on the first flip. Let $L_1$ be the length of the first run and $H$ be the event that the first flip is heads. $H^c$ would be the event that the first flip is tails. If the first flip is heads, the length of the first run is equal to the expected number of additional flips needed to obtain the first tails tails (since the first tails will end our streak of heads) added to the 1 1 head that already appeared. Since we are looking at a discrete waiting time, the number of additional flips until the first tails is ∼ Geom ( 1 − ) T∼Geom(1−p) distributed, since there is probability 1 − 1−p of tails per flip. However, there are − 1 T−1 heads that appear, as the last flip is the tails itself. questions.title: 7 Below I
questions.problem: You roll a fair standard $6-$sided die. You have two options: keep or roll again. If you decide to keep, you receive a payout equal to the upface (in dollars). Otherwise, you can roll again. If the sum of your two rolls is at least 7 7, you receive nothing. If the sum of the two rolls is less than 7 7, you receive the upface of your second roll (in dollars). Assuming optimal play, what is your expected payout?
questions.solution: Our goal here is to make a decision rule to determine what values from the first roll we should keep and which we should roll again. To not lose money, we need the sum of the two rolls to be at most $6$. We would only want to roll the die again if it can provide us a better expected payout on the second roll while taking on the risk that the sum is at least $7$. In particular, if the first roll is $3,4,5,$ or $6$, you should always keep the value. This is because you can never do strictly better on the second roll without the sum being at least $7$, which would make you have to pay money instead. Therefore, these $4$ values should always be kept. We now need to consider the cases of $1$ and $2$ separately. If a $1$ is rolled on the first roll, you need to determine whether the expected payout by rolling again is larger than $1$ or not. If you roll again and obtain any value at most $5$, then you get to keep that value, as the sum would be less than $7$. However, if you roll a $6$ on the second roll, then you receive nothing, as the sum would be at least $7$ in this case. Therefore, the expected value obtained by rolling again is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 0 6 = 5 2 > 1 6 1+2+3+4+5+0 = 2 5 >1 Since this expected value of rolling again is larger than $1$, you should roll again if a $1$ is obtained on the first turn. If a $2$ is rolled on the first roll, a similar decision needs to be made. If you decide to roll again, you would get to keep the payouts $1-4$ if they are obtained, as the sum would be at most $6$. However, if $5$ or $6$ is obtained, you receive nothing. Therefore, the expected payout by rolling again in this case is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 0 + 0 6 = 5 3 < 2 6 1+2+3+4+0+0 = 3 5 <2 Since the expected value by rolling again is less than 2 2, you should keep 2 2 if it is obtained on the first trial. Putting this together, we have that the optimal expected value is 5 / 2 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 6 = 15 4 6 5/2+2+3+4+5+6 = 4 15

questions.title: Paperless Play I
questions.problem: You play rock, paper, scissors with a friend, but they can't use paper. The winner receives $\$1$ from the loser. No payments happen if there is a tie. Under optimal strategy from both yourself and your friend, find your expected payout on one round of the game.
questions.solution: As your friend can only play rock and scissors, you should never play scissors yourself, as it is not possible for you to win against your friend with scissors. Therefore, we only have to work with rock and paper for yourself. In such a problem where an optimal strategy must be determined for multiple players, finding a Nash equilibrium is typically the best approach. Both players must run a mixed strategy, as if either ran a pure strategy, the other one could pick a pure strategy on the option that beats the one the other player selected, which is not optimal. Let p be the probability that you play rock. Similarly, let q be the probability that your friend plays rock. 1 − 1−p and 1 − 1−q are the respective probabilities of you playing paper and your friend playing scissors. The idea is to find an equation ( , ) E(p,q) that represents your expected payout of a round dependent on p and q. Afterwards, we want to take partial derivatives in p and q, set them equal to 0 0, and determine the values of p and q that are optimal for each player. If you and your friend both play rock, nothing occurs, so the expected profit is 0 0. If you play rock and your friend plays scissors, which occurs with probability ( 1 − ) p(1−q), you win $ 1 $1. If you play paper and your friend plays rock, which occurs with probability ( 1 − ) q(1−p), you also win $ 1 $1. Lastly, if you play paper and your friend plays scissors, which occurs with probability ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) (1−p)(1−q), your friend wins $ 1 $1. Thus, your expected profit, as a function of p and q, is given by ( , ) = ( 1 − ) + ( 1 − ) − ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) = 2 ( + ) − 3 − 1 E(p,q)=p(1−q)+q(1−p)−(1−p)(1−q)=2(p+q)−3pq−1 To solve for the optimal p and q, we take partial derivatives of this function in p and q and set them equal to 0 0. Namely, we have that ∂ ∂ = 2 − 3 = 0 ⟺ = 2 / 3 ∂ ∂ = 2 − 3 = 0 ⟺ = 2 / 3 ∂p ∂E =2−3q=0⟺q=2/3 ∂q ∂E =2−3p=0⟺p=2/3 These are the optimal values of p and q for each player, so the expected payout for you is ( 2 / 3 , 2 / 3 ) = 1 / 3 E(2/3,2/3)=1/3.

questions.title: Start or Not I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob alternate picking balls without replacement from an urn that has $k$ red balls and $1$ black ball. The winner is the person who draws the black ball. Alice gets to decide the order of drawing. If Alice plays optimally, what is her chance of winning when $k = 100$?
questions.solution: We can view the emptying of the urn as a sequence of $k+1$ draws, where the entire urn is emptied. Since drawing without replacement is an exchangeable process, the black ball is equally likely to be in any of the $k+1$ spots. The person who goes first will always have at least as many attempts to draw the black ball as the person who goes second, so it's never strictly optimal for Alice to go second. Note that the number of total draws is dependent on whether or not k is even or odd. If k is odd, $k = 2r+1$ for some other integer $r$, so there are $2r+2$ total draws needed to empty the urn. Both Alice and Bob will be able to draw out $r+1$ balls, regardless of the order. Therefore, when $k$ is odd, Alice is indifferent to going first or second. When $k$ is even, then $k = 2r$ for some integer $r$. There would be $2r+1$ total draws from the urn, and the first person to go would have $r+1$ draws out of the urn, while the second person has only $r$. Thus, there is a higher probability that the person who draws first wins in this case, as they get more attempts and the black ball is equally likely to appear in any draw prior to the process. Since $k = 100$ here, Alice should choose to go first, and she will get $50 + 1 = 51$ total attempts to draw out the black ball, so her probability of winning is $51/101$.

questions.title: No Ones Home
questions.problem: You repeatedly roll two fair $6-$sided dice. If both dice show values larger than $1$, add them to your running cumulative sum; otherwise, the game ends and you receive no payout. You can decide to stop rolling at any time. Under the optimal strategy, what is the minimum number of points at which you want to stop?
questions.solution: The idea here is to determine the value of $S$, your current sum, such that the expected value of rolling again is non-positive. The probability of neither die showing the value $1$ is $25/36$, as the die doesn't show the value $1$ with probability $5/6$ per die. By complementation, at least one $1$ appears with probability $11/36$. If at least one $1$ appears, you lose your current balance of $S$, so your expected profit is − −S is this case. Otherwise, if neither die shows a $1$, the value of each die is uniformly distributed on the integers $2-6$, which has mean $4$. Therefore, the expected sum of the two dice is $8$ by linearity of expectation. Combining these, the expected value of rolling again when your current sum is $S$ is 25 36 ⋅ 8 + 11 36 ⋅ ( − ) 36 25 ⋅8+ 36 11 ⋅(−S) For this expected value to be non-positive, we must have 25 36 ⋅ 8 + 11 36 ⋅ ( − ) ≤ 0 ⟺ ≥ 200 11 ≈ 18.2 36 25 ⋅8+ 36 11 ⋅(−S)≤0⟺S≥ 11 200 ≈18.2. The first integer for which this expected value is non-positive is $19$, so the answer is $19$.

questions.title: Most Likely First Ace
questions.problem: A standard deck of $52$ cards is shuffled, and cards are dealt out one-at-a-time. What is the most likely position of the first ace?
questions.solution: In problems like this, it's best to set up a function that represents the probability that the nth position has the first ace, and then maximize in n. Let $P(n)$ be this function. For the first ace to appear in the nth position, three things must happen: There must be three positions selected for the other aces after the nth among the remaining 52 − 52−n positions. Once position n and the three other positions are selected, the 4 4 aces must be arranged on those 4 4 positions. The other 48 48 cards must be arranged. There are ( 52 − 3 ) ( 3 52−n ) ways to pick the positions of the three other aces from the other 52 − 52−n spots after the nth position, as the order of selection is irrelevant. Once these 4 4 spots are selected, there are 4 ! 4! ways to arrange the 4 4 aces on these spots. After the aces are fixed, there are 48 ! 48! ways to arrange the other 48 48 cards to the open spots. There are clearly 52 ! 52! ways to arrange the deck, so by the multiplication principle, ( ) = ( 52 − 3 ) 4 ! 48 ! 52 ! = ( 52 − 3 ) ( 52 4 ) P(n)= 52! ( 3 52−n )4!48! = ( 4 52 ) ( 3 52−n ) Note that we could also get this by ignoring the other cards and dividing by ( 52 4 ) ( 4 52 ), the number of ways to pick the locations of the 4 4 aces in the deck without restriction. Regardless, one can note that ( 52 − 3 ) ( 3 52−n ) is decreasing in n, so we must make it as small as possible to maximize ( ) P(n). The smallest value is = 1 n=1, so the first position is best. The intuition for this result comes down to the restriction on the permutations. As the first ace goes further and further back, there are less ways to arrange the other 3 3 aces, so to maximize this, we should put the first ace as quickly as possible.

The sum of the digits in the number is exclusively determined by the subset of integers that's selected, so we can consider the ( 4 3 ) = 4 ( 3 4 )=4 subsets of size 3 3 that can be selected, and determine which yield a sum divisible by 3 3. If 1 1 is excluded, the sum of { 2 , 3 , 4 } {2,3,4} is 9 9, so this outcome yields an integer divisible by 3 3. If 2 2 or 3 3 are excluded, the sum of the elements in the subset is 8 8 or 7 7, respectively, which aren't divisible by 3 3. Lastly, if 4 4 is excluded, { 1 , 2 , 3 } {1,2,3} has a sum of 6 6, so the number formed is divisible by 3 3. 2 2 of the 4 4 equally likely outcomes yield a sum divisible by 3 3, so the probability of having the integer be divisible by 3 3 is 2 / 4 = 1 / 2 2/4=1/2.

They both tell the truth with probability p A p B , and both lie with probability ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) (1−p A )(1−p B ) by independence. Thus, we can conclude [ ∣ ] = + ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) P[T∣E]= p A p B +(1−p A )(1−p B ) p A p B With the specified values, the answer is 3 / 7 3/7.

questions.title: Sum First I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob alternate rolling pairs of standard fair $6-$sided dice, with Alice going first. The game ends when Alice rolls a sum of $6$ or when Bob rolls a sum of $7$, whichever comes first. A turn is when either Alice or Bob rolls. Find the expected number of turns in the game.
questions.solution: The expected duration of the game is dependent on what happens at the first roll of each player. Therefore, the approach is to apply Law of Total Expectation on the first roll of each player. Let N be the number of rolls played in the game. Let $X_A$ and $X_B$ be the first sum of Alice and Bob, respectively. There are three cases for the first roll of each player: = 6 X A =6 (Alice ends game on first roll), ≠ 6 X A  =6 and = 7 X B =7 (Bob ends game on his first roll), ≠ 6 X A  =6 and ≠ 7 X B  =7 (Both Bob and Alice don't reach their target on their first rolls). Call these three events , , A,B, and C. By conditioning on the first turn of both players, [ ] = [ ∣ ] [ ] + [ ∣ ] [ ] + [ ∣ ] [ ] E[N]=E[N∣A]P[A]+E[N∣B]P[B]+E[N∣C]P[C] If a sum of 6 6 occurs on the first roll, which occurs with probability 5 / 36 5/36 by a simple counting argument, the game ends in 1 1 turn, so [ ∣ ] = 1 E[N∣A]=1. questions.title: Tallest to Smallest
questions.problem: A teacher lines up $2n$ students of distinct heights in the following fashion: The two tallest students are placed in the $2$ center positions, and the heights of − 1 n−1 students to the left and − 1 n−1 students to the right of the two center students decrease outwards. How many arrangements of students are possible when $n = 5$?
questions.solution: To find the number of arrangements, two things must be done: The two center students must be arranged, and then we must select the subset of students to on the left and right of the center. There are 2 2 ways to arrange the center students. Afterwards, we can select any subset of size − 1 n−1 from the remaining 2 − 2 2n−2 students to go in the first − 1 n−1 positions. This can be done in ( 2 − 2 − 1 ) ( n−1 2n−2 ) ways. Once these students are selected, as they all have distinct heights, there is exactly 1 1 way to arrange them in descending heights outwards. Additionally, once the subset of students to go on the left is selected, the other − 1 n−1 remaining students must go on the right, and there is exactly one way to arrange them in a fashion that their heights decrease outwards. By the multiplication principle, the total number of arrangements is 2 ( 2 − 2 − 1 ) 2( n−1 2n−2 ) With = 5 n=5, the answer is 140 140.

questions.title: Million Product
questions.problem: Count the number of $12-$digit numbers which only contain prime digits such that the product of all digits is exactly $1,000,000$.
questions.solution: To find the digits that can be included, it's best to first consider the prime factorization of 1 , 000 , 000 = 10 6 = 2 6 ⋅ 5 6 1,000,000=10 6 =2 6 ⋅5 6 . Since there must be $6$ factors of each $2$ and $5$, this accounts for all $12$ of the possible digits in our number. Therefore, our number must consist of $6$ $2$s and $6$ $5$s, so the amount of numbers is equal to the number of ways to arrange $6$ $2$s and $6$ $5$s on $12$ blanks. Each one of these arrangements corresponds to a distinct value. Once the locations of the $2$s are selected, the $5$s fill the remaining $6$ spots. There are ( 12 6 ) = 924 ( 6 12 )=924 ways to pick the location of the $2$s, so this is the amount of numbers satisfying our condition by the above observation.

questions.title: Multi 66 I
questions.problem: Find the smallest multiple of $66$ that is at least $60,000$.
questions.solution: Since we have something that is roughly $1000$ times as large as $66$, a good starting place is $66 \cdot 1000 = 66000$. This is $6000$ over the threshold, so we can try removing another easy multiple of $66$. A simple one is $66 \cdot 100 = 6600$. Subtracting these, we get $66000 - 6600 = 59400$. We must be above $60000$, which is $600$ above $59400$. We see that $59400 + 9 \cdot 66 = 59994$, but $59400 + 66 \cdot 10 = 60060$ is larger than $60000$, so the answer is $60060$.

questions.title: Multi 66 II
questions.problem: Find the smallest multiple of $66$ that is at least $600,000$.

We must be above $600000$, which is $6000$ above $594000$. We know that $6600 = 66 \cdot 100$ is a valid multiple, so adding this, we get $594000 + 6600 = 600600$. We have to now subtract to get a smaller multiple of $66$. Note that $600600 - 66 \cdot 10 = 599940$, but $600600 - 66 \cdot 9 = 600006$, which is larger than $600000$, so the answer is $600006$.

questions.title: RPS Count
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play $10$ rounds of Rock (R) Paper (P) Scissors (S). It is known that each round had a winner. Bob played R, P, and S, respectively, $3,1,$ and $6$ times, while Alice played R, P, and S, respectively, $2,4,$ and $4$ times. How many wins did Bob have? If it is not possible to know the answer for sure, answer $-1$.
questions.solution: The key insight here is that if Bob plays S, Alice must have played either R or P to obtain a distinct winner. We can now determine how many wins Bob has from these rounds, as the sum of the sum of times that Alice played R and P equals the number of times that Bob played S. This implies that from the 6 6 times Bob played S, he would have 4 4 wins from the 4 4 times that Alice played P and 2 2 losses from the two times Alice played R. Afterwards, from the last 4 4 games, Alice played S 4 4 times, so she would have 3 3 losses from the three times that Bob played R, and 1 1 win from the time that Bob played P. Therefore, Bob has 4 4 wins from the rounds he played S and 3 3 wins from the 4 4 rounds he played P or R. Therefore, Bob has 7 7 total wins.

questions.title: Double Lily Pad

If a lake initially has $5$ lily pads in it, how many days must pass for the lily pads to cover a $5120$ square foot lake? Assume that the regions each lily pad covers are disjoint and fit to the shape of the pond.
questions.solution: We know that after $n$ days, the area of a given lily pad is $2^n$ , as it doubles in size each day for $n$ times. Since there are $5$ such lily pads, the total area covered by these lily pads after $n$ days is 5 ⋅ 2 5⋅2 n . We need to find the smallest integer $n$ such that 5 ⋅ 2 ≥ 5120 5⋅2 n ≥5120. This would be equivalent to finding the smallest $n$ such that 2 ≥ 1024 2 n ≥1024, which is $n = 10$. Therefore, after $10$ days, the entire area of the lake is covered by lily pads.
