questions.title: Prize Finder II
questions.problem: You have $n \geq 1$ boxes in front of you. A prize of $\$p$ is hidden in $1 \leq k \leq n$ of the boxes uniformly at random. You open boxes one-at-a-time until you find the prize. You are also required to pay a fee of $\$x$ to open each box. What value of $x$ makes the expected profit from opening these boxes $0$ when $n = 9, k = 2$ and $p = 50$?
questions.solution: As there is more than one box with a prize now, the argument from "Prize Finder I" will not work. You are looking for the expected number of boxes that need to be opened until one with a prize inside is opened, as this is directly related to the expected cost. The k boxes that have prizes inside can be treated as "dividers" of the sequence of opening. We want to do this because we are really sampling without replacement from the collection of boxes, which could really be seen as dealing without replacement from a deck of cards. In particular, we can take the approach of the "First Ace" problem in solving this. The k boxes with prize money are dividers, which means that there are − n−k boxes left that do not have dividers. The k boxes divide up the drawing process into + 1 k+1 regions of equal size in expectation by exchangeability, so there would be − + 1 k+1 n−k boxes per region, on average. Thus, in the region before the first box with a prize, there are − + 1 k+1 n−k boxes opened on average. After, we must add 1 1 for the box with the prize money itself to find the expected number of boxes that must be opened until the prize money is obtained. This implies there are + 1 + 1 k+1 n+1 boxes opened on average until the first box with a prize is opened. This means the expected cost of obtaining the prize money is + 1 + 1 k+1 n+1 x, as each box costs $ $x to open. The prize money is $ $p from opening the box. Therefore, for the expected profit to be 0 0, the expected cost must be equal to the prize, which means + 1 + 1 = k+1 n+1 x=p. By rearrangement, = ( + 1 ) + 1 x= n+1 (k+1)p . With the specified values, the answer is 15 15.

To count the number of ways to arrange the people in line, note that we are only identifying the people by whether or not they have a $\$5$ bill or a $ 10 $10 bill. Thus, we must pick the places of the n people in line with the $ 5 $5 bill. After this is done, the other n places in line must be the people with the $ 10 $10 bills. questions.title: Poweraid
questions.problem: Define the sets = { 1 , 3 , 5 , 7 , 9 } A={1,3,5,7,9} and = [ 4 ] = { 1 , 2 , … , 4 } B=[4n]={1,2,…,4n} for some positive integer $n$. Let $X$ be a uniformly random element from $A$ and $Y$ be a uniformly random element from $B$. Find the probability that ≡ 1 ( mod 10 ) X Y ≡1(mod10) when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: For each $x \in A$, there will be a different collection of integers in $B$ such that the condition is satisfied. For example, if $1$ is selected, then for any $y \in B$, 1 = 1 1 y =1, so this condition would be satisfied. However, if $5$ is selected, every power of $5$ also ends in $5$, so no integer from $B$ would satisfy this condition. Therefore, the best approach is to condition on the element from $A$ that is selected, and find which elements of $B$ would satisfy this condition for the selected element. Formalizing this, let $E$ be the event that ≡ 1 ( mod 10 ) X Y ≡1(mod10). We are going to condition on $X$, and find which $y \in B$ satisfy the condition. Namely, [ ] = [ ∣ = 1 ] [ = 1 ] + ⋯ + [ ∣ = 9 ] [ = 9 ] P[E]=P[E∣X=1]P[X=1]+⋯+P[E∣X=9]P[X=9] Since $X$ is selected uniformly at random from $A$, [ = 1 ] = ⋯ = [ = 9 ] = 1 / 5 P[X=1]=⋯=P[X=9]=1/5, as there are $5$ integers in $A$. To compute the conditionals, we must determine which integers in $B$ satisfy the condition. Since the element of $B$ is selected uniformly at random, we can just take the ratio of the number of integers in $B$ that satisfy the condition to the total number of integers in $B$ (which is $4n$) to compute the probability. If $X = 1$, then by the discussion above, all integers in $B$ satisfy the condition, so [ ∣ = 1 ] = 1 P[E∣X=1]=1. If $X = 5$, then none of the integers satisfy the condition, so [ ∣ = 5 ] = 0 P[E∣X=5]=0. If $X = 9$, we have to do a little experimentation to see which powers of $9$ will result in a ones digit of $1$. The first few powers of $9$ are $9, 81, 729,$ and $6561$. This makes us conjecture that even powers of $9$ will result in a $1$. This can be verified: If $n$ is even, then $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Then we have that, in mod $10$, 9 = 9 2 = ( 9 2 ) = 81 = ≡ 1 = 1 9 n =9 2k =(9 2 ) k =81 k =≡1 k =1. Therefore, all even integers make the power of $9$ end in $1$. This is exactly $1/2$ of all of the integers in $[4n]$, so [ ∣ = 9 ] = 1 / 2 P[E∣X=9]=1/2. If $X = 3$, we note that 3 2 = 9 3 2 =9, and even powers of $9$ end in a $1$. Thus, 9 2 9 2k ends in $1$ for integers $k$. Since 9 = 3 2 9=3 2 , this implies that ( 3 2 ) 2 = 3 4 (3 2 ) 2k =3 4k ends in $1$ for all integers $k$. Therefore, all multiples of $4$ in $[4n]$ will satisfy this condition for $3$. This is exactly $1/4$ of the total integers, so [ ∣ = 3 ] = 1 / 4 P[E∣X=3]=1/4. If $X = 7$, we have something similar: 7 2 = 49 7 2 =49, which ends in $9$, so the same exact argument above holds! Therefore, [ ∣ = 7 ] = 1 / 4 P[E∣X=7]=1/4. Plugging all of these in, we get that [ ] = 1 5 [ 1 + 1 4 + 0 + 1 4 + 1 2 ] = 2 5 P[E]= 5 1 [1+ 4 1 +0+ 4 1 + 2 1 ]= 5 2 This result is independent of n.

Since we are looking to count the expected number of some event that occurs and the events are not independent, counting with indicators is the best tool. Let $M_i$ be the indicator of the event that the ith entry in the permutation, $1 \leq i \leq n$, is a local maxima. = 1 + ⋯ + T=M 1 +⋯+M n gives the total number of local maxima. Note that 2 , 3 , … , − 1 M 2 ,M 3 ,…,M n−1 are exchangeable, and therefore identically distributed, as each of the interior terms have two neighbors. However, $M_1$ and $M_n$ only have one neighbor, so these two are identically distributed, but not the same distribution as the other − 2 n−2 spots. Random variables with the same distribution have the same mean, so via linearity of expectation, [ ] = ( − 2 ) [ 2 ] + 2 [ 1 ] E[T]=(n−2)E[M 2 ]+2E[M 1 ] [ 1 ] E[M 1 ] is just the probability that the entry in the first spot is larger than that of the second spot. Since all permutations are equally likely and all the values are distinct, each of the two spots are equally likely to be the larger one, so the probability is just [ 1 ] = 1 / 2 E[M 1 ]=1/2. [ 2 ] E[M 2 ] is the probability that 2 M 2 is a local maxima i.e. that it is the largest among 1 , 2 , M 1 ,M 2 , and 3 M 3 . Once again, since each permutation is equally likely, the maximum among these three random variables is equally likely to be in any of the three spots, so [ 2 ] = 1 / 3 E[M 2 ]=1/3, as there is a 1 1 in 3 3 chance that 2 M 2 is the maxima of the 3 3 above random variables. Therefore, [ ] = − 2 3 + 1 E[T]= 3 n−2 +1. With the specified values, the answer is 7 7.

questions.title: Hearty Variance
questions.problem: A hand of $n$ cards is dealt from a standard card deck. Find the variance of the number of hearts that are in the hand when $n = 26$.
questions.solution: Let $T$ be the total number of cards in the hand that are hearts. For each card in the hand, it either is or is not a heart. Therefore, we can count $T$ by counting $1$ per heart in the hand and $0$ if the card is not a heart. In other words, arbitrarily label the cards in your hand 1 − 1−n, and for $1 \leq i \leq n$, let $H_i$ be the indicator that card $i$ in your hand is a heart. Then = 1 + ⋯ + T=H 1 +⋯+H n gives the total number of hearts that are in hand. The $H_i$ random variables are not independent, as if we know the first card is a heart, this information decreases the probability that each of the remaining cards are hearts. Therefore, the variance of a sum formula is most appropriate. Applying this formula, we get Var ( ) = Var ( 1 + ⋯ + ) = ∑ = 1 Var ( ) + ∑ ≠ Cov ( , ) Var(T)=Var(H 1 +⋯+H n )= i=1 ∑ n Var(H i )+ i  =j ∑ Cov(H i ,H j ) Since the labels 1 − 1−n were assigned to the cards arbitrarily, the random variables 1 , … , H 1 ,…,H n are exchangeable, which implies they have the same distribution (and hence mean/covariance/covariances). Therefore, we can claim Var ( ) = Var ( 1 ) Var(H i )=Var(H 1 ) and Cov ( , ) = Cov ( 1 , 2 ) Cov(H i ,H j )=Cov(H 1 ,H 2 ) for all ≠ i  =j. Plugging these in, we obtain Var ( ) = Var ( 1 ) + ( − 1 ) Cov ( 1 , 2 ) Var(T)=nVar(H 1 )+n(n−1)Cov(H 1 ,H 2 ) The term ( − 1 ) n(n−1) arises from the fact that there are 2 n 2 total pairs of random variables H i and H j for 1 ≤ , ≤ 1≤i,j≤n, and the first sum contains n of those pairs where = i=j, so there must be ( − 1 ) n(n−1) pairs remaining where ≠ i  =j. All that remains is to compute each of these quantities. Since 1 H 1 is an indicator of the event that the first card is a heart, and each of the 4 4 suits is equally likely to appear for this draw, 1 ∼ Bernoulli ( 1 / 4 ) H 1 ∼Bernoulli(1/4), as 1 = 1 H 1 =1 with probability 1 / 4 1/4 and 0 0 otherwise. Thus, Var ( 1 ) = 1 / 4 ⋅ ( 1 − 1 / 4 ) = 3 / 16 Var(H 1 )=1/4⋅(1−1/4)=3/16. To compute Cov ( 1 , 2 ) Cov(H 1 ,H 2 ), we use the expansion of covariance to obtain Cov ( 1 , 2 ) = [ 1 2 ] − [ 1 ] [ 2 ] Cov(H 1 ,H 2 )=E[H 1 H 2 ]−E[H 1 ]E[H 2 ]. Since 1 H 1 and 2 H 2 are exchangeable, they have the same mean of [ 1 ] = 1 / 4 E[H 1 ]=1/4 from the known distribution of 1 H 1 . [ 1 2 ] E[H 1 H 2 ] is equal to the probability that 1 = 2 = 1 H 1 =H 2 =1, which is exactly that both of the first two cards are hearts. The probability that the first card is hearts is 1 / 4 1/4 from previous work. Given that the first card was a heart, the probability that the second cards is also a heart is 12 / 51 12/51, as there are 12 12 hearts that remain in the other 51 51 cards, so [ 1 2 ] = 1 / 4 ⋅ 4 / 17 = 1 / 17 E[H 1 H 2 ]=1/4⋅4/17=1/17. Plugging this in, we get Cov ( 1 , 2 ) = 1 / 17 − 1 / 16 = − 1 / 272 Cov(H 1 ,H 2 )=1/17−1/16=−1/272, Therefore, Var ( ) = 3 16 − 1 272 ( − 1 ) = ( 52 − ) 272 Var(T)= 16 3 n− 272 1 n(n−1)= 272 n(52−n) This result makes a lot of intuitive sense, as when = 0 n=0, there are always going to be no hearts, so the variance is 0 0. Similarly, when = 52 n=52, you have drawn the entire deck, so you will have always 13 13 hearts, meaning there is also 0 0 variance. Furthermore, this function is symmetric about = 26 n=26, which makes sense, as if you draw a hand of k cards, you are implicitly also leaving a hand of 52 − 52−k cards left in the deck that you did not select. Thus, you could create a hand of size k by either picking k cards and taking those or by picking 52 − 52−k cards to discard. Both methodologies should yield the same variance, as they both yield a hand of size k, and they do. With the specified value, the answer is 169 68 68 169 .

questions.title: Shuffle Up I
questions.problem: The numbers in the string $1234$ are shuffled uniformly at random. Let $p_i$ be the probability that exactly $i$ of the characters are out of place. For example, $3241$ has $3$ characters out of place. Find ∑ = 0 4 2 ∑ i=0 4 p i 2 .
questions.solution: Since all $4! = 24$ permutations of the string are equally likely, we only must count the number of permutations where exactly $0 \leq i \leq 4$ of the values are out of order. $p_0$ is just the probability that none of the characters are out of order i.e. all are in the correct spots. This just means that the string is correct. There is only $1$ such correct string, which is the original string $1234$, so 0 = 1 / 24 p 0 =1/24. For $p_1$ , note that it is impossible for exactly one element to be out of place, as if one element is out of place, it takes up the spot of a different element, so that other element also can't be in the correct spot. This implies 1 = 0 p 1 =0. $p_2$ is the probability that exactly $2$ characters are out of place. For this to occur, this means that two of the $4$ elements are in their correct place, and two of the elements were swapped in locations. For example, $3214$ is obtained by swapping $1$ and $3$. All outcomes with exactly $2$ characters out of place are generated by swapping two elements, so the number of outcomes satisfying this is just equal to the number of ways to select $2$ elements to swap, which is ( 4 2 ) = 6 ( 2 4 )=6. Thus, 2 = 6 / 24 = 1 / 4 p 2 =6/24=1/4. $p_3$ is the probability that there are exactly $3$ characters out of place. For this to be true, there must be exactly one character fixed in place. Afterwards, none of the remaining $3$ character can go into their original locations. There are $4$ ways to pick the character that is fixed. Afterwards, suppose that $abc$ are the three characters that are being permuted to different locations, with this as their original relative order. By writing out the $3! = 6$ permutations of these values, one can see that $2$ of these $6$ arrangements have no characters in their original spots, so there must be $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ ways to permute the characters such that $3$ of them differ in their location. Thus, 3 = 8 / 24 = 1 / 3 p 3 =8/24=1/3. Lastly, as ∑ = 0 4 = 1 i=0 ∑ 4 p i =1 by the fact that the only possibilities are that there are $0,1,2,3,$ or $4$ characters out of place, 4 = 1 − ∑ = 0 3 = 1 − 1 / 24 − 6 / 24 − 8 / 24 = 9 / 24 = 3 / 8 p 4 =1− i=0 ∑ 3 p i =1−1/24−6/24−8/24=9/24=3/8. The answer is ∑ = 0 4 2 = 1 2 + 6 2 + 8 2 + 9 2 24 2 = 91 288 i=0 ∑ 4 p i 2 = 24 2 1 2 +6 2 +8 2 +9 2 = 288 91

questions.title: Shuffle Up II
questions.problem: The numbers in the string $1234$ are shuffled uniformly at random. Given that the shuffled string is not $1234$, find the expected number of transpositions that need to be performed to make the permuted string the original string. For example, $3241 \rightarrow 1243 \rightarrow 1234$ can be transformed into the original string in two transpositions. Note that the transpositions do not need to be between adjacent entries in the string and that you take the most efficient sequence of transpositions to obtain $1234$.
questions.solution: To find the expected number of transpositions, it would be easier if we knew how many characters of the string were out of place. This is because the number of transpositions needed is dependent on how many characters are out of place. For example, if there are only 2 2 characters out of place, then only one transposition is needed, but if there are more characters out of place, there are more transpositions that are needed. Let O be the random variable representing the number of characters out of place given that the string is not 1234 1234. This restricts us to 23 23 strings. However, each of those strings are equally likely, and the counts are the same as in "Shuffle Up I", so [ = 1 ] = 0 , [ = 2 ] = 6 / 23 , [ = 3 ] = 8 / 23 , P[O=1]=0,P[O=2]=6/23,P[O=3]=8/23, and [ = 4 ] = 9 / 23 P[O=4]=9/23. Similarly, let T be the number of transpositions needed to obtain the original string. By performing the conditioning from above, [ ] = [ [ ∣ ] ] = ∑ = 1 4 [ ∣ = ] [ = ] E[T]=E[E[T∣O]]= i=1 ∑ 4 E[T∣O=i]P[O=i] We know from above that [ = 1 ] = 0 P[O=1]=0, so this term can be eliminated immediately. If = 2 O=2, then exactly 1 1 transposition is needed, as you just swap the two terms that are out of order. Therefore, [ ∣ = 2 ] = 1 E[T∣O=2]=1 and [ = 2 ] = 6 / 23 P[O=2]=6/23. Similarly, if = 3 O=3, then 3 3 of the letters are out place. It can quickly be seen that you need 2 2 moves to shuffle them back into the original arrangement, so [ ∣ = 3 ] = 2 E[T∣O=3]=2 and [ = 3 ] = 8 / 23 P[O=3]=8/23. The last case is when all 4 4 characters are out of place. However, one can quickly see that there are two sub-cases to consider here. Some of the outcomes with all 4 4 characters that are out of place consists of two swaps i.e. just switching around two pairs, while others need 3 3 transpositions. An example of the first kind is 3412 3412, as you can swap 1 1 and 3 3, as well as 2 2 and 4 4, to get back to the original arrangement. An example of the second kind is 3421 3421, as the sequence is 3421 → 1423 → 1243 → 1234 3421→1423→1243→1234. The second type always takes 3 3 transpositions, as we are always able to ensure one of the characters lands in the right position per turn. We know that there are 9 9 total outcomes with all 4 4 characters out of place, so we must determine how many of these 9 9 belong to each case. To obtain an outcome of the first kind, we must pick two pairs of elements to swap around. There are ( 4 2 ) = 6 ( 2 4 )=6 ways to pick a single pair to swap around. Once we pick the first pair, we also automatically pick the second pair to swap. For example, if we selected ( 1 , 3 ) (1,3) to swap, then the other pair that we swap is ( 2 , 4 ) (2,4). However, this exact sequence of swaps also could have been created by selecting ( 2 , 4 ) (2,4) to swap, and this would inadvertently also swap ( 1 , 3 ) (1,3). questions.title: Group Formation II
questions.problem: There are $n$ people in a class that have to make groups for a project. To do this, they each are assigned a label $1$ to $n$. Each person writes their label on a slip of paper, and all the pieces of paper are thrown into a bowl. One by one, each guest picks a name from the bowl. Each guest will be a part of a group with the guest they pulled the name out of from the bowl. If a guest pulls out their own name, they are in a group all by themselves. If Guest A pulls out Guest B's name, Guest B pulls out Guest C's name, and Guest C pulls out Guest A's name, they are all a part of the same closed group and no one else will be able to join them. What is the average size of a group when = 100 n=100? Round your answer to the nearest hundredth.
questions.solution: Drawing the numbers out of the bowl can be viewed as a random permutation of the labels. A group of people would be a cycle in this permutation, so this question is really asking for the expected size of a cycle in a uniformly random permutation of length n. From "Group Formation I", we know that there are an average of ∑ = 1 1 i=1 ∑ n i 1 cycles in the permutation. The expected length of the cycle is just the average number of elements in a cycle. Therefore, as there are n elements, the average number of elements per cycle is just ∑ = 1 1 / ∑ i=1 n 1/i n , the total number of elements divided by the expected number of cycles. This is because no cycle is any more/less likely to be larger/smaller than any other cycle. With = 100 n=100, the answer is approximately 19.28 19.28.

questions.problem: You flip a coin with probability $1/2 < p < 1$ of heads repetitively until the running total number of heads equals the running total number of tails. Find the probability that you ever stop flipping when $p = 3/4$.
questions.solution: Instead of viewing this as coin flips, it's easier to visualize what is occurring by framing it as a random walk of some particle. This is a natural choice, as random walks are often represented by random choice of direction, and we can map the two directions to the two outcomes of a coin. A heads will represent one movement to the right, while a tails will represent one movement to the left. An equal amount of heads and tails at some point would then visually represent the particle returning to the origin. Condition on the direction of the first movement, as the particle will need to move the opposite direction to return to the origin. Let 1 H 1 and 1 T 1 be the events that the particle moves right/left on the first turn (obtains head/tails) and R be the event of a return to the origin. We have that [ ] = [ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] + [ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] P[R]=P[R∣H 1 ]P[H 1 ]+P[R∣T 1 ]P[T 1 ]. As per the question, we know [ 1 ] = P[H 1 ]=p and [ 1 ] = 1 − P[T 1 ]=1−p. Now, we need to compute the conditional probabilities. For both [ ∣ 1 ] P[R∣H 1 ] and [ ∣ 1 ] P[R∣T 1 ], we need to compute the probability that the particle returns to the origin when it has some probability, say r, of moving in the direction of the origin, and probability 1 − 1−r of moving away from the origin. Thus, we will compute α r , the probability of returning to the origin from 1 1 step away when there is a probability 0 < < 1 0<r<1 of moving in the direction towards the origin and probability 1 − 1−r of moving away from the origin at each step. We would then have [ ∣ 1 ] = 1 − P[R∣H 1 ]=α 1−p , as the particle moves right at the first step, so it would need to move left to reach the origin, which occurs with probability 1 − 1−p per trial. By similar logic, [ ∣ 1 ] = P[R∣T 1 ]=α p , as the particle needs to move right to reach the origin. To compute α r , we should condition on what happens in the first step. This is because of the fact that if the particle moves 1 1 unit towards the origin at the first step, it already reaches the origin. Otherwise, it is now 2 2 steps away from the origin, which isn't the same probability, so we should condition on which direction the particle moves from the 1 1 step away position. If the particle moves towards the origin, which occurs with probability r by definition, then the origin is reached. Otherwise, with probability 1 − 1−r, the particle moves in the direction opposite of the origin, so it is now 2 2 units away. For the particle to reach the origin from 2 2 units away, the particle must eventually reach the state 1 1 unit away from the origin, and then eventually reach the origin from there. The problem of reaching the state 1 1 unit away from the origin from the one that is 2 2 units away is exactly the same as the original problem, except everything is shifted by 1 1 unit. This is a natural choice, as random walks are often represented by random choice of direction, and we can map the two directions to the two outcomes of a coin. A heads will represent one movement to the right, while a tails will represent one movement to the left. An equal amount of heads and tails at some point would then visually represent the particle returning to the origin. Condition on the direction of the first movement, as the particle will need to move the opposite direction to return to the origin. Let 1 H 1 and 1 T 1 be the events that the particle moves right/left on the first turn (obtains head/tails) and R be the event of a return to the origin. We have that [ ] = [ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] + [ ∣ 1 ] [ 1 ] P[R]=P[R∣H 1 ]P[H 1 ]+P[R∣T 1 ]P[T 1 ]. As per the question, we know [ 1 ] = P[H 1 ]=p and [ 1 ] = 1 − P[T 1 ]=1−p. Now, we need to compute the conditional probabilities. For both [ ∣ 1 ] P[R∣H 1 ] and [ ∣ 1 ] P[R∣T 1 ], we need to compute the probability that the particle returns to the origin when it has some probability, say r, of moving in the direction of the origin, and probability 1 − 1−r of moving away from the origin. Thus, we will compute α r , the probability of returning to the origin from 1 1 step away when there is a probability 0 < < 1 0<r<1 of moving in the direction towards the origin and probability 1 − 1−r of moving away from the origin at each step. We would then have [ ∣ 1 ] = 1 − P[R∣H 1 ]=α 1−p , as the particle moves right at the first step, so it would need to move left to reach the origin, which occurs with probability 1 − 1−p per trial. By similar logic, [ ∣ 1 ] = P[R∣T 1 ]=α p , as the particle needs to move right to reach the origin. To compute α r , we should condition on what happens in the first step. This is because of the fact that if the particle moves 1 1 unit towards the origin at the first step, it already reaches the origin. Otherwise, it is now 2 2 steps away from the origin, which isn't the same probability, so we should condition on which direction the particle moves from the 1 1 step away position. If the particle moves towards the origin, which occurs with probability r by definition, then the origin is reached. Otherwise, with probability 1 − 1−r, the particle moves in the direction opposite of the origin, so it is now 2 2 units away. For the particle to reach the origin from 2 2 units away, the particle must eventually reach the state 1 1 unit away from the origin, and then eventually reach the origin from there. The problem of reaching the state 1 1 unit away from the origin from the one that is 2 2 units away is exactly the same as the original problem, except everything is shifted by 1 1 unit. The probability of this is just α r as well. Then, once the particle hits the state 1 1 unit away from the origin, there is probability α r by definition that it hits the origin. By the Strong Markov Property (or intuitively reasoning that the hitting of the two states deal with independent sequences of coin flips), these are independent, so there is a probability 2 α r 2 of hitting the origin given that the particle moves away at the first step. By the Law of Total Probability, we have obtained = + ( 1 − ) 2 α r =r+(1−r)α r 2 . Rearranging this, we obtain a quadratic equation in α r given by ( 1 − ) 2 − + = 0 (1−r)α r 2 −α r +r=0. Therefore, we have that [ ∣ 1 ] = 1 − = 1 P[R∣H 1 ]=α 1−p =1, while [ ∣ 1 ] = = 1 − P[R∣T 1 ]=α p = 1−p p . Plugging these into the Law of Total Probability expression from the beginning, we get [ ] = 1 ⋅ + 1 − ⋅ ( 1 − ) = 2 P[R]=1⋅p+ 1−p p ⋅(1−p)=2p This result makes a lot of sense. questions.title: Generous Friend II
questions.problem: You and a rich friend play the following game: Each of you will select a positive integer according to any strategy of your respective choices. If you both select the same value n, you receive $ 2 $n 2 from your friend. Under an optimal strategy from both you and your friend, what is your expected payout to the nearest thousandth?
questions.solution: Consider this game on the finite set [ ] = { 1 , 2 , … , } [N]={1,2,…,N}. An initial strategy from each player could be to select a deterministic value $1 \leq i \leq N$. However, this is not optimal from each player, as you could just select $N$ every time and increase your expected value, while your friend could just select $1$ every time and decrease your expected value, so both players can do better. As this holds for all $N$, no type of "uniform" distribution on the positive integers will be optimal. The goal is to find some probability distribution on the positive integers such that you select $i \geq 1$ with probability $p_i$ . To do this, we should use the indifference principle. This idea states that in an optimal strategy, you should be indifferent to what your friend chooses. In other words, no matter what your friend selects as their number, your payout remains constant. The expected payout contributed by term k is just 2 k 2 p k , as you receive a payout of 2 k 2 with probability p k . Thus, the optimal strategy will have that 1 2 1 = 2 2 2 = ⋯ = 2 = ⋯ ⟺ = 1 2 1 1 2 p 1 =2 2 p 2 =⋯=k 2 p k =⋯⟺p k = k 2 1 p 1 However, we also must have that ∑ = 1 ∞ = 1 ⟺ 1 ∑ = 1 ∞ 1 2 = 1 ⟺ 1 = 6 2 k=1 ∑ ∞ p k =1⟺p 1 k=1 ∑ ∞ k 2 1 =1⟺p 1 = π 2 6 We use the known sum ∑ = 1 ∞ 1 2 = 2 6 k=1 ∑ ∞ k 2 1 = 6 π 2 Therefore, we have that = 1 2 1 = 6 2 2 p k = k 2 1 p 1 = π 2 k 2 6 for any ≥ 1 k≥1. This distribution is typically known as the Zeta ( 2 ) Zeta(2) distribution. In other words, the optimal strategy for both you and your friend is to select your values independently from a Zeta ( 2 ) Zeta(2) distribution. The expected payout would therefore be 6 2 π 2 6 , as this is the expected payout, regardless of the choice of your friend, for each ≥ 1 k≥1, so averaging all of these together gives the same value.

questions.problem: Alice and Bob have fair standard − n−sided and − m−sided dice, respectively, where $n \geq m$. Bob is allowed to roll his die twice and keep the maximum value, while Alice can only roll her die once. Find the probability that Alice rolls a strictly higher value than Bob on her die when $m = 15$ and $n = 20$.
questions.solution: Since $n \geq m$, we know that Alice has a higher potential ceiling of values that she can roll than Bob. Note that if Alice rolls a value that is strictly larger than m, she automatically has the higher value, as Bob can't roll higher than m. The probability she rolls a value that is at most m is $m/n$, as this accounts for $m$ of the $n$ equally likely sides. This implies that the probability she rolls a strictly larger value than $m$ is 1 − / 1−m/n. Otherwise, if she rolls a value at most $m$, there is positive probability that she can lose. She wins exactly when both of Bob's die rolls are strictly less than hers. In other words, the maximum of them is strictly less than hers. If we knew Alice's roll, this would be an easy item to compute, so the best approach is to condition on Alice's roll. Formalizing the above, let A be the event that Alice rolls a strictly larger value than Bob, and X be the value of Alice's roll. The probability of this per roll is − 1 m k−1 , as there are − 1 k−1 positive integers at most − 1 k−1 out of m total values on the die. Thus, as he rolls twice, the probability that both are at most − 1 k−1 is [ ∣ = ] = ( − 1 ) 2 P[A∣X=k]=( m k−1 ) 2 . questions.title: Maxidice II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob have fair standard − n−sided and − m−sided dice, respectively, where $n \geq m$. If it exists, compute lim ⁡ → ∞ r→∞ lim p r when $m = 15$ and $n = 20$.
questions.solution: This probability could be computed explicitly, but it's must better to think about this question on an intuitive level. As $r \rightarrow \infty$, it becomes more and more likely that Bob will roll at least one very high value for his die in the $r$ rolls. In fact, it becomes essentially guaranteed for very large $r$ that Bob will roll the value $m$ at some point in the $r$ rolls. As Alice needs to roll a strictly larger value than Bob, the only way to do this for large $r$ is for her to obtain a value larger than $m$ on her die, so that no matter what Bob rolls, he will never be able to break above the threshold of his die. The probability of Alice rolling a strictly larger value than m is 1 − 1− n m , as found in "Maxidice I", so lim ⁡ → ∞ = 1 − r→∞ lim p r =1− n m . By an extremely similar process to the one from "Maxidice I", one can explicitly show = 1 − + 1 ∑ = 1 ( − 1 ) p r =1− n m + n 1 k=1 ∑ m ( m k−1 ) r The only difference is that there are now r dice that need to be at most − 1 k−1 in value instead of 2 2, so the power changes. However, as m and n are fixed and − 1 < 1 m k−1 <1 for all 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤k≤m, as → ∞ r→∞, the terms on the interior of the summation tend to 0 0, as the common ratio − 1 < 1 m k−1 <1. Thus, the terms of the sum all tend to 0 0, meaning that the 1 − 1− n m term is all that remains. With the specified values, the answer is 1 / 4 1/4.

questions.title: Bertrand's Paradox III
questions.problem: A random chord is formed by selecting a uniformly random point $X$ from the interior of the unit circle that represents the other endpoint of a line segment extending from the circle's center to that point. Then, the chord whose midpoint is X and is perpendicular to the line segment with endpoints $(0,0)$ and $X$ is drawn. You may assume that there is only one such chord. Find the probability that this chord has length at least 3 3 .
questions.solution: We can view this question in the same light as "Bertrand's Paradox II", as we created the line segment in that problem by selecting a uniform direction and then a uniformly random distance from the origin in the selected direction. In this problem, we are just choosing a uniformly random point on the interior. If R represents the distance from the origin of the selected point, then we still want to compute [ ≤ 1 / 2 ] P[R≤1/2]. However, now, the event { ≤ 1 / 2 } {R≤1/2} represents a circle in the plane with radius 1 / 2 1/2 centered at the origin, as this is the set of all points of distance at most 1 / 2 1/2 away from the origin. Since the point X is selected uniformly at random from the interior of the circle, we can take ratios of areas to compute probabilities. The total area of the support is π, while the area of the event { ≤ 1 / 2 } {R≤1/2} is ⋅ ( 1 / 2 ) 2 = 4 π⋅(1/2) 2 = 4 π . Therefore, the probability that the chord is length at least 3 3 is 1 / 4 1/4. The three parts of this problem show that "random chord" needs to be defined carefully in the context of the problem, as different interpretations that all appear valid yield different answers!

questions.title: Coprime Fraction
questions.problem: Find the number of rational numbers b a such that $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime integers and $ab = 25!$.
questions.solution: For $a$ and $b$ to be relatively prime, their prime factorizations must not contain any primes in common. If they had a prime in common, then they would not be relatively prime. The possible primes in the prime factorization of $25!$ are just the primes that are less than $25$, which are: $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,$ and $23$. Since the product of $a$ and $b$ must be $25!$, we must assign the maximal power of each prime to exactly one of $a$ or $b$. This means, for example, that if the exponent of $2$ is $p_2$ in the prime factorization of $25!$, then $2^{p_2}$ must be in the prime factorization of exactly one of $a$ or $b$. Note that we need the exponent that is assigned to $a$ and $b$ to be maximal so that $a$ and $b$ are relatively prime. Otherwise, for example, if we assigned 2 2 − 1 2 p 2 −1 to $a$, we would have to assign a factor of $2$ to $b$ so that the product will be the same as what is in $25!$. However, $a$ and $b$ would no longer be relatively prime, as $2$ would divide both $a$ and $b$. Therefore, creating a fraction is really equivalent to just assigning each prime factor to one of $a$ or $b$. Since there are $2$ options for each of the $9$ prime factors, there are 2 9 = 512 2 9 =512 ways to assign the primes to either $a$ or $b$, so there are $512$ such fractions. Note that integers are rational numbers, so we don't need to worry about the case when $b = 1$. In general, if ( ) $\pi(n)$ represents the number of prime integers that are at most $n$, there would be 2 ( ) 2 π(n) ways to create such a fraction.

Since the walk is symmetric, with probability $1/2$ each, the particle moves one closer or one further from the line. This idea holds at every step, so we can frame this as a SSRW on the integers. The discussion below concerns the computation of expected hitting time of $1$ from $0$ in the random walk on the integers when there is probability $0 < p < 1$ of moving right for $p \geq 1/2$. \nl Let $T_i$ be the amount of steps needed to go from position $i$ to $i+1$. questions.title: Most Likely Odd
questions.problem: You repeatedly roll a fair standard − n−sided die until the cumulative sum of all observed upfaces is odd. What is the most likely sum to stop on when $n = 20$?
questions.solution: The most likely value needs to be accessible from the most possible ways in the fewest number of rolls. We need the fewest number of rolls condition because the die only has a certain probability of showing each side, so every additional roll that needs to be performed significantly reduces the probability of that cumulative sum appearing. The fewest number of rolls is 1 1, so this restricts our candidates to all the odd integers at most n. Let the largest odd integer at most n be denoted ∗ n ∗ . Any sequence of rolls that stops at a cumulative sum of k, where < ∗ k<n ∗ , has some amount of evens before it. For example, consider a standard 6 − 6−sided die. To stop at 1 1, 1 1 must be rolled on the first turn. In this case, ∗ = 5 n ∗ =5 can also be obtained on the first roll, so the probability of stopping on 5 5 must be at least as large as stopping on 1 1. To stop on 3 3, you either roll 3 3 on the first turn or roll 2 2 then 1 1. However, 4 4 then 1 1, which is equally probable to 2 2 then 1 1, results in a sum of 5 5 as well. Therefore, all the paths that lead to a cumulative sum of 3 3 have equivalents that lead to a cumulative sum of 5 5, so stopping on 5 5 must be at least as probability as stopping on 3 3. Lastly, 5 5 has additional sequences that lead to it, such as 2 2 then 3 3, which aren't encapsulated by the smaller values, so it must have strictly larger probability. This same idea generalizes: All paths that lead to stopping at a sum < ∗ k<n ∗ have equivalents that stop at ∗ n ∗ , with ∗ n ∗ having additional sequences that aren't equivalent to paths for any smaller odd value. Therefore, ∗ n ∗ , the largest odd integer at most n, is the most likely value to stop at. With = 20 n=20, the answer is 19 19.

questions.title: Cubic Ant III
questions.problem: A spider and an ant start at the opposing corners of a cube. Every minute, the spider and ant choose one of the three possible directions independently and uniformly at random to move in. Afterwards, they travel simultaneously. The spider catches the ant if they move along the same edge while travelling at the end of the minute. Find the expected number of minutes until the spider catches the ant.
questions.solution: The ant and the spider start a distance $3$ away from one another. Since they both move at each step, they can only ever be a distance of $3$ or $1$ away from one another. The expected amount of time until the spider catches the ant is dependent on how far away the spider is from the ant, so set up a $2-$state Markov chain. By the symmetry of the cube, the expected time for the spider and ant travel down the same edge is the same no matter which opposing edges they start it. WLOG, assume the ant and spider start at $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,1)$, respectively. Let $E_3$ and $E_1$ be the expected time for the ant and spider to intersect if they are current $3$ and $1$ units away from each other, respectively. The spider and ant are one unit away from each other if two of their coordinates are the same. By the symmetry of the cube and the movements being equally likely in any direction, the distribution of the distance of the ant and spider is the same, regardless of which movement the spider makes. WLOG, suppose the spider moves down to ( 1 , 1 , 0 ) (1,1,0) on the first turn. If the ant moves in the + +x or + +y directions to either ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) (1,0,0) or ( 0 , 1 , 0 ) (0,1,0), which occurs with probability 2 / 3 2/3, they are distance 1 1 away from each other. On average, an additional 1 E 1 minutes will pass before they intersect. Otherwise, if the ant moves upwards to ( 0 , 0 , 1 ) (0,0,1), which occurs with probability 1 / 3 1/3, the ant and spider are on opposite corners of the cube again, which means an additional 3 E 3 minutes will pass on average before intersecting. Therefore, we have the equation 3 = 1 + 1 3 3 + 2 3 1 E 3 =1+ 3 1 E 3 + 3 2 E 1 The additional 1 1 comes from the fact that 1 1 minute passed in the spider and ant moving. Now, we must derive a recurrence for 1 E 1 . If the ant and spider are 1 1 unit away from one another, they intersect exactly when they both choose to travel down the same segment. By the symmetry of the cube, the exact segment is irrelevant, so suppose the ant and spider are at ( 0 , 0 , 0 ) (0,0,0) and ( 0 , 0 , 1 ) (0,0,1), respectively. They choose to travel down the same segment with probability 1 / 9 1/9, for which 0 0 additional minutes would be needed. Otherwise, if the spider moves down and the ant moves in the + +x or + +y directions, the spider and ant still lie a distance 1 1 away from each other, meaning an additional 1 E 1 steps are needed. This occurs with probability 2 / 9 2/9, as the spider moves downwards with probability 1 / 3 1/3 and the ant moves in the + +x or + +y directions with probability 2 / 3 2/3. If the spider doesn't move downwards, the + +x and + +y movements for the spider are symmetry, so we can consider one of them only. Suppose the spider moves in the + +x direction to ( 1 , 0 , 1 ) (1,0,1). If the ant moves up or in the + +x direction to ( 0 , 0 , 1 ) (0,0,1) or ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) (1,0,0), they are separated by 1 1 unit, meaning an additional 1 E 1 minutes are needed on average. Otherwise, if the ant moves to ( 0 , 1 , 0 ) (0,1,0), they are on opposite sides of the cube, meaning 3 E 3 minutes more are needed on average. Therefore, 1 = 1 + 1 9 ( 0 ) + 2 9 3 + 2 3 1 = 1 + 2 9 3 + 2 3 1 E 1 =1+ 9 1 (0)+ 9 2 E 3 + 3 2 E 1 =1+ 9 2 E 3 + 3 2 E 1 We now have a system of two equations to solve for 1 E 1 and 3 E 3 . We want 3 E 3 , as the ant and spider initially start 3 3 units away from one another. One finds that 3 = 27 / 2 E 3 =27/2 after some basic algebraic work on the system.

questions.title: Die Duo II
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. Your friend's die has the values $111666$ on the sides. You get to select the sides of your own die under the following conditions: All values must be between $1$ and $6$, inclusive of both, and they must sum to $21$. An example would be $223455$. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to simultaneously maximize your winning probability and minimize your friend's winning probability? Enter the die's values in non-decreasing order from left to right.
questions.solution: Since there are no values strictly larger than $6$, the largest possible probability of winning is $1/2$, as you could have a die that has values all strictly larger than $1$, so you win guaranteed whenever your friend obtains a $1$. However, we also want to minimize the probability that your friend wins. For this to occur, we need to have as many values that are $6$ as possible and all sides are at least $2$. We can do better than one $6$, as a sum of $15$ still remains for the other $5$ sides of the dice. With two values of $6$, the remaining $4$ sides must sum to $9$. The only way to do this with all sides being strictly larger than $1$ is $2223$. Therefore, $222366$ is a good candidate. We can't use $3$ values as $6$, as the remaining three sides would be $111$, violating our other condition that all values must be strictly larger than $1$. Therefore, $222366$ is the optimal response.

questions.title: Die Duo III
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Your friend has a standard fair die. You get to select the sides of your own die under the following conditions: All values must be between $1$ and $6$, inclusive of both, and the die must have mean $7/2$. You may choose both the probabilities and the values on the die. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to maximize your winning probability? Enter the optimal winning probability.
questions.solution: Since your friend's die is unbiased in the sense that all values appear with equal probability, it has no particular weakness to exploit. If your values are biased with a lot of high values, you must also have lower numbers on your die so that the mean is 3.5 3.5. Therefore, those lower values will fare poorly against your opponents die. All of this discussion leads to the following claim: Any die you select has the same probability of winning against your opponent. Suppose that 1 , … , 6 p 1 ,…,p 6 are the probabilities that each value on your die appears. We know that 1 + ⋯ + 6 = 1 p 1 +⋯+p 6 =1 and ∑ = 1 6 = 3.5 ∑ i=1 6 ip i =3.5 by the conditions above. Let W be the event of you rolling a strictly higher value than your opponent. Furthermore, let X be the random variable representing one outcome of your die. questions.title: Die Duo IV
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. You get to select the sides and probability of appearance for both dice. There is one restriction: Only values $1-6$ can be used. You and your friend both receive the die you created. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to simultaneously maximize your winning probability and minimize your friend's winning probability? Report the variance of the die you create.
questions.solution: Since the dice are independent and identical, given that the two dice aren't the same value, it is equally likely as to whether you or your friend won. Furthermore, since you can select the probabilities that each side appears, WLOG, the values 1 − 6 1−6 all appear on the die. This is WLOG because you can set the probability of some side to 0 0 if you don't want it to appear. Let p be the probability that there is a tie between the dice. The probability that the dice show distinct values i.e. there is no tie is 1 − 1−p. Given that there is no tie, you win with probability 1 / 2 1/2 by the above discussion. Therefore, the probability you win is 1 − 2 2 1−p . To maximize your winning probability, we need to minimize the probability of a tie, p. Suppose that side i appears with probability p i . You can obtain a tie by both rolling 1 , 2 , … , 6 1,2,…,6. By the independence of the dice, = ∑ = 1 6 2 p= i=1 ∑ 6 p i 2 Our restrictions are 1 + ⋯ + 6 = 1 p 1 +⋯+p 6 =1 and 1 , … , 6 ≥ 0 p 1 ,…,p 6 ≥0, as these are probabilities. The goal is to minimize p under these restrictions. Intuitively, one can see that each of the p i values contributes the same to the total sum, as they are not weighted. Thus, in an optimal solution, there's no reason for p i to contribute more than any other, so it should be the case that 1 = ⋯ = 6 p 1 =⋯=p 6 . However, as we know their sum is 1 1, the result is 1 = 2 = ⋯ = 6 = 1 / 6 p 1 =p 2 =⋯=p 6 =1/6. In other words, you should choose the standard fair die. The mean of this die is 7 / 2 7/2. By LOTUS, the second moment is given by 1 2 + ⋯ + 6 2 6 = 91 6 6 1 2 +⋯+6 2 = 6 91 Using the variance formula, the variance of the value showing on this die is 91 6 − ( 7 2 ) 2 = 35 12 6 91 −( 2 7 ) 2 = 12 35 One can also verify the minimization by the method of Lagrange multipliers. Taking the gradient of the objective function ( ) (p) and setting it equal to λ multiplied by the constraint's gradient ( 1 ) (1), this yields the system 2 = 2x i =λ for all 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤n. Since = 2 λ=2x i for all 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤n, 2 1 = ⋯ = 2 ⟺ 1 = ⋯ = 2x 1 =⋯=2x n ⟺x 1 =⋯=x n .

questions.title: Die Duo V
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. You each get to select the sides of your own die under the following conditions: All values must be between $1$ and $6$, inclusive of both, and the die must have sides that sum to $21$. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What die would you select to maximize your winning probability? Enter the values of the die in non-decreasing order.
questions.solution: Both you and your friend can choose dice under the same restrictions. What's optimal for you is also optimal for them, so you and your friend will end up selecting the same dice. However, as both you and your friend receive the same dice, this problem is exactly that of "Die Duo IV": To maximize your probability of winning, you need to minimize the probability of a tie. Therefore, the answer is the standard die 123456 123456. This intuitively makes sense: By "Die Duo III", the standard fair die has constant winning probability, regardless of the die chosen by your opponent. In other words, the standard fair die has no "weaknesses", as it is uniformly distributed across all the values. If your friend were to select a die that has some repeated values, those could be exploited by changing your own die in response.

questions.title: Die Duo VI
questions.problem: You and your friend are both rolling $6-$sided dice. Both dice are fair in the sense that each side appears with probability $1/6$. You each get to select the sides of both dice under the following conditions: All values must be between $1$ and $6$, inclusive of both, and the die must have sides that sum to $21$. Note that the two dice no longer need to be the same. The winner is the person who rolls a strictly higher value. What dice would you select for you and your friend maximize your winning probability? Report the optimal probability of you winning.
questions.solution: To maximize your probability of winning, you want to have a minimal number of values on your friend's die that beat you, but have many of your values be just $1$ larger than theirs. The maximum value that can be put on your friend's die is $6$, so suppose one $6$ is placed on it. The other $5$ values must have sum $15$, so a natural choice is to make all of them $3$. This is the smallest constant value that can be placed without having any more "large values". To beat your friend, you would want as many $4$s as possible on your die, as that is the smallest value above $3$. This can be easily obtained with the die $144444$. Adjusting any values upwards is non-optimal, as $5$ nor $6$ give you any marginal benefit (they still only beat $3$), but you would also have to adjust another value down, meaning you lose an outcome of a $4$. With these two dice, you win exactly when you roll $4$ and your friend rolls $3$. This occurs with probability $5/6$ per die, so you win with probability $25/36$. We now claim that $25/36$ is optimal. The only way you would adjust your friend's die is if you put another $6$ on it, as that could lower the values you need on your die. If a second $6$ is added to your friend's die, $1/3$ of the time, they would roll a $6$, meaning you can't win. Therefore, your maximum winning probability would be $2/3 = 24/36 < 25/36$ with such a die for your friend.

Since this is an "at least" probability, the easier quantity to compute would be the complement, which is that no clubs are in the remaining 3 3 cards. For no clubs to be in the remaining 3 3 cards, the 3 3 cards must be drawn from the other 39 39 that aren't clubs. There are ( 39 3 ) ( 3 39 ) ways to do this. We also know that there are 51 51 cards remaining in the deck after the king of clubs has been removed, so there are ( 51 3 ) ( 3 51 ) ways to pick 3 3 cards without restriction. questions.title: Nobody 5
questions.problem: $10$ distinct marbles are being put into $4$ boxes. Compute the probability at least one box receives exactly $5$ marbles. Round to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: We are computing an "at least" probability here, so it's best to consider whether to use the complement or inclusion-exclusion. To see this, let's first set up some events representing our scenario probabilistically. Label the boxes 1 − 4 1−4, and let $B_i$ be the event that box $i$ gets exactly $5$ marbles. We want to compute [ ⋃ = 1 4 ] P[ i=1 ⋃ 4 B i ]. The events $B_i$ are not independent, as the knowledge that one box gets $5$ marbles significantly reduces the probability that another box gets $5$ marbles, as there would only be $5$ marbles left to distribute. Therefore, the best approach is inclusion-exclusion. Applying inclusion-exclusion to the union, the probability is equal to [ ⋃ = 1 4 ] = ∑ = 1 4 [ ] − ∑ < [ ] + ∑ < < [ ] + [ 1 2 3 4 ] P[ i=1 ⋃ 4 B i ]= i=1 ∑ 4 P[B i ]− i<j ∑ P[B i B j ]+ i<j<k ∑ P[B i B j B k ]+P[B 1 B 2 B 3 B 4 ] All of the triple and quadruple intersection terms are probability 0 0, as we only have 10 10 balls, so its impossible for 3 3 or more boxes to get exactly 5 5 balls. We only care about the individual terms and the pairwise intersection terms. As the boxes are exchangeable (the labels are irrelevant), the probability of all individual events and pairwise intersections are the same. There would be 4 4 terms in the first sum and ( 4 2 ) = 6 ( 2 4 )=6 terms in the second sum. As a result of this simplification, we only need to compute [ 1 ] P[B 1 ] and [ 1 ∩ 2 ] P[B 1 ∩B 2 ]. 1 B 1 is the event that box 1 1 has exactly 5 5 marbles. Thus, we fix 5 5 marbles in box 1 1, which can be chosen in ( 10 5 ) ( 5 10 ) ways. We need to account for this because the marbles are distinct. Afterwards, the other 5 5 marbles can go in any of the other 3 3 bins, so there are 3 5 3 5 ways to arrange the other marbles into the other bins. Unrestricted, there are 4 10 4 10 ways to arrange the 10 10 marbles into the 4 4 marbles, as there would be 4 4 options per marble. By the multiplication rule, [ 1 ] = ( 10 5 ) 3 5 4 10 P[B 1 ]= 4 10 ( 5 10 )3 5 As for [ 1 2 ] P[B 1 B 2 ], there must be 5 5 marbles that go into each bin. There are ( 10 5 ) ( 5 10 ) ways to pick the 5 5 marbles that go into the first bin. Afterwards, the other 5 5 marbles must go into bin 2 2, so there is only 1 1 way to arrange the other 5 5 marbles once the first ones are selected for bin 1 1. Therefore, [ 1 ∩ 2 ] = ( 10 5 ) 4 10 P[B 1 ∩B 2 ]= 4 10 ( 5 10 ) Substituting into the inclusion-exclusion formula, the probability is [ ⋃ = 1 4 ] = 4 ⋅ ( 10 5 ) 3 5 4 10 − 6 ⋅ ( 10 5 ) 4 10 ≈ 0.2322 P[ i=1 ⋃ 4 B i ]=4⋅ 4 10 ( 5 10 )3 5 −6⋅ 4 10 ( 5 10 ) ≈0.2322

questions.title: Mini And Maxi
questions.problem: You roll a standard fair − n−sided die $k \geq 1$ times. Define = max ⁡ { 1 , … , } M k =max{X 1 ,…,X k } and = min ⁡ { 1 , … , } m k =min{X 1 ,…,X k }. Compute [ + ] E[M k +m k ] when $n = 15$ and $k = 8$.
questions.solution: Each of the die rolls can be thought of as a DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n} random variable. We know that the mean of such a random variable is $(n+1)/2$. Additionally, as the PMF is constant, it is symmetric about the mean. The expected value of the sum of two such random variables would be $n+1$, and one can also note that if ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } , X∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n}, ( + 1 ) − ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } (n+1)−X∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n}. This symmetry can now be used for the maximum and minimum of the dice rolls. Let 1 , … , ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } X 1 ,…,X k ∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n} IID be the dice rolls. Note that [ min ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] = [ min ⁡ { ( + 1 ) − 1 , … , ( + 1 ) − } ] = [ ( + 1 ) − max ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] E[min{X 1 ,…,X k }]=E[min{(n+1)−X 1 ,…,(n+1)−X k }]=E[(n+1)−max{X 1 ,…,X r }] The first equality is by noting that X i and ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−X i have the same distribution for each 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤n. The second equality is by noting that the minimum value of ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−X i is the same as subtracting the maximum value of X i from + 1 n+1. Therefore, [ min ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] + [ max ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] = + 1 E[min{X 1 ,…,X k }]+E[max{X 1 ,…,X k }]=n+1 Notably, this is independent of the number of rolls k. This makes intuitive sense because of the fairness of the dice: The maximum should increase, on average, as much per roll as the minimum decreases, so it's essentially the same as taking the expected value of any two rolls summed up. With the specified values, the answer is 16 16.

questions.title: Saddle
questions.problem: Let $M$ be a $2 \times n$ matrix whose components a ij , $i = 1,2$ and $1 \leq j \leq n$, are IID continuous random variables. We say that a ij is a saddle point of $M$ if = max⁡1≤≤ = min⁡=1,2 a ij = 1≤j≤n max a ij = i=1,2 min a ij . In words, a ij is the maximum of the row and minimum of the column it belongs to. Find the probability that a matrix M generated according to the above has a saddle point when $n = 10$ and each ∼ ( 0 , 1 ) a ij ∼N(0,1).
questions.solution: As we are looking at IID random components and comparing them, this hints to us that the exact distribution is irrelevant here. A natural first question is: Can there be more than one saddle point? Since M is $2 \times n$, there are only two rows. WLOG, suppose there is a saddle point in row $1$. There must exist an element that is the max of it's row and minimum of the column. This implies that there is an element in row $2$ larger than every element of row $1$. Therefore, there can't be a saddle point in row $2$, as the maximum of row $2$ must be larger than the largest element of row $1$, meaning it won't be the minimum of the column it belongs to. If there is a saddle point, there is exactly one. Since the two rows have IID components, we can find the probability of a saddle point in the first row and multiply it by 2 2 to get the answer. As the components are IID, WLOG, assume the maximum of row 1 1 is 11 a 11 . For 11 a 11 to be a saddle, 21 > 11 a 21 >a 11 . In other words, 21 = max ⁡ { 21 , 11 , … , 1 } a 21 =max{a 21 ,a 11 ,…,a 1n }. As all the a ij are IID and continuous, the probability of this occurring is 1 + 1 n+1 1 . Therefore, the answer is 2 + 1 n+1 2 . With = 10 n=10, the answer is 2 / 11 2/11.

questions.title: Summed Dice II
questions.problem: Suppose you have two $6-$sided fair dice. You can assign numbers to the sides in any way you please. Is it possible to assign values to the sides such that the sums { 2 , … , 12 } {2,…,12} each appear with probability $1/11$? If so, report $1$. If not, report $0$.
questions.solution: In this case, we should think about the underlying probability space. There are 6 2 = $36$ 6 2 =36 outcomes that can appear from rolling two dice, assuming all sides (even repeated values) are distinguishable. Each of these outcomes are equally likely, as the dice are fair. Thus, any event contains a subset of these 36 36 outcomes, meaning their probability is in the form $k/36$ for some integer $k$. In this situation, we want the event that the sums are exactly $k$, $2 \leq k \leq 12$, to have probability $1/11$. Thus, if this were possible, 1 / 11 = / 36 ⟺ 11 = 36 1/11=k/36⟺11k=36 for some integer $k$. However, as 11 ∤ 36 11∤36, there does not exist such an integer $k$, meaning there is no satisfactory die here.

questions.title: Exceed Double Heads
questions.problem: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly, and the cumulative number of tails and heads are recorded. Find the probability that the cumulative number of heads obtained ever exceeds twice the amount of tails. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Just as gambler's ruin and random walks can easily be related, we can relate this question to the scenario of "Double Step Particle II" quite easily. In this scenario, we can view a head as a step leftwards, while a tail as 2 2 steps right. The reason we view tails as two steps right is because the number of heads must strictly exceed twice the number of tails, so adding a tails to the running total adds 2 2 to the threshold. Furthermore, the "particle" in this scenario starts one unit away from the origin. If a heads is flipped immediately, then the number of heads does exceed twice the number of tails, so the process ends in 1 1 step. By the above discussion, this is a special case of "Double Step Particle II" with = 1 k=1 and = 1 / 2 p=1/2, so the answer is 5 − 1 2 2 5 −1 .

questions.title: Remaining Gum
questions.problem: Omar has $N$ pieces of 5gum in his left pocket and $N$ pieces of Orbit gum in his right pocket. He's dealing out gum to $M > 2N$ people in his probability class. Every time he deals out a piece of gum to someone, he picks which pocket to deal from uniformly at random. When Omar is asked to give someone gum and he looks in his pocket to find there are no pieces of gum remaining in it, he counts up the number of pieces of gum in his other pocket. Find the probability there are exactly k pieces of gum in the other pocket, 0 ≤ ≤ 0≤k≤N, when = 8 N=8 and = 4 k=4.
questions.solution: Let's think about the scenario at the experimental level, as it's fairly complicated from looking above. WLOG, we can assume that his right pocket is the one he notices to be empty. We can say this WLOG because both pockets are equally likely to be noticed as empty, so we can just fix one of them and multiply by 2 2 to account for the other pocket. We can formalize this logic a bit more using the law of total probability - if we let X be the event that the right pocket gets emptied first, Y be the event that the left pocket gets emptied first, and G the number of pieces of gum in the other pocket. Then the law of total probability gives, [ = ] = [ ] [ = ∣ ] + [ ] [ = ∣ ] = 1 2 [ = ∣ ] + 1 2 [ = ∣ ] = [ = ∣ ] P[G=k] =P[X]P[G=k∣X]+P[Y]P[G=k∣Y] = 2 1 P[G=k∣X]+ 2 1 P[G=k∣Y] =P[R=k∣X] The second and third equalities follow from the fact that both pockets are equally likely to be picked. If Omar's right pocket is the one that's noticed to be empty, it must have been selected by Omar + 1 N+1 times: N times to empty it out, and then 1 1 more time to notice it's actually empty. For there to be exactly k pieces of gum in his left pocket, it must have been selected − N−k times. This would ensure there are − ( − ) = N−(N−k)=k pieces of gum in the left pocket. To summarize the above discussion, for there to be exactly k pieces of gum in Omar's left pocket upon him noticing his right pocket is empty, the following events must occur: Omar must select from his right pocket N times in the first 2 − 2N−k draws Omar must from his left pocket − N−k times in the first 2 − 2N−k draws Omar must select from his right pocket on the ( 2 − + 1 ) (2N−k+1)st draw More simply, in the first 2 − 2N−k draws, Omar must select from his right pocket N times and from his left pocket − N−k times. Since each draw is independent, we can use a Binomial distribution to determine the probability that Omar draws from his left pocket − N−k times in the first 2 − 2N−k draws. If we let R represent the number of times he draws from his right pocket in the 2 − 2N−k trials, then ∼ Binom ( 2 − , 1 / 2 ) R∼Binom(2N−k,1/2). Accordingly, [ = ] = ( 2 − ) ( 1 2 ) ( 1 2 ) − = ( 2 − ) ( 1 2 ) 2 − P[R=N]=( N 2N−k )( 2 1 ) N ( 2 1 ) N−k =( N 2N−k )( 2 1 ) 2N−k Afterwards, the probability he draws from his right pocket again on the ( 2 − + 1 ) (2N−k+1)st trial is 1 / 2 1/2, so the probability of Omar having exactly k pieces of gum in his left pocket upon realizing his right pocket is empty is, ( 2 − ) ( 1 2 ) 2 − + 1 ( N 2N−k )( 2 1 ) 2N−k+1 again since each draw is independent. We still aren't done though, since as stated at the beginning, we must multiply the above probability by 2 2 to account for the other case of his left pocket being the one that he realizes is empty. Therefore, the probability of Omar having exactly k candies in his other pocket upon realizing one pocket is empty is, ( 2 − ) ( 1 2 ) 2 − ( N 2N−k )( 2 1 ) 2N−k With the specified values, the answer is 495 / 4096 495/4096. You may be wondering - why did we have to use the Binomial distribution here? Why couldn't we use the `"probability by counting" technique where we simple count of the number of ways we could have picked 12 pieces of gum with 8 from one pocket and 4 from another, divided by the total number of ways to pick the 16 pieces of gum? The reason for this is that the different ways to pick the 16 pieces of gum do not have equal probability, since after one pocket becomes empty, we can only choose gum from the other pocket. For example, the sequence of draws, ffffffffoooooooo has probability ( 1 2 ) 8 ( 2 1 ) 8 since after we've picked all 8 pieces of five gum, we can only pick pieces of Orbit. However, the sequence offfffffooooooof has probability ( 1 2 ) 15 ( 2 1 ) 15 since we don't empty a pocket of gum until after the 15th draw. So, since not all sequences have the same probability of occurrence, we can't simply count up the number of "valid" sequences and divide by the total number of possible sequences to calculate the probability of interest.

questions.title: Full Subset
questions.problem: Suppose $S$ is a set of $n$ elements. How many ways can two (not necessarily distinct) subsets of $S$, say $A$ and $B$, be selected such that $A \cup B = S$. Report the answer when $n = 8$. The order of $A$ and $B$ is irrelevant.
questions.solution: For $A \cup B = S$, every $x \in S$ must belong to at least one of $A$ or $B$. In other words, exactly one of the following is true: ∈ ∩ x∈A∩B c , ∈ ∩ x∈A c ∩B, or $x \in A\cap B$. Thus, there are $3$ options for each of the elements of $S$, meaning there are $3^n$ possible ways to assign the elements of $x$. However, the order of the subsets is irrelevant, so we need to divide by $2$ to account for the ordering of $A$ and $B$. There is one caveat to this: If $A = B$, there are not two orderings of the subsets, so these must be excluded first before dividing by $2$, and then added back. Since $A \cup B = S$, the only possible way $A = B$ is if $A = B = S$, which is $1$ possibility. Thus, there are 3 − 1 2 + 1 = 3 + 1 2 2 3 n −1 +1= 2 3 n +1 ways to select the subsets: We subtract the $1$ equality case from $3^n$ , divide by $2$ to remove the ordering of $A$ and $B$, and then add back in the equality case. With $n = 8$, the answer is $3281$.

questions.problem: You flip a fair coin $n$ times. Given that no consecutive heads appear in your sequence of flips, what is the probability that the first flip was a heads? Report the answer when $n = 15$.
questions.solution: This problem can be solved by recursion. First, let's generalize a little bit and suppose that we make $n$ flips. Since we are dealing with a fair coin, rather than focusing on determining the probability directly, we will instead determine the probability by counting the total number of length n sequences that start with a heads and don't have any consecutive heads, and divide that by the total number of sequences that don't have any consecutive heads. We can see that this gives us what we want by recalling Bayes rule, [ first flip is H ∣ No consecutive H in flips ] = [ first flip is H , No consecutive H in flips ] [ No consecutive H in flips ] P[first flip is H∣No consecutive H in n flips]= P[No consecutive H in n flips] P[first flip is H,No consecutive H in n flips] Denote the number of sequences of n coin flips with no consecutive heads as ( ) f(n). In order for a length n sequence to not have any consecutive heads, one of two things must happen. Either the sequence ends in TH or it ends in T. How many sequences of n coin flips with no consecutive heads end in HT? This will just be ( − 2 ) f(n−2), since to get the number of length n sequences with no consecutive heads ending in HT, we can just append HT to the end of any valid length − 2 n−2 sequence. Similarly, the number of length n sequences with no consecutive heads ending in T is given by ( − 1 ) f(n−1). Putting this together yields, ( ) = ( − 1 ) + ( − 2 ) f(n)=f(n−1)+f(n−2) which can be recognized as the Fibonacci sequence. What are the initial conditions? Clearly, ( 1 ) = 2 f(1)=2, as both sequences don't have consecutive heads. We can additionally prescribe ( 0 ) = 1 f(0)=1, as the only sequence is the empty one. This is exactly the Fibonacci sequence shifted by 2 2 upwards, so ( ) = + 2 f(n)=F n+2 . We now need to find the number of length n sequences that start with a heads and don't have any consecutive heads. Denoting this number as ( ) g(n), note that any sequences satisfying this condition must start with HT. This is also reasonable because we solved the $k = 2$ case like this in a different problem. The recurrence here will depend on both $n$ and $k$, so let , N n,k be the number of sequences of length $n$ with no runs of $k$ heads. Since we want less than $k$ heads, the possible endings are , , , … T,TH,THH,…, until it's tails with − $1$ k−1 heads following. One can intuitively understand this as breaking up the problem by conditioning on the position of the last tails in the sequence. questions.solution: In this question, we're asked to compute the expected amount of some dependent events that occur, so counting with indicators and applying linearity of expectation is the best approach. The events are dependent because if A and B are friends, they can't have the same set of friends, as nobody can be friends with themselves. As there are n people at the party, there are ( 2 ) ( 2 n ) pairs of people at the party, so let I i be the indicator that the ith pair of people have the same set of friends. = 1 + ⋯ + ( 2 ) T=I 1 +⋯+I ( 2 n ) gives the total number of pairs of people that have the same set of friends. For this to occur, the two people must not be friends with each other and must have the same decision (friends or not friends) with each of the other − 2 n−2 people at the party. The probability that the people aren't friends is 1 − 1−p. To calculate the probability that the two people have the same decision on each of the other − 2 n−2 people at the party, we break up into two cases: friends and not friends. The probability that both are friends with a given person is 2 p 2 , as it's probability p for each, while the probability that they both aren't friends with a given person is ( 1 − ) 2 (1−p) 2 . Adding these two disjoint cases together yields a total probability of 2 + ( 1 − ) 2 p 2 +(1−p) 2 for the two people having the same decision on a given other person. However, that would be incorrect as the expected length of the second run should intuitively be different than the expected length of the first run because the first run fixes what coin outcome we're looking for in the second run. Just as in Runny Runs I, the expected length of the second run is then the expected number of flips after the last head of the first run until the next head. This is for the exact same reason: We add 1 1 for the first tails that appears, and the number of additional flips performed, T, is Geom ( ) Geom(p) distributed, since there is probability p of heads per flip, and the run ends when the next heads appears. By plugging into the Law of Total Expectation, [ 2 ] = 1 ⋅ + 1 1 − ⋅ ( 1 − ) = 2 E[L 2 ]= p 1 ⋅p+ 1−p 1 ⋅(1−p)=2 This is independent of p, so the answer is 2 2.

questions.solution: The current state of the system is describe by two features: The ant that is currently moving and the distance between the ants. The latter feature is easy to work with: The ants start $2$ steps away from one another, and can only ever be $0,1,$ or $2$ movements away from each other. The part that requires more creativity is encoding the current person moving. One could start with defining , p A,i and , p B,i as the probability that ant A moves onto ant B given they ants A or ant B, respectively, is going to move, and are currently i units apart, where = 1 , 2 i=1,2. This is because either A must move onto the space of ant B or vice versa, and when B starts, the roles of A and B are really just reversed, as A would be going second when B goes first, so A plays the role of B here. This helps us, as we only need to create a system for , 1 p A,1 and , 2 p A,2 . , 2 p A,2 is the probability we want, as the system initially has the ants 2 2 units apart, with ant A moving first. Lastly, with probability 1 / 4 1/4, ant A moves to be two units away from ant B, so the probability in this case is , 2 = 1 − , 2 p B,2 =1−p A,2 . questions.title: Knight Movement I
questions.problem: A knight in chess can move $(\pm 2, \pm 1)$ or $(\pm 1, \pm 2)$ at each turn, as long as that movement stays inside the board. The chess starts at $(1,1)$ in an $n\times n$ chess board (bottom left corner), where $n \geq 6$ and $n \equiv 1$ mod $3$. Find the number of shortest paths from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ when $n = 13$.
questions.solution: To go from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$, the number of paths will definitely depend on the remainder of $n$ when divided by $3$, as each movement changes the sum of the $x$ and $y$ positions of the knight by $-3,-1,1,$ or $3$. When possible, we want make as many moves as possible to be $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$, as those are the movements adding $3$ to our total position at each step. Since we need to increase the total sum of our position from $2$ to $2n$, and we can only edit it by at most $3$ in each step, a lower bound on the number of movements needed is ⌈ 2 − 2 3 ⌉ ⌈ 3 2n−2 ⌉. Since $n = 3k+1$, 2 − 2 3 = 2 3 2n−2 =2k exactly, so we can get from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ in $2k$ movements. It's also fairly clear how to do this: The moves that change the position by $3$ each step are $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$, so we need to take $k$ of each movement type to reach $(n,n)$, as the $x$ position would increase from $1$ to $1 + 2 \cdot k + 1 \cdot k = 3k+1 = n$, and likewise with $y$. Any permutation of these $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ movements is fine, as they don't go outside the board's boundary. There are ( 2 ) ( k 2k ) ways to arrange these movement, as there are $2$ groups with $k$ movements of each type. Therefore, when $n = 3k+1$ for some positive integer $k$, there are ( 2 ) ( k 2k ) shortest paths from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$. With $n = 13 = 3 \cdot 4 + 1$, the answer is $70$.

questions.title: Knight Movement II
questions.problem: A knight in chess can move $(\pm 2, \pm 1)$ or $(\pm 1, \pm 2)$ at each turn, as long as that movement stays inside the board. The chess starts at $(1,1)$ in an $n\times n$ chess board (bottom left corner), where $n \geq 6$ and $n \equiv 0$ mod $3$. Find the number of shortest paths from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ when $n = 12$.
questions.solution: To go from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$, the number of paths will definitely depend on the remainder of $n$ when divided by $3$, as each movement changes the sum of the $x$ and $y$ positions of the knight by $-3,-1,1,$ or $3$. When possible, we want make as many moves as possible to be $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$, as those are the movements adding $3$ to our total position at each step. Since we need to increase the total sum of our position from $2$ to $2n$, and we can only edit it by at most $3$ in each step, a lower bound on the number of movements needed is ⌈ 2 − 2 3 ⌉ ⌈ 3 2n−2 ⌉. Since $n = 3k$, ⌈ 2 − 2 3 ⌉ = 2 ⌈ 3 2n−2 ⌉=2k, so we need at least $2k$ movements. We can indeed get from $(1,1)$ to $(n,n)$ in $2k$ movements: We must change $x+y$ from $2$ to $6k$, meaning there is an increase of 6 − 2 6k−2. We increased $x+y$ from $2$ to $6k+2$ in "Knight Movement I" by taking movements that increase $x+y$ by $3$ at each step. Now, since we can increase it by $2$ less, one of the movements increasing $x+y$ by $3$ can be replaced with one that increases $x+y$ by $1$, as that will yield a total increase of 6 − 2 6k−2. The options are $(2,-1)$ or $(-1,2)$. These movements have the same net effect, so we can count the number of movement sequences that have $(2,-1)$, and the multiply by $2$ to account for the other case of including $(-1,2)$. Suppose our different move is $(2,-1)$. To get from $(1,1)$ to $(3k,3k)$ with 2 − 1 2k−1 other movements, they must all be $(1,2)$ or $(2,1)$. With $(2,-1)$ already included, we must move 3 − 3 3k−3 more horizontally and $3k$ vertically. Therefore, we must have − 2 k−2 movements of the form $(2,1)$ and $k+1$ movements of the form $(1,2)$. This is because the change in $x$ position is 2 ⋅ ( − 2 ) + 1 ⋅ ( + 1 ) = 3 − 3 2⋅(k−2)+1⋅(k+1)=3k−3, and similarly for the change in $y$. However, we have a restriction: The $(2,-1)$ movement can't be first or last. If it's first, we would be below the lower bound of the board, while if it's last, we would have had to be above the upper bound of the board right beforehand, which also isn't allowed. Of all of the arrangements of the $2k$ total movements, the $(2,-1)$ movement isn't allowed in $2$ of the 2 2k positions, so we must multiply the total number of ways to arrange all of the movements without restriction by 2 − 2 2 $2k$−2 , as this is the proportion of paths that don't have the $(2,-1)$ movement as the first or last. The total number of ways to arrange the − 2 , + 1 , k−2,k+1, and $1$ movement of the three types is just a multinomial counting problem, as the movements themselves are indistinguishable besides their type, so the total ways to do this is ( 2 + 1 , − 2 , 1 ) = ( 2 ) ! ( − 2 ) ! ( + 1 ) ! 1 ! ( k+1,k−2,1 2k )= (k−2)!(k+1)!1! (2k)! . We multiply this amount by 2 − 2 2 2k 2k−2 and also by 2 2 (to account for the other case of ( − 1 , 2 ) (−1,2) being the odd movement) to yield the final answer of 2 ⋅ 2 − 2 2 ⋅ ( 2 − 2 , + 1 , 1 ) = 4 ( − 1 ) ( 2 − 1 ) ! ( + 1 ) ! ( − 2 ) ! = 4 ( − 1 ) ( 2 − 1 − 2 ) 2⋅ 2k 2k−2 ⋅( k−2,k+1,1 2k )=4(k−1) (k+1)!(k−2)! (2k−1)! =4(k−1)( k−2 2k−1 ) With = 12 = 3 ⋅ 4 n=12=3⋅4, the answer is 252 252.

questions.problem: Suppose that a coin selected from a bin will come up heads on each flip with a probability that is Unif ( 0 , 1 ) Unif(0,1) distributed. questions.solution: Since we have infinite flips, it makes sense that we would want to make our heads probability as large as possible in limit. Therefore, the natural idea is to change out your coin each time it lands tails. All of the flips between consecutive tails will be heads, so the expected long-term proportion of heads would 1 − 1− the long-term proportion of tails. To get the long-term proportion of tails, we need to compute the expected time between tails, and the reciprocal of that quantity would be the limiting proportion of tails. Intuitively, if [ ] E[T] is the expected number of flips between tails, then 1 1 out of every [ ] E[T] flips is a tail, so the limiting proportion would be 1 / [ ] 1/E[T]. The main issue is that we don't know the distribution of T currently. If we knew the probability p of the coin, tails would occur with probability 1 − 1−p per flip, so the conditional distribution would be Geom ( 1 − ) Geom(1−p), which has mean 1 1 − 1−p 1 . questions.title: Heads Proportion III
questions.problem: Suppose that a coin selected from a bin will come up heads on each flip with a probability that is Unif ( 0 , 1 ) Unif(0,1) distributed. At any time, the coin currently in use can be discarded for a new coin whose probability will also be Unif ( 0 , 1 ) Unif(0,1) distributed, independently of other generated probabilities/flips. The probability of the coin is never revealed to you. Find the optimal strategy to maximize the long-run proportion of heads appearing on the coin. Under this strategy, what is the probability that you obtain an infinite amount of tails? If necessary, round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: We have the strategy from the previous part of the problem, so we need to find the probability that we obtain an infinite number of tails. When considering an event that occurs infinitely often, it's typically best to use the Borel-Cantelli Lemma. Since the coin flips are independent here given the probability p, the 2 2nd Borel-Cantelli Lemma is best. At any point in the game, we have a probability 0 < < 1 0<p<1 of landing heads per flip, meaning there is probability 0 < 1 − < 1 0<1−p<1 of tails per flip. To use the Borel-Cantelli Lemma, we must define an infinite sequence of independent events. Assuming p is fixed, let A i be the event that the ith flip with the coin is tails. These events are independent, and ∑ = 1 ∞ [ ] = ∑ = 1 ∞ 1 − = ∞ i=1 ∑ ∞ P[A i ]= i=1 ∑ ∞ 1−p=∞ The sum is infinite because 1 − > 0 1−p>0. Since the sum is infinite, A i occurs infinitely often with probability 1 1. Since this holds for all 0 < < 1 0<p<1, we can conclude that there will be infinitely many tails with probability 1 1. This is counter-intuitive because we said that the limiting proportion of tails is 0 0 in the previous part, but there are infinitely many heads with probability 1 1. The resolution is to note that the "density" of such tails occurring is too small for it to have positive probability in limit, as the expected time between tails is infinite.

questions.title: Squared Outcome II
questions.problem: A standard fair − n−sided die is rolled repeatedly. If the die comes up with the value $1$, you lose and receive no payout. If the die shows the value $1 < k \leq n$, you have the option to roll again under the same rules for a price of $\$r$, or stop with a payout of $ 2 $k 2 .
