questions.title: Pick The Unknown
questions.problem: You have $3$ cards in front of you labelled $n,n+1,$ and $n+2$. However, you do not know what $n$ is prior to playing. All of the cards are initially face down. You flip one card and observe the value. You are then given the opportunity to hold (in which you receive a payout equal to the value of the drawn card), or you can hit. If you hit, you flip one of the other 2 2 remaining cards, and you face the same decision. Note that you can't go back to the value of a previous card after you decide to hit. Design the optimal strategy. Find the expected payout of this strategy when = 20 n=20.
questions.solution: The key to this question is closely analyzing what information/choice do you have after each draw. After the first card is drawn, you have no information as to what n is, so the card you drew is equally likely to be any of the minimum, middle, or maximum. This would imply that the expected payout with this strategy is + 1 n+1, the value of the middle card. If you stop after all 3 3 cards are drawn, you also get no choice as to what card you get (just pick the last one), so your expected value with this strategy is also + 1 n+1, as each of the three cards would be equally likely to be the last card drawn. However, with the second draw, you do have an information advantage that is afforded to you by the cards drawn. For example, if you drew n and then + 2 n+2 in the first two draws, you would know that the last card has to be + 1 n+1, meaning you would stay at + 2 n+2. Therefore, there is information that is given by the first 2 2 cards based on how far apart they are. Thus, the optimal approach to this question is to condition based on the values of the first two cards that appear. For simplicity, let a be the value of the first card, and b be the value of the second card. The most naturally thing to consider is the difference − b−a between the two cards, as this tells us how far apart the two cards that we drew were. The inferences that we can make are dependent on this. The two easiest cases are − = 2 b−a=2 and − = − 2 b−a=−2, of which the − = 2 b−a=2 example was shown above. If − = 2 b−a=2, then b must be the maximum card value among the three, so the payout in this case is + 2 n+2. If − = − 2 b−a=−2, then a must be the smallest card value among the three, so you should draw the last card, which would be + 1 n+1 in value. This case yields a payout of + 1 n+1. If − = 1 b−a=1, then you either selected + 1 n+1 and then + 2 n+2, or you selected n and then + 1 n+1. Since n is unknown to you, you have no idea if the two cards you selected are the two highest or the two lowest. Therefore, from your current position, you can either gain 1 1 more or lose 2 2 with equal probability (the higher number you picked is either the highest card, in which the remaining is the lowest, or it is the middle card, in which the remaining is the highest card). Thus, hitting again is negative expected value, as you lose more than you gain on average, so you should stay at the second card selected. The payouts in these cases are + 2 n+2 and + 1 n+1, respectively. Otherwise, if − = − 1 b−a=−1, then it's just the same argument as above in reverse, as you either selected + 2 n+2 and then + 1 n+1 or + 1 n+1 and then n. In this case, you either lose 1 1 (go from + 1 n+1 to n) or gain 2 2 (go from n to + 2 n+2) with equal probability, so it is positive expected value to go for the last card. The payouts are n and + 2 n+2, respectively. All 3 ! = 6 3!=6 permutations of the card values are equally likely, so the expected payout of the game is just the average of all of the payouts, which is 3 ⋅ ( + 2 ) + 2 ⋅ ( + 1 ) + 6 = + 4 3 > + 1 6 3⋅(n+2)+2⋅(n+1)+n =n+ 3 4 >n+1 With = 20 n=20, the answer is 64 3 3 64 .

questions.title: Dominating Two
questions.problem: You and the friend play the following game: You and your friend each select an integer in [ ] = { 1 , 2 , … , } [n]={1,2,…,n}, where $n \geq 3$. The winner is the person who picks the strictly larger number OR who picks exactly $2$ below the larger number. For example, if your friend selected $75$ and you selected $73$, you would be the winner. If the two numbers are equal, nothing occurs. The winner receives $\$1$ from the loser. Assuming both you and your friend play optimally, the optimal strategy is a mixed strategy where you choose your value according to some appropriately selected random variable X. Find [ ] E[X] when $n = 100$.
questions.solution: The first important observation is that the game is symmetric between the two players, as they both receive the same payout from each other and are making the same choice, so their optimal strategies will be the same. Now, we must go about determining the strategy. Since the larger number is generally better (except for perhaps having a number 2 2 below it dominate you by the rules of the game), a natural thing to think about is when larger numbers dominate smaller numbers. Suppose that k were to be selected. Note that + 3 k+3 is strictly better than k, as + 3 k+3 beats everything k beats, as well as + 2 k+2. Note that both k and + 3 k+3 lose to + 1 k+1 and win against + 2 k+2, while + 3 k+3 also beats k, so + 3 k+3 strictly dominates k. Thus, if you were to select k, you should instead select + 3 k+3. This implies that the strategy of you and your friend should be to select one of − 2 , − 1 , n−2,n−1, or n, as these are the three largest integers in the set to select from, and you can't add 3 3 to any of these and get a valid option in the set. The question now becomes: Which of these should you play? The first item to note is that each of the three options wins against 1 1 option and loses against another option. Namely, − 2 n−2 wins against n and loses to − 1 n−1, − 1 n−1 wins against − 2 n−2 and loses to n, while n wins against − 1 n−1 and loses to − 2 n−2. This appears very reminiscent to rock-paper-scissors! The optimal strategy should be the same for both players, so if there were a pure strategy Nash equilibrium, then this would always result in a tie, as they select the same value. However, this is not optimal, as by the above, one of the players can improve their strategy by selecting a different value that would beat the "shared" value from before. Thus, the players must both run a mixed strategy. Let − 2 , − 1 , p n−2 ,p n−1 , and p n be the three probabilities that correspond to playing each of the options. Note that the probabilities for you and your friend are the same by the fact that you share the same strategy. We must have that − 2 + − 1 + = 1 p n−2 +p n−1 +p n =1 by definition. One may intuitively first think that a uniform distribution among these three choices is best i.e. each of them is selected with probability 1 / 3 1/3. This would indeed be correct! Note that if you select a non-uniform distribution between the choices, your opponent can re-weigh their selection of probabilities to exploit your choice. In other words, if you put more probability mass on one of the choices, your opponent can exploit that by adding more probability mass on the option that beats the one where you put more mass. For example, suppose that you assign a distribution of − 2 = 0.5 , − 1 = 0.3 p n−2 =0.5,p n−1 =0.3 and = 0.2 p n =0.2. If your friend were to run a pure strategy of choosing − 1 n−1, the expected payout for you would be 0.5 ⋅ ( − 1 ) + 0.3 ⋅ 0 + 0.2 ⋅ 1 = − 0.3 < 0 0.5⋅(−1)+0.3⋅0+0.2⋅1=−0.3<0. Thus, the best choice is to remain indifferent so that your friend can't exploit your preference. In other words, this means both you and your friend should select uniformly at random from { − 2 , − 1 , } {n−2,n−1,n} on each trial. This has mean − 1 n−1, as it is uniformly random, so the answer is − 1 n−1 in general. With the specific values, the answer is 99 99.

questions.problem: Alice and Bob pick alternate turns in the following game: Initially, there are $n \geq 1$ stones in the middle. Either player can choose to take $1$ to $r$ stones from the pile. Assume that + 1 ∤ r+1∤n. The player who draws the last stone wins. Alice gets to determine if she goes first or second. Assuming Alice selects her position in the game optimally and both Alice and Bob play optimally, in how many turns (total actions by the players) does Alice win the game, inclusive of the draw that makes Bob lose, when = 107 n=107 and = 7 r=7?
questions.solution: We want Alice's optimal strategy to be independent of what Bob does. Using the same idea as "Stone Pick II", Alice should want to leave Bob with a multiple of $r+1$ stones left for him to pick from at each turn. Therefore, on Alice's first turn, she should select the (unique) number of stones $k$ such that Bob has a multiple of + 1 ∣ − r+1∣n−k i.e. Bob has a multiple of $r+1$ stones for him to select from. Afterwards, the exact same strategy described earlier will apply, as Alice will always leave Bob with some multiple of $r+1$ stones at each turn. Therefore, Alice should choose to go first, and she will win in 1 + $2$ ⋅ ⌊ + 1 ⌋ 1+2⋅⌊ r+1 n ⌋ turns, as + 1 ∣ − r+1∣n−k, which is the number of cycles the game goes through. Each cycle contains 2 2 actions by the players, and then $1$ additional action is needed for Alice to select $k$ stones on the first turn, where $k$ is defined above. With the specific values, the answer is $27$.

questions.title: Roll Again IV
questions.problem: Kelly plays a game where she has $n$ standard fair $6-$sided die and rolls all of them. Once she observes the values, she can choose to hold or reroll. If Kelly holds, she receives the sum of the upfaces as her payout (in dollars) under the caveat that if 2 2 or more of the dice show the same value i, each of them are switched to 7 − 7−i. If Kelly chooses to roll again, she may hold any subset of the dice fixed and reroll the rest. Kelly must pay $ 1 $1 per die per reroll. There are no restrictions on how many times Kelly can reroll the dice. Under optimal play from Kelly, what is her expected payout when = 4 n=4?
questions.solution: A key complication in this problem is the switching condition. However, if we look at it carefully, it doesn't actually change any expected values! This is because obtaining $k \geq 2$ values of $i$ has the exact same probability as obtaining $k$ values of 7 − 7−i, and these two outcomes would switch to one another. For an example with concrete numbers, $(1,1)$ is equally likely to appear as $(6,6)$ on two dice. The pair $(6,6)$ would payout $1+1 = 2$, while $(1,1)$ would pay out $6+6 = 12$, so the average payout of these pairs is $7$, which is the exact same as two dice that weren't switched in value. Therefore, we can completely ignore this condition. The optimal stopping strategy is exactly the same as in "Roll Again III", as her expected payout is only dependent on the value showing on a given die and not on the other dice. The stopping condition is also the same for all of the dice because they are identical and independent. By the result of the previous part, the optimal strategy is to hold whenever the die shows at least 3 3 or 4 4, as they have the same expected value, and the expected payout is $ 4 $4 per die. By linearity of expectation, the expected value of the sum is 4 4n. With = 4 n=4, the answer is 16 16.

questions.title: Roll or Hold
questions.problem: You are presented with the following game: You repeatedly roll a fair − n−sided with the values $0$ , 1 , … , − 1 0,1,…,n−1 on the sides. After each roll, assuming it's non-zero, you have the option to end the game and receive a payout equal to the face showing on your die or to roll again. If you ever roll a 0 0, the game ends and you receive no payout. Find the optimal strategy for this game. Report your expected payout under this strategy when = 8 n=8.

questions.problem: Aahna plays the following game: She generates a uniformly random number $1$ ∼ Unif ( 0 , $1$ ) U 1 ∼Unif(0,1). She has two options: Hit or Hold. If her balance ever exceeds 1 1, she loses and receives no payout. Otherwise, while her balance is less than 1 1, she faces the same option to hit or hold. questions.title: Bring Coin?
questions.problem: You and your friend want to go watch the new Kung Fu Panda movie, but your parents are not very thrilled about it. They allow you to do so if you succeed in the following game: Both you and your friend are given a coin with probability $0 < r < 1$ of landing heads and are put in separate rooms. Each of you makes a decision as to whether you bring out the coin or not. If neither person brings out the coin, you can't go to the movie. If exactly one person brings out their coin, they must flip it and obtain a head to attend the movie. If both people bring out their coin, they must both flip and obtain heads to attend the movie. Assuming both you and your friend play rationally, find the optimal strategy. Report the probability that you and your friend can attend the movie when = 1 / 3 r=1/3.
questions.solution: The first key piece to solving is noting that you and your friend must share the same strategy, as the game is symmetric between the players. Because of this, it's clear to see that it's not optimal to never bring out the coin, as neither person would bring a coin, leading to no chance of attend the movie. However, always bringing out the coin may not be optimal either, as the probability that both people land heads is significantly lower than if just one person needs to land a head. Therefore, both you and your friend should run a mixed strategy. This means that each person independently decides to bring out the coin with probability 0 < < 1 0<p<1. The problem is find the optimal choice of p. The second key is noting that p should satisfy the principle of indifference: For the optimal value of p, the probability that you can attend the movies should be the same, regardless of whether or not you bring the coin. Thus, we must calculate the probability that you attend the movie in case. If you don't bring the coin, your friend must bring the coin, which occurs with probability p, and land hands, which occurs with probability r. Therefore, the probability you attend the movies in this case is pr. If you do bring out the coin, there are two cases with positive probability: If your friend also brings out their coin (probability p), both of you must land heads, which occurs with probability 2 r 2 by independence. If your friend doesn't bring their coin (probability 1 − 1−p), you must land a head, which occurs with probability r. Aggregating the two cases above yields a total probability of attend the movies of 2 + ( 1 − ) pr 2 +(1−p)r. Equating the two options, we must solve for p in = 2 + ( 1 − ) pr=pr 2 +(1−p)r. By expanding, we get that = 2 + ( 1 − ) ⟺ = 2 + − ⟺ ( 2 − ) = ⟺ = 1 2 − pr=pr 2 +(1−p)r⟺pr=pr 2 +r−pr⟺pr(2−r)=r⟺p= 2−r 1 Division by r is fine since it's assumed that > 0 r>0. Therefore, both you and your friend should independently bring out their coins with probability 1 2 − 2−r 1 , yielding a probability of attending the movies of = 2 − pr= 2−r r With the specified values, the answer is 1 / 5 1/5.

questions.title: Bucket Allocation I
questions.problem: You and $100$ other players are each given $3$ tickets to distribute into three buckets with prizes $\$20, \$80,$ and $\$200$. One winning ticket is drawn from each bucket, and the winner gets the associated prize. A single person can win multiple buckets. You are the last person to put in your tickets and are told that the number of tickets in each bucket are currently allocated proportionally to the size of the prize of the bucket. Assuming you want to maximize expected profit, how should you allocate your tickets? Report the expected profit to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: The key is to mimic the strategy of the other people as closely as possible: Since the number of tickets in each bucket is already such that there is constant expected payout per bucket, the best approach is to get as close to the same distribution as you can. Prior to you putting in any tickets, there will be 300 300 total tickets from the other 100 100 people; by the question, there will be 20 , 80 , 20,80, and 200 200 tickets in the three respective buckets. Since the total amount of money in the buckets is $ 300 $300, you should put 200 / 300 = 2 / 3 200/300=2/3 of your tickets in the $ 200 $200 bin, which means 2 2 of the three tickets go in the $ 200 $200 bin. One may wonder why putting all 3 3 tickets in the $ 200 $200 bin is sub-optimal; intuitively, when putting all 3 3 tickets in that bin, you limit yourself to that one bucket, while each additional ticket added yields a smaller incremental increase in probability of being the winner. Thus, the other ticket should go in either the $ 80 $80 or $ 20 $20 bucket. By a simple expected value calculation, if you put your ticket in the $ 80 $80 bucket, there is a probability 1 / 81 1/81 of you winning (your ticket and the 80 80 tickets already in the bucket) $ 80 $80, so your expected value is 80 / 81 80/81. Similarly, if you put your ticket in the $ 20 $20 bucket, the is a probability 1 / 21 1/21 of you winning $ 20 $20, so your expected value is 20 / 21 20/21. As 20 / 21 < 80 / 81 20/21<80/81, you should put the last ticket in the $ 80 $80 bucket. This allocation yields a net expected value of 2 202 ⋅ 200 + 1 81 ⋅ 80 ≈ 2.9679 202 2 ⋅200+ 81 1 ⋅80≈2.9679 For good measure, here are the expected values of some other common strategies: All 3 3 in the $ 200 $200 bucket: 2.9557 2.9557 One in each bucket: 2.9351 2.9351

questions.title: Bucket Allocation III
questions.problem: You and $100$ other players are each given $3$ tickets to distribute into three buckets with prizes $\$20, \$80,$ and $\$200$. One winning ticket is drawn from each bucket, and the winner gets the associated prize. A single person can win multiple buckets. Assuming each person plays optimally to maximize their expected payout, what is your strategy? If $e_i$ is the expected number of tickets you place in the bucket with $\$i$ in it, report 20 2 + 80 2 + 200 2 e 20 2 +e 80 2 +e 200 2 .
questions.solution: The idea of the indifference between the buckets from "Bucket Allocation I" is what should be applied here. If one were to employ a strategy that is more reliant to generate expected value from a certain bucket, say the $\$200$ one, another play could bias their distribution away from the $\$200$ bucket to have a higher probability of winning one of the other buckets. Every person must have the same optimal strategy because each person has the same set of information about the game. Therefore, everyone should be betting proportionally to the amount in each bucket. Since $2/3$ of the money is in the $\$200$ bucket, every person should put $2$ tickets in there. The last ticket is what differs from the previous problem. Since every person runs the same strategy, it's sub-optimal to always select the $\$80$ bin: If everyone else chooses the $\$80$ bin, you can unilaterally improve your strategy by putting your ticket in the $\$20$ bin, guaranteeing you $\$20$. Therefore, a mixed strategy is most appropriate. Since $4/5$ of the remaining $\$100$ is in the $\$80$ bucket, to bet proportionally to the prize of the bucket, you should place your last ticket in the $\$80$ bucket with probability $4/5$, while you place it in the $\$20$ bucket with probability $1/5$. We can conclude that 20 = 1 / 5 , 80 = 4 / 5 , e 20 =1/5,e 80 =4/5, and 200 = 2 e 200 =2, so the answer is $117/25$.

questions.title: Good Moves
questions.problem: A particle walks $(0, 0)$ to $(n, n)$ in a path of length $2n$ under the condition that it moves right or up one unit at each step. Two consecutive moves in the form ( , ) − > ( + 1 , ) − > ( + 1 , + 1 ) (a,b)−>(a+1,b)−>(a+1,b+1) are called a good pair of moves. How many paths can the particle take that have exactly $0 \leq m \leq n$ good pairs of moves? Report the answer when $n = 12$ and $m = 4$.
questions.solution: As we want to have exactly $m$ good movements in our sequence, it's in our best interest to first fix the $m$ sequences of good moves, denoted by $RU$ (right and up), and add in the other movements between them. Any valid sequence can be formed by first placing the $m$ good movements in our sequence, and then add in the − n−m right and − n−m upwards movements between them. The remaining $R$ and $U$ movements are identical (among movements of the same type) besides their ordering. However, we need to be careful that there are no sequences of $RU$ in any between regions, as that would make there be more than $m$ good moves in the sequence. The condition to make this happen is that all the in between movements must have all the $U$'s before the first $R$. Otherwise, if there is at last one $U$ remaining to be placed after the first $R$ is, there is a switch $RU$ somewhere in the "between" sequence. This implies a crucial fact for the problem: Given any amount of $R$ and $U$ for a "between" sequence, the only possible sequence of movements is in the form … … U…UR…R. Each of these sequences between is uniquely determined by the counts of R and U in them, so we need to compute the number of distinct ways to assign counts of R and U to each of the $m+1$ regions formed by the $m$ good moves. This sounds like a stars and bars problem on both $R$ and $U$ individually. Let 1 , … , + 1 x 1 ,…,x m+1 be the number of $R$ in each region. There are − n−m $R$ left to be assigned, so we must have 1 + ⋯ + + 1 = − x 1 +⋯+x m+1 =n−m, where each ≥ 0 x i ≥0. The number of solutions to this, by stars and bars, is ( − + ( + 1 ) − 1 ( + 1 ) − 1 ) = ( ) ( (m+1)−1 n−m+(m+1)−1 )=( m n ) The exact same stars and bars process works for the assignment of U as well. By the product rule, there are ( ) 2 ( m n ) 2 ways to assign the counts of R and U to the "between" regions, which also must be the number of paths from ( 0 , 0 ) (0,0) to ( , ) (n,n) that have exactly m good moves. With the specified values, the answer is ( 12 3 ) 2 = 48400 ( 3 12 ) 2 =48400.

questions.problem: $r$ elements of { 1 , 2 , … , } {1,2,…,n} are selected with replacement and arranged in order of selection. A fun run is a decreasing or an increasing subsequence of maximal length. For example, with $n = 6$ and $r = 10$, $54261453$ has $5$ fun runs: $542, 26, 61, 145, 53$. Given that no number is selected more than once in succession, find the expected number of fun runs when $n = 12$ and $r = 11$.
questions.solution: In the example, we can clearly see that the starts of fun runs are either larger or smaller that the values on either side of them. This is because they must end an increase/decreasing chain, so they break a pattern. Counting the number of fun runs is equivalent to counting the number of positions that start a fun run, so linearity of expectation seems to be a good approach. Similarly, the last position is never the start of a fun run, as no values come after it, so [ ] = 0 E[I n ]=0. Since values can't be the same in succession, we will want to break this into two cases: Positions − 1 i−1 and + 1 i+1 are distinct vs. the same. If positions − 1 i−1 and + 1 i+1 both have distinct values, position i must also have a value that's not the value of position − 1 i−1 nor + 1 i+1 by the given information. Given that the three values are distinct, the probability that position i is either the maximum or minimum is 2 / 3 2/3, as it's equally likely to be any of the three orders. If positions − 1 i−1 and + 1 i+1 agree, then position i must be different than both of positions − 1 i−1 and + 1 i+1 in this sub-case by our given information. Since position i is distinct from the (repeated) value of positions − 1 i−1 and + 1 i+1, it is either the maximum or minimum by definition, so it starts a new run with probability 1 1. Now, we need to consider the probabilities of each case above. When 3 ≤ ≤ − 1 3≤i≤n−1, − 1 ≥ 2 i−1≥2, so there are always − 1 r−1 possible values for each of position 2 2 to n (any of the other − 1 r−1 values that aren't in the prior position). questions.title: House Salesman I
questions.problem: Priyanshu is looking to purchase a very nice house in Bangalore. The price (in Lakh Rupees) is ∼ Unif ( , ) P∼Unif(a,b). He can bid any amount he wants for the house, and if he bids at least the true value of P, he gets the house. If he doesn't win the bid, nothing happens. Since Priyanshu is a great salesman, he can sell the house for a multiple of 1 + 1+p times the true house price, where 0 < < 1 0<p<1. How much should Priyanshu bid on the house when = 100 , = 1000 , a=100,b=1000, and = 0.5 p=0.5.
questions.solution: Priyanshu's expected profit is based on how much be bids for the house. If we knew his bid for the house, we could calculate the expected profit directly. Therefore, the natural idea is to calculate his expected profit as a function of his bid x, say $E(x)$, and then optimize in $x$. Our first key observation to simplifying the problem is that Priyanshu should always bid $a \leq x \leq b$. If he bids less than $a$, he will never win the bid, meaning his expected profit is $0$. If he bids more than $b$, he would always win the bid by just betting $b$, as the maximum possible value of the house is $b$. Thus, we can calculcate $E(x)$ for $a \leq x \leq b$. Priyanshu wins the house when it's true value is at most $x$. The probability of this is − − b−a x−a , as the price $P$ is Uniform, so we can take ratios of lengths to compute probabilities. Given he wins with a bid of $x$, the price of the house is Unif ( , ) Unif(a,x) distributed by the properties of Uniform distributions. The mean price of the house is + 2 2 x+a in this case, and Priyanshu would sell the house for $1+p$ times that amount. He paid $x$ for the house, so Priyanshu's expected profit given he wins is the expected amount he sells the house for minus the amount he paid. If he doesn't win the bid, nothing happens, so his profit is $0$. By the Law of Total Expectation, ( ) = − − ⋅ [ ( 1 + ) ⋅ + 2 − ] + ( 1 − − − ) ⋅ 0 = − 1 2 ( − ) ( − ) ( − ⋅ 1 + 1 − ) E(x)= b−a x−a ⋅[(1+p)⋅ 2 x+a −x]+(1− b−a x−a )⋅0= 2(b−a) p−1 (x−a)(x−a⋅ 1−p 1+p ) $E(x)$ is quadratic in $x$, so the maximum occurs at the midpoint of the roots. Thus, the optimal choice of $x$ is ∗ = + ⋅ 1 + 1 − 2 = 1 − x ∗ = 2 a+a⋅ 1−p 1+p = 1−p a Recall that this is the optimal choice of the bid. We take the minimum of this with b, as there's no reason to ever bid more than b, so the optimal bid is min ⁡ { 1 − , } min{ 1−p a ,b}. With the specified values, the answer is 200 200.

questions.title: Weighted Rolls
questions.problem: You and your friend both play a game: you both pick a number (doesn’t necessarily need to be an integer), and then roll two weighted $6-$sided dice with the values $1-6$ on the sides. The person who gets closest to the sum wins. The dice are non-uniform: there is a 40 % 40% chance of rolling a sum of $12$, and a 6 % 6% chance of rolling each of the other $10$ sums $2-11$. Assuming both you and your friend play optimally, if you go first, what is your strategy? Report your probability of winning as a percentage.
questions.solution: To find the optimal strategy, it's best to first find the smallest value $x$ at which there is at least 50 % 50% probability of the sum being at least $x$. It's natural to do this because this would be the point where you and your friend may want to center your bet around. We can easily see that the dice show at least $11$ with probability 46 % 46%, while the sum is at least $10$ with probability 52 % 52%. Thus, let's consider different cases on your guess $x$ and how your friend would respond. Suppose you guess $x > 10$. Since there is a 46 % 46% chance of the dice showing $11$ or $12$, there is a 54 % 54% chance of the dice showing $10$ or below, so your friend should give a response of − x−ε for some very small ε to ensure they are closer for anything $10$ or below. Suppose you guess $x = 10$. If your friend guesses anything larger than $10$, there is a 46 % 46% chance of them winning (either $11$ or $12$ appears), meaning there is a 54 % 54% chance you win. Alternatively, if they guess anything less than $10$, they have a 48 % 48% chance of winning (sum $2$ to $9$ appears), meaning you have a 52 % 52% chance of winning. Suppose you guess $x < 10$. If your friend guesses anything higher than you, say + x+ε, they are closer than you for at least $10-12$, which gives them at least a 52 % 52% chance of winning. By the above, the only case when you have a larger than 50 % 50% chance of winnning is when you guess $x = 10$. Your friend has at most a 48 % 48% chance of winning in this case by guessing 10 − 10−ε for some very small ε, as they capture the numbers $2-9$. Under the optimal strategy, you guess $10$, and you get a 52 % 52% chance of winning.

questions.title: Product Rolls I
questions.problem: Suppose you roll two standard fair $4-$sided dice. You can pay $\$2$ to reroll either of the dice, and this decision can be made as many times as you'd like. Your payout is the product of the upfaces of your final roll. Assuming optimal play, what is your expected value?
questions.solution: Suppose the two dice show the values $x_1$ and $x_2$ , where 1 < 2 x 1 <x 2 . If you make the decision to roll again, you should clearly roll the die showing $x_1$ , as the expected product of the dice would be larger if you have a larger multiplier. By iterating this methodology, the optimal strategy must be to continually reroll the dice until both are sufficiently large. More explicitly, the strategy is to reroll both dice until they both show at least t for some = 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 t=1,2,3,4. The goal is to find the expected value of our payout with each threshold. questions.title: Chess Mean Return I
questions.problem: A king starts at the bottom left corner of a standard $8 \times 8$ chessboard. A king can move to any adjacent square (vertical, horizontal, or diagonal) at any step, as long as it stays on the chess board. Find the expected time for the king to return to the bottom left corner if the king moves uniformly at random among all of it's possible moves at each step.
questions.solution: This Markov Chain is time-reversible: Any path that can be taken to get from the bottom left to any position can also be taken backwards to get back to the bottom left. Using this, we can use the classic theorem that relates the stationary distribution to expected return time. All that needs to be done is find the stationary distribution. We can view this random walk as one of a graph, where the degree of each square is equal to the number of squares that it can be reached by. By noting this, the stationary probability on each square is equal to it's degree as a proportion of the total degree of the graph. Intuitively, this makes sense; The proportion of time that the Markov Chain spends in a given state is directly proportional to how many "entry points" there are to that state. By a simple counting argument, there are 36 36 squares with 8 8 entry points (the inner 6 × 6 6×6 square), 24 24 squares with 5 5 entry points (the outer boundary of the 8 × 8 8×8 square, minus the corners), and 4 4 squares with 3 3 entry points (the 4 4 corners), yielding a total degree of 36 ⋅ 8 + 24 ⋅ 5 + 4 ⋅ 3 = 420 36⋅8+24⋅5+4⋅3=420. Thus, the limiting proportion on the bottom left corner is 3 / 420 = 1 / 140 3/420=1/140, so the expected return time is 140 140, the reciprocal of the limiting proportion.

questions.title: Murderous Circle
questions.problem: Suppose that there are $N$ people standing in a circle labeled $1$ through $N$ in order, where person $1$ has person $2$ on their left and person $N$ on their right. Define = 2 X=2 r , where $r$ is the maximum power such that 2 ≤ 2 r ≤N. Person $1$ takes a sword and kill the person to their left. Afterwards, they pass the sword to the next living person on their left, and the process continues circularly until one person remains. questions.solution: The general set-up of this problem suggests that there is something special about powers of $2$. In particular, it somewhat makes sense that the answer here would be related to a power of $2$, as at each rotation of the circle, you are essentially "halving" the number of people that remain in the circle, so as you are repeatedly rotating around a circle and halving, the answer should involve some modular arithmetic and powers of 2 2. First, let's consider the case where = 2 N=2 k for some positive integer k and explicitly work out some cases for small values of k. If = 1 k=1, then clearly person 1 1 wins, as they immediately kill person 2 2. If = 2 k=2, person 1 1 kills person 2 2, person 3 3 kills person 4 4, and then person 1 1 kills person 3 3. This means person 1 1 also wins here. More generally, once might assume that person 1 1 will always win in the case where N is a power of 2 2. This hunch would be correct. The reason that person 1 1 will always win is because of the fact that powers of 2 2 can always halve without a remainder, so the "relative position" of person 1 1 never really changes. Now, suppose that N is not a power of 2 2. This means that N is − N−X away from the largest power of 2 2 at most N by the definition of X. If − N−X people are killed in the circle, then the first person that begins with the knife immediately afterwards will be the last person standing. This is because there would now be a power of 2 2 number of people left in the circle, which means that the first person to start would be the last person standing. For example, with = 3 N=3, we have that person 1 1 kills person 2 2 and person 3 3 kills person 1 1. questions.title: Tripled? I
questions.problem: A child is playing baseball and tracking his batting average. This child is the next Babe Ruth, so at some point, his batting average is below 75 % 75%. However, later that day, his batting average is above 75 % 75%. Is it guaranteed that his batting average ever exactly 75 % 75%? Answer 1 1 if the answer is yes and 0 0 if the answer is no.
questions.solution: Imagine the balls being put into two stacks: "hit" and "not hit". For his batting average to be below 75 % 75% at one point, the "hit" stack must be less than $3$ times as tall as the "not hit" stack. However, later that day, the "hit" stack must exceed $3$ times the height of the not hit stack. Thus, no matter how tall the "not hit" stack is, at some point, there must have been exactly $3$ times as many balls in the "hit" stack as the "not hit" stack for there to be a change from below 75 % 75% to above 75 % 75%, as all of these are integers. Therefore, the answer is $1$.

questions.title: Tripled? II
questions.problem: A child is playing baseball and tracking his batting average. This child is the next Babe Ruth, so at some point, his batting average is below 60 % 60%. However, later that day, his batting average is above 60 % 60%. Is it guaranteed that his batting average was ever exactly 60 % 60%? Answer 1 1 if the answer is yes and 0 0 if the answer is no.
questions.solution: Imagine the balls being put into two stacks: "hit" and "not hit". For his batting average to be below 60 % 60% at one point, the "hit" stack must be less than $3/2$ as large as tall as the "not hit" stack. However, later that day, the "hit" stack must exceed $3/2$ times the height of the not hit stack. The approach of the previous question doesn't work because a $3/2$ multiple of the stack may be a non-integer. This hints at the fact that we can cook up an example where the $3/2$ multiple of the smaller stack is a non-integer. For example, suppose the child makes $1$ of his first two shots, so each stack is of size $1$. If the child makes the next shot, his proportion of shots made is $2/3$, which is larger than $3/5$. Thus, it's not guaranteed, and the answer is $0$.

Therefore, − 1 n−1 marbles are needed in this scenario, so the answer is 14 14.

questions.title: Hours and Minutes I
questions.problem: In how many positions do the minute and hour hands overlap on the face of an analog clock?
questions.solution: Starting at the $12:00$ position, in $t$ hours, the minutes hand complete $t$ revolutions around the clock, while the hour hand has completed $t/12$ revolutions (there are $12$ hours on the clock). The first time the minute and hour hands overlap, the minute hand has completed one lap more than the hour hand. Thus, $t = t/12 + 1$, or $t = 12/11$ hours. In general, on the nth time the hands meet, the minutes hand has completed n more laps than the hours hand, so the time $t$ at which the hands meet for the nth time, solves $t = t/12 + n$. The number of positions of intersection is exactly the number intersections in $12$ hours. With $t = 12$ (there are $12$ hours on a clock), we must have 12 = 12 / 12 + ⟺ = 11 12=12/12+n⟺n=11. Thus, there are $11$ intersections.

questions.title: Boy or Girl?

questions.solution: Naturally, the percentage of boys and girls will remain at a $50/50$ split in an infinitely large population because the probability that a girl is born is unaffected by the couples' preferences. Note that this doesn't hold if the population is of a finite size, as the argument here relies on the Law of Large Numbers to make the proportion of children in the population. Thus, the percentage of girls in the population is 1 2 2 1 .

questions.title: Special Multiple
questions.problem: Find the lowest multiple of $35$ that only has the digits $1$ and $0$.
questions.solution: We have two conditions: The number must have a units digit of zero, and it must be divisible by $7$. To check if a number is divisible by $7$, we can multiply the units digit by $2$, and subtract it from the rest of the number. Since the units digit is already $0$, this means we are simply looking for a number composed of one's and $0$s that is divisible by $7$, and we add a $0$ on to the end of it. The first number that satisfies this is $1001$, so the answer to this problem is $10010$.

questions.title: Integer-Valued Angles
questions.problem: Find the number of values of $n$ such that an $n$-sided polygon forms integer-valued interior angles.
questions.solution: The interior angles of a regular − n−gon are given by 180 ( − 2 ) $n$ 180(n−2) , where n is the number of sides. Intuitively, this makes sense: With $n = 3$, we get $60$, which is the degrees of each angle in an equilateral triangle, while $n = 4$ gives $90$, which is a square. Expanding this out, we can write it as 180 − 360 180− n 360 . For this expression to be an integer, $360/n$ must be an integer, meaning $n$ must divide $360$. This question now boils down to finding the divisors of $360$. This is easily done with the prime factorization 360 = 2 3 ⋅ 3 2 ⋅ 5 360=2 3 ⋅3 2 ⋅5. The number of prime factors is just the number of ways to choose an exponent $0$ to the maximum of each factor in the prime factorization, so there are $(3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 24$ divisors of $360$. However, two of these are invalid: $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ are not polygons, so there are $24- 2 = 22$ values of $n$.

questions.title: Digit Reversal
questions.problem: A $4-$digit number $abcd$ is such that $4 \cdot (abcd) = dcba$. Find $abcd$.

Therefore, $a = 2$ is fixed. Now, $4 \cdot (2bcd) = dcb2$, so $4 \cdot d$ must end with $2$. Only $d = 3$ and $d = 8$ satisfy this. However, as $a = 2$, $abcd \geq 2000$, so $4 \cdot (abcd) = dcba \geq 8000$, meaning $d = 8$ is correct. Our number is currently in the form $2bc8$. Since the first digit of $4 \cdot (2bc8) = 8cb2$ is $8$, the multiplication $4b$ must be at most $9$, as there is no carryover to make the $8$ turn into a $9$. Therefore, we can conclude $b = 1$ or $2$. As 4 ∣ 8 2 4∣8cb2, $4$ must divide $b2$. This is because 4 ∣ 100 4∣100, so we could right $8cb2 = 100 \cdot 8c + b2$. As 4 ∣ 12 4∣12 and 4 ∤ 22 4∤22, $b = 1$ is correct. Our final task is to determine $c$ in $4 \cdot (21c8) = 8c12$. Note that $4 \leq c \leq 7$, as $2100 < 21c8 < 2200$, so $8400 < 4 \cdot (21c8) < 8800$. By manually testing these $4$ values, one can confirm $c = 7$ is correct, which yields $4 \cdot 2178 = 8712$. questions.title: isprime() IV
questions.problem: You have two integers $x$ and $y$, with $y \geq 0$. From these two integers, you form three new ones of the form $x$, $x+y$, and $x+2y$. If the product of the the three new integers is prime, what is $xy$?
questions.solution: The first step in solving this problem is realizing that two of your three new numbers must be $1$ and $-1$. This is to satisfy the definition of a prime number, which is that it only has two factors: $1$ and itself. If this wasn't the case, the product would have at least $2$ distinct factors, meaning it isn't prime. As the definition of a prime number requires it to be at least $2$, and the difference between $1$ and $-1$ is $2$, we know that the last number must also be negative to counteract the $-1$ and make the product positive. We should subtract $2$ from $-1$ to get $-3$, meaning our sequence is $-3,-1,1$, so as $y \geq 0$, = − 3 x=−3 and $y = 2$. Thus, = − 6 xy=−6 is the answer.

questions.title: 2D Collisions II
questions.problem: On an infinite two-dimensional frictionless plane, $m$ unit squares slide in the positive direction, while $n$ more unit square slide towards them in the other direction. When the unit squares collide, they will elastically rebound in the other direction with the same speed. Let x be the number of squares that end up proceeding in the negative direction, while y be the number of squares that end up proceeding in the positive direction. Find the value of − y−x when = 100 m=100 and = 50 n=50.
questions.solution: The key with many of these movement and rebound problems is that the problem before and after the collision is symmetric: When two squares collide, it's really as if nothing happened, as there is still one square moving in each direction at the same speed as before the collision. Thus, you could envision it as the squares phasing through one another. Since the number of squares moving in each direction is unchanged after any collision, the number of squares moving in each direction at the end of the process is the same as at the start. Thus, = y=m and = x=n, so the answer is − m−n. With the specified values, the answer is 50 50.

questions.title: Coaster Time
questions.problem: You play a game with a friend where each of you have unlimited coasters and a circular table of any size. You win the game when your opponent runs out of space to put coasters on the table. What is the optimal strategy to win this game? Under this strategy, do you want to go first or second? Enter 1 1 for first and 2 2 for second. If there is no strategy guaranteeing a win, enter − 1 −1.
questions.solution: Let's play the game with the first and second players unassigned, and consider the optimal moves per player. Intuitively, the key lies in the shape of the table: Since it's circular, we can "mirror" valid opponent moves to get another valid move. The only one that can't be mirrored is putting a coaster right in the center of the table. Thus, the optimal strategy is for the first player to put a coaster right in the center of the table. From then on, any move player 2 2 makes, player 1 1 puts a coaster in the mirror opposite location (i.e. rotated 180 180 degrees about the origin). If the move of player 2 2 was valid, the move of player 1 1 will be too. By doing this, player 1 1 has a valid move if and only if player 2 2 does, and player 2 2 has to go first after player 1 1 puts their coaster in the center, so the first person to run out of moves with be player 2 2. As a result, you should go first.

questions.title: Diluted Juice II
questions.problem: You have two equally-sized cups, one has juice and one has water. You pour some of the water into the juice cup, and then pour some of that mixture back into the water cup so that they are of equal volume once again. What is the difference between the percentage of water in the diluted water cup and the percentage of juice in the diluted juice cup?
questions.solution: The answer hinges on the following clear observation: If the volumes of liquid in each container return to the exact same amounts, then, after the transfer of the juice and water, the amount of juice that was transferred to the water has to be the same amount of water that was transferred to the juice. Intuitively, this makes sense: If we transfer some amount of water to the juice, and then some amount of mixed juice and water back to the water, whatever amount of water is now in the juice must be the amount of juice now transferred to the water, as the volumes of each before and after transferring must be the same. More succinctly, you can think about it as: the amount of juice transferred to the water has to be the same amount of water transferred to the juice in order to keep both volumes the same in the end. As a result, the answer is 0 0.

questions.title: Taxman Game
questions.problem: You play a game against an opponent that begins with you selecting a number from $1-10$ on a board. Your opponent will then remove every number that evenly divides the number that you selected from the board. When you select a number, it must have at least one factor that is not itself remaining on the board. You repeat this process until there are no more numbers on the board. Your score is the sum of all of the numbers you select. What is your final score?
questions.solution: The first thing to notice is the number of choices you get to make. Since you can only choose numbers that have at least one factor that is not itself remaining on the board, you can (at best) hope to choose 5 numbers, since there are 10 numbers in total, and at least 2 numbers will be removed every time you make a choice (the number you chose, and all of its factors). So, our goal will be to choose numbers so that (1) we maximize the sum of chosen numbers and (2) we get to choose 5 numbers. In order to choose 5 numbers, we need to make sure that every time we choose a number it only has one factor which is not itself remaining. Given this, our first choice will be to choose the largest prime number we can, since the only factor the prime number will have other than itself will be 1. So, our first choice will be 7. The remaining numbers are now 10, 9, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2. Now, note that the numbers 10, 9, 8, and 6 are all individually greater than the sum of all their respective factors, which means it's better to choose these numbers than it is to choose their factors. Thus, our task is now to determine in what order we should choose the numbers 10, 9, 8, and 6. We can go ahead and choose 9, since it's only factor on the board is 3. Our list of numbers is now 10, 8, 6, 5, 4, 2. The only number with a single factor is now 6, so we choose 6 next, and our list of numbers is now, 10, 8, 5, 4. Now both 8 and 10 each only have a single factor on the board, and we can choose them in any order we want. Thus, our total score is 7 + 9 + 6 + 8 + 10 = 40.

questions.title: Fortune Cookies I
questions.problem: You buy a package of $n$ fortune cookies and open each one to see the fortune slip inside. The first slip says "a maximum of $0$ of these $n$ slips tell the truth." The next slip says "a maximum of $1$ of these $n$ slips tell the truth.", and so on, until the last slip, which says "a maximum of − 1 n−1 of these $n$ slips tell the truth." How many of these slips are telling the truth when $n = 1000$?
questions.solution: It may help to consider some small cases, such as $n = 2$ or $n = 3$, and then try to generalize the pattern. For two slips, only one will tell the truth: The two slips will say at most $0$ and at most $1$ tell the truth. From here on, we will refer to slip $i$ as the one that says at most $i$ tell the truth. If slip $0$ were true, it would be an automatic contradiction to itself, so slip $0$ must be false. As there's only one other slip, it must be the case that slip $1$ as true, as there can't be more than $1$ true statement. For three slips, slip $0$ can't be true for the same reason as in the previous part. If slip $1$ were true, slip $2$ would also be true, making there be $2$ truths, so slip $1$ can't be true. As there's only one slip left, slip $2$ must be true, making there be $1$ truthful slip. More generally, with $n$ slips, all of the slips past slip $k$ for some $k$ must be true: if slip $k$ is true, there are at most $k$ true statements, so there are also at most ′ > $k$ ′ >k statements true, making slip ′ k ′ true. Thus, our goal is to find the minimum value of $k$ such that statements k to − 1 n−1 are true, while statements $1$ to $k$ are false. Remember, the largest slip says that at most − 1 n−1 statements are true, so we stop at − 1 n−1. For this to be true, the number of true statements, − n−k (for this value of k, statements k to − 1 n−1 are all true) must be at most k, as we claim that there are at most k statements that are true when saying slip k is true. Mathematically, this means − ≤ ⟺ ≥ 2 n−k≤k⟺k≥ 2 n This is the minimum value of k such that statements k to − 1 n−1 are true, so there are exactly − ⌈ / 2 ⌉ n−⌈n/2⌉ true values. We take the ceiling because the minimum value must be an integer. With = 1000 n=1000, the answer is 500 500.

questions.title: Exponential Digits II
questions.problem: How many digits are in 99 99 99 99 ?
questions.solution: Intuitively, we would expect that we lose $1$ digit to the fact that $99$ starts with $2$ digits (rather than $3$), and $2$ digits to the fact that we only raise 99 99 99 99 as opposed to 99 100 99 100 . Based on our answer to "Exponential Digits I", an initial guess is $198$ digits. To verify this, we must ensure 10 197 ≤ 99 99 < 10 $198$ 10 197 ≤99 99 <10 $198$ . The latter inequality is obvious, as 99 99 < 100 99 = 10 198 99 99 <100 99 =10 198 . As for the first inequality, we need to use the helpful fact that ( 1 + 1 / ) < (1+1/n) n <e for all positive integers n (although it tends to e in limit). It makes sense that e would be involved somehow, as we have terms that look like exponentials. Using this, ( 100 99 ) 99 = ( 1 + 1 / 99 ) 99 < ( 99 100 ) 99 =(1+1/99) 99 <e Therefore, we can conclude 100 99 < 99 99 ⋅ 100 99 <99 99 ⋅e, so 99 99 > 1 / ⋅ 100 99 > 1 / 10 ⋅ 10 198 = 10 197 99 99 >1/e⋅100 99 >1/10⋅10 198 =10 197 Therefore, we can conclude 99 99 99 99 has exactly 198 198 digits. To verify our answer, we can use a trick: To find the number of digits in = n=x y , we take the floor of ( ⋅ log ⁡ 10 ( ) ) + 1 (y⋅log 10 (x))+1. This gives us ( 99 ⋅ log ⁡ 10 ( 99 ) ) + 1 ≈ ( 99 ⋅ 1.995 ) + 1 ≈ 197.505 + 1 = 198.505 (99⋅log 10 (99))+1≈(99⋅1.995)+1≈197.505+1=198.505. When floored, this gives us the number of digits, 198 198.

questions.title: Unconventional Sum
questions.problem: Find the sum of the digits of all numbers from $0$ to $10,000$.
questions.solution: The key to this problem is extend out integers so that they all have the same number of digits. This allows us to compare them directly. To do this, we append $0$s out front until the number has $4$ digits (we will add $1$ back in at the end to account for $10000$). Doing this, we have the integers $0000$ to $9999$, and it's okay to include $0000$, as it has a sum of digits equal to $0$. The sum of all digits in this range can be found by considering the mean value of each digit, which is simply 0 + 9 2 = 4.5 2 0+9 =4.5. As the mean value of each digit is $4.5$, the average sum of digits is 4.5 ⋅ 4 = 18 $4.5 \cdot 4 = 18$. As there are $10000$ numbers considered, the sum of all digits in this range must be $18 \cdot 10000 = 180000$. Adding in $1$ for $10000$, the answer is $180001$.

questions.title: Added Digits II
questions.problem: Consider all five digit numbers whose digits, when pairwise added, are unique and do not contain $0$. Find the smallest number that fits this condition.
questions.solution: Our goal is to make our $5-$digit number as small as possible, and have all distinct sums. The smallest numbers are $1,2,$ and $3$, and these all have distinct pairwise sums, so the number should start with $123$. Our fourth digit cannot be a $4$ because $1+4=2+3$, so our fourth digit will be $5$, as this doesn't violate the condition of having distinct pairwise sums, meaning our number is now in the form $1235X$. Since $1+6 = 2 + 5$, $6$ can't be the last digit. Since $1+7 = 3+5$, $7$ can't be the last digit either. However, with $8$, the condition is not violated, so $12358$ is the number.

questions.title: Liquid Measurement I
questions.problem: You are given the task of measuring out $200$ml of liquid using a faucet, a $1100$ml bottle, and a $700$ml bottle. A transfer of liquid is counted as filling a bottle, emptying a bottle, or transferring from one bottle to another. What is the minimum number of transfers to measure $200$ml?
questions.solution: The idea of bucket questions is to usually perform continual transfers from one to the other. This can be accomplished in $18$ transfers by filling up the $1100$ml bottle and continuously transferring it to the $700$ml bottle. Conversely, you can accomplish this in $14$ transfers by filling up the $700$ml bottle and continuously transferring that to the $1100$ml bottle. The algorithm would take the following steps: If the $1100$ml bottle is full, empty it. Otherwise, fill the $700$ml bottle, and transfer the contents to the $1100$ml bottle. Continue to do this until the $700$ml bottle has $200$ml in it.

questions.title: Optimal Payout
questions.problem: You are given a stack of $100$ poker chips. Each poker chip is worth $\$1$. You are allowed to divide your poker chips into any number of stack of any size. In which case, your payout is the product of the sizes of all stacks. For example, two stacks of $50$ yields a payout of $50\cdot50=2500$. Provide your answer as the product of all unique stacks values multiplied by the number of duplicated stacks
questions.solution: The key to this problem is recognizing that we must continuously break down the stack sizes. Let's begin with $20$ stacks of $5$. This yields 5 20 5 20 payout. However, if we divide the stack of $5$ into a stack of $3$ and $2$, we get $3\cdot2=6$, which is a greater payout multiplier. Thus, we divide our stacks into stacks of $3$, which yields $33$ stacks of $3$, and one stack of $1$. This is better, but having a stack of $1$ does not increase the expected value. So we create $32$ stacks of $3$ and $1$ stack of $4$, which gives us an answer of $32\cdot 3 \cdot 4=384$ and a payout of 4 ⋅ 3 32 4⋅3 32 .

questions.title: Ending Value
questions.problem: Let ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } N∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n} for some $n > 0$. Let $p(n)$ be the probability that $N^3$ ends in $81$. If it exists, compute lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) n→∞ lim p(n). If the limit doesn't exist, report $-1$.
questions.solution: To solve this problem, we should first thing about what types of numbers $n$ have their last two digits as $81$ when cubed. To have the final digit of $n^3$ be $1$, $n$ must also end in $1$: $n$ clearly can't end in an even number, or else it will be even. If $n$ ends in $3,5,7,$ or $9$, $n^3$ ends in $7,5,3,$ and $9$, respectively. Thus, $n = 10k + 1$ for some non-negative integer $k$. The idea now is to expand out $n^3$ to see what the terms look like, which yields 3 = ( 10 + 1 ) 3 = 1000 3 + 300 2 + 30 + 1 n 3 =(10k+1) 3 =1000k 3 +300k 2 +30k+1 As $k$ is an integer, 1000 3 1000k 3 and 300 2 300k 2 will not influence the last two digits of $n^3$ , as they are divisible by $100$ and $1000$, respectively. Thus, only $30k+1$ influences the last two digits. For the last two digits to be $81$, we must have 30 + 1 ≡ 81 ( mod 100 ) 30k+1≡81(mod100). This happens exactly when ≡ 6 ( mod 10 ) k≡6(mod10), which can be seen by noting $30 \cdot 6 + 1 = 181$. Thus, if $k = 10m + 6$ for some positive integer $m$, $n^3$ ends in $81$, so $n = 10k + 1 = 10(10m+6) + 1 = 100m + 61$ The above implies that every integer whose last two digits are $61$ satisfy this condition. Exactly one integer per $100$ integers has it's last two digits as $61$, so the limiting proportion integers whose cube ends in $81$ is $1/100$, which is the answer.

questions.title: Product Combinations II
questions.problem: There are four positive real numbers, $w, x, y, z$, which, when pairwise multiplied, you get $9$, $10$, $12$, $27$, $30$, or $n$. What is the missing number $n$?
questions.solution: Let's first start by considering integers. Since $12$ and $30$ are both divisible by $6$, a natural choice is to first consider $w = 6$ (it doesn't really matter what way you arrange them). With this, we can see that $6 \cdot 5 = 30$ and $6 \cdot 2 = 12$, so $x = 2$ and $y = 5$ are two of the other values. This choice also generates $2 \cdot 5 = 10$. The values not accounted for yet are $9, 27,$ and $n$. Since $9 = 2 \cdot 9/2$ and $27 = 6 \cdot 9/2$, the last value must be $z = 9/2$, and the only unaccounted pair is 5 ⋅ 9 / 2 = 22.5 $5 \cdot 9/2 = 22.5$.

questions.title: How Many Shakes?
questions.problem: You are with your spouse at a party, along with $n$ other couples. Some people shake hands at this party, although nobody shakes hands with themselves or their spouse. You observe that everyone (excluding yourself, but including your spouse) shook hands with a different number of people. How many people did your spouse shake hands with? Report the answer when = 14 n=14.
questions.solution: There are $2n+1$ people other than yourself ( $n$ couples and your spouse), and it's given that nobody shook the same amount of hands as anyone else. Since nobody shakes hands with their spouse, nobody else shakes hands with more than $2n$ people at the party. As there are $2n+1$ people and none of them shake the same amount of hands, the people must have shaken 0 , 1 , … , 2 0,1,…,2n hands. Label the person that shook $i$ hands as $p_i$ . Since we want to figure out your spouse, it's natural to try to pair up the people based on how many hands they shook. 2 p 2n must have shaken hands of everyone at the party besides themselves and their spouse. In particular, we know 2 p 2n didn't shake hands with $p_0$ , as $p_0$ doesn't shake hands with anyone, so 2 p 2n and $p_0$ must be partners. Similarly, 2 − 1 p 2n−1 must have shaken hands with everyone except themselves and their spouse. By the same logic, $p_0$ didn't shake hands with 2 − 1 p 2n−1 , nor did $p_1$ , as 2 p 2n shook the hand of $p_1$ , meaning that is the only person they could have shaken hands with. Thus, 2 − 1 p 2n−1 and $p_1$ are partners. We can continually iterate this logic to conclude 2 − p 2n−i is paired with $p_i$ . There are $2n+1$ people remaining, including your spouse, so looking over 0 ≤ ≤ − 1 0≤i≤n−1, we get $2n$ people in $n$ couples, leaving one person left: $p_n$ , the person who shook $n$ pairs. Since this is the only person left unpaired, your spouse must be $p_n$ . Thus, your spouse shook $n$ hands. When $n = 14$, the answer is $14$.

questions.title: Most Recent Three
questions.problem: A coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ is repeatedly flipped until two of the three most recent flips are heads. If the first two flips are $HH$, the process ends in two flips. Find the expected number of flips performed when $p = 1/3$.
questions.solution: It's very tempting to start with a Markov chain by conditioning on the first flip. However, this is an incorrect approach because the first three flips are really separate from anything more than $3$ flips. This is because there aren't $3$ previous flips yet to compare to. Therefore, the better approach is to consider the number of flips until the first head, as we really aren't interested in anything until at least one head appears in our "history" of the last three flips, and then condition on the next two flips afterwards. We condition on the next two flips because the head and the next two flips form a sequence of 3 3 flips. Let's bring this into math. Let N be the number of flips until the first heads appears, and E be the expected number of flips we perform in total. As there is a probability p of heads per flip, ∼ Geom ( ) N∼Geom(p). Thus, it takes 1 / 1/p flips to obtain the first heads on average. After the first heads appears, we can consider the 4 4 outcomes of the next two flips: If the next flip immediately afterwards is heads (occurs with probability p), only 1 1 additional flip is needed, as our condition is satisfied. If the next two flips are TH (occurs with probability ( 1 − ) p(1−p)), 2 2 additional flips are needed, and the ending sequence is HTH. If the next two flips are TT (occurs with probability ( 1 − ) 2 (1−p) 2 ), the process is essentially reset: Since the two flips after the H were TT, HTT is our history, so the next flip after this will take the H out of the history. We would have to wait for another H and then repeat the process above, so 2 + 2+E flips are performed on average ( 2 2 for the TT and E additional beyond that). By the Law of Total Expectation, we can conclude = 1 + ⋅ 1 + ( 1 − ) ⋅ 2 + ( 1 − ) 2 ⋅ ( 2 + ) ⟺ = 2 − ( 1 − ) 2 2 ( 2 − ) E= p 1 +p⋅1+p(1−p)⋅2+(1−p) 2 ⋅(2+E)⟺E= p 2 (2−p) 2−(1−p) 2 As a quick sanity check, we can see that the expected value is 2 2 when = 1 p=1, which makes sense, as the first two flips are always heads. Furthermore, when = 0 p=0, the expected value tends to ∞ ∞, as we'd have to wait extremely long amounts of time when p is small to observe two heads in the last three flips. With = 1 / 3 p=1/3, the answer is 42 / 5 = 8.4 42/5=8.4.

questions.title: Stunted Coin Flip I

If one shows heads and the other shows tails, the person who got a heads repeatedly flips their coin until it becomes a tails, and then both of them simultaneously flip again under the same rules. The value of $N$ is dependent on what happens in the first two flips, since the first two flips determine the sequence of actions that happen next. Thus, it's best to condition on the outcome of the flip two flips to compute [ ] E[N]. Using the Law of Total Expectation, let 0 , 1 , H 0 ,H 1 , and $H_2$ be the events that $0,1,$ and $2$ heads appear in the first two flips. Thus, the average number of flips for this case is [ ∣ 0 ] = 2 + [ ] E[N∣H 0 ]=2+E[N]. The probability of two tails in two flips is 1 / 2 2 = 1 / 4 1/2 2 =1/4 by independence. If one heads occurs, 2 2 flips are counted first. Afterwards, the person with a heads must flip until they get a tails. The number of flips needed for this to occur can be represented as a random variable ∼ Geom ( 1 / 2 ) M∼Geom(1/2), as there is probability 1 / 2 1/2 per trial of landing a tails. After the M trials needed for the person to get a tails, the game is back in the original state it started in, so N additional flips are needed to end the game. Thus, 2 + + 2+M+N flips are needed to end the game in this case, meaning [ ∣ 1 ] = 2 + [ ] + [ ] = 4 + [ ] E[N∣H 1 ]=2+E[M]+E[N]=4+E[N] flips are needed on average. The probability of 1 1 head and 1 1 tail in two flips is 1 / 2 1/2. Lastly, if 2 2 heads occur, the game ends immediately in 2 2 flips, so [ ∣ 2 ] = 2 E[N∣H 2 ]=2, and the probability of this case is 1 / 4 1/4 by independence. Plugging into the Law of Total Expectation expression from before, [ ] = 1 4 ⋅ ( 2 + [ ] ) + 1 2 ⋅ ( 4 + [ ] ) + 1 4 ⋅ 2 ⟺ [ ] = 12 E[N]= 4 1 ⋅(2+E[N])+ 2 1 ⋅(4+E[N])+ 4 1 ⋅2⟺E[N]=12

questions.title: Secured Timecapsule
questions.problem: A group of $7$ friends make a time capsule. They only want the time capsule to be opened when $4$ or more of the friends want to open it, so they put locks on the time capsule. What is the minimum number of locks needed $l$, and how many keys must each person carry $k$? Report the value of $l+k$.
questions.solution: To solve this, we must think about how locks and keys should be assigned. First, lets look at the condition where the timecapsule cannot be opened. A group of $3$ of the friends will possess a key to every lock except for one, as the minimum condition to open all of the locks requires $4$ individuals. Thus, the $4$ other friends must all possess a key to this final lock such that the timecapsule can be opened in the presence of $4$ individuals. This means that for each subset of $3$ friends, there should exist a lock which none of them have the key to. From this, the minimum number of locks must be ( 7 3 ) = 35 ( 3 7 )=35 locks. This gives us the number of locks, which is $35$. Now, we need to find the number of keys each person carries such that $4$ people can open all of these $35$ locks. This means each lock has $4$ keys, giving us $4\cdot35=140$ keys, or $20$ keys per person. Therefore, our answer is $35+20=55$.

questions.title: Transaction Change
questions.problem: Suppose that someone purchases a piece of candy for $n$ cents, where $n$ is in the range $1-100$. What is the fewest number of coins (of denomination $1, 5, 10, 25$) that you need to always provide change for this transaction?
questions.solution: Our goal is to optimize for a combination of coins where the quantity of the coins is minimized and we can provide change for any value of $n$ between $1$ and $99$. From this, we can begin by considering that we will need four coins of denomination $1$ to provide change for the following values of $n$, { 96 , 97 , 98 , 99 } {96,97,98,99}. We then need one coin of denomination $5$, which will allow us to provide change for all values of $n$ from $91-99$. The next step is to ensure that we can provide change for any value ending in $1-9$. To do this, we can begin with $3$ coins of denomination $25$. In conjunction with our previous coins, we can provide change for $66-75$, $41-50$, and $16-25$, as well as $91-99$. Lastly, we will need to use coins of denomination $10$ to close the gaps on the values of $n$ we can provide change for. In order for us to cover the range between $75-91$, we will need at least $2$ coins of denomination $10$. Our new ranges become $1-25$, $21-50$, $46-75$, and $71-99$. This covers all values of $n$ from $1-99$, but with some overlap between values which we can no longer reduce. In total, we need $10$ coins: four $1$'s, one $5$, two $10$'s, and three $25$'s.

questions.problem: How many digits are in 2 1000 2 1000 and 5 1000 5 1000 ? Provide your answer as the sum of both digit counts.
questions.solution: For this problem, we should have logarithm base $10$ memorized for all single digits. In general, the number of digits in an integer is ⌊ 1 + log ⁡ 10 ( ) ⌋ ⌊1+log 10 (n)⌋. You can verify this for small n. For 2 1000 2 1000 , the number of digits is ( 1000 ⋅ log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) ) + 1 ≈ ( 1000 ⋅ 0.301 ) + 1 ≈ 301.03 + 1 = 302.03 (1000⋅log 10 (2))+1≈(1000⋅0.301)+1≈301.03+1=302.03. When floored, this gives us the number of digits, 302 302. For 5 1000 5 1000 , we have ( 1000 ⋅ log ⁡ 10 ( 5 ) ) + 1 ≈ ( 1000 ⋅ 0.6989 ) + 1 ≈ 698.9 + 1 = 699.9 (1000⋅log 10 (5))+1≈(1000⋅0.6989)+1≈698.9+1=699.9. When floored, this gives us the number of digits, 699 699. In total, this is 699 + 302 = 1001 699+302=1001 digits.

questions.title: Check Error
questions.problem: When cashing a check, a man received an incorrect sum where the dollar and cent fields on his check were swapped. The man did not realize this error until he got home, in which he realized that he received exactly twice the original value of the check, plus 5 5 cents. What was his original check worth?
questions.solution: In order to solve this problem, we will create an equation for the check balance and equate it to the actual balance. Let $a$ and $b$ be the dollar and cent amounts on the original check, respectively. The total amount of money on the check was + 0.01 a+0.01b, whereas the amount of money he received was + 0.01 b+0.01a, since the dollar and cent positions were swapped. As per the question, the amount he received, + 0.01 b+0.01a, is equal to 0.05 0.05 more than twice as much as the original check, + 0.01 a+0.01b. Thus, our equation relating the value of the check and the received amount is 2 ( + 0.01 ) + 0.05 = + 0.01 ⟺ 2 + ( 0.02 + 0.05 ) = + 0.01 2(a+0.01b)+0.05=b+0.01a⟺2a+(0.02b+0.05)=b+0.01a We have the relationship between a and b above, but we must now solve for a and b. The solution will depend on whether or not the cents on the LHS roll over into a new dollar. In particular, if 0.02 + 0.05 < 1 0.02b+0.05<1, the dollars of each side are 2 2a and b, respectively, so = 2 b=2a. The cents of each side would have to be equal too, so 0.01 = 0.02 + 0.05 0.01a=0.02b+0.05. Since = 2 b=2a from above, 0.01 = 0.04 + 0.05 ⟺ 0.03 = − 0.05 0.01a=0.04a+0.05⟺0.03a=−0.05a, which isn't possible, as > 0 a>0. Because of this, the cents must roll over into a new dollar, so = 2 + 1 b=2a+1, as one additional dollar is created from the cents. The number of cents on the LHS is 0.02 + 0.05 − 1 0.02b+0.05−1, since 0.02 + 0.05 0.02a+0.05 is more than a dollar, and this dollar is counted with = 2 + 1 b=2a+1. As the number of cents on the LHS and RHS must be equal, substituting in our condition, 0.02 + 0.05 − 1 = 0.01 ⟺ 0.02 ( 2 + 1 ) − 0.95 = 0.01 ⟺ 0.03 = 0.93 ⟺ = 31 0.02b+0.05−1=0.01a⟺0.02(2a+1)−0.95=0.01a⟺0.03a=0.93⟺a=31 As we have a, we also can obtain = 2 ( 31 ) + 1 = 63 b=2(31)+1=63. Therefore, the man's original check balance was 31.63 31.63.

questions.title: Binomial Sum

questions.title: Middle Coins
questions.problem: You have $4$ fair coins before you, and you flip them under the following procedure: Flip all four coins. Count up the number of heads and tails that appear. Whichever parity has more coins showing it, flip all the coins of that parity again. If the number of heads and tails are equal, end the game. We define a round as any grouping of coins being flipped. Find the expected number of rounds needed for the game to end.
questions.solution: To frame this problem probabilistically, let $E$ be the total number of flips that need to be performed. The number of additional flips that need to be performed is dependent on the number of coins showing the more frequent outcome in the first flip: If there are 2 2 of each initially, we're done, but if we need to reflip 3 3 or 4 4 coins, there are additional rounds that need to be performed. Thus, the best approach is to condition on the number of coins showing among the more frequent parity. Since the coin is fair, it's irrelevant whether there are more heads or more tails showing. Let 2 , 3 , E 2 ,E 3 , and 4 E 4 be the expected number of additional rounds that need to be performed given there are 2 , 3 , 2,3, and 4 4 coins showing of the more frequent parity. Lastly, let X be the number of coins showing the more frequent parity on the first flip. By the Law of Total Expectation, = 1 + 2 [ = 2 ] + 3 [ = 3 ] + 4 [ = 4 ] E=1+E 2 P[X=2]+E 3 P[X=3]+E 4 P[X=4] If an equal number of heads and tails appear on the first flip, the game ends, so 2 = 0 E 2 =0, as no additional flips must be performed. If we have to flip 3 3 coins again, the first flip has to either have 3 3 heads and 1 1 tail, or vice versa. WLOG, assume it's 3 3 heads and 1 1 tail. When flipping the three heads again, there are four options: If no tails appear, we're in the same state as before, so 3 E 3 additional rounds are needed on average with probability 1 / 2 3 = 1 / 8 1/2 3 =1/8. If one tail appears, there are an equal number of heads and tails, so no additional rounds are needed with probability 3 / 8 3/8. If two tails appear, there are 3 3 tails and 1 1 head, so we're really in the same situation as before, since we are flipping 3 3 coins next round. 3 E 3 additional rounds are needed on average with probability 3 / 8 3/8 here. If three tails appear, all 4 4 coins are tails, so we are flipping all coins again. This is identical to the situation we had at the start: We flip all the coins, so E additional rounds are needed in this situation with probability 1 / 8 1/8. Aggregating all of these, by Law of Total Expectation, 3 = 1 + 1 2 3 + 1 8 ⟺ 3 = 2 + 1 4 E 3 =1+ 2 1 E 3 + 8 1 E⟺E 3 =2+ 4 1 E The 1 1 out front comes from the round we just performed. Now that we have 3 E 3 , we must find [ = 3 ] P[X=3]. This is the event that either 3 3 heads or 3 3 tails appear in the initial 4 4 flips. By using the Binomial distribution PMF, we can quickly see [ = 3 ] = 1 / 2 P[X=3]=1/2, as there are ( 4 3 ) = 4 ( 3 4 )=4 ways to get 3 3 heads, and likewise with 3 3 tails. By the description from the last bullet point, 4 = E 4 =E, as we are just flipping everything again, which is the same as the scenario used to model the equation for E. To reflip all 4 4 coins, all of the coins must show the same value, which is 2 2 of the 16 16 equally likely outcomes ( HHHH and TTTT), so [ = 4 ] = 1 / 8 P[X=4]=1/8. By substituting 3 E 3 in terms of E and 4 = E 4 =E into the initial LOTE equation for E, we get = 1 + 1 2 ( 2 + 1 4 ) + 1 8 ⟺ = 8 / 3 E=1+ 2 1 (2+ 4 1 E)+ 8 1 E⟺E=8/3

questions.title: Multiplicative Digits
questions.problem: When written out fully, how many digits does 2 53 ⋅ 3 3 ⋅ 5 50 ⋅ 13 $2$ 53 ⋅3 3 ⋅$5$0 ⋅13 2 have?
questions.solution: The terms with very large exponents are $2$ and $5$. When considering total digits, it's natural to first consider the number of trailing zeros. A trailing $0$ is formed by being divisible by $10 = 2 \cdot 5$. Thus, the number of trailing zeros is equal to the number of times $10$ divides the integer. We can selectively write this integer as 2 53 ⋅ 3 3 ⋅ 5 50 ⋅ 13 2 = ( 2 ⋅ 5 ) 50 ⋅ 2 3 ⋅ 3 3 ⋅ 13 2 = 10 50 ⋅ 216 ⋅ 169 2 53 ⋅3 3 ⋅5 50 ⋅13 2 =(2⋅5) 50 ⋅2 3 ⋅3 3 ⋅13 2 =10 50 ⋅216⋅169 The above implies there are $50$ trailing zeros in the expansion of the integer. Now, we note that 216 ⋅ 169 > 100 ⋅ 100 = 10 4 216⋅169>100⋅100=10 4 , while 216 ⋅ 169 < 216 ⋅ 200 < 10 5 216⋅169<216⋅200<10 5 , so the $216 \cdot 169$ term out front is an integer between $10000$ and $100000$, meaning it has $5$ digits. Therefore, the front contributes $5$ digits, yielding a total of $55$ digits.

questions.title: Even Gap
questions.problem: Sam has $2n$ blocks: $n$ distinct colors with $2$ replicates per color. He lines up the blocks uniformly at random. Find the probability that there are an even number of blocks between every pair of identically-colored blocks. Report the answer with $n = 5$.
questions.solution: Since the blocks are being arranged in a line, it's best to consider a line with $2n$ empty spots labelled $1$ to $2n$. For any given color to have an even amount of blocks between them, it must be the case that the two blocks are in spaces with opposite parity. For example, if the two blocks are in spaces $3$ and $7$, spaces $4,5,$ and $6$ lie between them, which is an odd amount of spaces. Thus, our condition really is that one block of each color lies on an odd-valued spot, while the other is in an even-numbered spot. Since the arrangement is generated uniformly at random, we can convert this into a counting problem. The total number of distinct ways to arrange the 2 2n blocks of n distinct colors onto the 2 2n spots is easiest computed via anagrams. Each of the spots will be given a label 1 − 1−n, and there are 2 2 labels of each color. This anagrams problem is easiest solved with the multinomial coefficient. The total number of arrangements is just ( 2 2 , 2 , … , 2 ) = ( 2 ) ! ( 2 ! ) = ( 2 ) ! 2 ( 2,2,…,2 2n )= (2!) n (2n)! = 2 n (2n)! The number of arrangements satisfying our condition requires a bit of creativity. For the condition to be satisfied, among each pair, there must be one even-located and odd-located block. Thus, among the odd positions in the string, there must be one of each of the n colors, and likewise with even. There are ! n! ways to arrange the n colors around the n even spots, and likewise with odd. By the multiplication principle, there are ( ! ) 2 (n!) 2 ways that satisfy our condition. Therefore, the probability of our event is ( ! ) 2 ( 2 ) ! 2 = 2 ( 2 ) 2 n (2n)! (n!) 2 = ( n 2n ) 2 n With the specified values, the answer is 8 / 63 8/63.
