questions.title: Rat Poison I
questions.problem: You have $r$ very loyal rats that are willing to taste cups of wine for you! Exactly one of the $n$ cups has poison in it, which kills rats that drink it one hour after sipping. Otherwise, the rat drinks wine and feels a little tipsy, but it powers through and is fine. The rats are busy, so they can only drink cups within a one-hour period. Find the maximum value of n such that the poisonous cup can be uniquely identified when = 10 r=10. Assume the sipping process is instantaneous.
questions.solution: The idea of this question is that we need to map each rat to try some subset of the cups such that we maximize the number of cups that are consumed total. Any rat that tries the poisonous cup will die, so a possible idea is: Can we assign the rats such that each subset tries a unique cup? In this way, we would be able to identify the poisonous cup by the subset of rats that died. We are indeed able to do this! There are 2 2 r subsets of the rats, so an initial guess is that 2 2 r is the maximum number of cups for which the poisonous one can be identified. Now, we must devise a strategy to assign the rats to the cups. Each rat is either included or not included in the subset of rats that tries a given cup. Therefore, we can create strings of length r such that the ith position is 1 1 if rat i tries it, and 0 0 if it doesn't try it. We end up with a string 1 2 … b 1 b 2 …b r . where each = 0 b i =0 or 1 1. We can view this as a binary string of length r, meaning that all the values 0 = 0 ⋅ 2 − 1 + 0 ⋅ 2 − 2 + ⋯ + 0 ⋅ 2 0 0=0⋅2 r−1 +0⋅2 r−2 +⋯+0⋅2 0 to 2 − 1 = 2 − 1 + 2 − 2 + ⋯ + 2 0 2 r −1=2 r−1 +2 r−2 +⋯+2 0 are possible. The idea is to label the urns 0 0 to 2 − 1 2 r −1, express the label of each cup in binary, appending 0 0's out front as necessary to make the string of length r, and the rats that try that cup are exactly the positions of the string with a 1 1. For example, if = 5 , 18 = 10010 r=5,18=10010 would be tasted by rat 1 1 and 4 4, while 6 = 00110 6=00110 is tried by rats 3 3 and 4 4. Once the rats taste and you observe which rats die, you can reconstruct which cup has the poison by constructing the binary string. For example, if rats 3 3 and 5 5 die, while the others live, the cup with the poison is 00101 = 4 + 1 = 5 00101=4+1=5. We can't test more than 2 2 r cups, as otherwise, by pigeonhole principle, there would be at least one cup who doesn't have a subset mapping to it. Because of this, we would not be able to uniquely determine which cup has the poison. With = 10 r=10, the answer is 1024 1024.

questions.title: Rat Poison II
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $k$. You have $r$ very loyal rats that are willing to taste cups of wine for you! Exactly one of the $n$ cups has poison in it at random, which kills rats that drink it one hour after sipping. Otherwise, the rat drinks wine and feels a little tipsy, but it powers through and is fine. The rats are busy, so they can only drink cups within a one-hour period. Find the maximum value of n such that the poisonous cup can be identified with probability at least 1 / 1/k when = 10 r=10 and = 5 k=5. Assume the sipping process is instantaneous.
questions.solution: The idea of this question is that we need to map each rat to try some subset of the cups such that we maximize the number of cups that are consumed total. In this problem, we only need to assign the rats such that there is probability at least $1/k$ of us identifying the poisonous cup. Any rat that tries the poisonous cup will die, so a possible idea is: Can we assign the rats such that each subset tries exactly k cups? We are indeed able to do this! There are $2^r$ subsets of the rats, so an initial guess is that ⋅ 2 k⋅2 r is the maximum number of cups for which the poisonous one can be identified with probability at least $1/k$. As for the strategy, we know that when $k = 1$, the strategy is to label the cups $0$ to 2 − 1 2 r −1, and then express each label in a binary string of length $r$, with the ith spot being $1$ denoting that rat $i$ drinks from that cup. Now, imagine we perform this same strategy of $k$ sets of $2^r$ cups. In other words, we label the cups $0_i$ to ( 2 − 1 ) (2 r −1) i , where $m_i$ is the cup labelled $m$ in the ith group, express each label in binary, and each rat tries the cups they are assigned to in every group at once. The exact sequence of rats that dies allows you to identify the label of the cup, but not which group it belongs to. Since there are k groups, and the poison is at random, each of the k cups with the proper label are equally likely to contain the poison, so there is probability 1 / 1/k you guess correctly. For the same reason, we can't have more than ⋅ 2 k⋅2 r cups, as at least one of the labels would have more than k replicates of a certain subset drinking it. With the specified values, the answer is 5120 5120.

questions.title: Rat Poison III
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $k$. You have $r$ very loyal rats that are willing to taste cups of wine for you! Exactly one of the $n$ cups has poison in it at random, which kills rats that drink it one hour after sipping. Otherwise, the rat drinks wine and feels a little tipsy, but it powers through and is fine. The rats are less busy now, so they can drink cups for up to p hours. Find the maximum value of n such that the poisonous cup can be identified with probability at least 1 / 1/k when = 3 , = 4 , r=3,k=4, and = 3 p=3. Assume the sipping process is instantaneous, and that rats can sip cups exactly at time p hours, if needed.
questions.solution: Based on the previous questions, we should try to assign the rats to the cups based on some subset argument. Now that the rats have $p$ hours instead of just $1$, we have significantly more optionality, in the sense that we can now assign rats to try cups at different times. We must wait an hour between sets of sips, as we need $1$ hour to let the poison sit in to kill the rat. Since the sipping process is instantaneous, at the mark of each hour 0 , 1 , … , 0,1,…,p, we have each rat sip according to some assignment rule. In the previous parts, we could only assign whether or not a rat sips a certain cup because there was only 1 1 hour to try the cups. Now, there are + 1 p+1 times at which they can try cups, which are hours 0 , 1 , … , 0,1,…,p. Thus, instead of assigning 0 0 or 1 1 based on whether or not the rat tries the given cup, we instead assign an integer 0 , 1 , … , 0,1,…,p to each spot in our string that represents the hour at which a given rat tries a given cup. This is repeated for each of the k groups by adding in a subscript of 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤k, dependent on the group number. In essence, this is just the same strategy as the previous part, but we express the labels in base + 1 p+1 for general p hours of trying. This does align with the last part, since = 1 p=1 there. For example, with = 2 , = 2 , k=2,p=2, and = 5 r=5, the label 16 = 00221 16=00221 (in base 3 3) means that rats 3 3 and 4 4 try this cup in hour 2 2, rat 5 5 tries it in hour 1 1, and rats 1 1 and 2 2 never try it. Once we record the hour in which each rat dies, we can identify the label, but not the group, for which the poison must be in. Note that we should actually record element the hour of death minus 1 1, as the poison takes 1 1 hour to set in, meaning if a rat dies in hour ℎ h, they drank from the poisoned cup in hour ℎ − 1 h−1. These hours are concatenated into a string in base + 1 p+1 to get the label, where the value of the ith position is the is ℎ − 1 h−1, with ℎ h being the hour of death of the ith rat. For example, using the values above, if rats 1 , 2 , 1,2, and 5 5 die in hour 3 3 (i.e. one hour after the drinking ends), while rats 3 3 and 4 4 die in hour 1 1, the string is 22002 22002 in base 3 3 (remember that we subtract 1 1 from each hour), and this equals 218 218 in base 10 10. Therefore, the label at which the poison is located is 218 218. We have now created a correspondence between base + 1 p+1 strings of length r and the identification of the cup in one group. There are ( + 1 ) (p+1) r such strings, since it can range from 00 … 0 00…0 to … ppp…p, meaning there are + 1 p+1 options for each of the r spots. As there are k groups of this size, the maximum number of cups that we can test is ⋅ ( + 1 ) k⋅(p+1) r . With the specified values, the maximum number of cups is 256 256.

questions.title: Testing Eggs I
questions.problem: You are given $2$ identical eggs and access to an − n−floor building. The goal is to determine the highest floor from which an egg will not break when dropped out of a window from that floor. Call this floor the critical floor critical floor. There is exactly one critical floor in the building. If an egg is dropped and does not break, it's undamaged and can be dropped again. Broken eggs can't be dropped again. If an egg breaks on floor n, it also breaks for all floors > m>n; similarly, if an egg doesn't break on floor n, it also doesn't break for any floor < m<n. What is the maximum value of n such that the critical floor can be identified in at most d drops? Report the answer when = 10 d=10.
questions.solution: Our goal is to find the optimal strategy such that the critical floor can be identified in at most $d$ drops. A very basic initial strategy would be to have constant gaps between floors we test, such as every $10$ floors. However, this can't be an optimal strategy, as for higher floors, we need more drops to get up there in the first place, so we have fewer drops to explore around the higher up we go. Therefore, a more natural idea is to decrease the spacing between consecutively searched floors the higher we go. Let's first determine where the first egg should be dropped. As we need to drop at most d times, we need to think about the maximum number of floors that can be explored in the worst case afterwards. For the first egg, we have d drops remaining, so if it breaks, we need to be able to search all of the floors from 1 1 to the floor we dropped at first in finding the critical floor. Thus, we should drop at floor d, so that if it breaks, we can explore floors 1 1 to − 1 d−1 in the subsequent − 1 d−1 drops. We need to explore every floor, as if the other egg breaks at any point before we've found the critical floor, we can't find the critical floor. What happens if the egg doesn't break at floor d? We now have − 1 d−1 drops remaining, meaning that we should jump another − 1 d−1 floors, and drop the egg at floor + ( − 1 ) = 2 − 1 d+(d−1)=2d−1. In the case that the egg breaks at 2 − 1 2d−1, we can now explore the − 2 d−2 floors + 1 , … , 2 − 2 d+1,…,2d−2 in the other − 2 d−2 drops. This method keeps iterating: When we have k drops left and no egg has broken yet, we jump k floors from the previous drop point so that if it breaks there, we can explore the − 1 k−1 floors between and identify the critical floor. Therefore, highest floor at which we can drop an egg in d drops is + ( − 1 ) + ( − 2 ) + ⋯ + 2 + 1 = ( + 1 ) 2 d+(d−1)+(d−2)+⋯+2+1= 2 d(d+1) Since the critical floor must be one of the n floors, if the egg doesn't break at floor ( + 1 ) 2 2 d(d+1) , the floor one above it must be the critical floor, so the maximum height at which we can uniquely identify the critical floor is ( + 1 ) 2 + 1 2 d(d+1) +1. With = 10 d=10, the answer is 56 56.

questions.title: Testing Eggs II
questions.problem: You are given $3$ identical eggs and access to an − n−floor building. The goal is to determine the highest floor from which an egg will not break when dropped out of a window from that floor. Call this floor the critical floor critical floor. There is exactly one critical floor in the building. If an egg is dropped and does not break, it's undamaged and can be dropped again. Broken eggs can't be dropped again. If an egg breaks on floor n, it also breaks for all floors > m>n; similarly, if an egg doesn't break on floor n, it also doesn't break for any floor < m<n. What is the maximum value of n such that the critical floor can be identified in at most d drops? Report the answer when = 10 d=10.
questions.solution: Our goal is to find the optimal strategy such that the critical floor can be identified in at most $d$ drops. A very basic initial strategy would be to have constant gaps between floors we test, such as every $10$ floors. However, this can't be an optimal strategy, as for higher floors, we need more drops to get up there in the first place, so we have fewer drops to explore around the higher up we go. Therefore, a more natural idea is to decrease the spacing between consecutively searched floors the higher we go. Let's first determine where the first egg should be dropped. As we need to drop at most d times, we need to think about the maximum number of floors that can be explored in the worst case afterwards. For the first egg, we have d drops remaining, so if it breaks, we need to be able to search all of the floors from 1 1 to the floor we dropped at first in finding the critical floor. Unlike the first scenario, we have 2 2 eggs that remain, so if one breaks, it's okay! We still have a second egg. In the remaining − 1 d−1 drops, with 2 2 remaining eggs, we can explore ( − 1 ) 2 2 d(d−1) floors. Note that we don't add the 1 1, as we haven't reached the top of the building if it breaks before the end. Accordingly, we should drop at floor ( − 1 ) 2 + 1 2 d(d−1) +1, so that if it breaks, we can explore floors 1 1 to ( − 1 ) 2 2 d(d−1) in the subsequent − 1 d−1 drops. Again, we don't have to necessarily explore every floor this time, as we have 2 2 eggs instead of 1 1 after the first breaks. What happens if the egg doesn't break at floor ( − 1 ) 2 + 1 2 d(d−1) +1? After we drop a second time, there are − 2 d−2 drops that remain, so we should jump another ( − 2 ) ( − 1 ) 2 + 1 2 (d−2)(d−1) +1 floors, so that if the egg breaks, we can explore the other ( − 2 ) ( − 1 ) 2 2 (d−2)(d−1) floors between the floor of the first and second egg drop. We choose this amount by the result of "Testing Eggs I" with − 2 d−2 drops. More generally, if we have k drop remaining, we should jump up ( − 1 ) 2 + 1 2 k(k−1) +1 floors from our previous drop point, as we can explore the ( − 1 ) 2 2 k(k−1) floor between in the remaining − 1 k−1 drops if the egg breaks. Therefore, the highest floor we can drop at is ( ( − 1 ) 2 + 1 ) + ( ( − 2 ) ( − 1 ) 2 + 1 ) + ⋯ + ( 3 + 1 ) + ( 1 + 1 ) + ( 0 + 1 ) = ( 2 + 5 ) 6 ( 2 d(d−1) +1)+( 2 (d−2)(d−1) +1)+⋯+(3+1)+(1+1)+(0+1)= 6 d(d 2 +5) Since the critical floor must be one of the n floors, if the egg doesn't break at floor ( 2 + 5 ) 6 6 d(d 2 +5) , the floor one above it must be the critical floor, so the maximum height at which we can uniquely identify the critical floor is ( 2 + 5 ) 6 + 1 6 d(d 2 +5) +1. With = 10 d=10, the answer is 176 176.

questions.title: Distinct and Gamey
questions.problem: A standard fair $6-$sided die is repeatedly rolled. After each roll, as long as the value showing isn't $1$, you have the option to roll again or cash out an amount (in dollars) equal to the number of distinct faces you've observed thus far. If you roll a $1$, you receive no payout. Under the optimal strategy, what is your expected payout?
questions.solution: In this problem, we need to determine an optimal strategy that maximizes the expected value. Since the game is essentially a Markov chain (from $k$ distinct faces i.e. payout of $k$), we can receive go up to $\$(k+1)$ and face the same choice, or receive nothing. As we need to make the decision that maximizes our expectation at each step, a Dynamic Programming (DP) approach is best here. For $0 \leq k \leq 5$, let $E(k)$ be the expected payout under the optimal strategy when we have observed $k$ distinct sides that aren't side $1$. We stop at $5$ because there are only $5$ other sides on the die that aren't the value $1$. We must derive a recurrence for $E(k)$. There are two options: Cash out or roll until we get to $k+1$ distinct sides observed. If we cash out, $\$k$ is received. If we decide to not cash out, there are two options: We roll $1$ before any of the other distinct values, or vice versa. If we roll $1$ before the other distinct values, we receive no payout. To find the probability of this, we perform sample space reduction. This is okay because all of the sides are equally likely. Nothing happens if we roll a value that has already been observed, so 6 − 6−k values remain that would change the state of the game. All of those besides the value 1 1 would allow us to increase to + 1 k+1 distinct sides, in which the expected value of the game is ( + 1 ) E(k+1), since this is the expected value under the optimal strategy when we have + 1 k+1 distinct sides observed. Thus, the expected payout by continuing to roll is 5 − 6 − ( + 1 ) 6−k 5−k E(k+1). At each step, we should take the choice (stop or roll until new value) that maximizes the expected payout, so we've derived the recurrence relation ( ) = max ⁡ ( , 5 − 6 − ( + 1 ) ) E(k)=max(k, 6−k 5−k E(k+1)) What is our starting condition? For = 5 k=5, we can't do any better, as we've obtained every distinct value, so ( 5 ) = 5 E(5)=5. We are looking for ( 0 ) E(0), as we initially have 0 0 distinct values. Working backwards, ( 4 ) = max ⁡ ( 4 , 1 2 ( 5 ) ) = 4 ( 3 ) = max ⁡ ( 3 , 2 3 ( 4 ) ) = 3 ( 2 ) = max ⁡ ( 2 , 3 4 ( 3 ) ) = 9 / 4 ( 1 ) = max ⁡ ( 1 , 4 5 ( 2 ) ) = 9 / 5 ( 0 ) = max ⁡ ( 0 , 5 6 ( 1 ) ) = 3 / 2 E(4) E(3) E(2) E(1) E(0) =max(4, 2 1 E(5))=4 =max(3, 3 2 E(4))=3 =max(2, 4 3 E(3))=9/4 =max(1, 5 4 E(2))=9/5 =max(0, 6 5 E(1))=3/2 By the above, our expected payout is 3 / 2 3/2.

questions.title: Last Die Limit
questions.problem: Fix two positive integers $r$ and $n$. A die with sides 1 − 1−n is formed such that side $i$ appears with probability $p_i$ . The die is repeatedly rolled until the sum of all upfaces is at least $r$. For $1 \leq k \leq n$, let $p(k,r)$ be the probability that the last value rolled was $k$. Evaluate lim ⁡ → ∞ ( , ) r→∞ lim p(k,r). Report the answer when $n = 12, k = 3,$ and = 6 − ∣ 7 − ∣ 36 p i = 36 6−∣7−i∣ for each $1 \leq i \leq 12$. This represents the case of two fair dice summed up.
questions.solution: To solve the problem of determining the limiting probabilities of each value on a die being the one that makes the cumulative sum cross a large threshold, we need to understand the behavior of the final roll in this context. First, let's consider a fair die. For a cumulative sum to reach or exceed a threshold, different values on the die have different probabilities of being the final roll. For instance, the value 1 1 is less likely to be the final value that makes the cumulative sum reach 10 , 000 10,000 compared to the value 6 6. This is because, for 1 1 to be the final roll, the sum must be exactly 9 , 999 9,999 on the roll before. In contrast, for 6 6 to be the final roll, the sum can be anywhere from 9 , 994 9,994 to 9 , 999 9,999 on the roll before. Intuitively, the probability that a given side is the last value showing should depend on two factors: \textbf{The value of the side}: Higher values on the die are more likely to be the final roll because they can reach the threshold from a wider range of sums that come beforehand. This dependence is linear in the value k because the number of sums that can come before the threshold crossing is directly proportional to the side value. For example, if the last roll is 1 1, only one sum is possible before the threshold, while if the last roll is 6 6, there are 6 6 sums that can precede the threshold. \textbf{The probability of the side appearing on any given roll}: The more likely a side is to appear on any roll, the more likely it is to be the final roll. This dependence is also linear in p k , as we are only considering probability of each side appearing on a single roll: the final one. Combining these two factors, the probability of a side k being the final roll should be proportional to kp k , which represents a weighted linear combination of the value and the probability of that value occurring. However, kp k itself does not necessarily form a probability distribution since the sum ∑ = 1 ∑ k=1 n kp k is not guaranteed to be 1 1. Instead, we need to normalize this expression to form a proper probability distribution. The normalization constant is just ∑ = 1 ∑ k=1 n kp k . Notably, this is the mean μ of each roll. Therefore, the probability that k is the last side rolled is, in the limit, given by: = ∑ = 1 μ kp k = ∑ i=1 n ip i kp k This result makes intuitive sense: the probability that a given side k is the last rolled is exactly the ratio of the expected contribution of side k to the total expected value μ of the die per roll. Values with large contributions to μ have higher probabilities, and vice versa. With the specified values, 3 = 1 / 18 p 3 =1/18 and = 7 μ=7, so the answer is 1 / 42 1/42.

questions.title: Triangular Selection
questions.problem: Fix $n \geq 4$. Three distinct vertices are selected uniformly at random from a regular − n−gon. These points are then connected pairwise via line segments to form a triangle. Find the probability that at least one of the sides of the triangle is also a side of the − n−gon when $n = 10$.
questions.solution: As the three points are selected uniformly at random from the $n$, we can just compute the ratio of the number of triangles that satisfy the condition to the total number of triangles that can be formed. This is admissible because each collection of $3$ vertices forms a distinct triangle, making it relatively easy to compute the probability. As stated previously, every subset of $3$ points forms a distinct triangle, so the number of triangles that can be formed is equal to the number of subsets of $3$ points from $n$, which is ( 3 ) ( 3 n ). As for the triangles that can be formed, by drawing out a simple diagram, we see there are two possible types of triangles: Triangles with $1$ side in common with the − n−gon and triangles with $2$ sides in common with the − n−gon. We should count these cases separately, since these types are triangles are formed differently. For the triangles with $2$ sides in common, we must have three consecutive vertices selected. This is because There are exactly $n$ such possible collections of three consecutive vertices, which correspond exactly to rotating the starting point of the three vertices through the $n$ vertices. For triangles with $1$ side in common, there are two parts: Pick the side that is common between the triangle and the − n−gon. Pick the location of the last vertex. There are n sides of the − n−gon, so there are n ways to pick the common side. Once the side is selected, we can pick any point besides exactly 4 4: The two vertices on the side that was selected, as well as the vertices directly adjacent on either direction of the selected side. We can't do the latter because we would then have 3 3 adjacent vertices, and the triangle would share 2 2 sides with the − n−gon. Thus, there are − 4 n−4 options for the last vertex of this case, meaning that there are ( − 4 ) n(n−4) total triangles that can be formed sharing 1 1 side. Adding the two cases together, there are + ( − 4 ) = ( − 3 ) n+n(n−4)=n(n−3) total triangles sharing at least one side with the − n−gon. Therefore, the probability of the triangle sharing at least one side with the − n−gon is given by ( − 3 ) ( 3 ) = ( − 3 ) ( − 1 ) ( − 2 ) 3 ! = 6 ( − 3 ) ( − 1 ) ( − 2 ) ( 3 n ) n(n−3) = 3! n(n−1)(n−2) n(n−3) = (n−1)(n−2) 6(n−3) With = 10 n=10, the answer is 7 / 12 7/12.

questions.title: Shooters Shoot
questions.problem: Alice, Bob, and Chad are in a shootout on O-Block. Each of them are strapped with guns that have varying accuracies. The three guns respectively have probabilities $1/3, 2/3,$ and $1$ of hitting their desired opponent per shot. If the target is not hit, the bullet goes astray and does not hit anyone else. Going in the order Alice $\rightarrow$ Bob $\rightarrow$ Chad, each person gets to decide if they want to shoot at a given turn, and if so, who they target. This cycle repeats until only person remains. Under the optimal strategy from each player, what is the probability that Alice is the last one alive?
questions.solution: Since each player plays rationally, everyone would prefer to be left with a weaker opponent than themselves. Thus, Alice would prefer to be left with Bob instead of Chad, and Chad would prefer to be left with Alice instead of Bob. Therefore, Alice's first course of action is to opt out of shooting until either Bob or Chad dies. This happens by the end of the first rotation: If Bob kills Chad (probability 2 / 3 2/3), Alice and Bob remain; if Bob misses, then Chad always hits his target, and that would be Bob. Summarizing the above, Bob and Chad go against Alice in the end with respective probabilities 2 / 3 2/3 and 1 / 3 1/3. Now, we need to find the probability Alice wins against Bob and Chad when it's just two players. If Alice is against Chad, then she must hit her first shot to win, as Chad will kill her next turn. Thus, Alice has probability 1 / 3 1/3 of winning against Chad. If Alice is against Bob, Bob just shot at Chad and hit, so Alice is up first. We are now looking for the probability that Alice hits her bullet before Bob. We can view this in the same light as flipping coins: Alice and Bob have coins with respective probabilities of 1 / 3 1/3 and 2 / 3 2/3 of landing heads per flip, with Alice flipping first, and we want to find the probability of Alice landing heads before Bob. This is exactly the scenario of "Coin Swap IV", so here is the solution to that problem, where p and q are the probabilities of the two coins, respectively, showing heads per player. In this case, = 1 / 3 p=1/3 and = 2 / 3 q=2/3. Alice's probability of winning is dependent on what happens in the first turn. Therefore, we should use the Law of Total Probability to condition on what happens on the first flip of each player. Let a be the probability that Alice wins the game. With probability p, she flips a head on her first turn and immediately wins. Otherwise, she flips a tails with probability 1 − 1−p. In this case, for Alice to have another shot at winning, Bob must also flip a tails, which occurs with probability 1 − 1−q. Afterwards, the coin would go back to Alice, and the probability of her winning would still be a, as the coin just performed one cycle and past outcomes don't influence future outcomes of the coin. Thus, we have the equation = + ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) ⟺ = 1 − ( 1 − ) ( 1 − ) a=p+(1−p)(1−q)a⟺a= 1−(1−p)(1−q) p With the specified values, the probability Alice wins is 3 / 7 3/7. By the Law of Total Probability, we can conclude that Alice's probability of being the last person standing is 2 3 ⋅ 3 7 + 1 3 ⋅ 1 3 = 25 63 3 2 ⋅ 7 3 + 3 1 ⋅ 3 1 = 63 25

questions.title: First Odd
questions.problem: Every integer from $1$ to $10$ 10 10 ( 10 10 billion) is written out on a (very very long) piece of paper in alphabetical order such that all spaces and hyphens are ignored. For example $7611$ is read as "seven thousand, six hundred eleven", and the spaces are ignored when writing. Scotty, who has too much free time, decides to read out all $10$ billion numbers in order of their appearance on the page. What odd number does he read first?
questions.solution: This question is a very advanced exercise in alphabet knowledge. The first integer from $1$ to $10$ that appears alphabetically is $8$ (eight). However, after this, the first available suffix word is billion (as opposed to million, thousand, hundred, or any digit $0-9$). Therefore, the integer must start with "eight billion". As for the millions and thousands spot, we see that "eight" is not optimal here, as you'd follow eight by thousand (or million), whereas "eighteen" beats out "eightthousand" and "eightmillion" alphabetically. Thus, "eighteen million" and "eighteen thousand" come next. We can't repeat this for the last three digits, as having 8 8 or 18 18 would make the number even, and we want the first odd number. Let's first start at the end. Since 8 8 can't be the last digit, we should look for eighty, as that starts with e as well. 80 80 itself doesn't work, but looking among the odd digits, we see "five" comes first alphabetically, so the number ends in 85 85. However, is there a hundreds spot? We must have a hundreds spot, as the ℎ h in hundreds comes before the y in eighty, so "eight hundred" must come before the "eighty five". Thus, our final integer is 8 , 018 , 018 , 885 8,018,018,885

questions.title: Choccy Break
questions.problem: Rui has a chocolate bar that is arranged into the shape of a $m \times n$ grid of $1 \times 1$ squares. Rui can break up the chocolate bar in any way he wants horizontally or vertically at each step. The goal is to obtain the constituent $mn$ $1 \times 1$ squares. What is the minimum number of breaks Rui must perform? Report the answer for $m = 10$ and $n = 8$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we initially have one piece of chocolate, and we want to obtain the $mn$ $1 \times 1$ squares of chocolate. When we break up a piece of chocolate into two pieces, our total count of pieces of chocolate increases by $1$: The piece that was broken is now $2$ pieces. This is the key insight we need: No matter how Rui breaks up his chocolate, the number of total pieces he has increases by $1$ at each step! Therefore, to go from $1$ piece to $mn$ pieces, no matter how Rui decides to break it, he will need to perform − 1 mn−1 breaks, as the "piece count" must increase by − 1 mn−1. In general, with these "devise an algorithm" type brainteasers, the idea is to create and track some metric that changes with each step. With the specified values, the answer is 79 79.

questions.title: Deterministic Poker
questions.problem: Alice and Bob trust each other a lot, so they play a game of deterministic poker. Deterministic poker proceeds under the following rules: A standard deck of cards is displayed in the center completely face-up. Alice draws any 5 5 cards of her choice from the center, and then Bob does the same. Alice can discard any amount of her 5 5 selected cards, in which they will remain out-of-play. If she discards k cards, she can select any k cards from the center to replace them. Bob does the same as the above step. The person with the stronger hand (in the sense of standard poker rules) is the winner. If they have equally strong hands, the game ends in a tie. The cards in the hands of both players are visible at all times. Under optimal play from both players, who has a winning strategy? Alice Bob Alice and Bob always tie None of the above SUBMIT
questions.solution: For this question, recall that the order of hands in poker is: Royal Flush (Ace-high straight flush) > Straight Flush (decreasing in power as the high card decreases) > Four-of-a-kind. Since Alice chooses first, if Bob is able to select any type of royal flush, she will never be able to win, as royal flush is the best hand. To block Bob from doing this, Alice must select one card from each suit that is in the royal flush. The best card to select would be the one that blocks the most straight flushes, as it weakens the maximum possible hand Bob can have. The rank 10 10 is in the most straight flushes, so Alice should select the 10 10 from each suit first. Bob is now limited to straight flushes that are 9 − 9−high at best. The last card Alice selects is irrelevant, as she will be able to discard later if she wants. Since Bob will likely want high ranks, WLOG, suppose Alice takes the Ace of spades as her last card. Since Bob is also playing optimally, he must ensure Alice does not get a royal flush after discarding some of her cards, so he must obtain one card in each suit that is above a 10 10 in rank. By doing this, Alice will always be missing a card for the royal flush in any suit. For simplicity, assume Bob chooses all of the kings. As for the last card, Bob knows that the best he can do is obtain a straight flush with high card at most 9 9. Therefore, his best choice is to pick a 9 9 of some suit. This would allow him to discard the kings on his next turn, and then get a 9 − 9−high straight flush. Alice is now in a great position: She has all of the rank 10 10 cards and some other card, so although she can't get a royal flush, she is able to get a 10 − 10−high straight flush by only keeping a 10 10 that isn't the suit of the 9 9 that Bob selected. She can't keep that suit of 10 10, as she would not be able to complete her 10 − 10−high straight flush in that suit. Once she discards the other 4 4 cards, she can pick up ranks 6 − 9 6−9 in the proper suit, and she obtains a 10 − 10−high straight flush. Since Bob can't do any better than a 9 − 9−high straight flush, it's over for him. The correct answer is Alice.

The only challenge in this question is that we don't know the initial amount of money! Now that we have found an explicit formula for a k , since = − b k =a n−k , we can conclude that the balance in the account at time k is = ( 1 − 1 2 − ) b k =r(1− 2 n−k 1 ) This formula satisfies the key property we expect: At time n, the balance is 0 0. questions.title: Coin Occurrences
questions.problem: You and your friend play the following game with a fair coin: You both get to select distinct sequences of length $2$ of heads and tails. A fair coin is then repeatedly flipped until one of the two sequences you or your friend selected appears in two consecutive flips. The person whose sequence appears first is the winner. For example, if you choose $HH$ and your friend chose $HT$, $THT$ would end the game in $3$ flips. You get to decide whether to choose your sequence first or second. The person who chooses second gets to hear the sequence the first person selected. Assume optimal play from both players. Report the value of $L + p$, where $L = 1$ if you should select first, $L = 2$ if you should select second, and $L = 3$ if it doesn't matter which order you select in, and $p$ is the probability of you winning under the optimal strategy.
questions.solution: There are only $4$ sequences of length $2$: $HH,HT,TH,$ and $TT$. Our goal is to find the best response to any given sequence. Since $H$ and $T$ have equal probability of appearing on any given flip, we can consider $HH$ and $HT$ and $TH$, and we automatically get the probabilities of $TT$ and $TH$ and $HT$, since the roles of $H$ and $T$ are reversed. For $HH$ against $HT$, there is nothing that contributes to either sequence until the first $H$ appears, and then the flip right after is equally likely to be $H$ or $T$, so $HH$ and $HT$ beat each other with probability $1/2$. For $HH$ against $TH$, note that if the first flip is $T$, $TH$ automatically comes first, as the coin flipping state repeatedly stays in $TT$ until an $H$ appears, and at that point, $TH$ would be the last two flips. Therefore, $HH$ wins exactly when the first two flips are $HH$, and $TH$ wins otherwise (as once $T$ is flipped, you can never get $HH$ before $TH$). Thus, $HH$ wins with probability $1/4$ against $TH$ (which wins with probability $3/4$). From the above, we can conclude that $TT$ and $TH$ beat each other with probability $1/2$, while $TT$ beats $HT$ with probability $1/4$. Additionally, it's clear that $TT$ and $HH$ beat, as well as $HT$ and $TH$, beat each other with probability $1/2$, as the coin is fair, so any flipping process leading to one of the sequences to win can be inverted (all $H$ to become $T$, and vice versa) to make the other sequence win. With all of this in mind, we can see that $HT$ and $TH$ are the best two options: No other sequences beats them with more than probability $1/2$. Thus, this is a Nash equilibrium: The first person to select picks $HT$ or $TH$, and the second person to select picks the other sequence. In this way, no player can unilaterally increase their probability of winning. Thus, both players win with probability $1/2$, and you are indifferent to selecting your sequence first or second. The answer is $3 + 1/2 = 7/2$. This intuition doesn't hold as proof (as this fails for some larger strings), but $HT$ and $TH$ take the least amount of flips on average to appear, so it makes sense that these might be best.

questions.title: Additive Dice I
questions.problem: You and your friend each roll a standard fair $6-$sided die and observe the values appearing individually. Before the values are revealed to the other person, you are given the option to pay $\$25$ to add $2$ to the value of your roll. Your opponent does not have this option. After your decision is made, the values (including your potential $+2$) are revealed. The person with the strictly higher value receives $\$100$ from a third party. If both values are the same, no exchange of money occurs. Assuming you play to maximize expected value, what is your expected payout?
questions.solution: In this problem, we essentially need to find when you should exercise the option to add $2$ to your score. The optimal strategy is to exercise the option whenever your value is $\leq t$ (for some threshold $t$), and otherwise not exercise it. If you rolled the value $k$, the probability you have a strictly higher value than your opponent is − 1 6 6 k−1 , as there are − 1 k−1 values on their die less than $k$. However, by adding $2$, your probability is now + 1 6 6 k+1 of winning, which increases your expected payout by 100 ⋅ 2 / 6 = 100 / 3 ≈ $ 33.33 > 25 100⋅2/6=100/3≈$33.33>25. The only time this doesn't occur is when $k = 6$, as you can't have probability $7/6$ of winning. More explicitly, by adding $2$ to $6$, you already beat every other value with a $7$, so $8$ has the same effect as $7$. When you rolled a $6$, this option increases your expected payout by 100 / 6 ≈ $ 16.67 < 25 $100/6 \approx \$16.67 < 25$. By the above calculations, unless you roll a $6$, you should always exercise the option. Under this strategy, your expected payout is 100 ⋅ 1 6 ⋅ ( 2 6 + 3 6 + 4 6 + 5 6 + 1 + 5 6 ) − 5 6 ⋅ 25 = 875 18 100⋅ 6 1 ⋅( 6 2 + 6 3 + 6 4 + 6 5 +1+ 6 5 )− 6 5 ⋅25= 18 875 In the above expression, $100$ represents the payout for winning. $1/6$ represents the probability of rolling each value on your die. The fractions inside represent the probabilities of winning with the values $1-6$ under the optimal strategy. Note that the probability is $5/6$ when rolling a $6$ because the other player could roll a $6$. The $5/6$ out back represents the probability you exercise the option. The $25$ out back represents the cost of the option. In simple terms, you can view the above expression as expected gain minus expected cost.

questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$ and a positive real number $a$. $n$ points are selected uniformly at random from the square with vertices $(\pm a, \pm a)$ in the plane. Afterwards, each pair of points is connected by a line segment. Find the expected number of total intersections between the line segments and the coordinate axes ( − x−axis and − y−axis). Note that we are not counting intersections between line segments themselves. Report the answer when = 10 n=10 and = 4 a=4.
questions.solution: In this problem, we are looking to compute the expected count of some events where we don't know a distributional form (namely, the PMF of the number of total intersections). Therefore, the best approach is to count by linearity of expected value, as we can just sum up over all pairs of points. As there are n points, there are ( 2 ) ( 2 n ) pairs, so label all of the pairs 1 1 to ( 2 ) ( 2 n ), and let N i be the number of intersections that the line segment connecting pair i has with the axes. = 1 + ⋯ + ( 2 ) T=N 1 +⋯+N ( 2 n ) gives the total number of intersections with the axes. We didn't use indicators because, as we will later see, it's possible for a segment to cross at 2 2 points. Since the points are selected IID, all of the pairs have the same mean, so by linearity, [ ] = ( 2 ) [ 1 ] E[T]=( 2 n )E[N 1 ] [ 1 ] E[N 1 ] is the expected number of intersections of the line segment between the first pair of points with the axes. The number of intersections of the segment is going to depend on which quadrants the points are in, since the axes divide the quadrants. Namely, by a quick drawing, we see the following: If the two points are in the same quadrant, there is no intersection with any axis. If the two points are separated by one quadrant (share exactly one of the same − x−coordinate sign or same − y−coordinate sign), there is one intersection with an axis. If the two points are diagonally opposed (both − x−coordinate and − y−coordinate signs differ), there are two intersection points. All quadrants are equally likely, since the square is symmetric about the origin and we select uniformly at random. WLOG, we can assume the first point of the pair is in the bottom left. With probability 1 / 4 1/4, the other point is also in the bottom left. Similarly, with probabilities 1 / 2 1/2 and 1 / 4 1/4, the other points are in one quadrant and two quadrants away from the bottom left. Therefore, the expected number of intersections is [ 1 ] = 0 ⋅ 1 / 4 + 1 ⋅ 1 / 2 + 2 ⋅ 1 / 4 = 1 E[N 1 ]=0⋅1/4+1⋅1/2+2⋅1/4=1 Plugging this in, we conclude the answer is [ ] = ( 2 ) E[T]=( 2 n ) With = 10 n=10, the answer is 45 45.

questions.title: Circular Mismatch I
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n \geq 3$. $n$ people stand around in a circle, each having their own coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip. Each person flips their coin, and the outcomes are recorded. Find the expected number of people for which their flip differs from both people adjacent to them. Report the answer when $p = 2/3$ and $n = 18$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we are looking to compute the expected count of some non-independent events. These events are not necessarily independent because the knowledge that a person has a flip that differs from the two people adjacent to them potentially gives information about what the flip is. Therefore, the best approach is counting via indicators. Since we are looking to compute the expected count of some event, it's best to set up the indicator as the event we want to count! Thus, label the people 1 1 to n, and let I i be the indicator that person i has a coin outcome that is distinct from the people next to them. = 1 + ⋯ + T=I 1 +⋯+I n gives the total number of people for which this is true. Since all of the people have identical coins (or, more specifically, the people are labelled arbitrarily), the indicators 1 , … , I 1 ,…,I n are identically distributed. This allows us to say that they all have the same mean, so [ ] = [ 1 ] E[T]=nE[I 1 ] [ 1 ] E[I 1 ] is the probability that person 1 1 has a flip that differs from both of their neighbors. There are two ways this can occur: Person 1 1 has H, and the neighbors both have T, or vice versa. If person 1 1 has H (probability p), the other two people don't match i.e. both obtain T with probability ( 1 − ) 2 (1−p) 2 . If person 1 1 has T (probability 1 − 1−p), the other two people don't match i.e. both obtain H with probability 2 p 2 . This breaking into cases is necessary because H and T don't have the same probability of occurring. Adding the two cases together, we can conclude that the probability person 1 1 has different outcomes from both of their neighbors is [ 1 ] = 2 ( 1 − ) + ( 1 − ) 2 = ( 1 − ) E[I 1 ]=p 2 (1−p)+p(1−p) 2 =p(1−p). Plugging into the linearity of expectation formula, we can conclude [ ] = ( 1 − ) E[T]=np(1−p) As a sanity check, when = 0 p=0 and = 1 p=1, the expression is 0 0, which makes sense: Everyone would have the same outcome, so nobody differs. The expression is maximized at = 1 / 2 p=1/2, which also makes intuitive sense: The flips are "most random" at = 1 / 2 p=1/2, so there is likely to be the most mismatches between people in the circle. With the specified values, the answer is 4 4.

questions.title: Keep or Play I
questions.problem: Sophie offers you the following game: You will be given a fair coin, and will be allowed to flip it until you first land tails. For each head you flip, you will receive $ ℎ $h. After you receive a tails, you can either choose to accept your payout or play another round for free under the same rules. If you decide to play again, you must accept the payout of the second round (i.e. your first round is null and void). Find the fair value of Sophie's game when ℎ = 10 h=10.
questions.solution: At an intuitive level, the decision to play the second round is dependent on how much was earned in the first round: If you earned a lot in the first round, there's no need to play again, as you'd likely earn less. Thus, we should find a threshold at which you would want to play the game again. The number of flips needed until the first tails appears is ∼ Geom ( 1 / 2 ) N∼Geom(1/2), as there is probability 1 / 2 1/2 per flip of landing a tails. Thus, the expected number of flips needed until the first tails is [ ] = 2 E[N]=2. Since there are 2 2 flips on average needed until the first tails, there is 1 1 head on average. As you are paid $ ℎ $h per head, the expected value of a single round is $ ℎ $h. You would only take up the second chance if you earned less than $ ℎ $h on the first round, which occurs exactly when the first flip is tails (i.e. you have no payout). The optimal strategy is to always accept the payout if you obtain at least 1 1 heads and only reflip if you have no heads. As for the expected value of this strategy, we must consider two cases and their probabilities: If you get no heads (probability 1 / 2 1/2, as the first flip must be tails), your expected value on the game is just the expected value of a single round, which is ℎ h. If you get at least 1 1 head (probability 1 − 1 / 2 = 1 / 2 1−1/2=1/2), conditional on your first flip being heads, you are in the exact same position after the first flip as before, but you now have $ ℎ $h in your bank. The position is exactly the same because past flips don't influence future flips, so the number of additional flips needed until the first tails is ∼ Geom ( 1 / 2 ) N∼Geom(1/2), in which you'd make an additional $ ℎ $h on average. Therefore, your expected payout in this case is ℎ + ℎ = 2 ℎ h+h=2h. By the Law of Total Expectation, the expected payout from Sophie's game is ℎ ⋅ 1 2 + 2 ℎ ⋅ 1 2 = 3 ℎ 2 h⋅ 2 1 +2h⋅ 2 1 = 2 3h With ℎ = 10 h=10, the answer is 15 15.

questions.title: Biased Poker Tournament I
questions.problem: There are $101$ players (you plus $100$ poker pros) in a round‐robin poker tournament. This means that each person plays every other person once. All of the poker pros start have $100$ chips to start with for each of the $100$ matches they play, but you receive $20,000$ chips before the tournament, and are allowed to distribute them in any way you'd like among the $100$ matches. For example, you could put $1000$ chips on each of $20$ matches. In each match, the chance to win is proportional to your chips; that is, if you have $a$ chip and your opponent has $b$ chips, your probability of winning the match is + a+b a The chips of the losing player do not get added to the stack of the winning player. A win awards $1$ point, while a loss does not award anything. After all the matches are complete, the prizes are awarded as follows: $1$st place: $\$1,000,000$ $2$nd place: $\$500,000$ $3$rd place: $\$400,000$ $4$th place: $\$300,000$ $5$th place: $\$200,000$ $6$th to $10$th place: $\$100,000$ No prize for anyone else. Any ties in points when converting to rank will be resolved by a uniformly random permutation of the ranks (ex: if three people are tied for $1$st, ranks $1,2,$ and $3$ will be assigned uniformly at random). Assuming you play optimally, Which of the following are characteristics of this game? Each of the pro players is expected to win $50$ games. Each of the pro players is expected to win less than $50$ games. Each of the pro players is expected to win more than $50$ games. The optimal strategy is to dynamically adjust how much you put on each game based on the results of the first few matches. The optimal strategy is to provide some fixed non-uniform distribution of the chips across the matches. The optimal strategy is to distribute $200$ chips per match, regardless of the outcome of prior matches. There is no single optimal strategy, there are multiple strategies that are optimal. None of the above. SUBMIT
questions.solution: The answer choices fall into two primary categories, so let's answer both of them separately. As for the first group of answers, let's look at this intuitively. Clearly, if you are playing optimal, you have a strictly larger than 50 % 50% chance of winning the tournament, as you have twice as many chips as everyone else. As all of the pro players are identical, there's no reason that you should be more likely to win against one player than another. Therefore, if you have a > 1 / 2 >1/2 probability of winning the tournament, and your odds are constant across players, you must beat each player with > 1 / 2 >1/2 odds. How does this come into play? Each of the pros plays against you and 99 99 other pros. Since the pros have equal money, they are at equal odds of winning, so each of those games is won by either player by probability 1 / 2 1/2. Thus, if < 1 / 2 x<1/2 is the probability of the pro winning against you, by Linearity of Expectation, the expected number of games each pro wins is 99 ⋅ 1 / 2 + = 49.5 + < 49.5 + 0.5 = 50 99⋅1/2+x=49.5+x<49.5+0.5=50 As for the second grouping of questions, we can reason this as a consequence of the above. We stated that since all players are identical, under an optimal strategy, you should be no more likely to win or lose against any particular pro. For this to happen, you odds would need to be constant, which means that the number of chips you bring into each game must be constant. Thus, distributing 200 200 chips to each of you 100 100 matches is optimal. We can also prove this rigorously. Suppose that you allocate x i chips to game i. We require that 1 + ⋯ + 100 = 20000 x 1 +⋯+x 100 =20000 based on your initial supply. In game i, your probability of winning would be 100 + = 1 − 100 100 + 100+x i x i =1− 100+x i 100 By the Linearity of Expecatation, the expected number of games you win is given by ∑ = 1 100 100 + = 100 ( 1 − ∑ = 1 100 1 100 + ) i=1 ∑ 100 100+x i x i =100(1− i=1 ∑ 100 100+x i 1 ) Let's consider a single term ( ) = − 1 / ( 100 + ) f(x)=−1/(100+x). Note that this function is concave for all > 0 x>0: ′ ′ ( ) = − 2 ( 100 + ) 3 < 0 f ′′ (x)=− (100+x) 3 2 <0 Since this function is concave, this means that there is diminishing marginal increase in probability for each additional chip you put in. More simply stated, if < a<b, the increase in probability of winning a given match by changing from a to + 1 a+1 chips is smaller than the increase in probability of winning a given match when changing from b to + 1 b+1 chips. The above implies that if you already allocated a lot of chips to one match, adding another chip gives you a small improvement. On the other hand, if you put very few chips in a match, one extra chip gives you a larger boost in win probability. Using the above example of going from → + 1 a→a+1 and → + 1 b→b+1 chips, one extra chip in the match with a chips boosts your win chance more than one extra chip in the match with b chips. Therefore, if the chip allocations aren’t balanced, you could always take a chip from a match where its effect is smaller and reallocate it to a match where its effect is larger, and this would increase your overall win probability. By doing this reallocation from games with higher amounts of chips to ones with lower amounts of chips, you are just converging on a uniform distribution of the chips across the games, since this process of moving from high to low will be repeated until there is no place left to go from high to low i.e. all games have equal amounts of chips. Options 2 2 and 6 6 are correct.

questions.problem: Each of the $9$ cells in a $3\times 3$ grid of squares is colored either blue or white with equal probability, independently between squares. Find the expected area of the largest square of blue cells contained within the grid.
questions.solution: Let $c$ be a coloring of the grid, let $A(c)$ be the area of the largest square of blue cells contained within the coloring. The possible values of $A(c)$ are $0,1,4,$ and $9$. To compute the expected value, we must compute $\mathbb{P}\left[A(c)=0\right](0)+\mathbb{P}\left[A(c)=1\right](1)+\mathbb{P}[A(c)=4](4)+\mathbb{P}\left[A(c)=9\right](9)$ where we know that $\mathbb{P}[A(c)=0]+\mathbb{P}[A(c)=1]+\mathbb{P}[A(c)=4]+\mathbb{P}[A(c)=9]=1$ by properties of the probability measure. There are 2 9 = 51$2$ $9$ =512 equally likely colorings of the grid, as there are $2$ color options per square. We can compute [ ( ) = 0 ] P[A(c)=0] and [ ( ) = 9 ] P[A(c)=9] pretty easily. Note that the event { ( ) = 0 } {A(c)=0} occurs exactly when all of the squares are white. Similarly, we have that { ( ) = 9 } {A(c)=9} occurs exactly when all of the squares are blue. Therefore, by independence of the square colorings, [ ( ) = 0 ] = [ ( ) = 9 ] = 1 2 9 = 1 512 P[A(c)=0]=P[A(c)=9]= 2 9 1 = 512 1 It now suffices to compute the number of colorings c of the grid such that ( ) = 4 A(c)=4. Computing this quantity is slightly easier than ( ) = 1 A(c)=1 because there are only 4 4 squares of size 4 4< but 9 9 squares of size 1 1, so we have to perform inclusion-exclusion on fewer terms with our proposed method. For ( ) = 4 A(c)=4 to be satisfied, at least one of the four 2 × 2 2×2 sub-grids in the top left, top right, bottom left, or bottom right must be colored completely blue. Let these regions be named , , , A,B,C, and D, respectively. Let A be the event that sub-grid A is colored fully blue, and define events , , B, C, and D similarly. We want to compute ∣ ( ∪ ∪ ∪ ) ∖ ( ∩ ∩ ∩ ) ∣ = ∣ ∪ ∪ ∪ ∣ − ∣ ∩ ∩ ∩ ∣ ∣(A∪B∪C∪D)∖(A∩B∩C∩D)∣=∣A∪B∪C∪D∣−∣A∩B∩C∩D∣. questions.title: Shady Column
questions.problem: Consider an array of white unit squares arranged in a rectangular grid with $r$ rows of unit squares and $c$ columns of unit squares. What is the smallest possible value of $c$ such that, if we shade $s$ unit squares in each column black, then there must necessarily be some row with at least $t$ black unit squares? You should receive a function $f(r,t,s)$. Evaluate $f(40,17,13)$.

Meanwhile, if each row has at most − 1 t−1 black unit squares, then by the Pigeonhole Principle, at most ( − 1 ) r(t−1) unit squares could have been shaded black. Thus, if > ( − 1 ) cs>r(t−1), then any valid shading configuration must yield a row with at least t black unit squares. Conversely, if ≤ ( − 1 ) cs≤r(t−1), then there exists a shading configuration in which no rows have at least t black unit squares, which we construct as follows: (1) number the rows 0 , … , − 1 0,…,r−1 and the columns 0 , … , − 1 0,…,c−1; (2) in each column ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , − 1 } i∈{0,1,…,c−1}, shade the s unit squares in the rows ( ( + ) mod ) ((si+j) mod r) for integers ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , − 1 } j∈{0,1,…,s−1}. If we follow this procedure by iterating i and j in ascending order, then for each integer ∈ { 1 , 2 , … , } k∈{1,2,…,cs}, the kth square shaded lies in row ( ( − 1 ) mod ) ((k−1) mod r). Therefore, row 0 0 has at least as many black unit squares as any other row, and row 0 0 has exactly ⌈ / ⌉ ⌈cs/r⌉ black unit squares per our construction. By the assumption ≤ ( − 1 ) cs≤r(t−1), ⌈ / ⌉ ⌈cs/r⌉ is at most − 1 t−1, so no row has more than − 1 t−1 black unit squares. Thus, the answer to this problem is = ⌊ ( − 1 ) ⌋ + 1 c=⌊ s r(t−1) ⌋+1. Evaluating with our given values, we get the value 50 50.

questions.title: Non-Consecutive Heads
questions.problem: A fair coin is flipped $n$ times. It is known that there are no consecutive heads anywhere in the sequence. Let $E(n)$ be the expected amount of heads that appear given this information. Compute lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) n→∞ lim n E(n) to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: To compute $E(n)$, it is better to derive a recurrence relation. This is because of the fact that the sequence with $n$ flips is intimately related to the sequences with − 1 n−1 and − 2 n−2 flips, as a valid sequence with $n$ flips must also have subsequences of size either − 1 n−1 or − 2 n−2 that are valid as well, dependent on the start of the sequences. Therefore, we derive a recurrence for $E(n)$ by conditioning on the start. For a sequence to not have any consecutive heads, the sequence could either start with $HT$ or $T$. Clearly, the sequence can't start with $HH$, and the $TH$ case is captured in the $T$. Therefore, we only need to consider these two initial sequences. If the sequence starts with $HT$, we can append to it any valid sequence of length − 2 n−2, as the $HT$ ends with $T$, so any additional sequence of length − 2 n−2 can be added to it. There would be ( − 2 ) + $1$ E(n−2)+1 heads on average in this sequence, as there is one H from the beginning and ( − 2 ) E(n−2) heads on average in the remaining − 2 n−2 spots. Given that there are no consecutive heads, by the result of "Conditional First Head", the probability that the sequence starts with H (and hence HT) is + 2 F n+2 F n , where F n is the nth Fibonacci number. If the sequence starts with T, we can append any sequence of length − 1 n−1 to this, as the tails does not interfere with the start of any sequence that is added. There would be ( − 1 ) E(n−1) heads on average in such a sequence, as the heads only come from the remaining sequence of length − 1 n−1, which has ( − 1 ) E(n−1) heads on average. By "Conditional First Head" once again, the probability that the sequence starts with T is + 1 + 2 F n+2 F n+1 . By applying Law of Total Expectation, we have that ( ) = + 1 + 2 ( − 1 ) + + 2 ( 1 + ( − 2 ) ) E(n)= F n+2 F n+1 E(n−1)+ F n+2 F n (1+E(n−2)) We are looking to find lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) n→∞ lim n E(n) . Traditional methods will not work here, as this is a second-order recurrence whose coefficients are not constant (they depend on n). Furthermore, this recurrence is not homogeneous. Therefore, we will need to take a different approach. If lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) = n→∞ lim n E(n) =c, then we have that ( ) E(n) cn as → ∞ n→∞. Therefore, we can find the constant c that makes this recurrence true in limit. As n is extremely large, we also know by "Fibonacci Ratio I" and "Fibonacci Ratio II" that the coefficients also converge to a limit. Since there is a shift by 1 1 between the numerator and denominator in the first limit, we have that + 1 + 2 → 2 1 + 5 F n+2 F n+1 → 1+ 5 2 , as it is the reciprocal of the limit in "Fibonacci Ratio I". Similarly, we have that + 2 → 2 3 + 5 F n+2 F n → 3+ 5 2 by taking a reciprocal. Substituting in ( ) E(n) as cn, we need to solve for c in = 2 1 + 5 ( ( − 1 ) ) + 2 3 + 5 ( 1 + ( − 2 ) ) cn= 1+ 5 2 (c(n−1))+ 3+ 5 2 (1+c(n−2)) By noting that 2 1 + 5 + 2 3 + 5 = 1 1+ 5 2 + 3+ 5 2 =1, we can rearrange this equation, isolate c, and find that = 2 5 + 5 c= 5+ 5 2 .

questions.title: Dual Face Stopper
questions.problem: Cards are dealt one-by-one from a standard deck of cards without replacement. The card dealing ends when either $2$ kings appear OR at least $1$ king and $1$ ace appear (whichever occurs first). Find the expected number of cards that are dealt in the game.
questions.solution: This problem is similar to the "First Ace" paradigm, so we should use some approach similar to it to solve this problem. To solve this problem, we need to break it down into steps of what occurs. First, we need to find the expected number of cards that need to be dealt until either an A or K is observed. To do this, we need to use the "First Ace" paradigm with 8 8 dividers ( 4 4 K and 4 4 A). This leaves 52 − 8 = 44 52−8=44 left to be distributed, and these 8 8 dividers cut up the deck into 9 9 regions (before the first divider, between first and second, etc.). Therefore, there should be 44 / 9 44/9 cards per region on average by the exchangeability of the spacings. Thus, the expected number of cards needed until the first divider is reached is 44 / 9 + 1 = 53 / 9 44/9+1=53/9, as we must add 1 1 to account for the divider actually being drawn. This divider can be either a K or an A. If the divider is an Ace, then we just need to observe one K to stop. If the divider is a K, then either an Ace or another K must be observed to stop. Since the expected number of cards that need to be drawn depends on what the first divider actually is, we should condition on this. Namely, there is an equal probability that the first divider is A or K, as there are 4 4 aces and 4 4 kings in the deck at the time the first one of these is drawn, so given it's one of them, it's equally likely to be either. If the first divider is an Ace, then we need to find the expected number of cards that need to be drawn until a K appears. In this case, there are 52 − 53 / 9 = 415 / 9 52−53/9=415/9 cards left in the deck on average, and there are 4 4 dividers still (corresponding to the 4 4 kings). Therefore, there are 415 / 9 − 4 = 379 / 9 415/9−4=379/9 non-divider cards left to be placed. These 4 4 kings divide the remaining deck into 5 5 equal sized parts on average, so there should be 379 / 45 379/45 cards per region in expectation. In turn, the expected number of additional cards needed to draw the king is 379 45 + 1 = 424 45 45 379 +1= 45 424 . Otherwise, if the first divider is a King, then we need to find the expected number of cards that need to be drawn until either an A or K appears. This is because we would obtain a stopping condition with either an A or K appearing. As with before, there are 52 − 53 / 9 = 415 / 9 52−53/9=415/9 cards left in the deck on average after the first card, and 7 7 of these are dividers ( 4 4 aces and 3 3 kings, since one was already drawn). Note that we need both A and K to be dividers because we want the expected number of cards appearing before either A or K appears. Thus, there are 415 / 9 − 7 = 352 / 9 415/9−7=352/9 non-divider cards left that need to be placed into 8 8 regions (which come from the 7 7 dividers). On average, there would be 352 / 72 352/72 cards in each of the 8 8 regions by the exchangeability of the spacings, so the expected number of cards that need to be drawn until the next A or K appears is 352 / 72 + 1 = 424 72 352/72+1= 72 424 . Combining all of the above, we have that the expected number of cards that are drawn is given by 44 9 + 1 + 1 2 ⋅ 424 45 + 1 2 ⋅ 424 72 = 1219 90 9 44 +1+ 2 1 ⋅ 45 424 + 2 1 ⋅ 72 424 = 90 1219 Note that the 53 / 9 53/9 occurs for all states because it is the expected number of cards that occur until the first A or K appears. questions.problem: $n$ random intervals are created by the following procedure: Two points are independently sampled uniformly at random from $(0,1)$. questions.solution: Let $L_i$ and $R_i$ be the left and right endpoints of each interval. Since we are looking at IID uniformly random values in $(0,1)$, it's easier to consider orderings. We need that < L i <R i for each $1 \leq i \leq n$ for the intervals to be valid (left endpoint must come before the right one). There are $(2n)!$ total orderings of the $2n$ uniformly random points, and there is a probability $1/2$ per pair that < L i <R i , as they are IID. Thus, the probability that this holds for all $n$ pairs is just 1 / 2 1/2 n . questions.title: Coinsecutive IV
questions.problem: Daniel flips a fair coin until he obtains $n \geq 1$ consecutive heads. Find the expected number of flips that Daniel performs when $n = 9$.
questions.solution: Let $e(k,n)$ be the expected number of flips that Daniel needs to perform to obtain $n$ consecutive heads when he has already obtained $0 \leq k \leq n$ consecutive heads. We want $e(0,n)$. The best approach here is to use a Law of Total Expectation/Markov Chain argument to condition on what happens at the next flip to derive a recurrence for $e(k,n)$. This is because of the fact that we either reach a state with $k+1$ consecutive heads or go back to the state with $0$ consecutive heads obtained, so the states are inherently quite related. A simple initial boundary is that $e(n,n) = 0$, as if $n$ heads are already obtained, no more flips need to be performed. For all 0 ≤ ≤ − 1 0≤k≤n−1, we perform $1$ flip, by the above discussion, we have that ( , ) = 1 + 1 2 ( + 1 , ) + 1 2 ( 0 , ) e(k,n)=1+ 2 1 e(k+1,n)+ 2 1 e(0,n). This occurs because of the fact that we perform $1$ flip, and with probability $1/2$, we obtain a head, which means we have $k+1$ consecutive heads now, which would imply there would be, on average, an additional $e(k+1,n)$ flips needed before obtaining $n$ consecutive heads. questions.title: Destined Ruin
questions.problem: A gambler starts with a bankroll of $\$n$ and goes to a casino. He bets $\$1$ each round. The gambler wins with probability $0 < p < 1$ and loses with probability 1 − 1−p independently between rounds. Find the probability that the gambler ruins after exactly $n+2k$ turns when $n = 6, k = 3,$ and $p = 1/3$. Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: For the gambler to ruin after exactly $n+2k$ turns, he must have exactly $n+k$ losses and $k$ wins in the $n+2k$ games. However, the gambler's balance is never allowed to be negative or $0$ at any time before the turn $n+2k$. To incorporate this condition, one has to be creative. When looking from the start of the game, this essentially just means that the number of losses can never be more than n larger than the number of wins. However, this condition is not easy to encode mathematically. Instead, it's easier to look backwards from the end of the game, as the current sum is 0 0 by this time. To ensure that the gambler has not bankrupted beforehand, the number of losses, when counting back from the end, must always be strictly larger than the number of wins. If the number of wins is larger at some point, then this implies that the gambler had negative money, and if they equalize, the gambler ruined before + 2 n+2k total rounds were played. As there are + n+k losses and k wins, the probability that the number of losses is always ahead of the number of wins is + − + + = + 2 n+k+k n+k−k = n+2k n . questions.title: Circular Ant I
questions.problem: We arrange $n$ ants around a circle at equally spaced increments, where $n$ is odd. All ants walk at a common constant speed that allows them to complete $1$ revolution per minute. We run an experiment where we randomly set each ant to face one of the two possible directions (clockwise or counterclockwise) with equal probability, and then have the ants walk for 1 1 minute. Whenever two ants bump into each other, they both turn around and start walking in the opposite direction at the same constant speed. At the end of the minute the ants stop and we check their positions. What is the probability that all n ants are in the same positions as they were originally when = 9 n=9?
questions.solution: This problem has a lot of sources of complexity, which include the potentially large number of ants, the randomness of the positions, and what happens when they bump into each other. Fortunately, there are many symmetries in this problem that simplify it greatly. The first key insight is that the set of the positions of the n ants at the end of the minute is the same as the set of the original positions. This can be seen by considering a simpler variant where the ants all look the same i.e. are indistinguishable. When two ants bump into each other and turn around, it would look the exact same as it would have if the ants just "walked through" one another. Therefore, we can consider the simplified experiment of all n ants walking in a full revolution uninterrupted and ending up with the same set of positions, as the bumping makes no difference in the grand scheme of the experiment. The other key insight into this problem is that the number of ants that are moving clockwise/counterclockwise at any given time is constant. Whenever two ants collide, we transition from one clockwise and one counterclockwise ant to one counterclockwise and one clockwise ant, respectively, so the total number of clockwise-walking ants has not changed. This also directly follows from the above, as it is as if the ants really phase through one another, so their directions didn't really change. Using the above two insights, we can solve the problem. For the n ant positions to be the same at the end of the experiment, we need every ant to have traveled the same number of revolutions, whether it's 1 1 revolution clockwise, 1 1 revolution counterclockwise, or 0 0 revolutions. Recall that the ants are distinguishable in the actual experiment, so they must have either all travelled clockwise, all travelled counterclockwise, or they didn't move in the end. The above implies that all n ants are in the same positions at the end of the experiment as before if and only if all n ants move clockwise (the first case), all n ants move counterclockwise, or equal amounts of ants move clockwise and counterclockwise (the last case). Since each configuration is equally likely, we can take the ratio of the number of ways that satisfy one of the above to the total number of arrangements. As n is odd here, there can't be an equal amount of ants that move clockwise and counterclockwise, and there are clearly only 2 2 configurations where the ants move all clockwise or all counterclockwise. Each of the n ants has 2 2 options as to which direction to move in, so there are 2 2 n total configurations of the ants initially, so for n odd, the answer is 2 / 2 = 1 / 2 − 1 2/2 n =1/2 n−1 . With the specified value, the answer is 1 / 256 1/256.

questions.title: Dyck Path I
questions.problem: A Dyck Path of length $2n$ in the plane is a path from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ in the plane where the path never crosses (but can touch) the $y=x$ line and the only possible movements from $(x,y)$ are $(x+1,y)$ and $(x,y+1)$. If the path stays strictly below $y=x$ outside of the endpoints, then it never crosses the line = − 1 y=x−1, as the next integer in the lattice above the line = − 1 y=x−1 would lie on $y = x$, which it is not allowed to touch. questions.title: Initial Head Equalization
questions.problem: You repeatedly flip a coin with probability $0 < p < 1$ of heads per flip until you obtain an equal running total of heads and tails for the first time. For a fixed integer $n \geq 1$, find the probability that you flip $2n$ times when $p = 1/4$ and $n = 5$. Round to the nearest hundred-thousandth.
questions.solution: To flip exactly $2n$ times, you must flip exactly $n$ heads and $n$ tails with a sequence where the running total of heads never equals the running total of tails beforehand. Thus, the approach is to find the probability of each such sequence with n heads and n tails, and then count the number of sequences that satisfy this condition. As there are n heads and n tails in the coin flip sequence and there is independence between flips, the probability of any particular sequence with n heads and n tails is ( 1 − ) p n (1−p) n . Now, we need to count the number of sequences that satisfy our condition. The condition of "the number of heads and tails never equalize before the end" is reminiscent of the Catalan numbers. Note that we could either have strictly more heads throughout or strictly more tails throughout the flipping process, and there are equal amounts of valid sequences where there are more heads vs. more tails. The equality can be seen b "reflecting" the sequences of heads and tails (so that every heads becomes a tails and vice versa). Every sequence that previously had more heads than tails throughout would now have more tails than heads throughout, and vice versa. Thus, we can just count sequences where there are more heads than tails throughout, and multiply by 2 2 to account for the other case. To count the number of sequences where there are strictly more heads than tails throughout, we can view this in the same light as "Dyck Path I", where a heads is a right movement and tails is an upwards movement. We want to count the number of sequences where the number of right movements is strictly more than the number of upwards movements throughout of length 2 2n. Equivalently, this path lies strictly below the = y=x line until the end. By the result of "Dyck Path I", there are 1 ( 2 − 2 − 1 ) n 1 ( n−1 2n−2 ) paths that satisfy this condition. Since we have to multiply by 2 2 for the other case, there are 2 ( 2 − 2 − 1 ) n 2 ( n−1 2n−2 ) satisfactory paths, so the probability of stopping after 2 2n turns is 2 ( 2 − 2 − 1 ) ⋅ ( 1 − ) n 2 ( n−1 2n−2 )⋅p n (1−p) n With the specified values, the answer is approximately 0.00324 0.00324.

Thus, the number of sequences where the number of heads always is strictly larger than the number of tails is − + ( + ) a+b a−b ( a a+b ). questions.title: Quant Pick III
questions.problem: A quant firm has $N$ candidates applying for an internship position. There are two positions available. Each applicant has a distinct quality rating from $1$ to $N$, where $1$ is the best and $N$ is the worst. This rating is not known to the interviewer, but they do know that there are exactly $N$ applicants. The applicants are interviewed one-by-one in random order. During the interview, the interviewer gains enough information to rank the applicant among all of the people that have interviewed thus far, but does not know anything about the quality of candidates that haven't been interviewed yet. Since the firm wants to be inclusive, their goal is to have the best intern train the worst intern. Design the optimal strategy to maximize the probability of selecting both the rank 1 1 quant and the rank N quant. As → ∞ N→∞, what does the probability that both the rank 1 1 and rank N quants are hired tend to? Round to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: We can think of this as two runs of the original problem: One where you want the best of all the applicants, and another where you want the worst of all the applicants. By "Quant Pick II", the probability that you select the best candidate under the optimal strategy tends to − 1 e −1 . Now, the optimal strategy for choosing the worst candidate is exactly the same as the one for choosing the best candidate, but you instead look for the first candidate after the discard period that is worse than the worst of the ones discarded. This has the same success probability of − 1 e −1 in limit of successfully picking the worst candidate, as we could essentially relabel rank i with rank ( + 1 ) − (N+1)−i (so that rank 1 1 becomes rank N, and vice versa), and picking the worst candidate among the original ranks would now be equivalent to picking the best candidate among the "reflected" ranks, which has probability − 1 e −1 of occurring by the result of "Quant Pick II". As → ∞ N→∞, we can view this as two (very close to) independent selection processes, as each candidate will be valid for at most one of the selection processes. Therefore, the probability that both the best and worst will be selected is roughly − 1 ⋅ − 1 = − 2 e −1 ⋅e −1 =e −2 .

questions.title: Coin Multisets
questions.problem: Two fair coins are repeatedly tossed until all multisets of outcomes are obtained. This means that only one of $HT$ or $TH$ must be obtained. Find the expected number of flips of the two coins that occur.
questions.solution: Since we are only considering multisets of the outcomes, $HT$ consists of $2$ outcomes: $HT$ and $TH$. This multiset is twice as likely as the other outcomes to appear. A simple linearity of expectation argument will not work here, as the expected number of flips is dependent on what is obtained at the first flip. Instead, the expected number of flips needed is dependent on which multisets still need to be seen. The best method is to derive a recurrence relation for the expected number of flips based on the number of solo multisets left to obtain ( HH or TT) versus the multiset that's more probable ( TH). Let ( , ) E(n,k) be the expected number of flips needed with n solo multisets and k more probable multisets. ( 2 , 1 ) E(2,1) is the value we want to compute. We can first derive a recurrence for ( 2 , 1 ) E(2,1) by condition on what happens at the first flip. If HH or TT is obtained at the first flip (probability 1 / 4 1/4 each), exactly 1 1 solo multiset remains, so an additional ( 1 , 1 ) E(1,1) flips are needed to end the process. Otherwise, with probability 1 / 2 1/2, TH or HT is obtained, which means only the two solo multisets remain. ( 2 , 0 ) E(2,0) additional flips are needed on average in this scenario. Therefore, we obtain the equation ( 2 , 1 ) = 1 + 1 2 ( 1 , 1 ) + 1 2 ( 2 , 0 ) E(2,1)=1+ 2 1 E(1,1)+ 2 1 E(2,0) Looking at ( 1 , 1 ) E(1,1), we can derive a similar recurrence. With probability 1 / 4 1/4, we obtain the same multiset that was obtained already, in which we still need an additional ( 1 , 1 ) E(1,1) flips on average. With probability 1 / 4 1/4, we obtain the other multiset, in which we need an additional ( 0 , 1 ) E(0,1) flips on average. Lastly, with probability 1 / 2 1/2, we obtain the more likely multiset, in which we need an additional ( 1 , 0 ) E(1,0) flips on average. Setting up the recurrence, we get ( 1 , 1 ) = 1 + 1 4 ( 1 , 1 ) + 1 4 ( 0 , 1 ) + 1 2 ( 1 , 0 ) ⟺ ( 1 , 1 ) = 4 3 + 1 3 ( 0 , 1 ) + 2 3 ( 1 , 0 ) E(1,1)=1+ 4 1 E(1,1)+ 4 1 E(0,1)+ 2 1 E(1,0)⟺E(1,1)= 3 4 + 3 1 E(0,1)+ 3 2 E(1,0) Computing expected values in the form ( , 0 ) E(i,0) and ( 0 , ) E(0,j) are fairly easy, as all of the remaining outcomes have the same probability of occurring. Namely, ( 1 , 0 ) E(1,0) is just the expected time to get the last solo multiset. There is probability 1 / 4 1/4 of this on each flip, so ( 1 , 0 ) = 4 E(1,0)=4, as the number of flips would be Geom ( 1 / 4 ) Geom(1/4) distributed. Similarly, ( 0 , 1 ) E(0,1) is the expected time to get the more probable multiset, which has probability 1 / 2 1/2 of appearing per flip. Therefore, ( 0 , 1 ) = 2 E(0,1)=2, as the number of flips needed to observe this multiset would be Geom ( 1 / 2 ) Geom(1/2) distributed. For ( 2 , 0 ) E(2,0), we have to apply a linearity of expectation argument, as there are two solo multisets that need to be seen. With probability 1 / 2 1/2, we see one of the solo multisets per flip (each of the two have probability 1 / 4 1/4 of appearing per flip). Thus, the expected number of flips to see one of them is 2 2. Once the first one has been observed, there is one solo multiset remaining, and it has probability 1 / 4 1/4 of appearing per flip. Therefore, the expected number of additional flips needed to see the last multiset is 4 4. By linearity of expectation, ( 2 , 0 ) = 2 + 4 = 6 E(2,0)=2+4=6. Plugging all of these values in, ( 1 , 1 ) = 4 3 + 1 3 ⋅ 2 + 2 3 ⋅ 4 = 14 3 ( 2 , 1 ) = 1 + 1 2 ⋅ 14 3 + 1 2 ⋅ 6 = 19 3 E(1,1) E(2,1) = 3 4 + 3 1 ⋅2+ 3 2 ⋅4= 3 14 =1+ 2 1 ⋅ 3 14 + 2 1 ⋅6= 3 19
