Drawing out a few paths on the plane, one can see that the paths of length − 1 n−1 that end by moving left/right have only $2$ options, as they are unable to move the direction opposite of where they just moved. However, if the last movement is upwards, there are three options, as there is no restriction from the previous movement. Therefore, all paths of length − 1 n−1 have 2 2 options, and then paths of length − 1 n−1 ending in an upwards movement have an additional option. There are − 1 s n−1 paths of length − 1 n−1, so there are 2 − 1 2s n−1 paths that come from every path having at least two options. However, how many paths of length − 1 n−1 end in an upwards movement? The answer is − 2 s n−2 , as you can append an upwards movement to any path of length − 2 n−2, and get a path of length − 1 n−1 that ends in an upwards movement. Plugging in this initial conditions yields the system 1 + 2 = 1 1 ( 1 + 2 ) + 2 ( 1 − 2 ) = 3 c 1 +c 2 c 1 (1+ 2 )+c 2 (1− 2 ) =1 =3 With some algebraic manipulation, one can show that 1 = 1 + 2 2 c 1 = 2 1+ 2 and 2 = 1 − 2 2 c 2 = 2 1− 2 . questions.title: Cubic Ant IV
questions.problem: A spider and an ant begin on opposite corners of a cube. Every minute, the spider moves to one of the vertices adjacent to it uniformly at random. The ant moves to one adjacent vertex uniformly at random every 2 2 minutes. The spider and ant both move exactly on the minute, so when both move, they are on the move at the same time. The spider eats the ant if they ever are on the same vertex. Find the expected amount of minutes until the spider eats the ant.
questions.solution: Similar to the other "ant on a cube" problems, this problem is best modelled by a Markov chain, as the next arrangement of the spider and ant is dependent on the current one. Since the spider and ant move uniformly at random, their current positions can be described by the distance between them presently. The possible distances between them are 0 , 1 , 2 , 0,1,2, and 3 3, so let E i be the expected amount of time (in minutes) for the ant and spider to be on the same vertex given that they are currently i movements apart from one another. We are looking to compute 3 E 3 , as the opposite corners are distance 3 3 apart. Very importantly, we will assume that neither the spider nor ant have moved yet, so there will be 2 2 minutes until the next ant movement in each case. This will become important later. The key goal here is to derive recurrences via Law of Total Expectation for each of the E i . For simplicity of explanation, assume the cube is the unit cube with vertices at ( , , ) (a,b,c), where , , = 0 , 1 a,b,c=0,1. Let's first compute 3 E 3 . There are two possible cases for the spider's movement in the two movements: It moves in two distinct directions or it moves back to where it started. In the second case, which occurs with probability 1 / 3 1/3 (one of three directions are opposite of where it just moved), no matter where the ant moves, it will be a distance 2 2 away from the spider, so it will take an additional 2 E 2 minutes on average to be eaten. In the first case, which occurs with probability 2 / 3 2/3, there are 2 2 distinct movements taken the by spider. There are two cases that can happen: The spider and ant meet, which occurs with probability 1 / 3 1/3 (one of the three movements by the ant makes it move to the spider's location), or the ant is two movements away from the spider, which occurs with probability 2 / 3 2/3. In the first sub-case, no additional minutes are needed, while in the second case 2 E 2 additional minutes are needed on average. Note that we can use 2 E 2 here because the process is starting again at a state where the ant and the spider are 2 2 units apart and there are 2 2 minutes until the ant moves again. By the Law of Total Expectation, 3 = 2 + 1 3 ⋅ ( 2 + 2 ) + 2 3 ( 2 3 ⋅ ( 2 + 2 ) + 1 3 ⋅ ( 0 ) ) = 2 + 7 9 2 E 3 =2+ 3 1 ⋅(2+E 2 )+ 3 2 ( 3 2 ⋅(2+E 2 )+ 3 1 ⋅(0))=2+ 9 7 E 2 We now perform a similar process for 2 E 2 . WLOG, assume that the ant is at ( 0 , 0 , 0 ) (0,0,0) and the spider is at ( 1 , 1 , 0 ) (1,1,0). In this calculation, we want to condition on the first movement of the spider. When calculating 3 E 3 , no matter where the spider moved in the first minute, it would be 2 2 units away from the ant; however, in this scenario, the spider could move to a position 1 1 unit or 3 3 units away from the ant in the first minute, so we must distinguish these. With probability 2 / 3 2/3, the spider moves to either ( 0 , 1 , 0 ) (0,1,0) or ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) (1,0,0), which are one unit away from the ant. WLOG, assume it moves to ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) (1,0,0). There are two sub-cases here: With probability 2 / 9 2/9, the ant and spider move to opposing corners, in which an additional 3 E 3 minutes are needed on average. With probability 7 / 9 7/9, the ant and spider are one unit away from each other, in which an additional 1 E 1 minutes are needed on average. For the other case, with probability 1 / 3 1/3, the spider moves to ( 1 , 1 , 1 ) (1,1,1), which is 3 3 units away from the ant. There are also two sub-cases here: With probability 1 / 3 1/3, the ant and spider stay in opposing corners, in which an additional 3 E 3 minutes are needed on average. With probability 2 / 3 2/3, the ant and spider are 1 1 unit apart, in which an additional 1 E 1 minutes are needed on average. Combining all of the above, 2 = 2 3 [ 2 + 2 9 3 + 7 9 1 ] + 1 3 [ 2 + 1 3 3 + 2 3 1 ] = 2 + 7 27 3 + 20 27 1 E 2 = 3 2 [2+ 9 2 E 3 + 9 7 E 1 ]+ 3 1 [2+ 3 1 E 3 + 3 2 E 1 ]=2+ 27 7 E 3 + 27 20 E 1 In the above, we can't just say have 1 E 1 and 3 E 3 inside the parentheses because after the first movement, there is only 1 1 minute until the ant moves again, which is not the scenario that we consider with the E i quantities. Lastly, we repeat the process for 1 E 1 . WLOG, suppose the ant is at ( 0 , 0 , 0 ) (0,0,0) and the spider is at ( 0 , 0 , 1 ) (0,0,1). With probability 1 / 3 1/3, the spider moves downwards to the ant directly and eats it, taking only 1 1 minute. Otherwise, with probability 2 / 3 2/3, the ant and spider are distance 2 2 apart. WLOG, say the spider moves to ( 0 , 1 , 1 ) (0,1,1). There are two sub-cases that can occur in the second minute: With probability 2 / 9 2/9, the spider and ant meet (they can meet at ( 0 , 0 , 1 ) (0,0,1) or ( 0 , 1 , 0 ) (0,1,0), both of which occur with probability 1 / 9 1/9). With probability 7 / 9 7/9, the spider and ant are two units apart, meaning an additional 2 E 2 minutes are needed on average. Combining the above cases, we get 1 = 1 3 ⋅ 1 + 2 3 [ 2 + 2 9 ⋅ 0 + 7 9 ⋅ 2 ] = 5 3 + 14 27 2 E 1 = 3 1 ⋅1+ 3 2 [2+ 9 2 ⋅0+ 9 7 ⋅E 2 ]= 3 5 + 27 14 E 2 Using a linear system solver on the three equations above, one obtains 3 = 1366 / 151 E 3 =1366/151.

questions.title: Geometric Progression
questions.problem: Three distinct integers from [ 100 ] = { 1 , 2 , … , 100 } [100]={1,2,…,100} are selected uniformly at random. Find the probability that the three numbers form a geometric progression. Report your answer to the nearest millionth. Here are some possible examples: $3 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 12$ (common ratio $2$) $81 \rightarrow 90 \rightarrow 10$ (common ratio $10/9$)
questions.solution: There are two very distinct cases to consider here: Integer common ratio and fractional common ratio. This is hinted at in the examples given in the question. Since the integers are selected uniformly at random from $[100]$, we can just count the number of geometric progressions, and then divide by the total ways to select $3$ integers from $[100]$, which is ( 100 3 ) ( 3 100 ). Let's start with counting integer common ratios. If $r$ is the common ratio, the three elements selected must be in the form , , 2 a,ar,ar 2 , where $a$ is the minimum value selected and $r$ is the common ratio. When $r$ is an integer, we don't have to be concerned about whether or not $ar$ and 2 ar 2 are integers. Thus, our only constraint is that they must be at most $100$. If $r$ is an integer, $r > 1$, as the integers are distinct. The goal is to count up the number of progressions that correspond to each common ratio. The progression is uniquely determined by a and r, so if we fix r, we can count the number of progressions by counting the number of valid values of a. With $r = 2$, the minimum value is $a = 1$, while the maximum is $a = 25$, as this yields $25 \rightarrow 50 \rightarrow 100$. We got this by looking at the maximum integer $a$ such that 2 = 4 ≤ 100 ar 2 =4a≤100. Therefore, we obtain $25$ progressions for this case With $r = 3$, the minimum value is $a = 1$, while the maximum is $a = 11$, as this yields $11 \rightarrow 33 \rightarrow 99$. $11$ is the maximum integer $a$ such that 2 = 9 ≤ 100 ar 2 =9a≤100. We can now generalize this pattern to integer values of $r$: The minimum value is $a = 1$, while the maximum value is ⌊ 100 / 2 ⌋ ⌊100/r 2 ⌋. The maximum valid value of $r$ such that ⌊ 100 / 2 ⌋ ⌊100/r 2 ⌋ is non-zero is $r = 10$, while yields the unique progression $1 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 100$. By the above, the number of geometric progressions with integer common ratio is ∑ = $2$ 10 ⌊ 100 2 ⌋ = 25 + 11 + 6 + $4$ + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 53 k=2 ∑ 10 ⌊ k 2 $100$ ⌋=25+11+6+4+2+2+1+1+1=53 Now, we move to the non-integer common ratios. This is a lot more complicated, as we don't have a particularly nice closed-form answer like we do for the integer case. This is because there are divisibility concerns: For example, if = 2 a=2 and = 3 / 2 r=3/2, this yields the sequence 2 → 3 → 9 / 2 2→3→9/2, which isn't fully contained in [ 100 ] [100]. Suppose the common ratio is a reduced fraction = / r=m/n. In particular, this means m and n have no common factors. Since a is supposed to be the smallest value in the progression, we also have > m>n. For ar and 2 ar 2 to both be integers, it must be the case that 2 ∣ n 2 ∣a, as 2 = 2 2 ar 2 = n 2 am 2 , and we also know that m and n have no common factors. Furthermore, we know ≤ 10 m≤10, as if 2 ∣ n 2 ∣a, ≥ 2 a≥n 2 , so 2 ≥ 2 ⋅ 2 2 = 2 ar 2 ≥n 2 ⋅ n 2 m 2 =m 2 , so if > 10 m>10, 2 > 100 m 2 >100, meaning 2 ar 2 is not in [ 100 ] [100]. The idea is to condition on the value of n, look at all the possible values of m corresponding to n, and then determine how many progression correspond to each one. Conditioning on n is better because it limits the possible search space of starting values a to multiples of 2 n 2 . To simplify notation, we will write the progress as ( , , 2 ) (a,ar,ar 2 ). questions.title: Shuffly Deck
questions.problem: A deck consists of $r$ red and $b$ blue cards. Each turn goes as follows: The deck is shuffled completely at random. The card on top is dealt, and it's color is noted. Continue dealing from the deck without replacement until the first card of the other color appears. Replace back the card of the other color that you just drew into the deck. Do not replace any cards drawn beforehand. This process is repeated until the deck is empty. Find the probability that the last card drawn from the deck is blue when = 50 r=50 and = 100 b=100.
questions.solution: This is a very complicated scenario, so it's not worthwhile to chase down the exact distribution of cards at each time. Recurrences also do not work here, as you would need to be recursive on both r and b, which is not easy to solve. Instead, let's look at the end of the game, and then work backwards. At the end of the game, when the last card is drawn, all of the cards in the deck must be of the same color: If they weren't at some point, a card of a different color would be drawn, and it would be replaced back into the deck. For this to be blue, in the last turn, all of the cards remaining must be blue. Therefore, on the turn before the final card is drawn, all of the red cards must have been drawn out. For this to happen, all of the red cards must come before all of the blue cards. To see this, consider what happens if this isn't the case: If the first card drawn on the second-to-last turn was blue, then a red being drawn would stop the drawing process, and the red card would be replaced for the next turn, meaning the deck wouldn't contain only blue cards. If the first card drawn on the second-to-last turn was red, then a blue card would stop the drawing process. Since we're assuming that there is at least one blue card before the last red card, there would be a red card that hasn't been discarded yet, also violating the condition that the deck doesn't only contain blue cards in the end. The above discussion implies that on the second-to-last turn of the process, all the red cards and all of the blue cards must be contiguous (i.e. all adjacent to one another). Thus, when the game is two turns away from ending, the cards are in the form … … R…RB…B or … … B…BR…R. Both of these arrangements of cards are equally likely, regardless of the number of reds and blue cards there are, as there are just two permutations with the same amount of cards of each type. A blue card is the last one drawn in the first case above (all reds come before the first blue). When the game is about to end, both states are equally likely, so the probability of the last card being blue is 1 / 2 1/2, regardless of the initial amounts r and b!

questions.title: See All Sides III
questions.problem: Fix $n > 1$. An − n−sided die with the values $1$ to $n$ is rolled repeatedly until all of the sides appear. The die is weighted such that the value $1$ has probability 2 + 1 n+1 2 of appearing, while the values $2$ to $n$ each have probability 1 + 1 n+1 1 of appearing. Find the expected number of rolls needed to observe all of the sides when $n = 6$.
questions.solution: The methodology of the previous parts will not work, as the sides are not all equally likely anymore. We formed the random variables 1 , … , X 1 ,…,X n based on the time it takes for the ith distinct side to appear. However, we were able to determine the distribution of each $X_i$ because the sides all had the same probability. In this situation, if a one appears first, the next Geometric random variable has success parameter − 1 + 1 n+1 n−1 , as there is probability $2/(n+1)$ of rolling $1$. If the first value appearing is anything but $1$, the next Geometric distribution would have parameter + $1$ n+1 n . Since the above approach doesn't work in it's current form, to utilize what we already know, we can "create" a die that is fair, and then modify it in some way to adjust for our scenario. Since the probability of a 1 1 is 2 $n+1$ 2 , we can instead envision our − n−sided die as an ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−sided die that has two sides labelled $1$. This modification ensures the probability of a $1$ is 2 + 1 n+1 2 per roll. To observe a 1 1, we only need to see one of the two sides that has a 1 1. Now, roll this fair ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−sided die until all of the sides are observed. By the result of "See All Sides II", the expected number of rolls performed is ( + 1 ) ∑ = 1 + 1 1 (n+1) i=1 ∑ n+1 i 1 This amount overestimates the true expected value because we may have rolled longer than we actually needed to. In particular, if we observed all of the values 2 2 to n on the die before the second 1 1 appears, there's no need to continue rolling. To account for this, we subtract out the expected number of additional rolls that are performed as a result of the die modification. We only have extraneous rolls when the last value to be observed on the ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−sided die is one of the two 1 1s. The probability of the last observed value being 1 1 is 2 + 1 n+1 2 , as each of the two 1 1s are equally likely to be the last side observed. When we are continually rolling to get the last 1 1, that particular 1 1 appears with probability 1 + 1 n+1 1 per turn, so, on average, + 1 n+1 extraneous rolls are performed when the remaining side is a 1 1. Using this, we can conclude the true expected number of rolls to see all of the sides on the original die is ( + 1 ) ∑ = 1 + 1 1 − 2 + 1 ⋅ ( + 1 ) = ( + 1 ) ∑ = 1 + 1 1 − 2 (n+1) i=1 ∑ n+1 i 1 − n+1 2 ⋅(n+1)=(n+1) i=1 ∑ n+1 i 1 −2 With the specified values, the answer is 323 / 20 = 16.15 323/20=16.15. This is slightly higher than the fair die case, which was 14.7 14.7. Intuitively, this makes sense because our die is biased to the value 1 1, which means it's "less random" than the completely fair die. Therefore, there's a higher probability of getting repeated values, meaning more rolls are needed.

questions.title: See All Sides IV
questions.problem: Fix $n > 2$. An − n−sided die with the values $1$ to $n$ is rolled repeatedly until all of the sides appear. The die is weighted such that the values $1$ and $2$ have probability 2 + 2 n+2 2 of appearing, while the values $3$ to $n$ each have probability 1 + 2 n+2 1 of appearing. Find the expected number of rolls needed to observe all of the sides when $n = 6$.
questions.solution: Since the die is once again biased in such a way that the larger probability is a multiple of the smaller probability, we apply a similar strategy to "See All Sides III". Instead of having an ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−sided die, we have a fair ( + 2 ) − (n+2)−sided die labelled with 2 2 sides for each of the values 1 1 and 2 2. Just as in the last problem, we repeatedly roll until we see all the sides, and we adjust afterwards for extraneously rolling. The expected number of rolls to see all + 2 n+2 sides is ( + 2 ) ∑ = 1 + 2 1 (n+2) i=1 ∑ n+2 i 1 The above over-counts the true number of rolls needed because it's possible to obtain at least one of each value before obtaining the second 1 1 and/or 2 2, in which case, we would be done earlier. Therefore, we need to subtract out the expected number of extraneous rolls performed. Unlike the last problem, there are now two cases where the rolls are extraneous: We could be rolling additionally for both 1 1 and 2 2, or just one of them. It's important to distinguish between these cases because they have different expected amounts of extraneous rolls. We roll extraneously for both a 1 1 and 2 2 exactly when the last two values appearing on the ( + 2 ) − (n+2)−sided die are 1 1 and 2 2 in some order. With = 6 n=6, for example, such sequences include 12345612 12345612 and 12345621 12345621. We roll extraneously for just one of the sides if the last value appearing is a 1 1 or 2 2, and the second-to-last value is anything but the other of 1 1 or 2 2 that's in the final spot. With = 6 n=6, some examples include 12234561 12234561 and 22345611 22345611. Let's start with the case where we roll for both 1 1 and 2 2 extraneously. To find the probability of this case, let's consider how it can happen. There are 2 2 ways to arrange the 1 1 and 2 2 once they are actually in the last two spots, so we can compute the probability of 1 1 being the ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−st value rolled and 2 2 being the last value rolled, and then multiply by 2 2 to account for the other order. The probability of a 1 1 appearing as the ( + 1 ) (n+1)st distinct value is 2 + 2 n+2 2 , as there are 2 2 sides of the + 2 n+2 that are 1 1. Given this, the probability the last value is 2 2 is 2 + 1 n+1 2 , as there are now only + 1 n+1 remaining sides that can fill the spot, and 2 2 of them are the value 2 2. Thus, the probability of the last two spots being 1 1 and 2 2 in some order is 2 ⋅ 2 + 2 ⋅ 2 + 1 = 8 ( + 1 ) ( + 2 ) 2⋅ n+2 2 ⋅ n+1 2 = (n+1)(n+2) 8 . In this case, there are two values to sides to roll still. After that, only 1 1 of the + 2 n+2 sides remains, which would take an average of + 2 n+2 rolls to obtain. Thus, the expected number of extraneous rolls in this case is 3 2 ( + 2 ) 2 3 (n+2). Thus, the probability of the last side appearing being either 1 1 or 2 2 is 4 + 2 n+2 4 . WLOG, suppose that it is a 1 1. This choice is irrelevant because 1 1 and 2 2 are equally likely. Given that the last side appearing is 1 1, the second-to-last side appearing must be anything but either of the 2 2s, which constitute − 1 n−1 of the remaining + 1 n+1 sides. Thus, the probability of the other case is 4 ( − 1 ) ( + 2 ) ( + 1 ) (n+2)(n+1) 4(n−1) . In this case, we only wait for 1 1 additional side, which has probability 1 + 2 n+2 1 of appearing per trial. questions.problem: There are $n$ pairs of gloves in a drawer, with each pair having a unique label $1$ to $n$ on it. Gloves in the same pair have the same label. questions.title: Many Consecutive Heads II
questions.problem: A fair coin is flipped $n$ times. Find the probability that there is no run of $k$ consecutive heads nor tails, $1 \leq k \leq n$, among the $n$ flips when $n = 11$ and $k = 4$.
questions.solution: Since all of the sequences of flips are equally likely, the best approach is to count the number of sequences that satisfy this condition. As we need to ensure there aren't k consecutive heads nor tails, we can't have a sequence of length k consistent of the same outcomes. A natural choice is to compare positions i and + 1 i+1 for each 1 ≤ ≤ − 1 1≤i≤n−1 to see if they are the same. Thus, we represent our sequence of n coin flips by − 1 n−1 1 1s or 0 0s, where a 1 1 at position i means that positions i and + 1 i+1 are the same outcome, while a 0 0 means they differ. As the coin is fair, the probability that two consecutive flips are the same, hence a 1 1, is 1 / 2 1/2. A sequence of k consecutive identical flips can be identified by a string of − 1 k−1 consecutive 1 1s in the sequence. Therefore, we've now transformed the question into: How many sequences of length − 1 n−1 don't have a run of − 1 k−1 or more 1 1s? Since 0 0 and 1 1 are equally likely to be in each position, we can identify 1 1 as a head and conclude that we can apply the result of "Many Consecutive Heads I" to this with n and k as − 1 n−1 and − 1 k−1. Note that we also must replace 2 2 n with 2 − 1 2 n−1 in the denominator, as there are only 2 − 1 2 n−1 such binary strings of length − 1 n−1. Alternatively, one can note that any sequence of 0 0s and 1 1s can be linked in two of the original sequences where H and T are flipped, so we would multiply the number of satisfactory sequences of 0 0s and 1 1s by 2 2 to get the number of satisfactory sequences of H and T. The extra factor of 2 2 in the numerator would reduce the denominator to 2 − 1 2 n−1 . questions.title: See All Sides VI
questions.problem: An − n−sided die with the values 1 , 2 , … , 1,2,…,n is such that side $i$ appears with probability $p_i$ per roll. Find the expected number of rolls that must be performed until all $n$ sides appear once. Report the answer when = 3 , 1 = 1 / 5 , 2 = 1 / 2 , n=3,p 1 =1/5,p 2 =1/2, and 3 = 3 / 10 p 3 =3/10.
questions.solution: The approach of the previous problems is not feasible here, as the probabilities are no longer proportional in any way. To generalize our method, we pose the problem as follows: Let $T_i$ be the number of rolls needed for the ith side to appear for the first time. The random variable max ⁡ { 1 , … , } max{T 1 ,…,T n } represents the number of rolls that must be performed to see all the sides, as we stop rolling the moment we see all n sides. Thus, we must solve for [ max ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] E[max{T 1 ,…,T n }]. Our largest issue is that 1 , … , T 1 ,…,T n are not independent, so we can't use the tail sum. To resolve this, we instead use the maximum-minimum principle. This states that for any real numbers 1 , … , x 1 ,…,x n , max ⁡ { 1 , … , } = ∑ = 1 − ∑ < min ⁡ { , } + ∑ < < min ⁡ { , , } + ⋯ + ( − 1 ) + 1 min ⁡ { 1 , … , } max{x 1 ,…,x n }= i=1 ∑ n x i − i<j ∑ min{x i ,x j }+ i<j<k ∑ min{x i ,x j ,x k }+⋯+(−1) n+1 min{x 1 ,…,x n } You can view this exactly in the same light as the inclusion-exclusion principle, but ∪ ∪ is now the maximum, while ∩ ∩ is now the minimum. We can write the above more succinctly as max ⁡ { 1 , … , } = ∑ = 1 ∑ 1 < ⋯ < ( − 1 ) + 1 min ⁡ { 1 , … , } max{x 1 ,…,x n }= k=1 ∑ n i 1 <⋯<i k ∑ (−1) k+1 min{x i 1 ,…,x i k } This is helpful because it's much easier to find the expected value of the minimum of first occurrences. By substituting in x i as T i and taking expected values on both sides, we obtain [ max ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] = ∑ = 1 ∑ 1 < ⋯ < ( − 1 ) + 1 [ min ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] E[max{T 1 ,…,T n }]= k=1 ∑ n i 1 <⋯<i k ∑ (−1) k+1 E[min{T i 1 ,…,T i k }] What remains is to compute [ min ⁡ { 1 , … , ] E[min{T i 1 ,…,T i k ]. This random variable intuitively represents the expected time to see ANY of the sides 1 , … , i 1 ,…,i k . There is a probability p i of seeing side i, so we see one of the sides 1 , … , i 1 ,…,i k with probability 1 + ⋯ + p i 1 +⋯+p i k per roll. Thus, the number of rolls needed to observe any of the sides 1 , … , i 1 ,…,i k is given Geom ( 1 + ⋯ + ) Geom(p i 1 +⋯+p i k ) distributed, which has mean [ min ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] = 1 1 + … E[min{T i 1 ,…,T i k }]= p i 1 +…p i k 1 Therefore, we can conclude [ max ⁡ { 1 , … , } ] = ∑ = 1 ∑ 1 < ⋯ < ( − 1 ) + 1 ⋅ 1 1 + … E[max{T 1 ,…,T n }]= k=1 ∑ n i 1 <⋯<i k ∑ (−1) k+1 ⋅ p i 1 +…p i k 1 With the specified values, the answer is 5 + 2 + 10 3 − ( 10 7 + 5 4 + 2 ) + 1 = 559 84 5+2+ 3 10 −( 7 10 + 4 5 +2)+1= 84 559

questions.title: Spirit Airlines I
questions.problem: On a sold out Spirit Airlines flight, $n$ people decide to risk it all and line up to board the plane. They may never make it to the destination. The first passenger in the line has lost their boarding pass, but is allowed in. They take a random seat. If available, every subsequent passenger takes their assigned seat. If their seat is not available, the passenger chooses an open seat uniformly at random to sit in. Find the expected number of passengers that sit in their own seat when = 100 n=100 to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: We are looking to count the expected count of some events that are not independent, so counting with indicators and linearity of expectation is the proper approach. Label the people 1 − 1−n, where $1$ is the person who lost their boarding pass, and define $I_i$ as the indicator of the ith person sitting in their seat. = $1$ + ⋯ + T=I $1$ +⋯+I n gives the total number of people that sit in their correct spot. By linearity of expectation, [ ] = [ 1 ] + [ 2 ] + ⋯ + [ ] E[T]=E[I 1 ]+E[I 2 ]+⋯+E[I n ] Our goal is to compute [ ] E[I i ] for each 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤n, the probability that person i sits in their correct seat. Since person 1 1 is separate from the rest, we should consider them first. Person 1 1 selects randomly, so they sit in their seat with probability [ 1 ] = 1 / E[I 1 ]=1/n. Now, let's consider [ ] E[I i ] for 2 ≤ ≤ 2≤i≤n, as these people's probability of sitting in their seat is dependent on the actions of the people coming before them. Let's first consider some simple cases of the second and third people to board. For the second person to sit in their correct spot, person 1 1 can't take their spot. Thus, with probability − 1 n n−1 , person 2 2 is in their correct spot. Now, for the third person, the probability is dependent on where both 1 1 and 2 2 sit. With probability 1 / 1/n, person 1 1 sits in their correct spot, meaning all of the remaining people also sit in their correct spot. Otherwise, with probability − 3 n n−3 , person 1 1 sits in a spot not belonging to people 1 , 2 , 1,2, nor 3 3, meaning person 3 3 will sit in their own spot. Otherwise, with probability 1 / 1/n, person 1 1 sits in the spot belonging to person 2 2. Given this, person 2 2 doesn't sit in the spot belonging to person 3 3 with probability − 2 − 1 n−1 n−2 , as − 2 n−2 of the remaining − 1 n−1 spots don't belong to person 3 3, so the total probability of person 3 3 sitting in their own spot is 1 ⋅ 1 + − 3 ⋅ 1 + 1 ⋅ − 2 − 1 = − 2 ( 1 + 1 − 1 ) = − 2 − 1 n 1 ⋅1+ n n−3 ⋅1+ n 1 ⋅ n−1 n−2 = n n−2 (1+ n−1 1 )= n−1 n−2 Furthermore, you may recall from the "basic" airplane probability that there is probability 1 / 2 1/2 of the final person getting their seat. These fractions are all in the form + 1 j+1 j for some positive integer j. Namely, we claim that the probability that the jth to last person to enter the plane has probability + 1 j+1 j of obtaining their seat, where 1 ≤ ≤ − 1 1≤j≤n−1. Alternatively, the jth person to enter the flight has probability + 1 − + 2 − n+2−j n+1−j of getting their seat, where 2 ≤ ≤ 2≤j≤n. Here's the key insight to get this relationship: At any given time, there is at most one person who is yet to board whose seat has been taken. For example, with = 5 n=5, if person 1 1 takes seat 4 4, people 2 2 and 3 3 get their correct seat, and person 4 4 is the only individual whose seat is already occupied upon entry. This is because when someone boards, either they sit in their correct seat, or they take the seat belonging to someone else, but remove themselves from the queue. In both cases, the net number of pre-taken seats doesn't change. Using this, upon the kth person entering, there are − ( − 1 ) n−(k−1) empty seats. Person k gets their seat exactly when they are not the person in the queue who seat is already taken. Imagine the last person whose selected randomly stands up. There would now be − ( − 2 ) n−(k−2) open seats that look identical to that person, as they select uniformly at random. The probability that person took the seat of person k is 1 − ( − 2 ) n−(k−2) 1 , so with probability − ( − 1 ) − ( − 2 ) n−(k−2) n−(k−1) , person k gets their seat. One can also verify this rigorously. Let ( , ) P(n,j) be the probability that the jth person gets their seat when there are n total people. This probability is influenced by the location of person 1 1, so we condition on their location. Namely, if person 1 1 sits in position > k>j or their own seat = 1 k=1, the jth person gets their seat with probability 1 1. If person 1 1 sits in the jth seat, they get their own seat with probability 0 0, as it's already occupied. Otherwise, if they sit in seat 2 ≤ ≤ − 1 2≤k≤j−1, it's as if the process starts all over again, with person k as the first "wanderer". − ( − 1 ) n−(k−1) seats would still be open at the time the kth person: Seat 1 1 and seats + 1 k+1 to n. questions.title: Guaranteed Card Profit
questions.problem: Cards are turned face up one at a time from the top of a well-shuffled standard deck You start with a bankroll of $\$1$ and are allowed to bet any amount of your wealth on the color of the next card. The next card is revealed to you, and you immediately get to collect your profit if you are correct. This repeats for all $52$ cards in the deck. How would you play this game to maximize your guaranteed earnings? Under this strategy, report your minimum guaranteed profit to the nearest cent.
questions.solution: A very basic strategy is to just bet all of your money on the last card, as you always know it's color, meaning you walk away with $\$1$ extra always. The primary question is: Can one do better than this? Instead of waiting until the end, is there amount proportion that we could bet before the end that would allow us to always make money? We can improve on $\$2$ by waiting to bet until three cards remain. If they are all one color, we can make $\$7$ profit. Otherwise, WLOG, we can say $2$ are black and $1$ is red (it doesn't matter since the colors are exchangeable). We can bet $\$1/3$ on the next card being black. If the card is red, we lose $\$1/3$, but we know the color of the final two cards, so we can bet it all, earning us a profit of $\$5/3$. Otherwise, if the card is black, we make $\$1/3$ and can wait for the last card to show and bet it all, yielding us a guaranteed profit of $\$5/3$ in this case too. In the above, we bet in proportion to how many cards were remaining: Since there was a slight bias towards black, we bet some money on black. In particular, there was $1$ more black card than red, and there were $3$ total cards, so we should bet $\$1/3$ on black. The idea is we want to extend this backwards somehow. No matter what strategy we use, we will obviously want to bet everything at every round as soon as the remaining deck becomes monochromatic, as we know all the colors. Let's call all strategies with this property sensible. Before we look at guaranteed profit, one may wonder if there is a strategy that maximizes the expected profit. Any strategy that maximizes expected profit would be sensible, as you'd want to bet everything for as long as you can where you're guaranteed to make money, hence increasing expected value. However, the converse is also true: Any sensible strategy maximizes expected profit. In particular, all of them have the same expected profit! Consider the following basic strategy: Bet all of your money at every round on some fixed sequence of black and red cards appearing. There are ( 52 26 ) ( 26 52 ) such sequences one could pick, as we only regard the color of the cards, and all are equally likely. The probability of this sequence hitting is 1 ( 52 26 ) ( 26 52 ) 1 , and your bankroll at the end would be $ 2 52 $2 52 , as you would double your money every single round. Thus, your expected profit on this strategy is 2 52 ( 52 26 ) ≈ $ 9.08 ( 26 52 ) 2 52 ≈$9.08 This strategy almost always makes you go broke, but it is indeed sensible by our definition: You'll bet everything you have, which is either a lot of money or nothing. The key here is that every sensible strategy one could implement is a combination of pure strategies of this form. To see why, imagine you had ( 52 26 ) ( 26 52 ) assistants that each had $ 1 ( 52 26 ) $ ( 26 52 ) 1 each bet on one of the distinct pure strategies above. Exactly one of them would multiply their money to $ 9.08 $9.08, while the others would bankrupt, as only one sequence comes out. It should seem reasonable that every sensible strategy amounts to distributing your $ 1 $1 among these assistants in some way. At any point, if your assistants are putting $ $x on red and $ $y on black combined, it's equivalent to you putting a $ ( − ) $(x−y) bet on red (when > x>y) or $ ( − ) $(y−x) bet on black (when < x<y). For example, if your assistants are betting $ 0.45 $0.45 on red and $ 0.55 $0.55 on black, you either receive $ 0.90 $0.90 if red appears or $ 1.10 $1.10 if black appears. This would be the exact same as if you bet $ 0.10 $0.10 on black, as you'd either earn $ 0.10 $0.10 or lose $ 0.10 $0.10 in the same scenarios as above. We can implement such a strategy above as follows: Suppose you look to bet $ $x on a color (WLOG, say red). You would assign your assistants $ 1 + 2 $ 2 1+x to the assistants betting on red as the first card $ 1 − 2 $ 2 1−x to the assistants betting on black. Suppose you were correct and want to bet $ $y on black. You would now allot $ $y more to the assistants guessing "red-black" at the start than those guessing "red-red". Note that the ones who guessed black at the start already bankrupted and no longer have money. One can iterate this repeatedly for each one to get their assigned stake. Since each pure strategy has the same expected value, any sensible strategy has the same expected value of $ 9.08 $9.08, yielding $ 8.08 $8.08 in profit. However, not all of these strategies guarantee this amount. Only one of them does, and it's exactly what we described before: Give each assistant the same amount of money at the start, and exactly one of them will always end with $ 9.08 $9.08. This strategy is easily implemented in the game as follows: If there are r red and b black cards currently in the deck, assuming ≥ b≥r, bet a proportion − + b+r b−r on the next card being black, and if < b<r, bet a proportion − + r+b r−b on the next card being red. This is exactly the strategy we described at the beginning, and it makes intuitive sense: You want to bet in proportion to how much of an advantage there is. With this, you're always guaranteed $ 8.08 $8.08 in profit.

questions.title: Reunite
questions.problem: You generate a uniformly random number in $(0,1)$ for free. You can either choose to cash out on this number first, or you can choose to generate a uniformly random number in $(0,1)$ for a price of $0 < p < 1$. Your payout is the maximum of all the numbers you generate before cashing out. Assuming you play optimally, find the expected payout when = 0.045 p=0.045.
questions.solution: The optimal strategy of this game will be to cash out when you first obtain a value $x \geq t$ for some threshold $0 \leq t \leq 1$. This is because, intuitively, each play is a new game with the same conditions as before, so your strategy should remain constant. Since the game is under the same conditions between rounds, the threshold must also be constant, as you have already paid for those previous rolls. The goal now is to find the optimal t. The optimal threshold t is the value such that we are indifferent to rolling again versus cashing out. Thus, ( ) = ∑ = 1 [ Applicant is selected and is the best applicant ] = ∑ = 1 [ Applicant is selected ∣ Applicant is the best ] [ Applicant is the best ] = ∑ = 1 − 1 0 + ∑ = [ Applicant is selected ∣ Applicant is the best ] [ Applicant is the best ] P(t) = i=1 ∑ N P[Applicantiis selected and is the best applicant] = i=1 ∑ N P[Applicantiis selected∣Applicantiis the best]P[Applicantiis the best] = i=1 ∑ t−1 0+ i=t ∑ N P[Applicantiis selected∣Applicantiis the best]P[Applicantiis the best] The first term is 0 0 because of the fact that all of the first − 1 t−1 people are discarded immediately, so there is no chance for any of the first − 1 t−1 applicants to be selected. Now, to compute the conditional probability, note that if i is the best applicant, then they need to be the first person that is better than the best of the first − 1 t−1 applicants. For this to occur, it must be the case that none of the people that came before person i were better than the best of the first − 1 t−1. If this did happen, the interviewer would have selected that other person before candidate i appears. Therefore, the needed condition is that the best of the first − 1 i−1 candidates is in the discarded pile i.e. the best of the first − 1 i−1 is also the person that is the best of the first − 1 t−1. As the best of the first − 1 i−1 candidates is equally likely to be in any of the − 1 i−1 spots, the probability that they lie in the first − 1 t−1 spots (so that they are discarded) is − 1 − 1 i−1 t−1 , which is the value of that conditional probability. However, we get around this by noting that if = 1 t=1, there are no candidates discarded, so the only possible strategy is to choose the first candidate that walks in, as they are better than all of the observed candidates up until that point. questions.title: Tourney Fight
questions.problem: Alice and Bob are in the Roman era. Each of them has a team of gladiators. Alice has $n$ gladiators of respective powers 1 , … , a 1 ,…,a n , while Bob has $m$ gladiators of respective powers 1 , … , b 1 ,…,b m . Assume that all powers are integer-valued. The tournament consists of Alice and Bob picking gladiators to fight against one another one-at-a-time. The two gladiators fight to the death, and there is no possibility of a tie. Each gladiator wins in proportion to their power i.e. if the two gladiators have powers x and y, the probability that the gladiator with power x wins is / ( + ) x/(x+y), and similar for y. The winning gladiator also inherits the power of its opponent. This means that if a gladiator of power of x wins against a gladiator of power y, the winning gladiator now has power + x+y. Alice picks her gladiator first for each fight. Afterwards, if he has one, Bob selects his gladiator to go against Alice's. The winner of the tournament is the player that has at least one gladiator left when the other person runs out of gladiators. Under optimal play from Bob, what is his probability of winning if = 4 , = 8 , = 2 , n=4,m=8,a i =2i, and = b i =i.
questions.solution: Instead of viewing this as "power", which is quite abstract, we can instead view this problem combinatorially as a stack of power for Alice and Bob. The key is to realize that they are betting power in each match and the bets are fair. Thus, for each gladiator in the arena, assign x balls if their power is x. This means that Alice and Bob will have ∑ = 1 i=1 ∑ n a i and ∑ = 1 j=1 ∑ m b j balls respectively in the stack whose total height is ∑ = 1 + ∑ = 1 i=1 ∑ n a i + j=1 ∑ m b j . Now, we shuffle all of the balls in the stack into a uniformly random order. The question now becomes: What is the winning condition. In other words, what happens when a gladiator wins? The winning gladiator absorbs the power of the losing one, so if the losing gladiator had power k, k balls belonging to the losing player are transferred to the winning player. Now, we also must encapsulate the / ( + ) x/(x+y) winning probability. We must cook up some event that has probability / ( + ) x/(x+y) for two gladiators whose powers are x and y. Note that if we restrict ourselves to the + x+y balls that belong to the two gladiators in play, x of those + x+y belong to the gladiator with x power. Thus, we can consider the relative ordering of the balls that belong to those two gladiators. In particular, we can say that the winner is the gladiator whose ball is highest up in the stack among the two gladiators in play. This has probability / ( + ) x/(x+y), as each of the + x+y balls in our restricted vision are equally likely to be the top, and x of them belong to the gladiator with power x. Thus, the winning gladiator is the one that has the ball highest in the stack relative to the two gladiators in play. Furthermore, the surviving gladiator's new collection of balls is uniformly distributed in the vertical order, so there is independence between trials. The winner of the entire tournament is the person who has the top-most ball in the stack, as there is no ball that is higher than it. In other words, whichever of Alice or Bob owns the gladiator whose ball is the top of the stack is the person who wins the tournament. As the balls are arranged uniformly at random, we have that the probability it belongs to Bob is just the number of balls Bob has divided by the total number of balls in the stack. Note that the above implies that all strategies that Bob can apply are equally good. There is no optimal strategy for Bob to send out his gladiators in! The probability Bob wins is ∑ = 1 ∑ = 1 + ∑ = 1 ∑ j=1 m b j +∑ i=1 n a i ∑ j=1 m b j With the specified values, the answer is 9 / 14 9/14.

questions.title: More Biased?
questions.problem: Two coins are before you, say $1$ and $2$, where coin $i$ has probability $p_i$ of heads. However, $p_1$ and $p_2$ are unknown to you, so you assign a Uniform prior to the values of $p_1$ and $p_2$ . You flip each coin $n$ times. For some $0 \leq k \leq n$, coin $1$ shows heads $k$ times, while coin $2$ shows heads − n−k times. Find the probability that coin $2$ is more biased (i.e. has a probability that deviates from $1/2$ by a larger amount) than coin $1$ when $n = 30$ and $k = 10$.
questions.solution: Let's first set up this problem via conditional distributions. We suppose that 1 , 2 ∼ Unif ( 0 , 1 ) P 1 ,P 2 ∼Unif(0,1) IID. Define $N_1$ and $N_2$ as the number of heads that appear in $n$ flips on coins $1$ and $2$, respectively. Given $P_1$ and $P_2$ , the distributions of $N_1$ and $N_2$ are easy to determine: They would count the distribution of number of heads in $n$ flips of a coin of some fixed probability, so 1 ∣ 1 ∼ Binom ( , 1 ) N 1 ∣P 1 ∼Binom(n,P 1 ), and likewise with 2 ∣ 2 N 2 ∣P 2 . The "bias" of coin i is ∣ − 1 / 2 ∣ ∣P i −1/2∣, which is the distance from $1/2$ to the value of the probability. We are looking to compute [ ∣ $1$ − 1 / $2$ ∣ < ∣ 2 − 1 / 2 ∣ ∣ 1 = , 2 = − ] P[∣P 1 −1/2∣<∣P 2 −1/2∣∣N 1 =k,N 2 =n−k] For starters, it helps to know the distribution of 1 ∣ 1 P 1 ∣N 1 and 2 ∣ 2 P 2 ∣N 2 , as we are computing a probability involving their posterior distributions above. Namely, 1 ∣ 1 = 1 ∼ Beta ( 1 + 1 , ( − 1 ) + 1 ) P 1 ∣N 1 =n 1 ∼Beta(n 1 +1,(n−n 1 )+1), which intuitively makes sense by the interpretation of the Beta distribution, as we had 1 n 1 successes (heads) on the coin, as well as − 1 n−n 1 failures (tails). Thus, given our information above, 1 ∣ 1 = ∼ Beta ( + 1 , − + 1 ) P 1 ∣N 1 =k∼Beta(k+1,n−k+1), while 2 ∣ 2 = − ∼ Beta ( − + 1 , + 1 ) P 2 ∣N 2 =n−k∼Beta(n−k+1,k+1). Note that the parameters between the two distributions are symmetric, as the a and b parameters of the Beta distributions are just swapped. To relate these, a key fact must be used: If ∼ Beta ( , ) , 1 − ∼ Beta ( , ) X∼Beta(a,b),1−X∼Beta(b,a). Intuitively, this makes sense: If X is the distribution of the success probability, 1 − 1−X is the distribution of the failure probability, so the a prior successes and b prior failures now switch roles when looking at the distribution of the failures. Using this, we can conclude that if = 1 ∣ 1 = A=P 1 ∣N 1 =k and = 2 ∣ 2 = − B=P 2 ∣N 2 =n−k, A and 1 − 1−B are IID. Given the information of 1 = N 1 =k and 2 = − N 2 =n−k, we can also conclude that any function of 1 P 1 and 1 − 2 1−P 2 are IID, so ∣ 1 − 1 / 2 ∣ ∣P 1 −1/2∣ is identically distributed to ∣ ( 1 − 2 ) − 1 / 2 ∣ = ∣ 2 − 1 / 2 ∣ ∣(1−P 2 )−1/2∣=∣P 2 −1/2∣ given 1 = N 1 =k and 2 = − N 2 =n−k. Thus, the really complicated conditional probability statement at the start is just asking the probability that one of two IID random variables is larger than the other, for which the answer is 1 / 2 1/2 by exchangeability. The answer 1 / 2 1/2 makes a lot of intuitive sense: Since the prior on the probabilities was Uniform, before seeing any observations, the density of each possible 0 ≤ ≤ 1 0≤p≤1 is equal. After observing the first coin has k heads, while the second coin has − n−k heads, they are both symmetric about the mean amount of heads / 2 n/2, which can be found by Law of Total Expectation. While the k heads of coin 1 1 biases the posterior to one side, the − n−k tails of coin 2 2 biases the distribution to the other side by a symmetric amount, which is why we get the answer of 1 / 2 1/2.

questions.title: Tourney Ending I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play in a tennis tournament such that the winner of each round receives $1$ point, while the loser loses $1$ point. The tournament ends as soon as one of the players reaches $2$ points or $2n$ games have been played, whichever comes first. Alice has probability $0 < p < 1$ of winning each round. Thus, we need to compute the expected number of blocks to see AA or BB in one of these blocks, multiply by 2 2 (there are two games per block), or end the tournament after n blocks have been performed. Since we are looking at a "first occurrence" distribution, we should think of the Geometric distribution. In particular, the probability of success per trial is the probability that either AA or BB occurs. Each game is independent, so we can add the two cases together to get a probability of success in a given block as = 2 + ( 1 − ) 2 p W =p 2 +(1−p) 2 , so ∼ Geom ( ) N∼Geom(p W ) gives the number of rounds that are performed under no restriction on the maximum. questions.title: First Digit
questions.problem: Suppose that ∼ DiscreteUnif { 1 , 2 , … , } N∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n} for some fixed integer $n \geq 1$. Let $p(n)$ be the probability that $2^N$ has a first digit $1$. For example, 2 4 = 16 2 4 =16 satisfies this. Find lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) n→∞ lim p(n) to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: The key here is to think about writing $N$ in scientific notation = ⋅ 10 N=m⋅10 n . This is a natural choice because only the leading part $m$ will affect what the first digit is; $10^n$ will not change what happens. Written in base $10$ notation, we can define the mantissa of a positive integer = ⋅ $10$ k=m⋅10 n as ( ) = log ⁡ 10 ( ) = log ⁡ 10 ( ) − ⌊ log ⁡ 10 ( ) ⌋ f(k)=log 10 (m)=log 10 (k)−⌊log 10 (k)⌋. Intuitively, this is just the fractional part of the logarithm of an integer. For example, the mantissa of 120 120 is 10 ( 120 ) − ⌊ log ⁡ 10 ( 120 ) ⌋ ≈ 2.079 − 2 = 0.079 log 10 (120)−⌊log 10 (120)⌋≈2.079−2=0.079. We are looking at integers 2 2 n for positive integers n, so we can see ( 2 ) = log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) − ⌊ log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) ⌋ f(2 n )=nlog 10 (2)−⌊nlog 10 (2)⌋. As log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) log 10 (2) is irrational, we can see that the mantissa of integers of the form 2 2 n are uniformly distributed on ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1). More specifically, { ( 2 ) : ∈ } {f(2 n ):n∈Z} is uniformly distributed on ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) in the sense of a limiting proportion p of the mantissas lie in any sub-interval of length p of ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1). This is by the equidistribution theorem. Now, the first digit of 2 2 n is 1 1 if and only if it's mantissa is less than log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) log 10 (2), as if ( 2 ) f(2 n ) is the mantissa of 2 2 n , we must have 10 ( 2 ) < 10 log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) = 2 10 f(2 n ) <10 log 10 (2) =2. We raise 10 10 to the mantissa because the mantissa is defined as a logarithm in base 10 10. As the mantissas are uniformly distributed in limit and our event of having the mantissa at most log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) log 10 (2) is an event of length log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) log 10 (2), we can conclude that lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) = log ⁡ 10 ( 2 ) ≈ 0.301 n→∞ lim p(n)=log 10 (2)≈0.301 As suggested by a user, we note that we have just shown Benford's law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benford%27s_law) when the leading digit is 1. A more general result can be found on the linked wikipedia page. Cool!

questions.title: Reduction Mania
questions.problem: A game starts with a Uniformly random integer ∼ DiscreteUnif { $1$ , $2$ , … , } N∼DiscreteUnif{1,2,…,n}. Alice and Bob take turns modifying the integer. A legal move depends on whether the integer is odd or even. If it's even, the player can either subtract $1$ or divide by 2 2. If the number is odd, the player can either subtract $1$ or subtract 1 1, then subsequently divide by $2$. The game ends when the number reaches $0$, and the player who reduces from $1$ to $0$ wins. Alice gets the first move in the game. Assume that Alice and Bob both play optimally. Let $p(n)$ be the probability that Bob wins when the upper bound is $n$. If it exists, find lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) n→∞ lim p(n).
questions.solution: To gain some intuition on what the optimal strategy might be, we work with some small cases of the initial value first. $1$: Alice wins, as she subtracts $1$. $2$: Bob wins, as Alice gets the integer to $1$ by either action, and Bob makes it $1$. $3$: Alice wins, as she subtracts $1$ (makes the number $2$), Bob divides by $2$ or subtracts $1$ (both get to $1$), and Alice wins from there. $4$: Alice wins. She can divide by $2$, and now Bob plays the role of the first player (it becomes his turn), so Alice plays the role of Bob, meaning she will win. $5$: Alice wins. She can subtract $1$ and divide by $2$ (making the number $2$), and the argument follows from above. $6$: Bob wins. If Alice subtracts $1$, the number is $5$ starting with Bob, so Bob wins. If she divides by $2$, the number is $3$ starting with Bob, so Bob wins here too. $7$: Alice wins. If she subtracts $1$, the number is $6$, and Bob becomes the first player to act, so she wins in this case. $8$: Bob wins. Both actions Alice can do make the number reduce to something where the first player to act on them wins, so Bob must be the winner. With the ones we have tested, Bob wins on the integers $2,6,$ and $8$. Among the integers $2,6,$ and $8$ we can see that all of these have an odd number of factors that are $2$: $2$ = $2$ 1 , 6 = $2$ ⋅ 3 , 2=2 1 ,6=2⋅3, and 8 = 2 3 8=2 3 . Thus, a natural conjecture is that all integers with an odd number of factors are the ones Bob wins on. In fact, this is correct. We prove this via strong induction: Suppose that Bob wins on all integers with an odd number of factors that are 2 2 for all integers at most N. We must show that it also holds true for all integers at most + 1 N+1. We break up into cases based on what type of integer + 1 N+1 is. If + 1 N+1 is odd, Alice can either go to N or / 2 N/2 in her first action. N has either an even or odd amount of factors of 2 2. If it's even, / 2 N/2 has an odd number of factors, and vice versa. WLOG, suppose N has an odd amount of factors of 2 2. In this case, Alice should go to N, and this is an integer for which the second player to act from the start has a winning strategy. Bob would be first to act here, so Alice wins the game. This is what we would expect, as + 1 N+1 is odd, meaning it has 0 0 (which is even) factors of 2 2. If + 1 N+1 is even, but it has an odd amount of factors of 2 2, there are two options: Go to N or + 1 2 2 N+1 . Since + 1 N+1 is even, N is odd, so the first player to on this, which would be Bob, wins. Since + 1 N+1 also has an odd amount of factors of 2 2, + 1 2 2 N+1 has an even amount of factors of 2 2, which still is a case where the first player to act on it wins. Thus, Bob always wins this, regardless of what Alice does. If + 1 N+1 is even, but it has an even amount of factors of 2 2, Alice can divide by 2 2, yielding + 1 2 2 N+1 , which has an odd amount of factors of 2 2. The second player to act starting from + 1 2 2 N+1 , which would be Alice, wins, so Alice has a winning strategy here. Our strong induction is now complete: Bob wins exactly when the starting integer has an odd amount of powers of 2 2. The question is: What is the limiting density of such integers? All such integers are in the form 2 2 + 1 2 2k+1 m, where m is any positive odd integer (so that there are no additional powers of 2 2 in it), and k is any non-negative integer. Since m is odd, = 2 + 1 m=2r+1 for some non-negative integer r, so we want to find the density of integers in the form 2 2 + 1 ( 2 + 1 ) = 2 2 + 1 + 4 + 1 2 2k+1 (2r+1)=2 2k+1 +4 k+1 r, where r and k are any non-negative integers. Let's test for some fixed values of k. = 0 : 2 , 6 , 10 , 14 , … k=0:2,6,10,14,… = 1 : 8 , 24 , 40 , 56 , … k=1:8,24,40,56,… As we can see, the gap between consecutive "winning" integers for a fixed k is 4 + 1 4 k+1 , so the limiting proportion of winning integers belongs to a fixed k is 1 / 4 + 1 1/4 k+1 , as, in limit, one out of every 4 + 1 4 k+1 integers is one where Bob wins. We can sum over k to get the total "density" integers where Bob wins. This yields lim ⁡ → ∞ ( ) = ∑ = 0 ∞ 1 4 + 1 = 1 / 4 1 − 1 / 4 = 1 3 n→∞ lim p(n)= k=0 ∑ ∞ 4 k+1 1 = 1−1/4 1/4 = 3 1 We can interpret this informally as: In limit, if a "uniformly random positive integer" (really, this is the limit of Discrete Uniforms on { 1 , 2 , … , } {1,2,…,n}), there is probability 1 / 3 1/3 that Bob wins.

questions.problem: An elevator starts on the ground floor, and the number of people who enter the elevator is ∼ Geom ( ) N∼Geom(p). Once the people get on, each of them randomly selects a floor 1 , 2 , … , 1,2,…,r to get off on uniformly at random. If at least one person wants to get off at a certain floor, the elevator stops and lets them off; otherwise, it skips and keeps going up. Find the expected number of floors the elevator stops at when = 1 / 3 p=1/3 and = 10 r=10.
questions.solution: The expected number of stops is dependent on the number of people on the elevator. Intuitively, the more people there are, the more stops (on average) that the elevator needs to make. However, if we knew the amount of people N on the elevator, we can find the expected number of stops that need to be made, as this is a coupon collector problem. Framing this probabilistically, let S be the number of stops that need to be made. We are looking to compute [ ] E[S] by conditioning on the value of N, meaning [ ] = [ [ ∣ ] ] E[S]=E[E[S∣N]]. Our new goal is to compute [ ∣ ] E[S∣N]. Given that N people are on the elevator, each of the N people selects a floor uniformly at random from the r floors to get off on. We want to find the expected number of distinct floors selected among the N people. As we are looking to count the expected amount of dependent events (knowing someone selected a certain floor influences the probability another floor is empty), linearity of expected value is the best approach. Since we seek to count the expected number of distinct floors, let 1 , … , I 1 ,…,I r be the indicators of the events that floor i, 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤n, has at least one person exiting on it. = 1 + ⋯ + S=I 1 +⋯+I r is the total number of floors with at least one person exiting on it. Since this is an "at least one" probability, it's best to consider the complement, which is that nobody exits on floor 1 1. We subtract the complementary probability from 1 1 to get the probability of at least one person exiting on floor 1 1. Each person has probability 1 / 1/r of exiting on floor 1 1, so there is probability 1 − 1 / 1−1/r of a particular person not selecting floor 1 1 to exit on. Given N, the probability that none of the N people choose floor 1 1 is ( 1 − 1 / ) (1−1/r) N by independence. questions.title: Liquid Measurement II
questions.problem: You have a $120$ml container, a $7$ml container, and a $5$ml container. You are given the task of measuring out $1$ml in both of the latter containers. The first container is full, while the other containers are empty. A transfer of liquid is counted as filling a bottle, emptying a bottle, or transferring from one bottle to another. What is the minimum number of transfers to accomplish this task?
questions.solution: We essentially want to write $120 - 2 = 118$ as a linear combination of $7$ and $5$, as we must have $1$ ml in each of the $7$ and $5$ containers. We want to make the coefficient of the linear combination for $7$ to be as large as possible, as we can remove more water from the total each time with the $7$ ml container than the $5$ ml container. We can see that $98$ is the largest multiple of $7$ that has the same result modulo $5$ as $118$, which gives us a hint as to the first step. First, we will pour from the $120$ml container into the $7$ml container, and then empty the $7ml$. This is done $14$ times for $28$ transfers. Afterwards, we will perform a $4$ transaction algorithm three times, where we pour from the $120$ml container into the $7$ml container, pour the $7$ml container into the $5$ml container, empty the $5$ml container, and then pour the $7$ml container into the $5$ml container. At which point, the $120$ml container will have $1$ml of liquid, the $7$ml container will have $1$ml of liquid, and the $5$ml container will be full. So we perform two more transfers by emptying the $5$ml and moving $1$ml into it, which finishes our problem. This is $28+12+2=42$ transfers.

questions.solution: Let's go through the answer choices one-by-one. Instead of doing intense calculations, we are going to focus on intuition here. Exactly one of choices $1-5$ can be correct, so let's walk through it. A simple case is to consider [ ( 1 , ) ] E[$\ev{R(1,n)}$]. This is the expected ratio of $1$s to the total amount of rolls. Regarding options $6$ and $7$, we note that as $r$ increases, there's more potential for there to be long strings of other values that aren't $1$, and this consistently increases as $r$ increases: In essence, the intuition is that it's much less likely you get the "high ratios" since they occur with lower probability as $r$ increases, so the expected ratio decreases. For example, consider $r = 100$. The probability you get a ratio of $1$ in this case is 1 / 100 1/n 100 , which is very small. Based on this, option $7$ is correct. questions.title: Up-Down Permutation
questions.problem: Letting [ ] = { 1 , 2 , … , } [n]={1,2,…,n}, we define an up-down permutation up-down permutation as a tuple ( 1 , … , ) (a 1 ,…,a n ) such that 1 < 2 > 3 < ⋯ > a 1 <a 2 >a 3 <⋯>a n (or vice versa for the last element, dependent on the parity of n). In plain English, in an up-down permutation, the next element alternates between being larger and smaller than the last element. Let U n be the number of up-down permutations of [ ] [n]. questions.solution: We will seek to find $U_n$ for a general $n$. This type of problem has a recursive flavor to it: An up-down permutation of length $n+1$ should relate to up-down permutations of smaller lengths in some way. Instead of considering just up-down permutations, we can consider all "alternating" sequences, and exactly half of them will be up-down permutations. There are exactly as many up-down as down-up permutations, since one could replace i with ( + 1 ) − (n+1)−i in each spot to get the corresponding down-up permutation. We came up with this pairing from noting a certain transformation of the values that converts values that are larger than the next to be smaller, and vice versa, as subtracting a larger number reduces the overall value. Thus, the number of alternating permutations of length n is 2 2U n . To derive a recurrence, we must consider the nature of alternating permutations of length + 1 n+1. The only element in [ + 1 ] [n+1] that's not in [ ] [n] is + 1 n+1. + 1 n+1 is the maximum element of the permutation, so it will always be larger than the element to either side. This element + 1 n+1 can be in any of spots 1 1 to + 1 n+1 in the permutation, so a natural idea is to find the number of permutations conditioned on the position 1 ≤ ≤ + 1 1≤k≤n+1 of the value + 1 n+1. The number of such sequences with element + 1 n+1 fixed in position k will likely depend on k. To illuminate the situation, let's consider a fixed scenario when the maximum element is 6 6. Here are some possible sequences in each case of the position k of 6 6: = 1 : 6 > 4 < 5 > 1 < 3 > 2 k=1:6>4<5>1<3>2 = 2 : 1 < 6 > 4 < 5 > 2 < 3 k=2:1<6>4<5>2<3 = 3 : 4 > 2 < 6 > 1 < 5 > 3 k=3:4>2<6>1<5>3 = 4 : 2 < 5 > 4 < 6 > 1 < 3 k=4:2<5>4<6>1<3 = 5 : 3 > 1 < 5 > 2 < 6 > 4 k=5:3>1<5>2<6>4 = 6 : 3 < 5 > 1 < 4 > 2 < 6 k=6:3<5>1<4>2<6 There's something very interesting to note from these examples: The type of sequence (up-down or down-up) is uniquely determined by the parity of k. In particular, we can see that all odd k must be down-up permutations, while all even k are up-down permutations. This is not a coincidence! We can generalize this argument to having the maximum + 1 n+1 in odd and even positions of k. To prove our claim, we note that there are − 1 n−1 total inequality signs in the permutation. Since the signs alternate, all odd-indexed inequality signs are the same, and all even-indexed inequality signs are the same (namely, the inequality that's opposite of the odd-indexed signs). If + 1 n+1 is in position k that's odd, there are − 1 k−1 inequality signs that come before it, and the ( − 1 ) (k−1)st inequality sign, which comes right before it, must be < <, as + 1 n+1 is the largest element. As k is odd, − 1 k−1 is even, meaning that the first inequality sign is > >, since it's opposite parity of − 1 k−1. This is clearly evidenced in the sequences above. A similar argument holds for when k is even: There are − 1 k−1 inequality signs coming before, of which the ( − 1 ) (k−1)st is < <. As k is even, − 1 k−1 is odd, meaning the first inequality sign is also < <, as it matches in parity. Now that we've proven our observation, we make a second observation: The elements to the left of + 1 n+1 form either an up-down or down-up permutation of length − 1 k−1, as there are − 1 k−1 elements before the kth position. Similarly, the elements to the right of + 1 n+1 form either an up-down or down-up permutation of length + 1 − n+1−k, since there are + 1 − n+1−k elements in the permutation of length + 1 n+1 to the right of position k. Once + 1 n+1 is fixed in position k, we need to do the following to create some up-down or down-up permutation of length + 1 n+1: Pick − 1 k−1 elements from [ ] [n] to go left of position k. Arrange those − 1 k−1 elements into an appropriate up-down or down-up permutation based on the parity of k. Arrange the remaining + 1 − n+1−k elements to the right of + 1 n+1 into an appropriate up-down or down-up permutation. There are ( − 1 ) ( k−1 n ) ways to pick the − 1 k−1 elements to go left of position k, as the order of selection is irrelevant. The exact values of these elements are irrelevant, as they are all distinct, meaning we can just relabel them with values 1 1 to − 1 k−1, where 1 1 and − 1 k−1 are the minimum and maximum, respectively, among the subset of size − 1 k−1 that we selected. There are − 1 U k−1 up-down (or down-up, dependent on k) sequences that can be formed of length − 1 k−1 to go left of position k. Once the elements that go left of position k are fixed, the elements going right are too, since they are the leftovers. Once again, their exact values are irrelevant, as they are all distinct. There are + 1 − = − ( − 1 ) U n+1−k =U n−(k−1) ways to make an appropriate up-down or down-up permutation from the remaining − ( − 1 ) n−(k−1) elements to the right. Combining all of the above via the multiplication principle, we can conclude that the number of alternating permutations that can be formed with element + 1 n+1 in position k is ( − 1 ) − 1 − ( − 1 ) ( k−1 n )U k−1 U n−(k−1) This is the specific case with element + 1 n+1 at position k. This element can be in any position 1 ≤ ≤ + 1 1≤k≤n+1, and all of these cases are disjoint, so to get the total number of alternating permutations, we sum the above quantity from = 1 k=1 to + 1 n+1. This yields the recurrence 2 + 1 = ∑ = 1 + 1 ( − 1 ) − 1 − ( − 1 ) = ∑ = 0 ( ) − 2U n+1 = k=1 ∑ n+1 ( k−1 n )U k−1 U n−(k−1) = k=0 ∑ n ( k n )U k U n−k In the above, we shifted the index so that the sum starts at 0 0 instead of 1 1. Recall that the LHS is 2 + 1 2U n+1 because we made a recurrence for the number of alternating permutations, which is twice the number of up-down permutations. A natural question is: What is 0 U 0 ? The goal is to determine the highest floor from which an egg will not break when dropped out of a window from that floor. Call this floor the critical floor critical floor. There is exactly one critical floor in the building. If an egg is dropped and does not break, it's undamaged and can be dropped again. Broken eggs can't be dropped again. If an egg breaks on floor n, it also breaks for all floors > m>n; similarly, if an egg doesn't break on floor n, it also doesn't break for any floor < m<n. What is the maximum value of n such that the critical floor can be identified in at most d drops? Report the answer when = 10 d=10 and = 4 m=4.
questions.solution: The approach of the previous problems suggests that, for general $m$, we can approach the counting via dynamic programming, as with each drop, we relate back to our result with one less drop. Let $F(e,d)$ be the number of floors that can be explored when we have $e$ eggs and $d$ drops remaining. $F(e,d) + 1$ will be the maximum value of $n$, since the critical floor must be one of the $n$ floors, meaning if the egg doesn't break on floor $F(e,d)$, the critical floor must be $F(e,d) + 1$. The idea is to figure out where to drop the first egg to obtain our recurrence. If the egg breaks on the first trial, there would be − 1 e−1 eggs and − 1 d−1 drops remaining. Thus, we need to be able to explore ( − 1 , − 1 ) F(e−1,d−1) floors in the event that the first egg dropped breaks. In other words, we should drop the first egg from floor ( − 1 , − 1 ) + 1 F(e−1,d−1)+1, so that if it breaks, we can explore the first ( − 1 , − 1 ) F(e−1,d−1) floors and uniquely find the critical floor. If the egg does not break, there are still e eggs and − 1 d−1 drops remaining, so we will be able to explore an additional ( , − 1 ) F(e,d−1) floors above ( − 1 , − 1 ) + 1 F(e−1,d−1)+1 in this case. Therefore, we've derived the recurrence relation ( , ) = 1 + ( − 1 , − 1 ) + ( , − 1 ) F(e,d)=1+F(e−1,d−1)+F(e,d−1) We now need some boundary conditions for the DP. If = 1 d=1, we are only able to explore 1 1 floor with certainty, as it either breaks or does not break. Therefore, our first boundary condition is ( , 1 ) = 1 F(e,1)=1 for all ≥ 1 e≥1. Now, if = 1 e=1, we can explore floors 1 1 to d with certainty in d drops. We can't jump up on any gaps, as if we break our egg, we can't identify the critical floor with certainty, so ( 1 , ) = F(1,d)=d for all ≥ 1 d≥1. With these boundary conditions, our DP is complete. By using the recursion, we can conclude ( 4 , 10 ) = 385 F(4,10)=385, so 386 386 is our answer.

questions.title: Cards Out
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$ and positive integers 1 , … , r 1 ,…,r n . A deck consists of $n$ colors of cards such that there are $r_i$ cards of color $i$. Cards are drawn out one-by-one without replacement without replacement until at least one card of each color has been observed. On average, how many cards are drawn from the deck? Report the answer when $n = 4$ and = 13 r i =13 for $i = 1,2,3,4$ (this represents a standard deck). Round to the nearest ten-thousandth.
questions.solution: In this problem, we want to find the expected time until we've observed every color at least once. The last color to appear is the limiting factor here. Namely, if 1 , … , N 1 ,…,N n are the random variables that represent the number of cards dealt until the first one of color i, $1 \leq i \leq n$, the number of cards dealt until at least one card of every color has been is max ⁡ { 1 , … , } max{N 1 ,…,N n }. The exact distribution of the $N_i$ random variables are not easy to compute, and they also aren't independent: If $1$ = 1 N 1 =1 for example, we know that every other > 1 N i >1, as there can only be one color that comes on the first draw. Due to the dependence, using the tail summation for expected value doesn't work either. Since we sample without replacement, if we were to ask for an expression involving the minimum of some sub-collection of the random variables, say min ⁡ { 1 , … , } min{N 1 ,…,N k } for some k, it would be easier to compute. This is because we could use the paradigm of "First Ace", as we are looking for the expected time until we reach one of the cards of the first k colors, so we'd be able to treat these as the dividers. How can we do this conversion? We can use the maximum-minimum principle. This states that for any real numbers 1 , … , x 1 ,…,x n , max ⁡ { 1 , … , } = ∑ = 1 − ∑ < min ⁡ { , } + ∑ < < min ⁡ { , , } + ⋯ + ( − 1 ) + 1 min ⁡ { 1 , … , } max{x 1 ,…,x n }= i=1 ∑ n x i − i<j ∑ min{x i ,x j }+ i<j<k ∑ min{x i ,x j ,x k }+⋯+(−1) n+1 min{x 1 ,…,x n } You can view this exactly in the same light as the inclusion-exclusion principle, but ∪ ∪ is now the maximum, while ∩ ∩ is now the minimum. questions.title: Within One
questions.problem: How many ways can the elements 0 , 1 , … , 0,1,…,n be written in a row such that each number (other than the left-most) is within $1$ of some number to the left of it? Report the answer for $n = 9$. An example is $3425671809$.
questions.solution: For the simplicity of problem-solving, we will use the value $n = 9$ to illuminate the process. The process will become clear for general $n$. This problem seems intractable as is: There are too many options for what happens at the beginning, and then the next step, based on what the value selected is: If $0$ is the starting integer, for example, only $1$ can go next, but if $1$ were selected to start, either $0$ or $2$ could go next. Instead, let's see what we can extract about such sequences, and then work backwards. Since $0$ and $9$ only have one integer adjacent to them in the set, we claim that any such sequence must end in either $0$ or $9$. If it didn't, there would be $2$ integers adjacent to the number $k$ that it does end in: $k+1$ or − 1 k−1. One of these two integers wouldn't be able to be placed. Specifically, we claim that whichever one of $k+1$ and − 1 k−1 is not placed first won't be able to be placed at all. WLOG, suppose it's $k+1$. For $k+1$ to be placed, either $k$ or $k+2$ must come before it. Since $k$ comes at the end, $k+2$ would have to come before $k+1$. For $k+2$ to be placed beforehand, either $k+1$ or $k+3$ must have come before it. Since it's not $k+1$, $k+3$ must have come beforehand. One can iterate this logic until there is a contradiction, since there is eventually no larger number (or smaller in the case that − 1 k−1 was not first). By the above, either 0 0 or 9 9 must be the last integer. Without 0 0 or 9 9, the set of remaining values becomes { 1 , 2 , … , 9 } {1,2,…,9} or { 0 , 1 , … , 8 } {0,1,…,8}. Since we're guaranteed to have the last value be adjacent to one of the values that came before it, we're essentially in the same problem now, but with the set of size 9 9 instead of 10 10. It's the same problem because, at the boundaries, there are only 1 1 value that's adjacent in the set, but all the interior values have 2 2 adjacent elements. Thus, the second-to-last spot should be either the maximum or minimum element in the remaining set. The logic above iterates for every single turn: Creating the string from right to left, the selected element must either be the maximum or minimum element not yet selected. This is the key insight needed for the general n case as well. Thus, the last element of the string is 0 0 or n, and so on. Thus, working from the back, at each step, there are 2 2 options of element. This continues until the left-most element, where there is only 1 1 choice. Since there are + 1 n+1 blanks to fill total, and n of them have 2 2 options each, there are 2 2 n total strings for general n. With = 9 n=9, the answer is 512 512.

questions.title: Laptop Weights
questions.problem: Alice has four laptops, but he has no idea how much each one weighs. Each laptop weighs an integer amount of grams. Bob has a balance that shows the weight difference between the two sides, but it’s a bit wacky — —it can be off by 1 1 gram (either above or below) on at most one weighing. Is it possible for Bob to uniquely determine the weight of each laptop? If so, report the minimum number of times Bob must use the scale to guarantee he knows the weight of each laptop. Otherwise, report − 1 −1.
questions.solution: Intuitively, we will need a minimum of $4$ weighings to determine the weights: We can't solve a system of $4$ unknowns with less than $4$ weighings. Can we do it in exactly $4$ weighings? For simplicity of notation, let = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 t=w 1 +w 2 +w 3 +w 4 be the total weight of all $4$ laptops. Since the scale can only make errors of $\pm 1$, we will somehow want to be able to tell if the scale made an error or not. One natural way to tell is based on the parity of some quantity: If we can make some quantity that is even without error, then it's odd with error. A natural quantity would be if we can create $2t$ (an even value) from the $4$ weighings, since $4t$ wouldn't be helpful: We'd just be putting all $4$ laptops on the same side each time, and that wouldn't help us identify what each laptop weighs. To execute this strategy, we must think of a weighing scheme that yields $2t$. Note that 2 = $4$ − 2 = ( 1 + 2 + $3$ − $4$ ) + ( 2 + 3 + 4 − $1$ ) + ( 1 + 2 + $4$ − 3 ) + ( 1 + 3 + 4 − 2 ) 2t=4t−2t=(w 1 +w 2 +w 3 −w 4 )+(w 2 +w 3 +w 4 −w 1 )+(w 1 +w 2 +w 4 −w 3 )+(w 1 +w 3 +w 4 −w 2 ) Thus, the idea is to do $4$ weighings with $3$ of the laptops on one side, and the last laptop on the other side. Let's denote = 1 + 2 + 3 − 4 = − 2 4 = 2 + 3 + 4 − 1 = − 2 1 = 1 + 2 + 4 − 3 = − 2 3 = 1 + 3 + 4 − 2 = − 2 2 a b c d =w 1 +w 2 +w 3 −w 4 =t−2w 4 =w 2 +w 3 +w 4 −w 1 =t−2w 1 =w 1 +w 2 +w 4 −w 3 =t−2w 3 =w 1 +w 3 +w 4 −w 2 =t−2w 2 , , , a,b,c, and d are the "true values" of these measurements, not what was observed on the scale. If we indeed see that the sum of our four measurements is even, then there was no error, as + + + = 2 a+b+c+d=2t, which is even. The system of equations can then be solved for 1 , 2 , 3 , w 1 ,w 2 ,w 3 , and 4 w 4 by using standard linear algebra techniques. If there is an error, we detect it if the sum of the four measurements above, which should be even, is odd. We can find the problematic measurement by noting that all 4 4 measurements should have the same parity: t is constant, and 2 2w i is even for all i, so the measurement that differs in parity must be the one with an error. To identify the direction of the error, we need to think about breaking up further than just even vs. odd, as both adding and subtracting 1 1 from our faulty sum of + + + a+b+c+d will yield an even value. Instead, we should look at divisibility by 4 4, since exactly one of the two values above or below the odd value of our faulty sum will be divisible by 4 4. You can see this intuitively: No matter which odd number you select, exactly one of the even numbers on either side will be divisible by 4 4. How can we get a quantity from our measurements that should be divisible by 4 4 with the correct values?
