Afterwards, we now have the correct values of the sums , , , a,b,c, and d, and then can solve in the method above. Here is an example of the algorithm in action: Suppose we have the measured values 5 , 21 , 14 , 5,21,14, and 13 13 for , , , a,b,c, and d. We note that 14 14 is different parity than the other 3 3 values, so it must be in error. We can now see that = 5 , = 21 , a=5,b=21, and = 13 d=13 are the correct values. The possible values of c are 13 13 or 15 15, dependent on the error type. Computing the value of + + − a+b+c−d, we see that 5 + 21 + − 13 = 13 + 5+21+c−13=13+c. With the two options, we get 26 26 and 28 28 as the two sums, and since 4 ∣ 28 4∣28, = 15 c=15 is the correct value. Now, we know that + + + = 2 a+b+c+d=2t under the correct values, so 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = = 5 + 21 + 15 + 13 2 = 27 w 1 +w 2 +w 3 +w 4 =t= 2 5+21+15+13 =27 Since = − 2 1 a=t−2w 1 , 5 = 27 − 2 1 ⟺ 4 = 11 5=27−2w 1 ⟺w 4 =11. We can repeat this process on the other three quantities to get 1 = 3 , 2 = 6 , w 1 =3,w 2 =6, and 3 = 7 w 3 =7. By the above process, 4 4 is the minimum number of weighings needed!

questions.title: Non-Intersecting Chords
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$. We say that a circular configuration circular configuration of order $n$ is a circle with $n$ vertices and some (possible empty) collection of chords between the vertices under the condition that no two chords intersect at any point, including on the boundary. Let $O_n$ be the number of order $n$ circular configurations. Find the value of $O_6$ . As a sanity test for your formula, 0 = 1 = 1 , 2 = 2 , O 0 =O 1 =1,O 2 =2, and 3 = 4 O 3 =4.
questions.solution: This problem has a very combinatorial flavor to it, as we are looking to count the number of ways to draw any collection of chords in some region based on the amount of vertices. By a simple picture, it's reasonable to believe that the values of $O_n$ are related to each other by some recurrence, as it doesn't appear there is a direct way to count them with any of our more basic combinatorial tools (mainly due to the non-intersecting condition). Thus, our goal should be to derive a recurrence for $O_n$ . The difference between the order $n$ configuration and order − $1$ n−1 is the number of points available on the circle. Therefore, it's natural to believe that we can break up the recurrence based on whether or not this new point is connected via a chord or not. For simplicity, imagine this was a unit circle, and assume that the points are labelled 1 1 to n CCW, with vertex 1 1 located at the ( 1 , 0 ) (1,0) spot. There are two cases of configurations of order n: Vertex 1 1 is not connected to any other vertex via a chord. Vertex 1 1 is connected to another vertex via a chord. In the first case, since 1 1 is not connected to any other vertex via a chord, the number of order n configurations that can be made is equal to the number of configurations on − 1 n−1 vertices, since 1 1 is essentially ignored. In this case, there would be − 1 O n−1 configurations. In the second case, 1 1 must be connected to another vertex. Since 1 1 connects to another vertex, that chord divides up the circle into two components that are on opposite sides of the chord. Those two regions differ in size based on how far away the vertex that connects to 1 1 is from vertex 1 1. For example, if 1 1 connects to 2 2, then there is no region formed between them, as there are no vertices, while there are − 2 n−2 vertices on the other side. Thus, we should condition on the vertex i that 1 1 connects to. Suppose that 1 1 connects to vertex 2 ≤ ≤ 2≤i≤n. This chord breaks the circle up into two regions: Vertices k such that 2 ≤ ≤ − 1 2≤k≤i−1 (must be strictly larger than 1 1 and less than n, since it's CCW), and then vertices k such that + 1 ≤ ≤ i+1≤k≤n (all the vertices after i and ending at n). Since we have a non-intersecting condition on the chords, it's not possible for a vertex in one group to connect to a vertex in the other group. Therefore, the number of order n circular configurations that can be made in this case is equal to the product of the number of ways to make a circular configuration in each of the two regions, since we can pick any circular configuration on the appropriate amount of vertices for each of the two regions to form a configuration of order n. The number of ways to make a non-intersecting arrangement of chords in the first region of vertices 2 ≤ ≤ − 1 2≤k≤i−1 is − 2 O i−2 , as this is a region consisting of − 2 i−2 vertices. Similarly, the number of ways to make a non-intersecting arrangement of chords in the second region of vertices + 1 ≤ ≤ i+1≤k≤n is − O n−i , as this is a region of − n−i vertices. Combining these, the number of ways to make an order n arrangement when vertex 1 1 connects to vertex i is − 2 − O i−2 O n−i . However, the above is just for a single case of the vertex i that 1 1 connects to, so to account for all possible arrangements, we must sum the number of arrangements over all possible values of i, which are 2 ≤ ≤ 2≤i≤n. By the above work, we can conclude that our recurrence relation is = − 1 + ∑ = 2 − 2 − = − 1 + ∑ = 0 − 2 ( − 2 ) − O n =O n−1 + i=2 ∑ n O i−2 O n−i =O n−1 + i=0 ∑ n−2 O i O (n−2)−i In the above, we performed an index shift by 2 2 so that the summation starts at 0 0. To summarize our work, − 1 O n−1 accounts for all of the arrangements that can be made without vertex 1 1 connecting to anything else. ( − 2 ) − O i O (n−2)−i is the number of arrangements that can be made when vertex 1 1 connects to vertex + 2 i+2 (remember that we shifted by 2 2), and we sum over all possible values of i because the collection of configurations is disjoint over varying i (vertex 1 1 can only connect to a single vertex due to the non-intersecting condition). As for the initial conditions, we have that 0 O 0 and 1 O 1 are both 1 1, since the only possible arrangement is the one with an empty collection of chords. Using this recurrence, we eventually get 6 = 51 O 6 =51.

questions.title: Subset RPS
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$. $n$ people play − n−way RPS under the following rules: Each person uniformly at random chooses $R,P,$ and $S$, independently of everyone else. If exactly two of the three possible choices are played, all of the people in the losing group are eliminated, while all in the winning group move into the next round. If there are 1 1 or 3 3 distinct moves shown, nobody is eliminated, and everyone keeps playing. Find the expected amount of rounds played until there is only one player remaining when = 5 n=5.

questions.title: Placed Turnover
questions.problem: Rishi has $n$ fair coins lined up in positions $1$ to $n$. He flips all $n$ of them, and then performs the following iterative process: He counts how many heads there are among the $n$ coins. If there are exactly $k$ heads among the $n$ coins, the coin in position $k$ is turned over. This process iterates until all of the coins show tails. For example, with $n = 3$, if Rishi gets $TTH$, the sequence of turnovers is: $TTH \rightarrow HTH \rightarrow HHH \rightarrow HHT \rightarrow HTT \rightarrow TTT$, ending the process in $5$ turnovers. Find the expected number of turnovers Rishi needs to perform. Report the answer when $n = 40$.
questions.solution: Since this problem is very complicated and involves many iterations, it may be worth enumerating all of the possible outcomes for small $n$, see if there is a pattern, and then try to generalize. When $n = 1$, there are two outcomes: $H$ and $T$, which take $1$ and $0$ turnovers, respectively, so $1/2$ is the answer. When $n = 2$, there are four possible outcomes: $HH,TT,TH,$ and $HT$. $TT$ takes $0$ turnovers, $HH$ takes $2$ turnovers, $HT$ takes $1$ turnover, and $TH$ takes $3$ turnovers. This yields an expected value of $(0+1+2+3)/4 = 3/2$. When $n = 3$, there are eight possible outcomes. questions.title: Andrew Tate's Elevator II

The approach of the previous problem does not work because there are now multiple elevators, so it only matters which one is closest to the mth floor. To approach this problem, we need to think creatively about the condition we are given. Note that each elevator is at a uniformly random point along it's path at the time Andrew wants to go home, which is the same as the previous part. We can first note some intuitive properties our formula should satisfy: If = m=n, the answer should be 0 0, as there's no way for the elevator to be moving down. If = 1 m=1, the answer should be 1 1, as the elevator must always be moving down to floor 1 1. Assuming n is odd, if = ( + 1 ) / 2 m=(n+1)/2, the answer should be 1 / 2 1/2, as there is a length ( − 1 ) / 2 (n−1)/2 above and below this floor, so the floor is right in the middle. Therefore, intuitively, it should be equally likely for the elevator to come above or below. The most informative case is the last one. This, combined with the first two, hints to us that there are two regions: One where the elevator is equally likely to come from above or below, and one where it's not. Namely, if m is at or above the midpoint ( + 1 ) / 2 (n+1)/2, the portion of the path from floor m to the top and back and the region extending 2 ( − ) 2(n−m) floors below (and bouncing up from the ground, if necessary) floor m comprise of the region where it's equally likely for the first elevator to come from above or below. You use very similar logic if m is below the midpoint, where you take the portion of the path below m and to the ground and extending above m by 2 ( − 1 ) 2(m−1) floors (potentially bouncing off the top). The above is a bit abstract, so here are some concrete examples: If = 10 m=10 and = 50 n=50, the equally likely region comprises of the following two components: Below floor 10 10 and back up (length 2 ⋅ 9 = 18 2⋅9=18), and the region from floors 10 10 to 28 28. If the floor m is above the midpoint, there can't be any elevator above it, which means that every elevator must be below the mth floor, so the elevator will always be going up when it reaches the mth floor. questions.title: Game Prediction
questions.problem: A single-elimination tournament of $2^n$ teams consists of $n$ rounds. You, as a good sports better, want to bet on the outcome of all 2 − 1 2 n −1 matches in the tournament. In other words, for each game, you want to choose a winner for that game. Your payout is computed as follows: $\$1$ for each game you predict correctly in round $1$. $\$2$ for each game you predict correctly in round $2$. More generally, you receive $ 2 − 1 $2 k−1 for each game you predict correctly in round $k$, with $k = n$ (the finals) being the last round. All of the bets must be placed in advance of the tournament, and the initial bracket is visible to you. In game $i$, the two teams participating, say $A_i$ and $B_i$ , have respective probabilities of $p_i$ and 1 − 1−p i of winning the game. Since you know nothing about sports, you flip a fair coin to decide which team to bet on in each game. You do this by starting with all games in round $1$, then move to round $2$, and so on. Assuming that each game has an independent outcome, what is your expected payout when $n = 10$ and = 1 / 3 p i =1/3 for all $i$?
questions.solution: Since we are looking to compute the expected total payout throughout all the rounds, we are looking to compute the expected value of some dependent events: Our guess on who wins each game is dependent on who wins previously. Therefore, linearity of expectation is the best approach. To do this, we can label the games 1 1 to 2 − 1 2 n −1, where games 1 1 to 2 − 1 2 n−1 are in round 1 1, games 2 − 1 + 1 2 n−1 +1 to 2 − 1 + 2 − 2 2 n−1 +2 n−2 are in round 2 2, and so on. We receive a payout when we guess correct, and we don't receive a payout when guessing incorrectly, so let 1 , … , 2 − 1 I 1 ,…,I 2 n −1 be the indicators that games 1 1 to 2 − 1 2 n −1 are guessed correctly. Our payout would be given by = ( 1 + … 2 − 1 ) + 2 ( 2 − 1 + 1 + ⋯ + 2 − 1 + 2 − 2 ) + ⋯ + 2 − 1 2 − 1 T=(I 1 +…I 2 n−1 )+2(I 2 n−1 +1 +⋯+I 2 n−1 +2 n−2 )+⋯+2 n−1 I 2 n −1 We group the games as above because all games of the same round yield the same payout. One important question is: What is the probability we guess correctly in game i, given we know who participates in it? Suppose we assign heads to guessing team A i and tails to guessing team B i . Our guess is correct in two cases: Heads and A i actually wins, which occurs with probability / 2 p i /2. Tails and B i actually wins, which occurs with probability ( 1 − ) / 2 (1−p i )/2 Adding these two cases up yields that there is probability 1 / 2 1/2 of guessing correctly, regardless of who wins. Intuitively, this makes sense: Imagine you let the game play out until there was a winner, and then flipped the coin after. No matter who won, the coin gives you the side that corresponds to the winner with probability 1 / 2 1/2. The above fact allows us to conclude that the indicators in any given round are exchangeable, as they only require the knowledge of who is participating in the game. With this information, we can conclude all of the indicators corresponding to a given round have the same mean, so [ ] = 2 − 1 [ 1 ] + 2 ⋅ 2 − 2 [ 2 − 1 + 1 ] + ⋯ + 2 − 1 [ 2 − 1 ] = 2 − 1 ( [ 1 ] + [ 2 − 1 + 1 ] + ⋯ + [ 2 − 1 ] ) E[T]=2 n−1 E[I 1 ]+2⋅2 n−2 E[I 2 n−1 +1 ]+⋯+2 n−1 E[I 2 n −1 ]=2 n−1 (E[I 1 ]+E[I 2 n−1 +1 ]+⋯+E[I 2 n −1 ]) Now, our job is to compute the expected value of each indicator. For simplicity, we will refer to these indicators by the round they belong to (so 1 1 to n instead of the indices listed above). The expected value of the indicator in the kth round is the probability that we guess the outcome of that game in the kth round correctly. To guess the winner of the game in the kth round correctly, two things must happen: The winner of the kth round must be guessed correctly. Call this person P. In each of the first − 1 k−1 rounds that person P played, you must have guessed them to be winner. If you didn't guess them to be the winner at any point, you would have predicted they lost and crashed out of the tournament, not making them an option available to guess in the kth round. As we've already shown that the probability of guessing correctly per game is 1 / 2 1/2, independent of other games, the probability of guessing the kth game correctly is 1 / 2 1/2 k . Plugging these in for the indicators that they correspond to, we see [ ] = 2 − 1 ( 1 / 2 + 1 / 4 + ⋯ + 1 / 2 ) = 2 − 2 ∑ = 0 − 1 1 2 = 2 − 2 ⋅ 1 − 1 / 2 1 − 1 / 2 = 2 − 1 2 E[T]=2 n−1 (1/2+1/4+⋯+1/2 n )=2 n−2 i=0 ∑ n−1 2 i 1 =2 n−2 ⋅ 1−1/2 1−1/2 n = 2 2 n −1 With = 10 n=10, the answer is 1023 / 2 1023/2.

questions.problem: Fix three positive integers $r,b,$ and $g$. A box contains $r$ red, $b$ blue, and $g$ green marbles. You repeatedly draw out marbles one-at-a-time without replacement until you've drawn out all of the marbles of any color (i.e. the box only contains $2$ colors of marbles left). Find the expected number of marbles that are drawn out when $r=3,b=6,$ and $g=9$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: Let's first frame this problem probabilistically. Define $R,B$ and $G$ to be the number of marbles drawn out until the last red, blue, and green marbles (respectively) are selected from the box. The random variable that represents the number of draws we perform is min ⁡ ( , , ) min(R,B,G), as we draw out until any of the three colors. A natural first thought is to use the tail summation, but there's no clear way to see how to evaluate the probability of there being at least one marble of each color remaining in the box at any time. Thus, we need to come up with a more ingenious approach. The only other relationship that involves the expected value of a minimum of random variables is the maximum-minimum principle. This states that for any real numbers 1 , … , x 1 ,…,x n , max ⁡ { 1 , … , } = ∑ = 1 − ∑ < min ⁡ { , } + ∑ < < min ⁡ { , , } + ⋯ + ( − 1 ) + 1 min ⁡ { 1 , … , } max{x 1 ,…,x n }= i=1 ∑ n x i − i<j ∑ min{x i ,x j }+ i<j<k ∑ min{x i ,x j ,x k }+⋯+(−1) n+1 min{x 1 ,…,x n } Applying this with = 3 n=3 and 1 , 2 , 3 x 1 ,x 2 ,x 3 as the random variables , , R,B, and G yields [ max ⁡ ( , , ) ] = [ ] + [ ] + [ ] − [ min ⁡ ( , ) ] − [ min ⁡ ( , ) ] − [ min ⁡ ( , ) ] + [ min ⁡ ( , , ) ] E[max(R,B,G)]=E[R]+E[B]+E[G]−E[min(R,B)]−E[min(R,G)]−E[min(B,G)]+E[min(R,B,G)] This is good progress, as we see the term [ min ⁡ ( , , ) ] E[min(R,B,G)] on the RHS. However, we have a lot of different expected values to compute. Furthermore, it's hard to compute terms in the form of a minimum of random variables, as we don't know which color runs out first. The goal here is to use a "First Ace" approach, and to do that, we must know how many dividers there are. If we consider the minimum of random variables, it's unclear how many dividers there should be, since we don't know which color runs out first. However, if we were able to somehow transform the other minima into maxima, when computing [ max ⁡ ( , ) ] E[max(R,B)] (for example), we would know there are + r+b dividers, as we wait until all + r+b blue and red marbles are drawn. To do this, we can use the maximum-minimum principle on all of the pairwise minimums. Namely, we replace [ min ⁡ ( , ) ] = [ ] + [ ] − [ max ⁡ ( , ) ] E[min(R,B)]=E[R]+E[B]−E[max(R,B)] Doing this for all 3 3 pairwise minimums and rearranging yields [ min ⁡ ( , , ) ] = [ ] + [ ] + [ ] − [ max ⁡ ( , ) ] − [ max ⁡ ( , ) ] − [ max ⁡ ( , ) ] + [ max ⁡ ( , , ) ] E[min(R,B,G)]=E[R]+E[B]+E[G]−E[max(R,B)]−E[max(R,G)]−E[max(B,G)]+E[max(R,B,G)] Now, we need to set up the "First Ace" approach formally. questions.title: Yo Mama II
questions.problem: Yo mama performs a simple symmetric random walk starting at the origin. There is an absorbing boundary at position − 2 −2n for some positive integer n. If yo mama ever reaches this boundary, it stays there for the rest of time. After $4n$ steps, what is the variance of the position of the particle? Report the answer when $n = 5$ to the nearest thousandth.
questions.solution: In this question, there is a specific difference from the standard random walk problem: There is a "lower bound" at the absorbing boundary. In a standard SSRW with no boundary, the answer to this question is 0 0, as yo mama moves with equal probability up or down at each step. Now, it's not clear how this boundary affects the variance of the final position: On one hand, the boundary limits the random walk from going lower than − 2 −2n, but on the other, there are some paths that could go down for a while and, in the standard SSRW, end at a position above − 2 −2n, but would get absorbed beforehand with this boundary. To illustrate the above, take the example of = 5 n=5. A path that ends at − 8 −8 would have 14 14 down movements and 6 6 up movements. In a standard SSRW, the path that takes the first 14 14 steps down and 6 6 steps up at the end is valid, but with the absorbing boundary, this path would just end at − 10 −10. Now, how do we relate these two opposite forces? When considering the boundary, we only care about paths that fall into one of two categories: In the standard SSRW, they would end above − −n, but hit − −n before reaching the endpoint. In the standard SSRW, they would end below − −n, but get stopped at − −n before reaching the endpoint. Since the random walk is symmetric, we can create some relationship between these two types of paths. These two types of paths mentioned above constitute all of the paths that end at − 2 −2n. Suppose a path was supposed to end at position − 2 − 2 −2n−2k, where 0 ≤ ≤ 0≤k≤n is an integer. This is a path of the second type currently. Our goal is to relate this to a path of the first type, which requires us to find some symmetry. As our path currently ends at − 2 − 2 −2n−2k, we would want to find a path ending at − 2 + 2 −2n+2k. To relate these, we must think about how we can make downwards movements upwards, and vice versa. The most simple operation is a reflection, as this is a SSRW. Namely, we can simply see that if we reflect a path that ends at position − 2 − 2 −2n−2k at the first time it hits − 2 −2n, we get a path ends in position − 2 + 2 −2n+2k, which is equally probable to the un-reflected path, as the walk is symmetric. By doing this, we have paired up equally probable paths in the unrestricted SSRW that end at − 2 − 2 −2n−2k to paths ending at − 2 + 2 −2n+2k who would be absorbed by the boundary. Recall that for any random variable X, Var ( ) = [ 2 ] − ( [ ] ) 2 Var(X)=E[X 2 ]−(E[X]) 2 . If 4 S 4n is the position of yo mama at time 4 4n, we showed [ 4 ] = 0 E[S 4n ]=0 in the first part. Thus, we have Var ( 4 ) = [ 4 2 ] Var(S 4n )=E[S 4n 2 ]. There is a distinct challenge in this question that was not transparent in the first part: The quantity [ 4 2 ] E[S 4n 2 ] is no longer linear. For example, when we computed [ 4 ] E[S 4n ] in the first part, consider the special case of = 5 n=5 again. Take two paths that get absorbed at − 10 −10 who are supposed to end at − 8 −8 and − 12 −12. The change caused by the absorption of one path ( − 10 − ( − 12 ) = 2 ) (−10−(−12)=2) negates the other ( − 10 − ( − 8 ) = − 2 ) (−10−(−8)=−2). However, the squares do not cancel out, as the change from − 12 −12 to − 10 −10 is a decrease of ( − 10 ) 2 − ( − 12 ) 2 = − 44 (−10) 2 −(−12) 2 =−44, but − 8 −8 going to − 10 −10 is an increase by only ( − 10 ) 2 − ( − 8 ) 2 = 36 (−10) 2 −(−8) 2 =36. This change in the mean square only occurs for paths that are caught by the threshold. Therefore, a natural idea is to take the variance of an unrestricted random walk, and then subtract out the "differential" in mean square that occurs by the absorbing threshold. As for the variance of the original walk, we can note that each movement is independently ± 1 ±1 with equal probability, so we quickly find the variance of each step is 1 1. By the linearity of variance on independent random variables, the variance of a walk of length 4 4n is 4 4n. Now, we must subtract out the difference in mean square caused by the absorbing threshold. We've shown there are an equal amount of paths ending at − 2 − 2 −2n−2k (unrestricted SSRW) as there are ending at − 2 + 2 −2n+2k that get absorbed by − 2 −2n, where 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤k≤n. It's quite easy to count the number of paths ending at − 2 − 2 −2n−2k in a standard random walk: Just classify by the number of down movements. Suppose there are d down movements. questions.problem: You generate $r$ independent uniformly random integers with replacement from the set [ ] = { 1 , 2 , … , } [n]={1,2,…,n}. questions.solution: In this problem, we are given the maximum value among the $r$ values. Note that this is quite different from the (more standard) problem where you are given the maximum is AT MOST $k$, rather than exactly $k$. The key difference here is that the value $k$ actually has to appear among the $r$ values. In that problem, the standard argument is that all values $1$ to $k$ are equally likely because we don't have any additional information beyond the fact that the draws are fair and the values are at most $k$. In this problem, we can take a similar approach, but must be careful: The value $k$ itself is not necessarily equally likely as the other values, since it actually must appear. There is no requirement that the other values from $1$ to − 1 k−1 appear, so those ones are all equally likely, but we can't necessarily say $k$ is equally likely to those. Thus, a natural approach is to find the probability of $k$ appearing on a given draw, subtract that from $1$, and then divide by − 1 k−1. This will give us the probability of each of the values $1$ to − $1$ k−1 appearing. From there, we can use LOTUS to get the expected value of one draw, and then use linearity of expectation (the draws are all identical) to say that the expected sum is just r times the expected value of one draw. To phrase the above probability more formally, let M be the maximum among the r draws, and let X be the value of a single draw. For each 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤k, we seek to compute [ = ∣ = ] P[X=i∣M=k]. This is because the maximum being less than some value means all of the individual terms are less than that value, and analogous for minima and ≥ ≥. Thus, we can say [ = ] = [ ≤ ] − [ ≤ − 1 ] = − ( − 1 ) P[M=k]=P[M≤k]−P[M≤k−1]= n r k r −(k−1) r In the above, we basically say: The probability that the maximum of the r dice is exactly k is the probability that it's at most k minus the probability it's at most − 1 k−1. Namely, [ = , = ] = [ = ] − [ = , < ] P[X=k,M=k]=P[M=k]−P[M=k,X<k] We have < X<k in the above because the maximum can't be k if the roll is > >k. questions.title: Acute Triangles
questions.problem: Three points are selected uniformly at random from the circumference of the unit circle. Find the probability that the triangle formed by the three points is acute.
questions.solution: In this problem, we need to find the probability that all angles in a triangle formed via the selection of three uniformly random points are acute. In other words, all of the angles must be less than $90$ degrees. Recall from introductory geometry that the sum of the degrees of the angles in a triangle is $180$. As an obtuse angle must be $> 90$ degrees, there can only be at most $1$ obtuse angle in the triangle. Thus, a natural idea is to find the complementary probability: We want the probability that some particular angle is obtuse, and then multiply it by $3$ to account for the three possible angles that could be obtuse. Let $A,B,$ and $C$ be the three points that are selected from the circumference of the circle. Let's find the probability angle $C$ is obtuse. WLOG, since the distribution of points is uniformly random on the circumference, we will say that point $A$ is fixed at $(1,0)$, as we could rotate the circle. We chose to fix point $A$ just so that we are able to place points $B$ and $C$. Now, to find the probability that $C$ is obtuse, we can get some quick results just by playing around with different locations of $B$ and $C$: If $B$ and $C$ are on opposite sides of the − x−axis (i.e. one has positive − y−coordinate and the other has negative), angle $C$ is acute. If $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of the − x−axis, the point that is closer to $A$ forms an obtuse angle. Therefore, for $C$ to be obtuse, two conditions must be satisfied: $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of the − x−axis (probability $1/2$, as the selection is uniform), and $C$ must be closer to $A$ than $B$ is (probability $1/2$, both orderings are equally likely). These two events are clearly independent: Regardless of whether or not the points are in the same half of the circle, each point has probability $1/2$ of being closer to $A$. Therefore, we can conclude that angle $C$ is obtuse with probability $1/2 \cdot 1/2 = 1/4$. By our work earlier, angles $A$ and $B$ are obtuse with probability $1/4$ each as well, with all events disjoint. Therefore, the probability that some angle of the triangle is obtuse is $3/4$, meaning that the triangle is acute with probability $1 - 3/4 = 1/4$.

questions.title: Third Party Dice
questions.problem: Alice and Bob play the following game: Both players simultaneously roll a standard fair $6-$sided die. Each player gets to observe their own roll, but not the value of the other player's roll. Both players hand their die to Chad, who puts in an amount of dollars in an opaque box equal to the sum of the two rolls. Alice and Bob alternate turns bidding for the box, with Alice starting. Bids can only be placed as integer values. Each turn, Alice or Bob can decide to pass or increment the bid. The first person to pass let's the other player buy the box at the value of their last bid. Find the optimal strategy for each player. Under Alice's optimal strategy, what is the maximum amount she should bid if her roll is a 4 4?
questions.solution: A key observation is that from the viewpoint of a player with a private roll $r$ the value of the box is $v = r+s$ In the above, $s$ is the opponent’s (unknown) roll. In view of the uniform distribution on { 1 , 2 , … , 6 } {1,2,…,6} the ex-ante expectation of the box is $r + 7/2$. However, as the bidding war unfolds, the following features are important: When the bidding is low, both players are willing to bid. As the bid increases each player compares the current bid b to their reservation price (i.e. the maximum he is willing to pay), which depends on their own roll. In a complete–information war of attrition with two players (whose ``values'' differ) the equilibrium outcome is that the player with the lower value concedes first and the winner ends up paying an amount equal (roughly) to the loser’s value. (Indeed, if player i’s value were v i and the loser’s value were v j , then the winning profit is − v i −v j .) The above bidding game has a similar flavor. In equilibrium we conjecture that each player adopts a cutoff strategy: for a player whose die shows r there is a cutoff ( ) β(r) so that they continue bidding (i.e. raises the bid by $ 1 $1) as long as the current bid b satisfies < ( ) b<β(r), and drops out when ≥ ( ) b≥β(r). A reasonable assumption is that the equilibrium cutoff ( ) β(r) is strictly increasing in r. This makes intuitive sense: If you have a larger number, you are willing to pay a larger amount for the box given this information. If player i has roll r and his opponent has roll s with > r>s, the bidding war will continue until the current bid reaches ( ) β(s). At that point, the opponent with roll s will drop out, as < s<r, as ( ) < ( ) β(s)<β(r). This means that the player with roll r wins the box at price ( ) − 1 β(s)−1. Their net profit will be ( + ) − ( ( ) − 1 ) (r+s)−(β(s)−1) For the opponent of roll s to be exactly indifferent at their cutoff, we require that if they were to win (had they been the higher type), their profit would be zero. This is the principle of indifference. In a symmetric game such as this one (each player has the information of one roll), the margin occurs when the two players are equal; setting = r=s we obtain the indifference condition: ( + ) − ( ( ) − 1 ) = 0 ↔ 2 − ( ) + 1 = 0 ↔ ( ) = 2 + 1 (s+s)−(β(s)−1)=0↔2s−β(s)+1=0↔β(s)=2s+1 Since the roles of the players are symmetric, we conclude that a symmetric equilibrium is given by ( ) β(s) above. Simply stated, this means no player will ever bid more than twice their initial roll, as they bid with roll s only when < 2 + 1 b<2s+1 i.e. ≤ 2 b≤2s. For the question specifically, this means that Alice should never bid more than $ 8 $8, so 8 8 is the answer.

questions.title: Biased Poker Tournament III
questions.problem: There are $101$ players (you plus $100$ poker pros) in a round‐robin poker tournament. This means that each person plays every other person once. All of the poker pros start have $100$ chips to start with for each of the $100$ matches they play, but you receive $20,000$ chips before the tournament, and are allowed to distribute them in any way you'd like among the $100$ matches. For example, you could put $1000$ chips on each of $20$ matches. In each match, the chance to win is proportional to your chips; that is, if you have $a$ chip and your opponent has $b$ chips, your probability of winning the match is + a+b a The chips of the losing player do not get added to the stack of the winning player. A win awards $1$ point, while a loss does not award anything. After all the matches are complete, the prizes are awarded as follows: $1$st place: $\$1,000,000$ $2$nd place: $\$500,000$ $3$rd place: $\$400,000$ $4$th place: $\$300,000$ $5$th place: $\$200,000$ $6$th to $10$th place: $\$100,000$ No prize for anyone else. Any ties in points when converting to rank will be resolved by a uniformly random permutation of the ranks (ex: if three people are tied for $1$st, ranks $1,2,$ and $3$ will be assigned uniformly at random). One of the other players offers to buy $5000$ chips off you at the start. If you agree to sell, they will receive $5000$ chips from you, and will be allowed to allocate those $5000$ chips to any of their $100$ games in any way they please. Assuming optimal play from the pro player, how much would you sell those chips to him for? Choose the closest answer below. $\$0$ $\$1,000$ $\$10,000$ $\$25,000$ $\$50,000$ $\$100,000$ $\$200,000$ $\$500,000$ $\$750,000$ $\$1,000,000$ You should not sell them regardless of the offer. SUBMIT
questions.solution: To compute the fair value of those $5000$ chips, we need to estimate the change in expected payout from the tournament if you have $20000$ chips vs. if you and someone else each have $15000$ chips. If you are the only one with bonus chips, it's very probable that you win the entire tournament, and if you don't, it's nearly guaranteed that you landed in the top $5$. Thus, we can conservatively estimate the expected winnings from the tournament when you have $20000$ chips as $\$900,000$. If you only have $15000$ chips, firstly, it's much less probable you win the entire tournament, as you'd have $150$ chips to allocate per match instead of $200$. This means your probability of winning each match is $3/5$ instead of $2/3$. However it's still very likely you end up in the top $5$, but the probability mass is shifted more towards $2$nd to $5$th instead of $1$st. The other complication is that there is another player with an equal probability to you of winning, as they start with the same stack. To estimate the probability of any particular gambler (not the one you're making the deal with) beating you, we can repeat the same process as in the last part of the question. Your new mean would be 3 / 5 ⋅ 100 = 60 3/5⋅100=60, while your variance is 100 ⋅ 3 / 5 ⋅ 2 / 5 = 24 100⋅3/5⋅2/5=24. The individual gambler's have mean points 49.5 + ( 1 − 0.6 ) = 49.9 49.5+(1−0.6)=49.9 and variance ≈ 25 ≈25 as well. Thus, the event that a particular other gambler beats you is now approximately 1.5 1.5 standard deviations, rather than 2.5 2.5. This is a massive increase in probability that you aren't first, but it's still likely that you end near the top. Because there is also another player with the same amount of chips as you, it's likely that you and them will be ranked 1 1 and 2 2 in the tournament. As a crude estimate, we can say that there is approximately a 20 % 20% chance of you winning, 30 % 30% of ranking second, and 50 % 50% chance that you're in ranks 3 3 to 10 10 uniformly at random. This is likely not the real distribution. We skew it slightly more towards second because of the fact that there are many other players in the game, and you edge has decreased. Under this probability distribution, we find an expected payout of 1000000 ⋅ 0.2 + 500000 ⋅ 0.3 + 400000 + 300000 + 200000 + 5 ⋅ 100000 16 = $ 437 , 500 1000000⋅0.2+500000⋅0.3+ 16 400000+300000+200000+5⋅100000 =$437,500 This distribution is not really realistic because the drop off from 2 2nd to 3 3rd is a bit large (it won't go from 30 % 30% to 6.25 % 6.25%), but it suffices for estimation/rounding purposes. The difference in expected value here is $ 462 , 500 $462,500, which is closest to $ 500 , 000 $500,000, so this is the answer. By Monte Carlo simulation, one can verify that the true values are approximately $ 870 , 000 $870,000 and $ 410 , 000 $410,000, making the fair value of the 5000 5000 chips approximately $ 460 , 000 $460,000.

questions.title: More Dice, More Problems
questions.problem: Suppose Alice comes across an infinite collection of dice that are − n−sided with values 1 , 2 , … , 1,2,…,n on the sides. The dice are all biased the same way i.e. side i shows up with probability $p_i$ . For some positive integer threshold $s$, Alice and Bob play the following game, with Alice starting: Alice rolls $1$ die from the collection. Call her roll $T_1$ . If 1 > T 1 >s, Alice wins the game. Otherwise, Bob rolls $T_1$ dice from this collection. Call the sum of his $T_1$ rolls $T_2$ . If 2 > T 2 >s, Bob wins the game. Otherwise, Alice rolls $T_2$ dice from the collection. Call the sum of her $T_2$ rolls $T_3$ . If 3 > T 3 >s, Alice wins the game, otherwise, repeat in the same fashion as the above until someone rolls a sum of dice at least $s$. Find Alice's probability of winning the game in the case where $s = 2, n = 6$, and the dice are fair. Note that unlike other problems, there is nowhere near a closed-form expression for this probability for general dice and values of s.
questions.solution: To compute the probability of Alice winning, we need to keep track of the state of the game at all times. Namely, the state of the game is uniquely determined by who is rolling and how many dice are being rolled. Therefore, let $a_r$ be the probability that Alice wins the game given that she is currently rolling $1 \leq r \leq s$ dice. Note that 1 − 1−a r is the probability that Bob wins the game given that it's his turn and he is currently rolling $r$ dice. This is because 1 − 1−a r is the probability of Alice losing the game, which means Bob must win it. We now want to find a recurrence relation for $a_r$ . Alice's probability of winning is directly related to the sum of the dice that she rolls. Thus, we should condition on the sum of Alice's $r$ dice. There are two cases to consider: If the sum of Alice's $r$ dice is at least $s$, she wins on that turn. Letting $D_i$ be the value of the ith die she rolls, $1 \leq i \leq r$, this occurs with probability [ ∑ = 1 > ] P[ i=1 ∑ r D i >s] Otherwise, if the sum of her rolls is at most $s$, it will be Bob's turn to go. The minimum sum that Alice can roll is $s$, as the minimum value on each die is $1$. If the sum of Alice's rolls is some value $r \leq t \leq s$, Bob rolls $t$ dice on his turn. Based on the discussion at the beginning, Alice will win with probability $1$ − 1−a t in that case, as it will be Bob starting with t die rolls. The probability that Bob ends up rolling t dice is the probability Alice rolls a sum of t, which is [ ∑ = 1 = ] P[ i=1 ∑ r D i =t] We sum the second component over all integers ≤ ≤ r≤t≤s to account for all the cases. Putting it all together, we find that = [ ∑ = 1 > ] + ∑ = [ ∑ = 1 = ] ⋅ ( 1 − ) a r =P[ i=1 ∑ r D i >s]+ t=r ∑ s P[ i=1 ∑ r D i =t]⋅(1−a t ) The probability that Alice wins the game is 1 a 1 , as she initially rolls 1 1 die. This is a system of s equations (since 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤r≤s in the above) with s unknowns ( 1 , … , ) (a 1 ,…,a s ). One would typically solve this by starting at a s and working backwards, as this is a classic dynamic programming approach, and a s has the least "dependence" on the other terms. Employing this approach in our problem, we have that = 2 s=2 and that there are 6 − 6−sided fair dice. By using standard facts about fair dice and the sum of two fair dice, we reach the equations 1 = 2 / 3 + 1 / 6 ⋅ ( 1 − 1 ) + 1 / 6 ⋅ ( 1 − 2 ) 2 = 35 / 36 + 1 / 36 ⋅ ( 1 − 2 ) a 1 a 2 =2/3+1/6⋅(1−a 1 )+1/6⋅(1−a 2 ) =35/36+1/36⋅(1−a 2 ) The second equation is easy to solve for 2 a 2 by moving the 2 a 2 terms to the same side. This yields 2 = 36 / 37 a 2 =36/37. Plugging this into the first equation yields 1 = 2 / 3 + 1 / 6 ⋅ ( 1 − 1 ) + 1 / 6 ⋅ ( 1 − 36 / 37 ) ⟺ 7 / 6 1 = 2 / 3 + 1 / 6 + 1 / 37 ⟺ 1 = 186 / 259 a 1 =2/3+1/6⋅(1−a 1 )+1/6⋅(1−36/37)⟺7/6a 1 =2/3+1/6+1/37⟺a 1 =186/259 The answer with the specific values is 186 / 259 186/259.

questions.problem: There is a unit circle in the plane that is colored white initially. Every minute, we take a red paintbrush and paint some uniformly randomly selected semi-circle of the entire circle red. questions.solution: In this problem, we need to compute the expected amount of time to cover the circle in red entirely. The time is dependent on how much of the circle is left to be painted. Therefore, the best approach is to set up a function $f(x)$ that represents the expected number of minutes to paint the circle entirely red given that an arc of radian length $x$ has not been covered yet. Each semi-circle covers π radians of the entire circle. Furthermore, note that the first painting will always reduce us down to π radians unpainted, since none of the circle is painted at that point. Therefore, we will restrict ourselves to 0 ≤ ≤ 0≤x≤π, and the answer we seek is ( 2 ) = 1 + ( ) f(2π)=1+f(π), as it takes 1 1 minute to do the first painting. Since the paintings are in the form of semi-circles, the region that is unpainted must be connected/continuous, as each one covers exactly half of the entire circle and only at most π radians remain. You may want to try drawing out a few examples to convince yourself of this fact. We will use this fact here and assume that the arc from 0 0 to x radians is painted WLOG, as the circles are selected uniformly at random. There are three possible cases here for the next painting round: Your circle completely compasses the remaining white space. Your circle does not paint any of the remaining white space i.e. stays completely in the red. Your circle covers some amount of radians, say 0 ≤ ≤ 0≤y≤x. The circle you draw can be completely classified by it's angle with the + − +x−axis, where we will take the convention − ≤ ≤ −π≤θ≤π here for simplicity of calculation. This is because the circle covered will go through radians [ , + ] [θ,θ+π]. To cover the arc [ 0 , ] [0,x] radians, the starting point of the arc must be at most 0 0 radians (so that the bottom of the arc is captured) and at least ( + ) − 2 = − (x+π)−2π=x−π radians, as this is what's diametrically opposed to the upper bound at x radians. We subtract 2 2π to be consistent with our convention above. The probability that the starting angle uniformly randomly selected is in the interval [ − , 0 ] [x−π,0] is just the length over 2 2π, as the selection is uniform. Thus, the probability is − 2 2π π−x . In this case, the circle is painted red within 1 1 minute. As for the second case, for the circle to be completely contained in the red i.e. not cover any of the remaining region, the starting point must be in the range [ , ] [x,π]. The start is x because that is the upper bound of the arc that currently exists. The end is π because + − 2 = 0 π+π−2π=0, so anything larger than a starting point of π radians will hit the lower bound of the uncolored arc. Thus, the probability the starting point is in this range is − 2 2π π−x as well. In this case, it takes 1 + ( ) 1+f(x) additional minutes on average to paint the circle, as we spent 1 1 minute painting nothing else red, and there are still x radians uncolored, which take ( ) f(x) minutes on average to color. As for the last case, if the starting point of the arc is in the interval [ − , − ] [−π,x−π] OR [ 0 , ] [0,x], some proportion of the arc will be covered, but not all of it. questions.title: Minecraft Steve
questions.problem: Lucky day! Steve struck luck while mining. He has $m$ diamonds and $n$ gold ingots in his inventory. Since he is so lucky, he is going to perform the following procedure $r$ times: He removes one item from his inventory uniformly at random. He replaces the discarded item with one diamond and one gold ingot. Find the expected number of diamonds in Steve's inventory at the end of r draws. Report the answer when $m = 20, n = 25,$ and $r = 44$.
questions.solution: In this problem, we have a fair few moving parts, so let's first formalize our method and approach. At the start, Steve has $m+n$ items in his inventory. After $r$ turns, since he drops one item and replaces it with one diamond and one gold ingot, he will have $m+n+r$ total items in his inventory. One might think that a Linearity of Expectation approach would work well here, but the issue is that the probability of drawing a diamond on each turn is non-constant: The probability of selecting a diamond changes over time as Steve adds and removes items from his inventory. Thus, we will need a different approach. We know that after each turn, the count of the item that Steve took out (gold or diamond) will stay the same after replacement, while the count of the other item will rise by one. Therefore, the difference between the number of diamonds in his inventory and the number of gold ingots in his inventory changes by ± 1 ±1 at each turn. More specifically, for some non-negative integer 0 ≤ ≤ 0≤k≤r, let D k and G k represent the number diamonds and gold ingots, respectively, in Steve's inventory. By the discussion above, = − R k =D k −G k will change by ± 1 ±1 on each turn. More specifically, If a diamond is selected, + 1 = D k+1 =D k and + 1 = + 1 G k+1 =G k +1, so + 1 = − ( + 1 ) = − 1 + ( − ) = − 1 + R k+1 =D k −(G k +1)=−1+(D k −G k )=−1+R k . If a gold ingot is selected, + 1 = 1 + D k+1 =1+D k and + 1 = G k+1 =G k , so + 1 = ( + 1 ) − = 1 + ( − ) = 1 + R k+1 =(D k +1)−G k =1+(D k −G k )=1+R k Since we already have a value for the difference, we can get try to get a second equation for which we know the value of. If we are to define = + T k =D k +G k as the total number of items in Steve's inventory at each time, by the discussion earlier, = + T k =m+n k . We now have a system of two equations: = + T k =D k +G k and = − R k =D k −G k . Let's express the number of diamonds and gold ingots in the bag in terms of T k and R k , as those quantities may be easier to compute. By simple algebra, we find = + 2 = − 2 D k = 2 T k +R k G k = 2 T k −R k As this expresses the number of diamonds and gold ingots after k turns, after k turns, a diamond and a gold ingot are respectively selected with probabilities / D k /T k and / G k /T k . As we already know how to find T k , all we need is to find R k . More specifically, we need [ ] E[R k ]. questions.title: Consecutive Lineup
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $n$. There are $2n$ students in a class labeled 1 , 2 , … , 2 1,2,…,2n. When it is time for their school portraits, the teacher must line up half of the students to be in the first batch. The teacher has a peculiar rule: If students k and $k+1$ are in the first batch, then student $k$ must take their picture before student $k+1$ in line. Find the number of acceptable lineups that can be made when $n = 5$.
questions.solution: This problem has a unique twist because of the extra condition: if both students $k$ and $k+1$ are chosen, then student $k$ must appear before student $k+1$ in the lineup. A common approach in selection problems is to represent the situation with binary strings. Here, we view the $2n$ students as a binary string of length $2n$, where a $1$ indicates a selected student and a $0$ an unselected one. In our setting there are exactly $n$ ones and $n$ zeros. The key observation is that the constraint forces a particular structure on the ones. Notice that any block (i.e. a maximal sequence) of consecutive ones must appear in increasing order in the final lineup; there is no freedom to rearrange them. If we denote the lengths of these blocks by 1 , 2 , … , b 1 ,b 2 ,…,b k then we must have 1 + 2 + ⋯ + = b 1 +b 2 +⋯+b k =n Without any restrictions, the n selected students could be arranged in ! n! ways. However, in each block of length b i , only one ordering (the increasing order) is acceptable instead of the usual ! b i ! orders. Therefore, given a fixed block structure, the number of valid arrangements is ! 1 ! 2 ! ⋯ ! = ( 1 , 2 , … , ) b 1 !b 2 !⋯b k ! n! =( b 1 ,b 2 ,…,b k n ) While this expression correctly counts the valid arrangements for one particular block configuration, the challenge is that the blocks can have arbitrary lengths and positions in the string. Summing over all possible block structures directly becomes unwieldy. An alternative and clearer approach is to fix the positions of the zeros. With n zeros in the string, they divide it into + 1 n+1 regions (or gaps): one before the first zero, one between each pair of zeros, and one after the last zero. Let 1 , 2 , … , + 1 o 1 ,o 2 ,…,o n+1 be the number of ones in each region. These must satisfy 1 + 2 + ⋯ + + 1 = o 1 +o 2 +⋯+o n+1 =n At first glance one might think to use stars and bars to count the number of solutions for ( 1 , … , + 1 ) (o 1 ,…,o n+1 ). However, stars and bars would only account for the number of ways to distribute indistinguishable objects into bins and ignore the fact that the actual identities (or order) of the students matter. In our problem, having, say, students 2 2 and 3 3 in a gap is different from having students 3 3 and 4 4, even though both situations have two ones. To properly account for the order within each gap, we use multinomial coefficients, as these will treat the students as distinct while removing the orderings of students within gaps. For fixed numbers 1 , … , + 1 o 1 ,…,o n+1 , the number of arrangements where the order inside each gap is respected (that is, the students appear in increasing order within that gap) is ( 1 , 2 , … , + 1 ) ( o 1 ,o 2 ,…,o n+1 n ) Summing over all solutions to 1 + 2 + ⋯ + + 1 = o 1 +o 2 +⋯+o n+1 =n gives the total number of arrangements. This sum essentially says: How many ways can each of the n ones be placed into the + 1 n+1 regions with no restrictions? Each 1 1 is a distinct object (person) that we want to place into one of the + 1 n+1 gaps (between people not selected). For each 1 1, there are exactly + 1 n+1 choices of location, and these choices are made independently. Hence, the total number of assignments is ( + 1 ) (n+1) n . With = 5 n=5, the answer is 6 5 = 7776 6 5 =7776.

questions.title: Power Square Divisibility
questions.problem: Find the number of positive integers integers $n$ at most $10,000$ such that 2 − 2 2 n −n 2 is divisible by $7$.
questions.solution: For 2 − 2 2 n −n 2 to be divisible by $7$, it must be the case that $2^n$ and $n^2$ leave the same remainder when divided by $7$. Therefore, it is instructive to consider the remainders of $2^n$ and $n^2$ for varying $n$ modulo $7$. Let's start with $2^n$ . The first few values of $2^n$ are $2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128,$ and $256$. Modulo $7$, these values are $2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 1, 2, 4$. We can formally show that the cycle repeats $2, 4, 1$ infinitely: For $n = 1, 2, 3$, the remainders are $2, 4,$ and $1$ modulo $7$. The key is that the cycle is of length $3$, so we should consider what happens when we multiply by 2 3 = 8 2 3 =8. Since $8$ is equivalent to $1$ modulo $7$, multiplying by 2 3 2 3 gives you the same remainder, meaning $x$ and 2 3 2 3 x have the same remainder when divided by $7$, so the result is proven. Now, let's take a look at $n^2$ and see what we gather. The first few values of $n^2$ are $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49,$ and $64$. Modulo $7$, these values are $1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 0, 1$. Now, we see a cycle that is supposedly of length $7$. Let's prove that this is the case. We've already shown the base sequence $1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 0$ for the first $7$ positive integers. Now, we claim that $x^2$ and ( + 7 ) 2 (x+7) 2 have the same remainder modulo $7$. To prove this, we can expand out ( + $7$ ) 2 (x+7) 2 and obtain ( + 7 ) 2 = 2 + 14 + 49 = 2 + 7 ( 2 + 7 ) (x+7) 2 =x 2 +14x+49=x 2 +7(2x+7) Since the second part of the expression is clearly divisible by $7$, the remainder of ( + 7 ) 2 (x+7) 2 when divided by 7 7 is just the same as that of $x^2$ . Therefore, this cycle repeats infinitely. According to our work thus far, $2^n$ repeats remainders on a cycle of length $3$, while $n^2$ repeats remainders on a cycle of length $7$. Specifically here's the breakdown: 2 3 ≡ $1$ ( mod 7 ) 2 3n ≡1(mod7) 2 3 + 1 ≡ 2 ( mod 7 ) 2 3n+1 ≡2(mod7) 2 3 + 2 ≡ $4$ ( mod 7 ) $2$ 3n+2 ≡4(mod7) ( 7 ) 2 ≡ 0 ( mod 7 ) (7n) 2 ≡0(mod7) ( 7 + 1 ) 2 ≡ 1 ( mod 7 ) (7n+1) 2 ≡1(mod7) ( 7 + 2 ) 2 ≡ 4 ( mod 7 ) (7n+2) 2 ≡4(mod7) ( 7 + 3 ) 2 ≡ 2 ( mod 7 ) (7n+3) 2 ≡2(mod7) ( 7 + 4 ) 2 ≡ 2 ( mod 7 ) (7n+4) 2 ≡2(mod7) ( 7 + 5 ) 2 ≡ 4 ( mod 7 ) (7n+5) 2 ≡4(mod7) ( 7 + 6 ) 2 ≡ 1 ( mod 7 ) (7n+6) 2 ≡1(mod7) Now, for some integer m to be satisfactory, it must satisfy one of the following properties for some integers 1 n 1 and 2 n 2 : = 3 1 = 7 2 + 1 m=3n 1 =7n 2 +1 or = 3 1 = 7 2 + 6 m=3n 1 =7n 2 +6 = 3 1 + 1 = 7 2 + 3 m=3n 1 +1=7n 2 +3 or = 3 1 + 1 = 7 2 + 4 m=3n 1 +1=7n 2 +4 = 3 1 + 2 = 7 2 + 2 m=3n 1 +2=7n 2 +2 or = 3 1 + 2 = 7 2 + 5 m=3n 1 +2=7n 2 +5 This is just seen by equating the remainders. Since the cycle will repeat every 21 21 positive integers, we can just look at integers satisfying this from 1 1 to 21 21. For the first equality, we find that 6 = 7 ⋅ 0 + 6 6=7⋅0+6 and 15 = 7 ⋅ 2 + 1 15=7⋅2+1. For the second equality, we find that 10 = 7 ⋅ 1 + 3 10=7⋅1+3 and 4 = 7 ⋅ 0 + 4 4=7⋅0+4. For the last equality, we find 2 = 7 ⋅ 0 + 2 2=7⋅0+2 and 5 = 7 ⋅ 0 + 5 5=7⋅0+5. Thus, in each set of 21 21 consecutive integers, there are 6 6 that satisfy the condition: All integers equivalent to 2 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 10 , 2,4,5,6,10, or 15 15 modulo 21 21 will satisfy the condition in question. All that is left is to count how many integers satisfy the condition while being at most 10 , 000 10,000. This is just equivalent to counting the number of groups of 21 21 integers there are, as we know that there are 6 6 per group, and we can handle the last group separately. To do this, we note that 21 ⋅ 500 = 10500 21⋅500=10500, so the value is slightly less than 500 500 groups. As 21 ⋅ 20 = 420 21⋅20=420, 21 ⋅ ( 500 − 20 ) = 10500 − 420 = 10080 21⋅(500−20)=10500−420=10080. From here, it's easy to see that subtracting 4 ⋅ 21 = 84 4⋅21=84 gets us to 9996 < 10000 9996<10000, so we know that 10000 = 9996 + 4 = 20 ⋅ ( 500 − 20 − 4 ) + 4 = 21 ⋅ 476 + 4 10000=9996+4=20⋅(500−20−4)+4=21⋅476+4 In each of the 476 476 full groups, there are 6 6 integers satisfying the condition, so there are 476 ⋅ 6 476⋅6 integers satisfying the condition from the full groups. Now, in the last group of 9997 9997 to 10000 10000, we note that these represent remainders 1 1 to 4 4 when divided by 21 21, of which we know remainders of 2 2 and 4 4 will be satisfactory for our condition. Thus, there are 6 ⋅ 476 + 2 = 2858 6⋅476+2=2858 integers at most 10000 10000 satisfying the condition.

It is not necessarily always the case that [ ≤ ] = 1 / 2 P[X≤m]=1/2. Thus, all we know about the median at a first glance is that it partitions up our distribution into two pieces in another attempt to "center" it. Since we think that the median can represent some type of centering, it's instructive to look at the quantity ∣ − ∣ ∣μ−m∣. Our new goal is to bound this quantity. questions.title: Prefix Sums
questions.problem: Fix a positive integer $k$. The number 1 , 2 , … , 3 + 1 1,2,…,3k+1 arranged in some permutation uniformly at random, say 1 , … , 3 + 1 a 1 ,…,a 3k+1 . Define the leading sums = 1 + ⋯ + S n =a 1 +⋯+a n for $1 \leq n \leq 3k+1$. Compute the probability that none of the $S_i$ are divisible by $3$. Report the answer when $k = 5$.
questions.solution: We are looking to compute the probability that none of the prefix sums $S_i$ are divisible by $3$. A natural first thing to consider is the set of integers modulo $3$. There are $k, k+1,$ and $k$ integers equivalent to $0, 1,$ and $2$ modulo $3$, respectively. We will refer to these as $[0], [1]$, and $[2]$ integers, respectively. $[0]$ integers do not affect the prefix sum's divisibility by $3$ at all, as $[0]$ integers are divisible by $3$ themselves. This leads us to the $[1]$ and $[2]$ integers. Now, note that the sum of a $[1]$ integer and $[2]$ integer is divisible by $3$. Define $s_n$ as ( mod 3 ) S n (mod3). We know that $[0]$ integers don't change the value of $S_n$ . There are two cases: If = 1 s n =1, a $[1]$ integer must be the next integer among $[1]$ or $[2]$ integers, as a $[2]$ integer would make the sum divisible by $3$. Similarly, if = 2 s n =2, a $[2]$ integer must be the next integer among $[1]$ or $[2]$ integers, as a $[1]$ integer would make the sum divisible by $3$. Hence, ignoring $[0]$ integers, once the non- $[0]$ integer is chosen, the entire pattern is forced. As there are $k+1$ $[1]$ integers and $k$ $[2]$ integers, the sequence must start with a $[1]$ integer. Thus, the pattern of integer types (ignoring $[0]$ integers) is as follows: 1 , 1 , 2 , 1 , 2 , … 1,1,2,1,2,…. Now, we can create our sequence in a few steps: Select the locations for the $k$ $[0]$ integers anywhere in the sequence of $3k+1$. Arrange the $[0]$ integers on those $k$ spots. Arrange the $k+1$ $[1]$ integers in their respective spots in the ordering. Arrange the $k$ $[2]$ integers in their respective spots in the ordering. Divide by the total number of permutations. These can be counted as follows: The order in which the k spots for the $[0]$ integers is selected is irrelevant. questions.title: Random Seater
questions.problem: In a waiting room, there are $N>2$ chairs in a row. A chair is “available” if nobody is sitting on that chair or a chair right next to it. People enter one at a time and sit in one of the available chairs uniformly at random. This continues until there are no more available chairs. Compute the expected number of people that are seated at the end. Report the answer when = 6 N=6.
questions.solution: Let $E(N)$ denote the expected number of people seated when the process terminates, starting from $N$ empty chairs in a row. At the start, all $N$ chairs are available, so the first person chooses a seat uniformly from { $1$ , $2$ , … , } {1,2,…,N}. Once the first seat is chosen, it permanently blocks itself and its neighbors. The remaining available chairs, if any, lie in two disjoint sub-intervals (one to the left and one to the right of the blocked triple). From that point onward, the process inside each sub-interval evolves independently of the other, and (crucially) it evolves with the \emph{same rule} as the original problem: at each step, a person chooses uniformly among available chairs within that sub-interval. This “split into independent subproblems after the first choice” is the standard structure that produces a recursion depending only on the interval length. questions.solution: The central difficulty of this problem is that equality is a $\emph{global}$ numerical condition, while the allowed operation is extremely local and weak: we may only increase a number by $1$ or leave it unchanged, independently at each cell. From first principles, this immediately suggests that attempting to make all neighboring values distinct in magnitude distinct in magnitude is far too ambitious. Instead, we should look for a simpler invariant that is (i) easy to control with a $+1$ operation and (ii) strong enough to prevent equality. Parity is the natural candidate, since adding $1$ flips parity and two integers of opposite parity can never be equal. Once parity is identified as the correct numerical invariant, the geometry of the grid takes over. The $m\times n$ grid is bipartite: it admits a checkerboard coloring into black and white cells such that no two neighboring cells share the same color. This structure perfectly matches the binary nature of parity. The guiding idea is therefore to synchronize parity with color synchronize parity with color: force all black cells to have one parity and all white cells to have the opposite parity. If this can be done, then every pair of neighboring cells must differ in parity and hence in value. We now formalize this idea. Label the cells by coordinates ( , ) (i,j) with 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤m and 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤j≤n, and let , ∈ a i,j ∈Z be the original value in cell ( , ) (i,j). Color the grid so that cell ( , ) (i,j) is black if + i+j is even and white if + i+j is odd. For each cell, we choose an increment , ∈ { 0 , 1 } x i,j ∈{0,1} and define the modified value , = , + , . b i,j =a i,j +x i,j . Our goal is to ensure that , ≡ + ( m o d 2 ) , b i,j ≡i+j(mod2), so that black cells (even + i+j) contain even numbers and white cells (odd + i+j) contain odd numbers. This is always achievable: if , a i,j already has the desired parity, take , = 0 x i,j =0, and if not, take , = 1 x i,j =1. Equivalently, we may write the choice explicitly as , = ( + − , ) ( m o d 2 ) , x i,j =(i+j−a i,j )(mod2), which always lies in { 0 , 1 } {0,1} and guarantees the parity condition above. Now consider any two neighboring cells. If ( , ) (i,j) and ( + 1 , ) (i+1,j) are neighbors, then ( + 1 ) + = ( + ) + 1 , (i+1)+j=(i+j)+1, so their colors—and hence their enforced parities—are opposite. The same holds for horizontal neighbors ( , ) (i,j) and ( , + 1 ) (i,j+1). Therefore, for every adjacent pair, one modified value is even and the other is odd. Since integers of opposite parity cannot be equal, it follows that no cell has the same value as any of its neighbors. The key insight is that the problem is fundamentally about a binary constraint binary constraint. The grid already decomposes naturally into two classes via a checkerboard coloring, and parity is the simplest numerical feature that aligns perfectly with this decomposition and is fully controllable using the allowed operation. By weakening the goal from ``different values'' to ``different parity'' and exploiting the bipartite structure of the grid, we obtain a solution that works for every initial configuration. Hence, it is always possible to modify any grid so that no cell shares the same value as any of its neighbors.

questions.title: Vote Count I
questions.problem: Alice and Bob are running for presidency of a school club. It is known that Alice has $a$ votes and Bob has $b$ votes, where $a > b$. The votes are counted one-by-one, and a running tally is recorded. Find the probability that Alice is always strictly ahead in the vote count when $a = 40$ and $b = 20$.
questions.solution: Utilize the reflection principle in this question. For Alice to be strictly ahead of Bob throughout the counting of the votes, they are never able to tie. If the first vote is for Bob, Alice and Bob must tie at some point, as Alice has more votes than Bob, so they must equalize at some point. For any sequence of drawing where the first vote is for Alice and it reaches a tie, reflect the votes up until the first point of equalization. This means that all votes for Alice are flipped to be for Bob, and vice versa. An important note is that the reflected sequence is still one with a votes for Alice and b votes for Bob, respectively, as they have an equal amount of votes up until the point of equalization. This reflected sequence becomes one where the first vote is for Bob, as the first vote in the original sequence was for Alice. This reflected sequence could be any sequence that starts with a vote for Bob, as you're flipping all of the votes around. What this proves is that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the sequences where a tie is reached with the first vote being for Alice and sequences where the first vote is for Bob. The probability that Alice always leads the vote is just 1 − [ Alice and Bob tie at some point ] 1−P[Alice and Bob tie at some point]. Any sequence that ties starts with a vote for either Alice or Bob. However, by the above, the number of sequences where the first vote is Alice and there is a tie is equal to the number of sequences where there is a tie and the first vote is for Bob. Thus, [ Alice and Bob tie at some point ] = 2 [ Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob ] P[Alice and Bob tie at some point]=2P[Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob]. However, all sequences where Bob is the first vote tie at some point, so [ Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob ] = [ First vote is for Bob ] P[Alice and Bob tie at some point and the first vote is for Bob]=P[First vote is for Bob]. Since b of the + a+b total votes are for Bob, the probability that the first vote is for Bob is + a+b b . Plugging this in, we obtain that the probability Alice always leads is 1 − 2 ⋅ + = − + 1−2⋅ a+b b = a+b a−b . With the specified values, the answer is 1 3 3 1 .

questions.title: Vote Count II
questions.problem: Alice and Bob are running for presidency of a school club. It is known that Alice has $a$ votes and Bob has $b$ votes, where $a > b$. The votes are counted one-by-one, and a running tally is recorded. Find the probability that Alice is never behind in the vote count when $a = 40$ and $b = 20$. Note: Solve Vote Count I before attempting this question.
questions.solution: The situation of this question is very similar to that of the first part, so we should try to use the result of the first part of the question. The difference between a sequence where Alice always has strictly more votes than Bob versus can tie would be 1 1 vote. In other words, any sequence where Alice is never behind Bob can be converted into a sequence where Alice is always strictly ahead of Bob by appending a vote for Alice at the beginning of the sequence. Similarly, we can also convert a sequence where Alice is always ahead of Bob with + 1 a+1 votes for Alice and b for Bob into a sequence where Alice is never behind Bob with a and b votes for each person, respectively, by eliminating the first vote for Alice. Note that we know the first two votes of any such sequence where Alice is strictly ahead are for Alice, as there would be a tie if the first was for Alice and the second was for Bob. Thus, this action is valid. This implies that the number of sequences where Alice is never behind Bob with a and b votes for each, respectively, is equal to the number of sequences where Alice is always ahead of Bob when they respectively have + 1 a+1 and b votes. Note that this does not imply that the probabilities are equal, as the number of sequences of votes that can be drawn when there are + 1 a+1 and b votes for the candidates is not equal to when there are a and b votes. In other words, the sample spaces of the two experiments are not the same. By "Vote Count I", the probability of the latter event is already known to be + 1 − + + 1 a+b+1 a+1−b . Thus, as all sequences are equally likely to occur, the number of sequences that satisfy the latter event is just equal to the probability multiplied by the number of sequences. The total number of votes that are drawn out in the latter experiment is + + 1 a+b+1. Since it only matters which candidate the vote is for, we can pick the locations of the b votes for Bob in ( + + 1 ) ( b a+b+1 ) ways, as the order of selection is irrelevant, and the other + 1 a+1 spots belong to Alice. Thus, there are ( + + 1 ) ( b a+b+1 ) sequences total in the sample space of the latter experiment, so the number of sequences that satisfy our event of interest is − + 1 + + 1 ( + + 1 ) = − + 1 + + 1 ⋅ ( + + 1 ) ! ! questions.title: Tourney Switch
questions.problem: Fix $0 < p < 1$. Alice and Bob play in a best of 2 − 1 2n−1 tennis tournament. The winner of each round receives $1$ point, and the first to $n$ points wins. The player with a fewer points has probability $p$ of winning the next match, while the player with more points has probability 1 − 1−p of winning the next match. If Alice and Bob have an equal amount of points, Alice has probability p of winning. Find the probability that Alice wins the tournament when $n = 10$ and $p = 2/3$.
questions.solution: The situation with up to 2 − 1 2n−1 games gets very complicated for large $n$, so let's first consider the situation for when $n = 1$ and $2$, as these are solvable by hand. With $n = 1$, the probability is just $p$, as this just asks for the probability Alice wins the first game which is $p$, as they start out tied. When $n = 2$, there are three possible sequences leading to Alice winning: $WW, WLW,$ and $LWW$, where $L$ is a loss and $W$ is a win for Alice. The probability of $WW$ is just ( 1 − ) p(1−p), as she wins her first game with probability $p$, and then she wins her second game with probability 1 − 1−p, as she's leading after the first game. By a similar methodology, the probability of $WLW$ and $LWW$ are $p^3$ and 2 ( 1 − ) p 2 (1−p). Adding these up, the probability Alice wins the best of $3$ is ( 1 − ) + 2 ( 1 − ) + 3 = [ ( 1 − ) + − 2 + 2 ] = $p$(1−p)+p 2 (1−p)+p 3 =p[(1−p)+p−p 2 +p 2 ]=p This doesn't seem like a coincidence any more! A natural guess is that the probability Alice wins is p, regardless of n. We can prove this via strong induction. The base case of $n = 1$ is already shown above. Our strong induction hypothesis is that Alice has probability $p$ of winning a best of 2 − 1 2k−1 tournament for all $1 \leq k \leq n$. Our goal is to prove that she has probability $p$ of winning in a best of $2n+1$ tournament. We have to think carefully about how to actually utilize our induction hypothesis. Conditioning on the first step isn't sufficient here because the tournament is unbalanced afterwards i.e. one player only needs n wins, while the other needs $n+1$ wins. A more natural thing to condition on is if Alice and Bob tie at any point in the process. If they tie at some point in the process, we can reduce this problem down to one that is a smaller tournament. Let 2 + 1 A 2n+1 be the event that Alice wins the best of $2n+1$ tournament and $T$ be the event that Alice and Bob are tied at some point after the start. By the Law of Total Probability, [ 2 + 1 ] = [ 2 + 1 ∣ ] [ ] + [ 2 + 1 ∣ ] [ ] P[A 2n+1 ]=P[A 2n+1 ∣T]P[T]+P[A 2n+1 ∣T c ]P[T c ] For simplicity, let [ ] = P[T]=t, which makes [ ] = 1 − P[T c ]=1−t. If there is no tie at any point in the tournament, the winner of the first game is the winner of the tournament, so Alice must win the first game in this case. This occurs with probability [ 2 + 1 ∣ ] = P[A 2n+1 ∣T c ]=p. If there is a tie at some point in the tournament, which occurs with probability t, starting from the tie point, the remainder of the tournament is just a smaller version of the original one. By our strong induction hypothesis, the probability Alice wins a best of 2 − 1 2k−1 tournament for 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤k≤n is p, so the [ 2 + 1 ∣ ] = P[A 2n+1 ∣T]=p by the strong induction hypothesis. Plugging this in, [ 2 + 1 ] = + ( 1 − ) = P[A 2n+1 ]=pt+p(1−t)=p The result is now proven, allowing us to conclude the probability Alice wins the tournament is p, regardless of n. With the specified values, the answer is 2 / 3 2/3.

questions.title: Cubic Ant V
questions.problem: An ant walks along the edges of a cube that has vertices at { 0 , 1 } 3 = { ( , , ) : , , ∈ { 0 , 1 } } {0,1} 3 ={(x,y,z):x,y,z∈{0,1}}, starting at $(0,0,0)$. There is a spider located that $(1,1,0)$ that eats ants whenever they visit $(1,1,0)$. The ant moves to one of the three adjacent vertices with equal probability at each step. Find the probability that the ant makes it to $(1,1,1)$.
questions.solution: In more simple terms, we are asking the probability that the ant hits $(1,1,1)$ before $(1,1,0)$. Since the ant is performing a random walk, a Markov chain approach is most appropriate. One natural concern is that there are $8$ states as of now, which correspond to the $8$ vertices. Thus, we would want to find some symmetry in the path of the ant to reduce the complexity of the Markov chain. Drawing out the cube and placing the spider on it, we see $4$ group of vertices: Group $1$: $(1,0,1)$ and $(0,1,1)$ Group $2$: $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$ Group $3$: $(0,0,0)$ Group $4$: $(0,0,1)$ Groups $1$ and $2$ are obtained by essentially reflecting the cube about the diagonal plane passing through $(0,0,0)$ and $(1,1,0)$, since their paths to both $(1,1,1)$ and $(1,1,0)$ are just reflected. $(0,0,0)$ and $(0,0,1)$ are solitary, as they are directly on the path of reflection. Thus, we've reduced our problem to $4$ states. Let 1 , 2 , 3 , p 1 ,p 2 ,p 3 , and $p_4$ be the probabilities of reaching $(1,1,1)$ before $(1,1,0)$ from each of the $4$ groups, respectively. We now need to apply Law of Total Probability repeatedly to get equations that represent the movement of the ant. $p_3$ is our answer to the question, since the ant starts at $(0,0,0)$. If the ant is currently in group $1$, one of the three directions brings it to $(1,1,1)$, in which it wins automatically. The other two directions bring the ant to groups $2$ and $4$, in which there are respective probabilities $p_2$ and $p_4$ of success in these cases. By the Law of Total Probability, 1 = 1 3 + 1 3 2 + 1 3 4 p 1 = 3 1 + 3 1 p 2 + 3 1 p 4 If the ant is currently in group $2$, one of the three directions brings it to the spider, in which it dies. In the other two directions, the ant reaches groups $1$ and $3$, in which it has respective probabilities $p_1$ and $p_3$ of success. By the Law of Total Probability, 2 = 1 3 1 + 1 3 3 p 2 = 3 1 p 1 + 3 1 p 3 If the ant is currently in group $3$, two of the three directions bring the ant to group $2$, while the other brings the ant to group $4$. There are respective success probabilities of $p_2$ and $p_4$ in these cases, so by the Law of Total Probability, 3 = 2 3 2 + 1 3 4 p 3 = 3 2 p 2 + 3 1 p 4 Lastly, if the ant is currently in group $4$, two of the three movements bring it to group $1$, while the last movement brings it to group $3$. There are respective probabilities of success $p_1$ and $p_3$ in these cases, so by the Law of Total Probability, 4 = 2 3 1 + 1 3 3 p 4 = 3 2 p 1 + 3 1 p 3 By solving this system of four equations through your favorite method, we find that 3 = 3 / 7 p 3 =3/7.

questions.solution: For these types of problems, it's best to encode this using the probability generating function probability generating function (PGF) of the random variable. This is because the PGF enables us to evaluate probabilities involving a sum quite easily. The way to think of this is the MGF: The MGF stores the moments, and allows us to find the moments of a product of random variables via multiplication. In other words, the coefficient of z i is the probability that the random variable equals i. Therefore, we can get the PGF of the sum of the dice by multiplying the PGFs of the individual dice, since they are independent. We want the sum to be uniform over { 2 , 3 , … , 12 } {2,3,…,12}, so the PGF of the sum needs to be equal to ( ) = 1 11 ( 2 + 3 + ⋯ + 12 ) p S (z)= 11 1 (z 2 +z 3 +⋯+z 12 ) Therefore, we must find coefficients 1 , … , 6 p 1 ,…,p 6 and 1 , … , 6 q 1 ,…,q 6 such that ( ) ( ) = ( ) = 1 11 ( 2 + 3 + ⋯ + 12 ) = 2 11 ( 1 + + ⋯ + 10 ) = 2 11 ⋅ 11 − 1 − 1 p(z)q(z)=p S (z)= 11 1 (z 2 +z 3 +⋯+z 12 )= 11 z 2 (1+z+⋯+z 10 )= 11 z 2 ⋅ z−1 z 11 −1 The term on the RHS was simplified via Geometric sum formula. We know the roots of 11 − 1 z 11 −1 are the 11 11th roots of unity, which are all complex besides = 1 z=1. Therefore, we should try to isolate the 11 − 1 z 11 −1 and see if we can match roots. This yields 11 ( − 1 ) ⋅ ( ) ⋅ ( ) = 11 − 1 11(z−1)⋅ z p(z) ⋅ z q(z) =z 11 −1 The − 1 z−1 term on the LHS accounts for the real root. Division by z is okay here, as we were able to factor out a term of z from the PGFs ( ) p(z) and ( ) q(z) before. Since each of ( ) / p(z)/z and ( ) / q(z)/z are degree 5 5 polynomials, there are 10 10 roots on the LHS, and there are also 10 10 roots on the RHS that aren't = 1 z=1. Thus, all of the roots of ( ) / p(z)/z and ( ) / q(z)/z are the non-real 11 11th roots of unity. questions.solution: In this problem, we must be creative about how to generate an approach. The hardest part about the two methods is that it's unclear how long each lasts, since it's dependent on the sequence of wins and losses that occurred. Furthermore, based on this sequence of wins and losses, it influences the probability of winning in the next turn. Thus, it's not reasonable to compute this explicitly. Instead, we want to draw some common thread connecting the games. In the worst case, the tournament ends in 2 − 1 2n−1 turns, as someone must have n points by this time. Therefore, to put the two methodologies on equal footing, we will run the tournament for 2 − 1 2n−1 turns, regardless if someone has won before this point. Let's call this the "extended tournament". In the extended tournament, even if someone has won before 2 − 1 2n−1 turns has passed, in method A, the players will continue to alternate turns. In method B, after someone has lost, we will let the loser will serve all remaining rounds. Why do we construct method B in the extended tournament as above? Our goal is to relate these two tournaments somehow. Since you choose first, in method A, you will have chosen in exactly n of the 2 − 1 2n−1 turns. Thus, to put the two tournaments on equal footing, we need to ensure that regardless of when someone wins and who winsw in method B, you will have chosen in exactly n of the 2 − 1 2n−1 games. To do this, we note that in our construction, the number of times you choose is always equal to n, regardless if you win or lose and when. How is the above the case? Suppose you lose in ≤ ≤ 2 − 1 n≤k≤2n−1 turns. Under method B, you get to pick while you're winning, so if you lose in k turns, you must have won − k−n times, since your friend got n points. Thus, the turns at which you get to select are The first turn ( 1 ) (1) The − k−n turns that follow after the − k−n wins The remaining ( 2 − 1 ) − (2n−1)−k turns after you lose Therefore, the total number of times you select is 1 + ( − ) + ( 2 − 1 − ) = 1+(k−n)+(2n−1−k)=n. Similarly, if you are the winner, you select in the first turn and the − 1 n−1 games that follow your first − 1 n−1 wins. You don't get to select on the turn after your nth win because selection power immediately gets turned over to the loser once a winner is declared. Why do this entire "extended tournament" construction? Other than just putting the tournaments on equal footing, the extended tournaments and the original ones are equivalent: You win the extended version of the tournament if and only if you win the original version (play until a winner is declared). This is very clear: Since there are 2 − 1 2n−1 total turns in the extended tournament, the person who reaches n points first can't be overtaken by the other person, as there would be at most − 1 n−1 other turns for them to win. Thus, we can make a determination on the optimal choice in the extended tournament, and the same result will carry over to the original question. In each extended tournament, with both methodologies, you are now choosing n times, while your friend is choosing − 1 n−1 times. As the probability of winning is constant per each person that selects, the order in which the turns appear is irrelevant: You have the same probability of winning the tournament under either methodology. This is because you have the same stopping condition (need to obtain n points from the tournament), and both extended tournaments consist of n selections for you and − 1 n−1 selections for your opponent. Since the counts of how many times each player selects is the same per tournament, the ordering of these selections is irrelevant. Therefore, the answer is "You are indifferent to the two methodologies" (quite counter-intuitive!) If you don't believe in the above statement, consider an extreme case where 1 = 1 p 1 =1 and 2 = 0 p 2 =0 i.e. you win on every turn you select, and lose on every turn you don't. No matter how you order your n selections in the extended tournament, you always win, as you get to select n times, meaning you have n guaranteed wins.
