questions.title: Sticky Ants
questions.problem: A colony of $n$ ants participates in the following game: Each of the $n$ ants takes a uniformly random position along a stick of length $L$ meters, independently of one another. At the start, each ant chooses to walk left or right with equal probability. Each ant walks at a constant rate of v meters per second. Any time an ant bumps into another ant, the collision is perfectly elastic, so the two ants bounce off each other in opposite directions from which they approached, both still moving at constant speed v. Find the expected time until all n ants fall off the table when = 100 , = 2 , n=100,v=2, and = 4 L=4.
questions.solution: There is quite a bit going on here, so let's start by making some keen observations about the problem itself. Let's consider just a singular ant. Since the placement of the ant on the stick is uniformly random and the direction is also uniformly random, the amount of time (in seconds) it takes the ant to fall off the stick on it's own is Unif ( 0 , / ) Unif(0,L/v). This is because the maximum amount of time it can take is / L/v seconds (ant travels all L meters), and the points of distance x and − L−x from the LHS have the same probability density. Since they have the same probability density and the direction is selected uniformly at random, the amount of time it takes to fall off from both positions is the same: / x/v and ( − ) / (L−x)/v with equal probability. To prove the above intuition more rigorously, one can formally find the CDF of T, but the above intuition is sufficient. Now that we've reduced the first part about the direction, we must interpret the collision. Imagine seeing 2 2 identical ants colliding with each other in this manner. Initially, one ant was moving left, while the other was moving right, and the same happens afterwards, since the bounce off each other and change directions. Therefore, in the thought experiment above, this is no different than the ants phasing through one another and just walking on their original paths without bouncing. Thus, we can view the ants as ghost ants that phase through each other, and the bouncing condition doesn't even matter. If T i is the time it takes for ant i, 1 ≤ ≤ 1≤i≤n, to fall off the table, the time it takes for all n ants to fall off is max ⁡ ( 1 , … , ) max(T 1 ,…,T n ). Since we can just view the ants as phasing through one another, the placement of each ant is uniformly random, and each ant moves in the same way (velocity v, direction at random), we can conclude 1 , … , ∼ Unif ( 0 , / ) T 1 ,…,T n ∼Unif(0,L/v) IID. As we are looking to compute the expected maximum of Uniform random variables, we are able to use our classic order statistics formula: The n Uniform random variables, on average, split up the interval ( 0 , / ) (0,L/v) into + 1 n+1 equally-sized pieces. As n of these pieces come before the maximum of the random variables, we can conclude that [ max ⁡ ( 1 , … , ) ] = + 1 ⋅ E[max(T 1 ,…,T n )]= n+1 n ⋅ v L With the specified values, the answer is 200 / 101 200/101.

questions.title: Spirit Airlines II
questions.problem: On a sold out Spirit Airlines flight, $n$ people decide to risk it all and line up to board the plane. They may never make it to the destination. The first $1 \leq m \leq n$ passengers in the line have lost theirs boarding passes, but are allowed in. They each take a random seat. If available, every subsequent passenger takes their assigned seat. If their seat is not available, the passenger chooses an open seat uniformly at random to sit in. questions.solution: We are looking to count the expected count of some events that are not independent, so counting with indicators and linearity of expectation is the proper approach. questions.title: Continuous Blackjack
questions.problem: A gambler and a dealer play continuous blackjack. The gambler goes first and generates a uniformly random number in $(0,1)$. After each turn, they can choose to hit or hold. If hit, they will generate another uniformly random number in $(0,1)$. If the sum of the generated numbers is at least $1$, the gambler busts. Otherwise, he faces the same decision once again. This repeats until the gambler either busts or holds. If the gambler holds at a value $0 < s < 1$, the dealer starts by generating uniformly random numbers in $(0,1)$. The dealer keeps adding the values up until he either obtains a sum in the interval $(s,1)$ (in which case, the dealer wins) or he obtains a sum larger than $1$ (in which case, the gambler wins). The optimal strategy from the gambler is to hit when their current sum is $\leq t$ for some threshold $t$ and hold otherwise. Compute $t$ to $4$ decimal places.
questions.solution: The optimal strategy from the gambler will be in the following form: Hit when the current sum is $\leq t$ for some threshold $t$ and stay when the current sum is $> t$. The reason for this is because of the fact that each time the gambler has the option to hit/stay, the state of the game is identical to the previous turns except his current sum, so he should employ the same strategy on each round. If the game was just one round, under rational action, the gambler would choose to hold if their first roll was sufficiently large, and they would hit otherwise. Therefore, as this strategy must remain constant between rounds of the game, their strategy here is a generalized form of the one above. The goal is to now determine the optimal threshold t. The threshold t must satisfy the following indifference principle: If the gambler's current sum is t, then the gambler should be indifferent to holding versus hitting again. If the gambler was partial to one choice, they could increase their probability of winning by acting on that choice, so they must have no preference. Formalizing the above into mathematical language, let ℎ ( ) h(x) be the probability that the gambler loses when they hold with a current sum of x. Similarly, let ( ) g(x) be the probability that the gambler loses when they hit with a current sum of x and then hold. Since each draw is independent, our strategy only depends on the current sum of the gambler and not how they got to that point. The threshold will be the value 0 ≤ ≤ 1 0≤t≤1 such that ℎ ( ) = ( ) h(t)=g(t) by the indifference principle stated above. The first task is to determine ℎ ( ) h(x) and ( ) g(x). questions.title: Shuffling In BIG 2024
questions.problem: It's BIG $2024$, and Priyanshu is dealing from a deck of $m+n$ cards, where there are $n$ cards labelled $1$ to $n$, as well as $m$ jokers. The deck comes pre-shuffled uniformly at random. Each second, he draws out a card from the top of the deck. Priyanshu plays the following game: Initialize S as the empty set. If the card he draws has the value x on it, he removes the card and adds x to S. If he draws a joker, he checks the set S. If ≠ { 1 , 2 , … , } S  ={1,2,…,n}, he places all the cards back into the deck and reshuffles the total deck of + n+m cards uniformly at random to form a new deck. Otherwise, the game ends. Shuffling the deck takes no time. Note that when he shuffles the deck, the set S remains unchanged. Find the expected duration of the game when = 40 m=40 and = 60 n=60. Report the answer to the nearest second.
